finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that student engagement increased after AI integration, with average engagement scores rising by about 20%–23% across institutions (e.g., School A 65 to 78, School B 60 to 74, University C 70 to 85). The author attributes this to AI-driven personalization, immediate feedback, and adaptive learning, though notes possible novelty effects and unmeasured confounders.
finding.measure: Student engagement scores from institutional records and surveys

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improvements in innovative thinking skills after AI integration, with the percentage of students exhibiting innovative thinking increasing from 44% to 57% overall, and by 44%–57% across institutions (e.g., 40% to 60%, 35% to 55%, 45% to 65%). The author suggests AI-enabled platforms may foster critical thinking and problem-solving by presenting complex real-world problems, but also cautions that the measure was subjective and not standardized.
finding.measure: Percentage of students exhibiting innovative thinking / creativity / problem-solving skills

finding.finding_summary: Academic performance improved following AI integration, with GPA increasing by roughly 9%–14% across the reported institutions (e.g., School A 3.0 to 3.4, School B 2.8 to 3.2, University C 3.2 to 3.5). The paper links these gains to personalized learning and instantaneous feedback, but also states that statistical significance was not reported and that confounding variables could explain part of the change.
finding.measure: Grade Point Average (GPA) from institutional records and surveys

finding.finding_summary: Educator perceptions of AI were generally positive, ranging from 65% to 75% positive across the institutions, suggesting institutional support for AI adoption. The paper also reports strong positive correlations between AI integration level and outcomes such as engagement (r=0.78), academic performance (r=0.72), and innovation skills (r=0.80), but emphasizes that correlation does not establish causation.
finding.measure: Educator perception surveys; Pearson correlations between AI integration and educational outcomes

paper_profiles.title: A Review of AI Tools: Definitions, Functions, and Applications for K-12 Education
paper_profiles.venue: AI, Computer Science and Robotics Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review paper surveys artificial intelligence tools, functions, and applications relevant to K-12 education. It is motivated by the rapid growth of AI in schooling, the need for teachers to understand what AI tools are available, and concerns about ethical issues such as data privacy, bias, plagiarism, and surveillance. Rather than evaluating one intervention, the paper organizes the field by AI type (e.g., machine learning, intelligent tutoring systems, automated essay scoring, natural language processing), by function (instruction, personalization, assessment, and prediction), and by tool category (instructional, administrative, analytical).

The article focuses on how teachers and schools can use commonly available AI platforms and what those platforms are designed to do. Examples include ChatGPT, Chat for Schools, Class Companion, DreamBox, Khanmigo, MagicSchool, PowerBuddy, SchoolAI, Diffit, Eduaide.AI, and others. Across these tools, the paper emphasizes personalized feedback, immediate or timely responses, scaffolded support, rubric-based writing feedback, adaptive instruction, and teacher oversight/mediation. For instance, the review notes that AI-generated feedback tools and intelligent tutoring systems can provide instant, personalized feedback, while some platforms allow teachers to create or align rubrics, monitor student interactions, and review saved chats.

Because this is a review article, it does not present original experimental data or a single empirical evaluation of outcomes. Its main conclusion is that AI can support teaching and learning in K-12 settings by personalizing instruction, reducing teacher workload, and improving access to feedback and adaptive support, but implementation should be careful and human-centered. The authors also stress that educators should choose age-appropriate tools aligned with curriculum goals and remain attentive to privacy, bias, and the possible erosion of students’ critical thinking if AI is overused.

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies AI writing and reading tools as useful for literacy support, especially through rapid feedback on written work, text adaptation, and automated scoring. Examples include Class Companion, Eduaide.AI, SchoolAI, and AES/NLP-based systems that can provide feedback on grammar, style, mechanics, and writing quality; however, the paper reports no original effect sizes because it is a narrative review.
finding.measure: Writing feedback, automated essay scoring, and text-leveling / reading support functions

finding.finding_summary: The review states that intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive learning systems can improve elementary students’ mathematical understanding and achievement, citing prior studies rather than reporting new data. DreamBox is highlighted as an example of a math-focused adaptive tutor that adjusts instruction to student performance and proficiency level.
finding.measure: Mathematics understanding and achievement

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools may increase engagement by giving immediate feedback, allowing students to practice at their own pace, and making learning more responsive and interactive. This claim is discussed at a general level across tools such as chatbots, adaptive platforms, and AI feedback systems, but the article does not provide primary data.
finding.measure: Student engagement and interaction with AI-supported learning tools

finding.finding_summary: The review presents AI as potentially supporting critical thinking and problem solving through personalized tutoring, scaffolding, and feedback, but it also warns that overreliance on AI may weaken students’ critical thinking and creativity. This outcome is discussed conceptually rather than tested empirically, and the paper offers no direct effect size or sample size.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem solving, and creativity

finding.finding_summary: A central conclusion of the paper is that AI can reduce teacher workload by automating grading, generating lesson plans, creating assessments, and providing feedback more quickly. The review repeatedly cites tools such as AES, MagicSchool, Copilot, PowerBuddy, and SchoolAI as time-saving supports for instructional and administrative tasks, but it does not report original quantitative estimates.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading time, lesson-planning efficiency, and assessment generation

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that AI can help schools and districts support personalized learning, monitoring, and data-informed decision-making, while also requiring policies for privacy, bias, and safe use. Its main institutional contribution is a classification and selection guide for K-12 stakeholders rather than an empirical evaluation of school- or system-level outcomes.
finding.measure: School/district use, governance concerns, and AI tool selection for K-12 implementation

paper_profiles.title: CaseMaster: Designing and Evaluating a Probe for Oral Case Presentation Training with LLM Assistance
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of training medical students to deliver effective oral case presentations (OCPs), a core communication and clinical reasoning skill in medical education. The authors argue that conventional OCP training is hindered by inconsistent participation, limited structured guidance, and delayed or sparse feedback, especially for novice learners. They also note that while large language models (LLMs) can generate personalized content, their role in supporting structured, skill-building OCP instruction has been underexplored.

To investigate this, the authors conducted a formative study with six medical educators, then designed CaseMaster, an interactive web-based probe that uses GPT-4o to support OCP practice. CaseMaster organizes training into two stages: a preparation stage with patient exploration, SOAP-structured drafting, and preset LLM-assisted actions; and a reflection stage that compares student responses against reference answers and uses a rubric-aligned score sheet for automated feedback. The system emphasizes structured prompts, concise exemplar-based outputs, transparent criteria, and iterative self-reflection.

The evaluation included 12 medical students using CaseMaster and a baseline workflow in a controlled user study, plus interviews with five experienced educators. Results suggest the probe can improve presentation quality, confidence, and efficiency relative to traditional self-directed methods, while educators’ feedback highlighted both promise and the need for cautious, critically reflective use of LLM output. The paper concludes with design guidelines for adaptive, user-centered LLM-supported training tools in medical education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates an LLM-assisted oral case presentation training probe that supports students in organizing and delivering spoken medical presentations. In the 12-student user study, participants reported that CaseMaster improved presentation quality and confidence compared with a baseline self-directed workflow, and educators judged the system to support clearer, more coherent oral case presentations. Exact effect sizes were not reported in the provided text.
finding.measure: Oral case presentation quality, clarity, and participant-reported confidence in presentation delivery
finding.study_size: n=12 students in the controlled user study; n=6 educators in formative study; n=5 educators in follow-up evaluation

finding.finding_summary: CaseMaster was explicitly designed to support clinical reasoning, systematic reasoning, reflective evaluation, and reduction of common presentation errors. The formative study and subsequent design concepts emphasize that structured SOAP-based drafting, reference-answer comparison, and rubric-guided feedback help learners identify missing information, revise reasoning, and reflect on mistakes, which the authors argue can strengthen critical thinking and metacognition. No numeric learning gains were reported in the provided text.
finding.measure: Reasoning quality, reflection, identification of errors, and self-assessment during OCP preparation and review
finding.study_size: n=12 students; n=6 educators; n=5 educators

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that the LLM-assisted workflow may reduce workload and make preparation more efficient than traditional methods. In the controlled study and expert feedback, CaseMaster was described as helping students generate structured content more quickly and reducing the burden of searching, organizing, and evaluating case presentation materials, though no formal time-savings effect size was reported. The authors also frame the system as lowering educator workload by automating parts of feedback and scoring.
finding.measure: Perceived preparation efficiency, workload reduction, and system-supported drafting/scoring workflow
finding.study_size: n=12 students; n=5 educators for evaluation; n=6 educators for formative study

finding.finding_summary: The primary substantive focus is medical oral case presentation training, which is outside standard literacy, numeracy, or scientific reasoning categories but is clearly academic/vocational skill development. CaseMaster’s preparation and reflection stages were designed to improve the structure, accuracy, and completeness of oral case presentations using SOAP-based templates, preset prompts, and rubric-aligned evaluation. The paper reports positive qualitative and expert-evaluated indications of improved presentation quality, but no standardized learning effect sizes were provided.
finding.measure: Oral case presentation performance, completeness, and organization
finding.study_size: n=12 students in user study; n=6 educators in formative study; n=5 educators in follow-up evaluation

paper_profiles.title: A Review of AI Tools: Definitions, Functions, and Applications for K-12 Education
paper_profiles.venue: AI, Computer Science and Robotics Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article provides an overview of artificial intelligence tools for K-12 education, focusing on what AI is, how it is commonly used in classrooms, and the practical considerations teachers should keep in mind when selecting tools. The paper organizes AI into types (e.g., machine learning, intelligent tutoring systems, automated essay scoring, natural language processing) and functions (improving teaching and learning, personalized instruction, assessment/evaluation, and early warning/predictive analytics).

The article is not an empirical evaluation of a specific intervention; instead, it synthesizes prior literature and product examples to help educators understand the landscape of AI tools such as ChatGPT, Khanmigo, DreamBox, SchoolAI, MagicSchool, and others. It emphasizes potential benefits including personalized feedback, adaptive instruction, faster assessment, and teacher workload reduction, while also highlighting risks like plagiarism, misinformation, data privacy concerns, surveillance, and algorithmic bias.

In its discussion of classroom impact, the paper notes that AI tools may support learning and some academic outcomes, but it does not present original quantitative evidence on K-12 student outcomes. It also cautions that overreliance on AI could weaken students’ critical thinking and creativity, and it calls for careful implementation, robust policy, equitable access, and further longitudinal research to understand long-term effects in K-12 settings.

finding.finding_summary: The review describes AI tools for writing support and automated essay scoring as potentially improving writing through instant, personalized feedback, but it does not report original effect sizes or controlled-study results. It also warns that generative AI can facilitate plagiarism and may provide misleading or outdated information, creating risks for writing quality and academic integrity.
finding.measure: Writing feedback, essay scoring, and writing assignment support

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools can support critical thinking, problem solving, and personalized learning, but it also states that overreliance on AI may diminish students’ critical thinking and creativity. No original study data, sample size, or effect size are reported; the paper is a narrative synthesis drawing on prior literature and examples.
finding.measure: Critical thinking and problem-solving (conceptual discussion, not direct measurement)

finding.finding_summary: A central theme of the review is that AI tools can reduce teacher workload by automating grading, generating lesson plans, creating assessments, and streamlining administrative tasks. The paper repeatedly describes immediate feedback and automated scoring as time-saving functions, but it does not quantify the magnitude of workload reduction.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading time, lesson-planning efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests that AI tools may increase student engagement by providing immediate responses, personalized practice, and interactive tutoring experiences. These claims are descriptive and based on prior literature cited by the authors rather than on original empirical evaluation in this paper.
finding.measure: Student engagement and interaction with learning tools

paper_profiles.title: Learning design to support student-AI collaboration: perspectives of leading teachers for AI in education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers (primary and secondary) in South Korea
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines what K-12 teachers believe is needed to design effective student-AI collaboration (SAC) in schools. The authors frame AI as a collaborative learning agent rather than only a tool, and use a distributed cognition perspective to explore how curriculum, interaction, environment, and over-time development should be designed when AI is introduced into classroom learning.

The study is based on semi-structured, in-depth interviews with 10 Korean leading teachers involved in AI-in-education initiatives (5 primary, 5 secondary). Teachers discussed desirable learning goals, content, assessment, student-AI interaction supports, learning spaces, institutional policies, and school culture needed for SAC. They emphasized higher-order learning goals such as critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, and subject-matter understanding, but the paper does not test any intervention or measure student outcomes directly.

Main conclusions are design-oriented: SAC should center on authentic, interdisciplinary, and creative tasks; process-oriented and collaboration-focused assessment; explicit instruction in AI principles, data literacy, debugging, and AI ethics; intuitive interfaces and rich digital tools; flexible classrooms and secure infrastructure; systemic policy support; and a collaborative, safe-to-fail culture. The authors argue that students may progress through stages of learning about AI, learning from AI, and eventually learning together with AI, but this is a teacher-anticipated trajectory rather than empirical outcome evidence.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not provide direct empirical evidence that AI-personalized feedback improves critical thinking or other durable skills relative to any comparison condition. Instead, through interviews with 10 Korean teachers, it reports perceptions that SAC should aim to build higher-order thinking such as critical thinking, creativity, analytical thinking, and collaboration via authentic, interdisciplinary, and creative tasks. The finding is design-oriented and anticipatory rather than outcome-based.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about desired learning goals and student capabilities in student-AI collaboration

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified substantial institutional supports as necessary for student-AI collaboration, including systematic AIED policy, flexible school systems, collaborative school culture, secure digital infrastructure, and teacher capacity building. These are qualitative recommendations from interviews with 10 teachers, not measured effects, but they represent a strong positive perceived need for institutional change to enable AI use in education.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on policy, governance, school structure, and infrastructure

paper_profiles.title: Gamifying education: what is known, what is believed and what remains uncertain: a critical review
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and Undergraduate (review includes both, with limited K-12 studies)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a critical review of empirical and theoretical research on gamification in education, with a particular focus on what the evidence actually supports versus what is assumed or hoped for. The authors argue that gamification has been widely adopted and discussed, but the underlying empirical base is fragmented, often methodologically weak, and frequently overstates positive outcomes.

The review synthesizes 51 empirical studies published between mid-2014 and the end of 2015, plus 11 theoretical papers. It examines studies by educational level, subject area, learning activity, game elements used, and reported outcomes. The paper emphasizes that most studies are concentrated in higher education, with only 7 K-12 studies, and that most gamification designs rely on points, badges, and leaderboards rather than deeper game mechanics.

Overall, the review concludes that there is insufficient evidence for strong or long-term educational benefits of gamification, and that reported gains are highly context-dependent. The authors highlight that many studies report mixed, inconclusive, or weak findings, and that the field lacks systematic, cumulative experimentation that would allow confident claims about which game elements work, for whom, and under what conditions.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed empirical studies, gamification was most often linked to motivation, engagement, participation, and retention rather than to strong or consistent academic gains. The review concludes that evidence for motivational benefits is mixed and often overstated; many studies report promising results, but the overall evidence base is fragmented and does not yet support clear long-term effects.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, participation, retention, and related learner perception measures reported in the included studies
finding.study_size: n=51 empirical studies reviewed (7 K-12 studies within the set)

finding.finding_summary: The review includes some studies targeting collaboration, discussion quality, and related learner behaviors, but these outcomes are secondary and inconsistently reported. The authors do not find a systematic pattern showing that gamification reliably improves durable skills such as collaboration or self-directed learning across contexts.
finding.measure: Collaboration, online discussion participation/quality, and related behavioral outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Navigating the State of Cognitive Flow: Context-Aware AI Interventions for Effective Reasoning Support
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that AI-based reasoning assistants can improve human decision-making only when their interventions are aligned with the user’s cognitive state. The central problem is that static, one-size-fits-all AI feedback may interrupt users mid-thought, disrupt cognitive flow, and reduce the quality of reasoning rather than improve it.

The authors propose a context-aware cognitive augmentation framework grounded in flow theory. The framework would adapt the type, timing, and scale of AI interventions using multimodal behavioral cues such as gaze behavior, typing hesitation, interaction speed, and other engagement signals to infer when a user is stuck, overloaded, bored, or otherwise in need of support.

This paper is conceptual rather than empirical: it does not report a study, participants, or outcome data. Instead, it synthesizes prior work to make a case for “cognitive flow alignment,” recommending that future AI reasoning systems be evaluated on their ability to sustain engagement and support deep reasoning without being intrusive. The paper’s main contribution is a design and evaluation agenda for personalized, minimally disruptive AI assistance.

finding.finding_summary: No empirical effect was tested or reported. The paper is a conceptual position paper arguing that context-aware AI interventions could support critical thinking and reasoning by preserving cognitive flow, but it does not present participant data, comparative conditions, or measured outcomes.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: No empirical effect was tested or reported. The paper discusses engagement, motivation, cognitive load, and flow as important targets for adaptive AI support, but these are proposed design goals rather than measured outcomes in a study.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Shots and Boosters: Exploring the Use of Combined Prebunking Interventions to Raise Critical Thinking and Create Long-Term Protection Against Misinformation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2025 ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses the challenge of misinformation and asks how AI might support interventions that improve people’s critical thinking and resistance to misleading content. The authors argue that debunking alone is insufficient because misinformation spreads quickly, fact-checking coverage is incomplete, and exposure can have lasting effects. They therefore frame critical thinking and media literacy as important educational targets for prebunking interventions.

The paper does not report an empirical study; instead, it synthesizes prior work and proposes a new AI-driven design concept that combines two intervention stages: an inoculation-style training game and a follow-up reinforcement stage. In the first stage, users evaluate suspicious posts/news items, justify their judgments to an AI tutor, and receive personalized corrective and structural feedback; the system adapts to the user’s reasoning style over time. In the second stage, the AI delivers brief, personalized nudges to reinforce previously learned strategies using everyday news or social-media examples.

The paper’s main conclusion is conceptual rather than empirical: AI appears promising for delivering personalized learning, feedback, and reinforcement in prebunking interventions, but current approaches are still limited and fragmented. The authors argue that combining longer-form inoculation training with lighter-weight nudges may better support sustained gains in critical thinking and media literacy, though they do not provide original outcome data or evaluate the proposed system with students or other users.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not present empirical evidence that AI-personalized feedback improves critical thinking relative to standard instruction or non-AI feedback. It is a position/design paper proposing a combined prebunking concept, so no measured effect sizes, sample sizes, or outcome scores are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Developing Critical Thinking in Second Language Learners: Exploring Generative AI like ChatGPT as a tool for Argumentative Essay Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a structured ChatGPT-guided framework can improve second-language learners’ critical thinking and argumentative writing. The authors combine the Paul-Elder Critical Thinking Model with Tan’s framework for argumentative writing to create the ChatGPT Guideline for Critical Argumentative Writing (CGCAW), which supplies prompts intended to help learners plan positions, explanations, evidence, and conclusions while using ChatGPT.

The study used a small quantitative experiment with 10 university students from a state university, randomly assigned to an experimental group using the CGCAW prompts and a control group using ChatGPT without the structured guideline. Participants wrote a short argumentative essay on social media within 40 minutes, and essays were scored by Grammarly, ChatGPT, and a course instructor. Results were mixed: the experimental group performed better on ChatGPT’s ratings for clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence, but the control group scored slightly higher on Grammarly and substantially higher on the instructor’s rubric. The authors conclude that the structured AI guidance may support some higher-order aspects of argumentative writing and critical thinking, but the framework needs refinement, the sample was too small, and time/familiarity constraints likely affected performance.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly assessed argumentative essay writing quality after use of a ChatGPT-based guideline. On ChatGPT’s rubric, the experimental group using CGCAW scored slightly higher than the control group (mean 74 vs. 72.2; n=10), especially on clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence, but the control group scored higher on Grammarly (mean 92.2 vs. 90.6) and much higher on the course instructor rubric (mean 56 vs. 35).
finding.measure: Argumentative essay quality, scored by Grammarly, ChatGPT, and a course instructor across clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, persuasiveness, thesis, reasoning, counterarguments, and summary
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT total SD: 7.6 (experimental), 5.5 (control); Grammarly and instructor SDs not fully reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on critical thinking in argumentative writing and frames the intervention as a way to improve higher-order reasoning. The experimental group showed better performance on components linked to critical thinking—clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence—on ChatGPT’s scoring, but the instructor rubric favored the control group, suggesting the evidence for critical thinking gains is inconsistent across measures.
finding.measure: Critical-thinking-related writing dimensions (clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, argument structure, thesis, counterarguments, summary)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was a short, 40-minute writing task using ChatGPT and structured prompts, but the paper does not present a direct productivity or efficiency outcome. It instead notes implementation limitations: some participants could not complete the essay within the time limit, and prior familiarity with ChatGPT varied, which likely affected task completion and the usability of the framework.
finding.measure: Task completion within a 40-minute timed writing session

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Critical Thinking with AI: A Tailored Warning System for RAG Models
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether user-facing, context-specific warning messages can improve reasoning in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems used in an educational quiz setting. The motivating problem is that LLM/RAG outputs can contain hallucinations at both the retrieval and generation stages, which may mislead learners and weaken critical evaluation. The authors argue that generic safety warnings are often too broad, and that tailored warnings might better support reflective, informed use of AI-generated content.

The study presents a pilot interface that adds fact-checking and warning messages at both the retrieval and LLM-output level. Participants answered AP U.S. history multiple-choice questions under three conditions: no warning, a standard warning (“ChatGPT can make mistakes. Check important info.”), or a tailored warning generated from the specific hallucination or bias in the response. The sample included 18 participants split across the three groups, followed by a trust survey and short interviews. The context was a textbook-based history QA task, chosen because history textbooks can contain bias and because the task requires evaluating factual claims.

Results indicate that tailored warnings improved participants’ accuracy in detecting hallucinations relative to standard warnings and no warnings, especially for harder high-level hallucinations. The authors report a statistically significant overall difference in accuracy across conditions (ANOVA p=0.006162) and a higher average trust score in the tailored-warning group, while also noting that warnings sometimes introduced cognitive friction and confusion. Qualitative feedback suggests a tension between helping users think critically and preserving usability/trust, implying that warning design needs to be more carefully contextualized. The paper is explicitly preliminary and framed as ongoing research rather than a definitive efficacy study.

finding.finding_summary: In a pilot AP U.S. history quiz task (n=18), tailored warnings improved participants’ ability to detect hallucinations compared with a standard generic warning and no warning. Accuracy was 100% for no-hallucination items, 89% for low-level hallucinations, and 81% for high-level hallucinations in the tailored-warning group, versus 97%/81%/69% for standard warning and 100%/64%/56% for no warning. The authors report an overall ANOVA p=0.006162 across warning conditions.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice question accuracy on a history QA task with genuine, low-level hallucination, and high-level hallucination responses

finding.finding_summary: Tailored warnings were associated with slightly higher reported trust than the other conditions, with the authors noting a difference of 0.67 on a 5-point Likert scale. However, participants also reported that warnings could create confusion and cognitive friction, and the no-warning condition was rated easiest to use. This suggests the intervention may improve calibrated trust for some users while imposing usability costs.
finding.measure: Self-reported trust in the system and interface ease/usability ratings from post-task survey/interview

paper_profiles.title: Investigating Students’ Preferences for AI Roles in Mathematical Modelling: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how students prefer different AI roles during mathematical modelling, and how those preferences relate to their baseline design thinking (DT), computational thinking (CT), and mathematical modelling self-efficacy (MMSE). Although the study is framed around AI support in mathematics education, it does not test learning gains from AI-personalized feedback against teacher feedback or standard instruction; instead, it compares student perceptions of five AI personas: Tutor, Teaching Assistant (TA), Peer Student, Struggling Student, and Excellent Student.

The study used a within-subjects randomized controlled design with 26 university students who had not taken university-level mathematics courses, serving as proxies for high-school-level mathematical proficiency. Participants completed a baseline modelling task without assistance and then five short mathematical modelling tasks with the AI taking on different roles in counterbalanced order. Data came from questionnaires, rankings, chat logs, and open-ended responses.

Main findings show that students strongly preferred competent, supportive AI roles over the Struggling Student role. The Tutor role was ranked most favorably overall, followed closely by the Excellent Student, Peer, and TA roles; all four competent roles were rated similarly to one another. The Struggling Student role was rated significantly worse on preference, task confidence, helpfulness, and ease of interaction. Baseline DT and CT were positively associated with MMSE, but only one moderator effect emerged: students with higher DT preferred the TA role more than lower-DT students. Overall, the paper suggests that role framing matters for how students experience AI support in mathematical modelling, but it does not provide direct evidence that AI-personalized feedback improves K-12 critical thinking relative to non-AI feedback.

finding.finding_summary: The study did not evaluate achievement or learning gains on mathematical modelling tasks against a non-AI control; instead it compared student preferences and perceptions across AI roles. In a within-subjects RCT with n=26, the Tutor role was ranked most favorably overall (M=2.35 on a 1=best to 5=worst ranking scale), while the Struggling Student role was ranked least favorably (M=4.42), χ2(4, N=26)=28.83, p<.001.
finding.measure: AI role preference rankings and task-based user experience during mathematical modelling tasks

finding.finding_summary: This paper substantively examines constructs closely related to durable skills, especially computational thinking and mathematical modelling self-efficacy. CT and DT were both significant positive predictors of MMSE in a PLS-SEM model (DT β=0.730, p<.001; CT β=0.300, p<.001; R2=0.808), and only one group difference emerged: higher design-thinking students preferred the TA role more than lower-design-thinking students (Mhigh=2.38 vs. Mlow=3.46, p=.049).
finding.measure: Computational thinking, design thinking, mathematical modelling self-efficacy, and AI-role preference rankings

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly measured task confidence, perceived helpfulness, and ease of interaction as user-experience outcomes during AI-supported modelling. All three varied significantly by AI role (task confidence χ2(4,N=26)=24.85; helpfulness χ2(4,N=26)=32.63; ease of interaction χ2(4,N=26)=36.43; all p<.001), with the Tutor and Excellent Student roles rated highest and the Struggling Student role rated lowest across measures.
finding.measure: Task confidence, perceived AI helpfulness, and ease of interaction ratings
finding.std_deviation: M=3.69/3.65/3.42/3.12/1.88; M=4.12/3.96/3.73/3.58/1.92; M=4.08/3.81/3.69/3.38/1.81 (role-wise means for confidence/helpfulness/ease, respectively)

paper_profiles.title: Do intelligent tutoring systems benefit K-12 students? A meta-analysis and evaluation of heterogeneity of treatment effects in the U.S.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether intelligent tutoring systems (ITS)—AI-based software that provides personalized hints, feedback, examples, and practice—improve K-12 student learning in U.S. schools, and under what conditions they work best. The authors also evaluate whether study design features linked to internal validity and implementation/context features linked to external validity explain variation in effects.

Using a meta-analysis of 18 experimental studies (77 effect sizes) covering 11 ITS, the study finds an overall positive effect on student achievement (g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). The review focuses on U.S. elementary, middle, and high school students and compares effects across assignment level, attrition, grade level, student disadvantage status, support type, intervention duration, instructional condition, instructor type, measurement type, outcome subject, timing, and location.

The main conclusions are that ITS generally improves K-12 learning outcomes, with similar effects in elementary and middle school and for many student subgroups, but effects are smaller in rural settings and decline with longer duration. Among implementation features, worked-out examples, intervention duration, intervention condition, and immediate measurement were the most important moderators in the MetaForest analysis. The study also reports that just-in-time hints were not statistically significant, while on-demand hints, worked-out examples, motivation support, and reading materials were significant positive supports. Overall, the paper supports ITS as beneficial, but with meaningful heterogeneity and some implementation limits.

finding.finding_summary: Across 18 experimental studies and 77 effect sizes, intelligent tutoring systems produced a statistically significant positive effect on U.S. K-12 students’ learning outcomes (g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). The meta-analysis indicates that ITS improves academic achievement broadly, although effects vary by implementation and context.
finding.measure: Student learning outcomes / academic achievement

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines support features tied to higher-order learning processes, including worked-out examples, hints, and feedback, which are relevant to critical thinking-like skill development. However, the reported outcomes are general learning achievement rather than a direct critical-thinking measure, so evidence for durable skills is indirect; the overall achievement effect was positive (g=0.271).
finding.measure: Learning outcomes associated with higher-order support features (worked-out examples, hints, feedback)

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Recommendations in EdTech: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether introducing personalized content recommendations into an educational app increases children’s engagement relative to the app’s existing editorially curated recommendation system. The authors study a key implementation question in edtech: whether personalization can outperform human curation when the app’s users have varied preferences and when there is enough historical interaction data to support collaborative filtering.

The intervention was a new recommendation system for the “Recommended Story” section of Freadom, an English reading app for Indian children ages 3 to 12. The system used matrix factorization trained on historical user-story interaction logs and was deployed only for users with at least 60 prior story interactions; the control group continued to receive stories selected by editors. The experiment ran for two weeks and randomized 7,750 eligible users to treatment or control. The study’s primary outcomes were engagement-based proxies for learning, including Total Story Engagement, number of stories completed, and reading time, measured both within the personalized section and across the whole app.

The paper finds large positive effects on engagement. Personalized recommendations increased Total Story Engagement in the Recommended Story section by 60% (S.E. 17%), completed stories by 78% (S.E. 26%), and reading time by 87% (S.E. 25%). Across all app sections, treatment increased Total Story Engagement by 14% (S.E. 7%), completed stories by 19% (S.E. 8%), and reading time by 20% (S.E. 9%), suggesting the gains were not merely substitution within the app but reflected more overall usage. Effects were larger for heavy users, users with longer histories, and users with niche preferences; however, the authors do not measure learning outcomes directly, so the study provides evidence on engagement rather than critical thinking or achievement.

finding.finding_summary: Personalized recommendations substantially increased user engagement with the app. In the Recommended Story section, Total Story Engagement rose by 60% (S.E. 17%), the number of completed stories rose by 78% (S.E. 26%), and total reading time rose by 87% (S.E. 25%) among randomized users (n=7,750 eligible; n=3,023 launched the app during the experiment).
finding.measure: Total Story Engagement, completed stories, and reading time in the Recommended Story section
finding.study_size: n=7750 randomized; n=3023 launched app during experiment
finding.effect_size: 60% increase in Total Story Engagement; 78% increase in completed stories; 87% increase in reading time

finding.finding_summary: The treatment also increased overall app usage, indicating that gains in the personalized section were not offset by reduced activity elsewhere. Across all sections, Total Story Engagement increased by 14% (S.E. 7%), completed stories by 19% (S.E. 8%), and reading time by 20% (S.E. 9%).
finding.measure: Total Story Engagement, completed stories, and reading time across all app sections
finding.study_size: n=7750 randomized; n=3023 launched app during experiment
finding.effect_size: 14% increase in Total Story Engagement; 19% increase in completed stories; 20% increase in reading time

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly measure critical thinking or other durable skills, but it uses engagement with reading content as a proxy for beneficial educational outcomes. Because the study’s central focus is on personalized content recommendations for children’s reading app usage, the closest substantive category is durable skills only indirectly; no direct effect on critical thinking was reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: A Large Scale Randomized Controlled Trial on Herding in Peer-Review Discussions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether the order in which reviewers enter a peer-review discussion causally affects the final decision on a manuscript, a phenomenon the authors describe as herding in peer-review discussions. The motivating question is whether discussion initiators disproportionately influence the consensus outcome, which would make review decisions sensitive to arbitrary discussion-management choices.

The authors ran a large randomized controlled trial during the ICML 2020 review process. They split 1,544 borderline papers into two conditions and used discussion-management strategies designed to preserve the set of participating reviewers while changing only who was asked to initiate discussion first: in one condition the most positive reviewer was nudged to start (S+), and in the other the most negative reviewer was nudged to start (S−). They then compared reviewer-score updates and final acceptance outcomes across conditions. The intervention successfully changed who initiated discussion, but the paper found no statistically significant difference in acceptance rates, no difference in overall mean score changes, and therefore no evidence of herding in this peer-review setting. The study also notes that reviewers tended to converge toward the mean of initial independent opinions regardless of condition, and that any herding effect, if present, was likely small.

finding.finding_summary: A large randomized experiment on 1,544 borderline ICML 2020 submissions found no statistically significant effect of discussion initiator selection on final acceptance decisions. Acceptance rates were 0.21 in the positive-initiator condition (M+) versus 0.25 in the negative-initiator condition (M−), a difference of −0.04 with 95% CI [−0.08, 0.01] (p = .122).
finding.measure: Final paper acceptance rate in ICML 2020 peer review
finding.study_size: n=1544 papers (755 in M+, 789 in M−)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention changed who initiated discussions but did not materially change discussion activity or the overall amount of score change across conditions. Mean discussion length was similar (4.41 vs 4.24 messages), and the mean change in score across all reviewers was 0.01 in both groups (difference 0.00, 95% CI [−0.03, 0.04], p = .949).
finding.measure: Discussion length and change in reviewer scores during peer-review discussion
finding.study_size: n=1544 papers overall; n=1140 papers for initiator-specific score-change analyses
finding.confidence_interval: [−0.03, 0.04] for mean score change across all reviewers

finding.finding_summary: Although the study was motivated by a durable-skill-like mechanism (herding/critical-thinking influence), it found no evidence that the discussion initiator's opinion shifted final outcomes in a way consistent with biased consensus formation. The initiator's mean initial score differed sharply by condition (4.03 vs 2.76; difference 1.27, 95% CI [1.15, 1.39]), yet this did not translate into a detectable difference in acceptance decisions.
finding.measure: Herding-related influence on consensus in structured discussion; reviewer score updates as a proxy for opinion change
finding.study_size: n=1544 papers overall; n=1140 papers for initiator analyses
finding.confidence_interval: [1.15, 1.39] for initiator score difference; acceptance difference CI [-0.08, 0.01]

paper_profiles.title: On the existence and multiplicity of extensions in dialectical argumentation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies a formal logic problem in dialectical argumentation: when a theory has zero, one, or multiple stable extensions. The main question is not about learners or classrooms, but about the mathematical properties of extension existence and multiplicity in a defeasible reasoning system called DEFLOG.

The paper introduces dialectical justification as a local notion of argument support/defeat and proves characterizations of when a theory has an extension and how many extensions it has. It shows that a theory has an extension exactly when there is a context in which every sentence is either dialectically justifiable or defeasible, but not both; multiplicity corresponds to the maximal number of mutually incompatible such contexts. The paper also compares dialectical justification with Dung-style admissibility and argues that justification is the more powerful notion for these characterizations in the full DEFLOG language.

The work is purely theoretical and formal, with examples drawn from default reasoning, logic programming, and argumentation frameworks. It does not evaluate any educational intervention, AI system, or K-12 population, though it notes a relation to the author's work on automated argument assistance.

paper_profiles.title: An Investigation of Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) Method as a Customer Baseline Load (CBL) Calculation for Residential Customers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a randomized controlled trial (RCT) method can serve as an accurate customer baseline load (CBL) calculation approach for residential demand response programs, especially in comparison with the commonly used HighXofY/NYISO averaging baseline. The motivation is operational: CBL accuracy affects how much load reduction is credited and how much rebate is paid in peak time rebate (PTR) programs.

Using hourly electricity consumption data from 199 residential customers in an Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) dataset for 2012, the author compares RCT and NYISO baselines in two contexts: granular individual-customer settlement and aggregated settlement. The paper evaluates baseline error using mean absolute error (MAE), bias, and an overall performance index (OPI), and also estimates the financial consequences of baseline error in a hypothetical PTR program with a $0.35/kWh rebate and a $0.097/kWh tariff.

The results show that RCT performs better as the control group gets larger in the granular case, but NYISO is more accurate and more stable overall in the aggregated case. Aggregating consumption substantially improves both methods, especially NYISO, and leads to much lower error and lower apparent rebate payments than in the granular case. The paper concludes that RCT may be preferable when administrative simplicity matters and granular settlement is required with sufficiently large control groups, but NYISO is the more reliable baseline method for aggregated applications. The author also notes limitations of the study, including the use of a hypothetical PTR program and the absence of a real demand response event.

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily evaluates baseline-calculation efficiency and reliability for residential demand response settlement rather than educational outcomes. It finds that RCT has lower administrative cost and no need for historical data, but its error performance depends strongly on control-group size in the granular case and is less stable than NYISO in the aggregated case.
finding.measure: Baseline calculation error and administrative cost/complexity of CBL methods
finding.study_size: n=199 customers; 12 event days; control groups of 10, 20, 30, 40, or 50 customers
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI reported for bar plots, exact values not reported

finding.finding_summary: The study addresses implementation and market-settlement implications of demand response policy under FERC Order 745. It shows that baseline choice can materially affect false load reduction and rebate payments, with very large payment distortions in the hypothetical PTR program when CBL is inaccurate.
finding.measure: False load reduction as % of consumption; rebate as % of utility revenue
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI reported for bar plots, exact values not reported

paper_profiles.title: Tinkering in Primary School: From Episode to Science Practice
paper_profiles.venue: The Primary School as a Playful Space
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how tinkering, a constructionist and open-ended making practice, can be integrated into primary school science teaching through a model the authors call TIDE (Tinkering, Ideas generation, Disciplinary connection, Exploration). The central problem is whether teachers can move beyond treating tinkering as a recreational episode and instead use it as a bridge to disciplinary learning and classroom inquiry, especially in physics and the nature of science.

The authors describe an action-research project carried out in four primary schools in Bologna with 13 classrooms, 24 teachers, and approximately 300 students, using repeated tinkering workshops on light, professional development, documentation tools, questionnaires, and fishbowl reflection protocols. Due to pandemic constraints, the planned design was compressed, but the study still yielded teacher feedback and qualitative documentation about student participation, teacher comfort, and classroom dynamics.

The main findings suggest that tinkering can surface authentic student research questions, increase engagement, and re-engage students often seen as disengaged, while also revealing vulnerabilities among some high-performing students. However, teachers often felt unprepared to pursue the scientific questions that emerged, especially in physics, and tended to connect tinkering more readily to humanities or expressive activities than to science content. The chapter concludes that tinkering has promise for inquiry and scientific citizenship, but that effective integration into formal schooling requires additional disciplinary support and more robust documentation of learning over time.

finding.finding_summary: Tinkering prompted students to generate authentic scientific research questions, including a class-wide question about how to produce white light using colored filters. The authors report that many questions were only partially resolved during workshops, indicating that the practice supports inquiry and the emergence of scientific reasoning, though the study does not provide a controlled outcome measure or effect size.
finding.measure: Emergence and discussion of student research questions during tinkering workshops; fishbowl protocol documentation
finding.study_size: n=13 classrooms; approximately n=300 students; teacher feedback from n=20 teachers

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported high engagement, participation, motivation, and collaboration during tinkering, especially among students usually considered less engaged in regular schoolwork. The questionnaire found that 70% of teachers noticed unexpected or partially expected behavior, describing students as enthusiastic, sustained in attention, and more willing to participate in pairs or groups.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire about student engagement/participation; qualitative teacher reports from workshops

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that tinkering fosters critical thinking, collaboration, self-reflection, and problem solving, and teachers’ responses suggested that students focused more on process, reasoning, and managing frustration. However, the evidence is qualitative and descriptive rather than based on a formal critical-thinking assessment, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher descriptions of student reasoning, collaboration, and frustration tolerance during tinkering

finding.finding_summary: The intervention appeared to change teacher perceptions of students and classroom practice, with teachers reporting that tinkering could be integrated into classroom life and reveal hidden student strengths. At the same time, teachers often felt insufficiently prepared to address the scientific content that emerged, leading the authors to recommend additional disciplinary training and support for institutional implementation.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire and fishbowl reflection on integration into classroom practice and teacher preparedness

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Systems that Augment Human Performed vs. Demonstrated Critical Thinking
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2025 ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conceptual/position paper; no empirical study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses a conceptual problem in research on generative AI and critical thinking: many studies evaluate whether AI improves the final product of a task, but do not distinguish between critical thinking that is independently performed by the user and critical thinking that is merely demonstrated through AI-assisted output. The authors argue that this distinction matters because a system may make a response look more analytical without actually improving the user’s own reasoning ability.

The paper synthesizes prior work on critical thinking, Bloom’s taxonomy, and human augmentation frameworks to propose a two-part framework: performed critical thinking and demonstrated critical thinking. It argues that existing GenAI evaluations often overstate cognitive benefits because they measure AI-assisted outputs rather than independent post-interaction reasoning. The authors suggest that future research should use study designs that separately assess independent critical thinking, including pre/post or longitudinal approaches, and should draw on education research to design AI systems that scaffold reasoning rather than simply provide answers.

No original empirical data are reported. Instead, the paper offers design guidance for AI systems intended to support critical thinking in educational and other knowledge work contexts. It concludes that AI can improve demonstrated critical thinking and productivity, but this should not be assumed to translate into improved performed critical thinking, especially if users become overreliant on AI assistance.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is a conceptual synthesis rather than an empirical study, but it argues that generative AI may improve demonstrated critical thinking while not necessarily improving performed critical thinking. The authors cite prior studies as showing mixed findings on AI and critical thinking, and caution that AI assistance can increase the quality of final outputs without strengthening users' independent reasoning skills.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Discussion Tracker: Supporting Teacher Learning about Students’ Collaborative Argumentation in High School Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents Discussion Tracker (DT), a classroom discussion analytics system designed to help teachers learn about and support students’ collaborative argumentation in high school classrooms. The motivating problem is that collaborative argumentation is important for learning and group problem-solving, but teachers often struggle to monitor the quality of student talk and reflect on it without a record of the discussion.

DT uses NLP classifiers to automatically code classroom discussion transcripts along three dimensions: argument moves (claim/evidence/explanation), specificity, and collaboration (e.g., agree, extension, challenge/probe). The system then generates visualizations and analytics such as coded transcripts, collaboration maps, and strengths/weaknesses summaries for instructional planning. In the reported study, 18 high school English Language Arts teachers from 4 schools used a desktop version of DT after a discussion had been transcribed and manually coded; they also completed surveys and cognitive interviews.

The evaluation focused on teacher usability and NLP classifier performance rather than student learning outcomes. Teachers rated DT as helpful overall, especially the annotated transcript and overview/pie-chart displays, and generally agreed that it improved their insight into student learning and their facilitation of discussion. The automated classifiers showed moderate to substantial agreement with human annotations for argument moves and specificity, with weaker performance for collaboration, especially for rare labels like agree and challenge/probe. The paper concludes that DT is promising for supporting teacher reflection and future work should improve automation, transcription, segmentation, and ease of use.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that Discussion Tracker was helpful for analyzing classroom discussions and supporting their planning/goal-setting. In a survey of 18 high school ELA teachers, the overall item “Discussion Tracker is helpful for my teaching of literature discussions” averaged 4.72/5, and the system was also rated helpful for recognizing student strengths and weaknesses and for making changes to facilitation.
finding.measure: Teacher usability survey ratings of DT features and overall helpfulness

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on collaborative argumentation, a durable skill closely related to critical thinking and collaboration. Teachers used DT to inspect argument moves, specificity, and collaboration in student discussion, and they reported that the analytics gave them more insight into student learning than they usually get from reflecting on discussion alone (mean 4.67/5).
finding.measure: Teacher-reported usefulness of analytics for understanding students’ collaborative argumentation; coded discussion dimensions (argument moves, specificity, collaboration)
finding.study_size: n=18 teachers; 18 classroom discussions for classifier evaluation

finding.finding_summary: Although not a student outcome study, the system analyzes face-to-face classroom discussion transcripts and is explicitly intended to support oral discussion quality. Teachers found the annotated transcript and collaboration diagram helpful for examining student talk, suggesting the system can support instructional attention to speaking and listening in discussion-based classrooms.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of transcript-based discussion analytics

paper_profiles.title: The cognitive paradox of AI in education: between enhancement and erosion
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (opinion paper; synthesizes evidence across multiple educational levels including undergraduate and vocational learners, with some K-12 implications discussed)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an opinion piece arguing that AI in education has a paradoxical effect: it can enhance learning through personalization and efficiency, but it may also erode cognition through over-reliance and cognitive offloading. The authors frame the discussion using Cognitive Load Theory, Bloom’s Taxonomy, and Self-Determination Theory to explain how AI may reduce extraneous load while also diminishing germane cognitive effort, autonomy, and relatedness if used passively.

Rather than reporting a new empirical study, the article synthesizes prior literature and illustrative findings on memory retention, problem-solving, critical thinking, creativity, motivation, and language learning. It cites studies suggesting that AI-supported learning can improve some performance outcomes, but it also highlights evidence that overuse may weaken conceptual understanding, retention, and higher-order thinking. The paper concludes that AI should complement, not replace, human instruction, and recommends implementation strategies such as teacher-guided integration, reflection prompts, AI-free practice, and monitoring to preserve critical thinking and deep learning.

Because the paper is a conceptual and argumentative review, it does not provide original participant data, effect sizes, or a focused K-12 intervention comparison. Its main value is as a theoretical synthesis of potential benefits and risks of AI in learning, with broad implications for educational design and policy.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can both support and erode critical thinking and other higher-order skills. It cites prior studies and examples suggesting that AI-based personalization may help learning, but over-reliance can reduce active reasoning, source verification, and concept understanding; no original effect size is reported.
finding.measure: critical thinking, problem-solving, higher-order thinking, concept understanding

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses motivation, autonomy, competence, relatedness, and engagement as outcomes affected by AI use. It posits that AI may increase competence through customization but excessive dependence can undermine autonomy and intrinsic motivation; no primary data or effect size are reported.
finding.measure: motivation, autonomy, engagement, relatedness

finding.finding_summary: Across illustrative examples, the paper claims AI can improve some academic performance outcomes such as procedural performance and standardized-test scores, while also warning that conceptual understanding may decline when AI is used as a substitute for effortful learning. No original study statistics are reported.
finding.measure: standardized test scores, exam performance, conceptual understanding

paper_profiles.title: Editorial: Generative AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial introduces a Frontiers Research Topic on generative AI in education and summarizes the included papers. Its purpose is not to test a single intervention, but to frame the emerging research landscape around how generative AI may support personalized learning, feedback, assessment, mentoring, and other educational functions.

Across the volume, the editors highlight examples such as AI-generated feedback, student use of chatbots, AI support for mathematical proof construction, personalized assessment, career mentoring, interactive listening tasks, and issues of integrity, deception, and emotional content in AI responses. The editorial argues that generative AI holds promise for individualized support and engagement, but that important limitations remain, including response accuracy, emotional appropriateness, interpretability, privacy, fairness, and the need for human-in-the-loop oversight.

For the specific question of AI-personalized feedback and K-12 critical thinking, this paper does not report a direct empirical study. It only cites/opines that personalized feedback may improve engagement and foster strategic and critical use of AI tools, while also noting that more research is needed. No causal evidence, effect sizes, or K-12 outcome data are presented in the editorial itself.

finding.finding_summary: This editorial argues that AI-based personalized feedback may help foster students’ strategic and critical use of AI tools, but it also emphasizes that stronger evidence is still needed. The paper does not present original data or effect sizes; its claims are based on discussion of included articles and examples rather than a direct evaluation of critical thinking outcomes.
finding.measure: critical thinking / strategic use of AI tools (conceptual discussion, not directly measured in this editorial)

paper_profiles.title: AI in the Classroom: A Boon or a Threat to Pedagogical Practices?
paper_profiles.population: Secondary (6th grade students; teachers in Almaty schools)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI in education helps or harms pedagogical practice, with particular attention to student engagement, independent work, critical thinking, and retention. The authors frame AI as potentially useful for personalized feedback and support, but also as a possible source of over-reliance that could weaken deeper learning and independence.

Methodologically, the study combines a literature review, a survey of teachers from schools in Almaty, and a small classroom experiment with 6th-grade students. In the experiment, students used AI tools to write short stories, then were asked one week later to retell the stories; brief interviews followed to probe engagement and understanding. The teacher survey asked about perceived effects of AI on engagement, independence, motivation, and academic progress.

Findings were mixed. Teachers generally reported moderate engagement and divergent views on whether AI improves or hinders independence, with overall perceptions leaning neutral-to-positive. In the student activity, about half of students could retell the story after one week, suggesting only moderate retention, and many students made minimal customization of the AI-generated content, indicating limited critical engagement. The paper concludes that AI should supplement, not replace, traditional pedagogy, and that structured guidance is needed to prevent over-reliance and support critical and creative thinking.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported moderate to fairly positive engagement with AI-assisted assignments, but responses were not uniform. On a 1-5 scale comparing AI tools with traditional methods, 41.7% of teachers rated engagement at level 3, 33.3% at level 4, 16.7% at level 2, and 8.3% at level 5, indicating some perceived uplift but not a strong consensus.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of student engagement with AI-assisted assignments compared with traditional methods

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly addresses critical thinking, independent problem-solving, and metacognitive engagement as potential consequences of AI use. Teachers were evenly split on whether AI improves or hinders independence (25% at level 1 and 25% at level 5 on a 1-5 scale), and the student task showed low customization of AI-generated stories, suggesting limited deep processing. The experiment also found that only about half of 6th-grade students could accurately retell the story one week later, indicating moderate retention rather than strong durable learning.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of independence; student retelling of AI-assisted stories after one week; qualitative interview responses about customization and understanding
finding.study_size: n=6th-grade students (exact n not_reported); n=12 teachers

finding.finding_summary: The classroom experiment involved AI-assisted story writing, so the paper substantively touches literacy through writing and narrative production. However, the reported results do not show clear improvement in writing quality; instead, students mostly accepted AI-generated suggestions with minimal customization, and the main measured outcome was one-week retelling rather than a standardized literacy assessment.
finding.measure: AI-assisted story writing and later story retelling

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conceptual review with no human participants)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a narrative review and perspective piece on the emerging role of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular emphasis on chatbots and ChatGPT. The paper asks how AI tools may transform teaching and learning, including personalized instruction, instant feedback, assessment, and student engagement, while also highlighting ethical, practical, and pedagogical concerns.

The authors synthesize prior literature rather than reporting a new empirical study. They discuss AI applications across student learning, teacher support, and administration, arguing that tools such as chatbots, adaptive platforms, and automated grading systems may improve efficiency and support individualized learning pathways. They also note risks including bias, privacy concerns, unreliable outputs, limited human interaction, and the need for teacher training and responsible implementation.

Because the paper is not an original intervention study, it does not provide direct evidence that AI-personalized feedback improves K-12 critical thinking relative to other feedback conditions. Instead, it offers a broad overview of potential benefits and limitations of AI in education, concluding that further research is needed to determine where and how these tools are effective and ethically deployable.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools may foster durable skills such as critical thinking and creativity by providing personalized and instant feedback that encourages self-reflection and self-directed learning. However, this claim is presented as a literature-based expectation rather than as evidence from a new K-12 study, and no effect size or controlled comparison is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review states that AI-supported personalized learning can increase student motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduce anxiety, citing prior studies in the broader literature. These outcomes are discussed conceptually for educational AI generally, not as results from a single K-12 critical-thinking intervention.
finding.measure: motivation, engagement, confidence, anxiety

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes AI as reducing teacher workload through automated grading, assignment scoring, and feedback delivery, thereby saving time for lesson planning and student support. This is a conceptual synthesis with no original sample or effect estimate reported.
finding.measure: teacher workload / grading and feedback efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Multimodal Feedback Using Multiple External Representations: Strategy Profiles and Learning in High School Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether students’ voluntary use of elaborated, personalized feedback in a high-school physics platform is associated with better learning outcomes than relying on verification feedback alone. The broader motivation is to understand how adaptive feedback should be designed when multiple external representations (MERs)—text, graphics, and mathematics—are available, especially as AI-enabled tutoring systems become more common.

The study followed 661 students in grades 10–11 across 26 German schools over 16–24 weeks. Students completed kinematics exercises in a custom web platform (KI4SCool) that always provided verification feedback and optionally offered elaborated feedback in verbal, graphical, and mathematical formats. Students chose which feedback representations to open, and the authors analyzed platform logs, pre-/post-test performance, and representational competence using linear mixed-effects models, clustering, and ANCOVA.

Results showed a small positive association between more frequent use of elaborated feedback and higher post-test scores, even after adjusting for prior knowledge, platform performance, exercise count, and confidence. The effect was consistent across two cohorts, but the authors stress that the design is observational, so the relationship cannot be interpreted causally; motivated or more engaged students may have been more likely both to use the feedback and to score better. The paper also found that students tended to cluster into distinct feedback-use strategies, with some students consulting all representations, some favoring verbal feedback, and some never opening elaborated feedback. Initial representational competence did not clearly explain these strategy differences, and moderators by competence were not robust overall.

finding.finding_summary: More frequent use of elaborated multimodal feedback was associated with higher post-test performance in kinematics, a science learning outcome, after adjusting for pre-test score, platform score, exercise count, and confidence. In Cohort 1 (n=351), feedback frequency had a standardized association of β=0.13, 95% CI [0.05, 0.22]; in Cohort 2 (n=310), the association was smaller and marginal, β=0.08, 95% CI [0.00, 0.16], p=.054.
finding.measure: Post-test score on kinematics tests (percent correct / science concept test performance)

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined representational competence and students’ selection strategies across multiple external representations, which are closely related to critical thinking-like durable skills such as comparing, translating, and coordinating information across formats. However, it did not measure critical thinking with a dedicated instrument; instead, it found no clear evidence that initial representational competences differentiated feedback-strategy clusters (MANOVA Pillai’s trace=0.018, F=0.74, p=.67), while one cluster showed a positive slope between feedback frequency and post-test performance (estimate=33.83, SE=13.02, p=.01).
finding.measure: Initial representational competence; feedback-strategy cluster membership; post-test performance as a proxy for learning with MERs
finding.study_size: n=351 for competence analyses; n=661 overall

paper_profiles.title: Exploring LLM-Generated Feedback for Economics Essays: How Teaching Assistants Evaluate and Envision Its Use
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how large language model (LLM)-generated feedback can be used as a support tool for human instructors’ grading and feedback workflows. The authors ask not whether the AI directly improves student outcomes, but whether teaching assistants (TAs) perceive AI feedback as useful, accurate, and actionable when compared with their own handwritten feedback and with instructor-provided historical feedback.

The study was conducted in a college-level introductory economics course with frequent short essay assignments that required students to demonstrate understanding of economic concepts. The authors built a rubric-based feedback pipeline that first identified relevant sentences, then judged whether rubric criteria were met, and finally generated feedback comments; they also visualized AI highlights and intermediate outputs inside a Word document. Five TAs participated in think-aloud sessions across 20 one-hour sessions, reviewing AI feedback on essays they had already graded.

Findings suggest that TAs viewed AI feedback as often more detailed, more personalized, and more aligned with rubrics than their own feedback, especially because it used praise, guiding questions, and explanations. At the same time, the AI could be overly rigid, overly fragmented, and sometimes incorrect when rubrics were underspecified or when students expressed ideas in noncanonical ways. TAs said the highlights and intermediate outputs made errors easier to detect and made the system more useful as a suggestion tool. Overall, the paper concludes that AI-generated feedback may be promising as a human-in-the-loop aid for grading efficiency, consistency, and feedback quality, but it does not evaluate student learning effects.

finding.finding_summary: TAs reported that AI-generated feedback and sentence highlights could speed up reading, evaluation, and comment writing. They repeatedly described the system as helping them save time, especially for generating individualized comments and for quickly locating evidence tied to rubric items; however, these were subjective perceptions from a qualitative study (n=5 TAs, 20 one-hour sessions), not measured time gains.
finding.measure: TA perceptions of grading speed, reading efficiency, and feedback-writing workload in think-aloud interviews

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on critical evaluation and instructor decision-making around AI feedback rather than student critical thinking, but it does substantively address instructors’ evaluative judgment and metacognitive comparison of AI versus human feedback. TAs found AI suggestions helpful for prompting them to think more carefully about rubrics and their own judgments, yet they also stressed the need to critically review and not over-rely on the system.
finding.measure: TA reflections during think-aloud review of AI feedback and comparison with their own grading judgments

paper_profiles.title: Feedback control of nuclear hyperfine fields in double quantum dot
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a theoretical model for feedback control of nuclear hyperfine fields in a coupled double quantum dot system.
