The central question is how the interplay between electron and nuclear spins near singlet-triplet resonances can be used to manipulate nuclear spin fluctuations and thereby improve electron spin coherence.

The authors analyze two-electron states in a double dot under moderate external magnetic fields, deriving effective Hamiltonians for singlet-triplet resonances and showing that first-order and second-order hyperfine processes interfere to produce feedback effects. Depending on the resonance and material hyperfine-sign conventions, the mechanism can yield negative feedback that suppresses fluctuations in the longitudinal nuclear field gradient or positive feedback that amplifies it, and similarly for transverse nuclear fields.

The paper is not an empirical K-12 education study and does not investigate learners, teachers, feedback in instruction, or critical thinking outcomes. Instead, it is a condensed-matter physics theory paper motivated by quantum-dot qubit coherence. It discusses possible experimental relevance for double quantum dot systems, including implications for dephasing times and nuclear polarization, but provides no educational intervention or student outcome data.

paper_profiles.title: RLHF-Blender: A Configurable Interactive Interface for Learning from Diverse Human Feedback
paper_profiles.venue: Interactive Learning with Implicit Human Feedback Workshop at ICML 2023
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a tooling gap in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF): researchers lack standardized, configurable software for systematically studying how different kinds of human feedback can be collected, encoded, and used for reward learning. The authors argue that progress in RLHF is limited by ad hoc interfaces and simplified assumptions about feedback quality, irrationality, and bias.

The paper introduces RLHF-Blender, a modular client-server interface and experimentation framework that supports multiple feedback modalities, including ratings, rankings/comparisons, corrective feedback, demonstrations, and descriptive/feature-level feedback. It also defines a standard feedback encoding, a feedback processor, and sampling/querying modes (random, progressive, query-based, state-machine) so researchers can run controlled human-subject studies and train reward models from the resulting data.

The work is not an empirical evaluation of an educational intervention and does not study K-12 learners, teachers, or classroom settings. Instead, it proposes a research infrastructure for future RLHF experiments and discusses possible studies on feedback quality, human irrationality, calibration, and explainability. The main conclusion is that RLHF-Blender may enable more systematic, reusable, and comparative research on human feedback for reward learning, but the system itself is not yet fully validated in a large-scale user study.

paper_profiles.title: Joint Beamforming for Multiaccess MIMO Systems with Finite Rate Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies multiaccess MIMO wireless communication systems with finite-rate feedback. Its central question is how to use a limited feedback channel efficiently to maximize achievable sum rate when the transmitter has only imperfect channel state information. The authors analyze two suboptimal strategies: antenna selection and a general joint beamforming strategy with joint quantization of users’ strongest eigen-channel vectors.

The work is theoretical and mathematical rather than an educational intervention study. It develops asymptotic results using order statistics, random matrix theory, and Grassmann-manifold quantization bounds to approximate the performance of the proposed strategies. The paper shows that joint quantization is better than individual quantization, that random codebooks are asymptotically optimal in probability, and that the sum-rate loss from quantization decays with feedback rate. Simulations are used to support the analytical upper bounds, but no human participants, classrooms, schools, or K-12 outcomes are studied.

Because the paper is about wireless communication and information theory, it does not address AI, education, instruction, or student learning outcomes. There are no measures of critical thinking, academic achievement, engagement, or school implementation; accordingly, it is not relevant to the requested K-12 AI-in-education evidence question beyond being unrelated technical literature.

paper_profiles.title: Feedback Capacity and a Variant of the Kalman Filter with ARMA Gaussian Noises: Explicit Bounds and Feedback Coding Design
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a control/information-theory problem: how to characterize and lower-bound the feedback capacity of additive Gaussian channels with colored ARMA noise. The authors develop an alternative derivation using a variant of the steady-state Kalman filter, showing how certain Kalman-filter parameters can be mapped to a feedback communication channel and used to construct recursive coding schemes.

The paper is purely theoretical and does not study human participants, schools, classrooms, teachers, or students. It derives explicit lower bounds on feedback capacity for finite-order ARMA Gaussian noise channels, proves observability/detectability properties for the transformed state-space system, and shows how to design coding schemes that achieve the bounds under certain parameter choices. Special cases are discussed for first-order ARMA and second-order MA noise, with the derived bounds matching known capacity results in those settings.

Because the work is mathematical and does not evaluate any educational intervention, there is no empirical evidence about K-12 learning outcomes, AI-personalized feedback, critical thinking, or implementation in educational contexts.

paper_profiles.title: An Achievable Rate Region for the Broadcast Channel with Feedback
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (communication systems / information theory; no human participants)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an information theory study about the two-receiver broadcast channel with generalized feedback. It asks whether feedback can enlarge the achievable communication rate region relative to the classic no-feedback broadcast channel, and if so, how to characterize that gain with a single-letter region.

The authors propose a block-Markov superposition coding scheme built on Marton coding, where fresh messages are sent in one block and list-resolution information is sent in later blocks. The key idea is that the resolution information for the two receivers is correlated, so it can be transmitted more efficiently using joint source-channel coding ideas inspired by Han-Costa coding. The paper proves a new single-letter achievable rate region for discrete memoryless broadcast channels with generalized feedback and then specializes it to an AWGN broadcast channel with noisy feedback from one receiver.

The paper’s empirical/numerical component is limited to information-theoretic rate calculations, not human-subject experimentation. The authors show numerically that the proposed region can yield rates outside the no-feedback capacity region even with noisy feedback, and they compare the resulting sum rates against known schemes for noiseless feedback. The work is relevant to communications engineering rather than education, and it does not study AI, K-12 learners, critical thinking, or instructional feedback in classrooms.

paper_profiles.title: AttentionCode: Ultra-Reliable Feedback Codes for Short-Packet Communications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a wireless communications problem: how to design ultra-reliable short-packet feedback codes for noisy channels. The authors argue that conventional feedback schemes such as Schalkwijk-Kailath (SK), modulo-SK, and prior deep-learning-based feedback codes suffer from finite-precision limitations, sensitivity to feedback noise, or suboptimal performance at short block lengths.

To improve performance, the paper proposes AttentionCode, a deep-learning-based feedback coding framework built around a pure-attention encoder/decoder (AttentionNet), input restructuring, masking, and adaptation to fading channels. The system is trained with several optimization techniques including large-batch training, distributed learning, a look-ahead optimizer, training-test SNR mismatch, and curriculum learning. Numerical experiments compare AttentionCode with SK, modulo-SK, DeepCode, DEFC, and DRFC under AWGN and fading-channel settings.

The paper reports that AttentionCode achieves state-of-the-art block error rate (BLER) among the compared deep-learning-based feedback codes. In AWGN settings with noiseless feedback, it improves BLER performance relative to the best prior code by up to 1.6 dB at BLER 10^-8; with noisy feedback (feedback SNR 20 dB), it improves by 0.7 dB at BLER 10^-6. The paper is a communications engineering study and does not involve K-12 learners, classrooms, or educational outcomes; it is therefore not directly relevant to AI-personalized feedback for critical thinking in education.

paper_profiles.title: The Development of English Learning Model Based on Contextual Teaching and Learning (CTL) in Junior High Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for more contextual English instruction in junior high schools in South Sulawesi, Indonesia, where teachers were reported to rely on non-contextual materials that did not sufficiently support students’ communication or critical thinking. The authors argue that the 2013 curriculum requires more learner-centered approaches and that English learning should connect classroom content to local, real-world problems.

The study develops English learning devices based on Contextual Teaching and Learning (CTL), specifically a lesson plan (RPP), student worksheet (LKS), and student book, using a Four-D development model (define, design, develop, disseminate). The paper reports qualitative validation by an expert, classroom observations, student response data, and learning outcomes from 99 junior high school students. The intervention was implemented in a junior-high context in South Sulawesi, and the authors describe field trials and dissemination to teachers in Makassar.

The main conclusion is that CTL-based learning devices were viewed as effective for improving students’ English communication competence and critical thinking ability, especially through opportunities for discussion, problem solving, and reporting project results. Descriptively, 88.89% of students scored at or above the paper’s criterion for completion (score >=65), and the authors conclude that CTL-based materials can support more active, contextual, and socially interactive English learning. The paper also notes constraints such as students’ first language, social interaction patterns, and initial English proficiency.

finding.finding_summary: The CTL-based English learning devices were reported to improve students’ communication competence in English, with students showing more opportunities to speak, discuss, and interact with classmates and teachers. The study reports that 88.89% of the 99 junior high school students met the completion criterion (score >=65) on English learning outcomes, with an average score of 77.99/100 (SD=20.12).
finding.measure: English learning outcomes / communication competence score

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly identifies critical thinking as a central outcome of the CTL-based model and concludes that the developed learning tools can improve students’ critical thinking ability. Students were said to engage in speaking, discussing real problems, and reporting project results, which the authors interpret as supporting critical thinking development.
finding.measure: Critical thinking ability / ability to think critically during CTL-based English learning

paper_profiles.title: Learning design to support student-AI collaboration: perspectives of leading teachers for AI in education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers (primary and secondary school educators in South Korea)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 learning should be designed when artificial intelligence is introduced as a collaborative learning partner rather than only as a tool. The authors ask what curriculum, interaction supports, learning environments, and developmental stages are needed for student-AI collaboration (SAC) in school learning.

The study is based on in-depth semi-structured interviews with 10 Korean leading teachers in AI in education, drawn from primary and secondary schools involved in software education, AI pilot programs, or AI-convergence high schools. Using a hybrid inductive-deductive thematic analysis, the authors develop a student-AI collaboration model organized around curriculum, student-AI interaction, environment, and evolution over time.

Teachers argued that SAC should emphasize capacity building, especially higher-order thinking, collaboration, and subject-matter knowledge, through interdisciplinary, authentic, and creative tasks assessed with process-oriented and collaboration-focused methods. They also identified supports needed for meaningful student-AI interaction, including instruction on AI principles, data literacy, error analysis, AI ethics, intuitive interfaces, and AI with instructional scaffolding. At the institutional level, they emphasized the need for a supportive digital infrastructure, flexible school structures, teacher capacity building, a collaborative school culture, and a safe-to-fail environment. The paper concludes that SAC is envisioned as progressing from learning about AI, to learning from AI, and eventually learning together with AI.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived student-AI collaboration as a way to build higher-order thinking, including critical thinking, creativity, analytical thinking, and problem-solving. They expected SAC to help students evaluate AI-generated information critically, generate broader solution sets, and engage in systematic reasoning through authentic and interdisciplinary tasks. No quantitative effect size was reported because this was a qualitative interview study with n=10 teachers.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about higher-order thinking, critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, analytical thinking, and collaboration in SAC

finding.finding_summary: Teachers argued that SAC could support motivation, engagement, persistence, grit, coping with uncertainty, and willingness to try again after failure. They also emphasized the importance of safe-to-fail classroom cultures and AI designed to encourage students when they struggle, but the study reports perceptions rather than measured student outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about motivation, engagement, persistence, grit, and safe-to-fail learning culture

finding.finding_summary: Teachers viewed SAC as supporting subject-matter knowledge building across disciplines through authentic, real-world tasks and interdisciplinary learning. They described students using AI to solve classroom and real-life problems in science, home economics, social studies, and language arts, but the paper does not report direct student achievement data or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about subject-matter knowledge building and interdisciplinary authentic tasks

finding.finding_summary: Teachers said AI should automate repetitive instructional work and that cloud-based platforms should integrate with existing school systems to reduce teacher burden. They also framed process-oriented co-assessment and digital workflows as ways to manage learning more efficiently, but the paper does not quantify workload reduction.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about automation, platform integration, and assessment workflow

finding.finding_summary: A central finding was that SAC requires broad institutional support, including systematic AIED policy, governance coordination, flexible school structures, teacher professional development, collaborative school culture, and secure digital infrastructure. These were identified as prerequisites for implementation rather than measured outcomes, and no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about policy, governance, school organization, infrastructure, and professional development

paper_profiles.title: Development of Inclusive Learning Based on Problem-Based Learning to Improve Critical Thinking Skills and Scientific Attitudes of Students in the 3T Areas of Riau Province
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study addresses the challenge of improving higher-order thinking and scientific dispositions among high school students in Indonesia’s 3T regions, where access to educational resources, qualified teachers, and technology is limited. The authors argue that conventional science instruction in these areas does not sufficiently support critical thinking or scientific attitudes, and they focus on the need for an instructional model that is both inclusive and contextually appropriate.

The intervention was the development of an inclusive Problem-Based Learning (PBL) model adapted from the Borg & Gall R&D framework. The model incorporated contextual problems, scaffolding through guiding questions, visual media, differentiation strategies, and an inclusive classroom implementation guide. It was developed through preliminary study, expert validation, revision, limited trial, and effectiveness testing at SMAN 1 Kampar Kiri with high school students in an inclusive 3T school setting.

For effectiveness testing, the study used a non-equivalent control group design comparing an experimental class using the inclusive PBL model with a control class using conventional instruction over four science sessions. Data sources included a critical thinking test, a scientific attitude questionnaire, observations, and interviews. The authors report that the model was valid, practical, and effective, with improvements in students’ critical thinking and scientific attitudes, including greater curiosity, openness to evidence, and responsibility. The strongest quantitative result reported was for scientific attitude scores, which increased from 68 to 84 in the experimental class versus 66 to 73 in the control class; the paper concludes that inclusive PBL is a promising approach for equitable science learning in underserved regions.

finding.finding_summary: The inclusive PBL model improved students’ critical thinking skills in an effectiveness test conducted with high school students in an inclusive 3T school. The paper reports that the experimental class outperformed the control class after implementation, but it does not provide a specific effect size, confidence interval, or standard deviation in the extracted text.
finding.measure: Critical thinking skills test based on Ennis indicators

finding.finding_summary: Students’ scientific attitudes improved after the inclusive PBL intervention, with the experimental class increasing from 68 pretest to 84 posttest, compared with 66 to 73 in the control class. The attitude measure captured curiosity, openness to evidence, responsibility, and collaboration, and qualitative feedback suggested students found the learning more engaging and meaningful.
finding.measure: Science attitude questionnaire based on Fraser’s indicators

finding.finding_summary: The study centers on science learning in an inclusive classroom and reports that the PBL-based model supported better science-related learning processes, including problem solving with contextual scientific content. However, the direct quantitative outcome emphasized in the paper is critical thinking and scientific attitude rather than a narrowly defined scientific reasoning assessment, so the evidence for this category is secondary.
finding.measure: Science learning activities and science-topic classroom implementation

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual article argues that the rapid adoption of AI tools such as ChatGPT in education requires a new emphasis on AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The paper frames AI as both an opportunity and a risk: it can personalize learning, support diverse learners, and help with classroom tasks, but it can also encourage uncritical outsourcing of cognitive work, hallucinated outputs, and unclear authorship in academic work.

The paper is built from the author’s experience at a Swiss University of Applied Sciences, where informal discussions with students and staff informed a case study about institutional responses to generative AI. The university’s response was a formal AI guideline requiring transparency about AI use, documentation of models and prompts, and critical evaluation of outputs. The article then supplements this case discussion with a narrative literature review to propose practical strategies, including AI literacy courses, workshops, and classroom activities that treat AI as a sparring partner rather than a substitute for student thinking.

The article’s main conclusion is that simple prohibition or unrestricted use of AI are both inadequate. Instead, institutions should build a culture of AI use that is guided, transparent, and critically reflective. The author argues that education should explicitly teach students how to work with AI responsibly, understand its limitations, and use prompt engineering as a way to strengthen learning rather than bypass it.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that prompt engineering and AI literacy can strengthen critical thinking by pushing students to evaluate AI outputs, compare responses, and reflect on limitations. However, it also warns that uncritical AI use may weaken cognition by encouraging students to hand over thinking to machines; no empirical effect size is reported because the paper is conceptual and case-based.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, reflective evaluation of AI outputs, and prompt engineering competence

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes the implementation of institutional AI guidelines at a Swiss university and argues that such policies improve transparency and responsible AI use in academic work. The main evidence is a case study and institutional practice description rather than a measured outcome, so no quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Institutional AI policy/guidelines, transparency requirements, and governance of student AI use

finding.finding_summary: The article suggests that AI tools can support curriculum design, case-study creation, and classroom preparation, potentially reducing teacher workload and increasing efficiency. This is presented as a practical recommendation grounded in experience and literature, but no empirical workload measure or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workflow, curriculum creation, and instructional preparation

paper_profiles.title: Tablet use in schools: A critical review of the evidence for learning outcomes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper critically reviews empirical research on tablet use in primary and secondary schools, with a specific focus on whether tablet use improves students’ knowledge and skills. The authors conduct a systematic review of literature published from 2009 onward, identifying 33 relevant studies and retaining 23 that met minimum quality thresholds for detailed analysis.

Across the included studies, tablets were used in a wide range of classroom contexts and subjects, including science, social studies, mathematics, literacy, special education, and collaborative learning activities. The review finds that most studies report positive learning outcomes, though a substantial minority report no difference and a few report negative outcomes. The authors argue that positive results are often linked to tablet affordances such as portability, touch interaction, customization, and support for collaborative and individualized learning, but they also emphasize that the evidence base is fragmented, methodologically uneven, and often too limited in detail and duration to support strong causal conclusions.

The paper also examines factors associated with successful or unsuccessful tablet implementation, including infrastructure, device selection, software/content quality, and pedagogical design. It concludes that tablets can support learning in principle, but that future research needs to be more rigorous, longitudinal, and classroom-embedded to better identify when and how tablet use improves outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The review includes literacy and reading studies, with some reporting no difference and at least one reporting negative reading comprehension outcomes. For example, Sheppard (2011) reported negative or neutral impact on reading comprehension after tablet use three times a week for 45–60 minutes over several weeks, while other literacy-related studies found no significant differences.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension, reading speed, and related literacy outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Tablet-supported mathematics activities generally showed positive learning outcomes, including an iPad fractions game that improved students’ fractions knowledge. In Riconscente (2013), 122 fourth-grade students (n=122) improved fractions test scores by an average of 15% over one week compared with a control group; self-efficacy and liking of fractions each improved by about 10%.
finding.measure: Fractions knowledge/test scores and related attitudes

finding.finding_summary: Science-focused tablet studies were mostly positive, including work on the water cycle and plant morphology. For example, Furio et al. (2013) studied 79 Spanish students aged 8–10 and found positive results for a tablet-based educational game reinforcing water-cycle knowledge, with no significant differences from a mobile-phone comparison and learning gains in both conditions.
finding.measure: Science knowledge and inquiry-related learning outcomes (e.g., water cycle, plant morphology)
finding.study_size: n=79 (example study); broader review n=23 included studies

finding.finding_summary: The review also includes positive outcomes in non-core subjects such as social studies and other curriculum areas. For instance, Lin et al. (2012) reported learning gains in a social studies concept-mapping activity with 64 Taiwanese students, and the broader review notes positive outcomes across multiple subjects and special education contexts.
finding.measure: Social studies knowledge, concept maps, and subject-specific learning outcomes
finding.study_size: n=64 (example study); broader review n=23 included studies

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies reported gains in motivation, attitudes, self-efficacy, and engagement alongside learning outcomes. For example, Riconscente (2013) found that children’s self-efficacy for fractions and liking of fractions each improved by about 10%, and other studies reported positive attitudes and enjoyment when using tablets.
finding.measure: Self-efficacy, liking/attitudes, engagement, and participation

finding.finding_summary: Although the review is not limited to critical thinking, it substantively addresses collaborative learning and, in some cases, critical-thinking-related outcomes. The paper notes preliminary evaluation of tablet use in Zambia showing gains in subject knowledge and critical thinking skills, and it reports that tablet-supported collaboration could improve communication, participation, and the quality of artifacts produced.
finding.measure: Critical thinking skills, collaboration, communication, and group artifacts

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies several operational benefits of tablet use for schools and teachers, including reduced photocopying, greater lesson variety and pace, and easier collection of assessment data. Teachers in included studies reported workload benefits, and tablets supported ongoing feedback and cumulative assessment.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, lesson pace/variety, photocopying costs, assessment and feedback processes

finding.finding_summary: The review discusses implementation and institutional conditions affecting tablet adoption, such as wireless infrastructure, content management, change management, and school culture. These are not presented as direct outcome measures of a single intervention, but the paper argues that institutional readiness strongly shapes whether tablet initiatives succeed.
finding.measure: Implementation conditions, infrastructure readiness, and school-level adoption factors

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ roles and identities in student-centered classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative case study examines how high school STEM teachers experience role changes and identity shifts when implementing the Peer Enabled Restructured Classroom (PERC) model, a student-centered, peer-mediated instructional approach. The paper asks how teachers think about themselves as they adopt this pedagogy, what challenges they face, and how they either grow into or resist the model.

The intervention/context is the PERC Program in two urban secondary schools serving high-needs, predominantly Black and Hispanic student populations. In PERC classes, students work in small groups led by peer instructors (Teaching Assistant Scholars), while teachers shift toward facilitation, assessment, coaching, and mentoring; teachers also teach a separate TAS class focused on teaching skills, self-regulation, content, and college knowledge. Data came from interviews, focus groups, observations, and program documents across 13 teachers over multiple years.

The main conclusion is that radically student-centered classroom structures change teachers’ work and professional identities in predictable ways. Most teachers found benefits such as improved ability to monitor student learning, support individuals, reduce classroom management burdens, and focus on deeper content work; some transitioned easily, others with difficulty, and one resisted the model and left it. The study argues that successful implementation of student-centered STEM reforms depends heavily on aligning the pedagogy with teachers’ beliefs and providing sustained professional development and coaching.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the PERC model improved student engagement, self-regulation, and on-task behavior through peer leadership and immediate support. Although the paper does not quantify student outcomes with effect sizes, teachers consistently described students as more engaged, less bored, and more accountable in groups led by TAS.
finding.measure: Teacher reports and observation of student engagement, on-task behavior, and self-regulation in PERC classes

finding.finding_summary: The study centrally focuses on the development of durable skills in the classroom, especially collaboration, metacognition, problem solving, and communication. Teachers described students working in peer-led groups, asking scaffolding questions, giving feedback, and taking responsibility for learning, but the paper provides qualitative evidence rather than quantitative effect estimates.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions and classroom observations of collaboration, metacognition, communication, and problem solving in PERC/TAS classes

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that PERC improved classroom efficiency by reducing time spent repeating instructions, managing behavior, and answering routine questions. They said TAS allowed them to focus on bigger misconceptions and deeper content discussion, suggesting higher instructional productivity, but no quantitative workload measure was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher reports of classroom management burden, repetition of instructions, and time available for deeper instruction

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that student-centered programs like PERC can improve teacher evaluation outcomes and support school-level adoption of reform-oriented pedagogy. Administrators reportedly observed improved Danielson observation ratings and stronger classroom dynamics, but this is based on qualitative reports rather than measured institutional effect sizes.
finding.measure: Administrator, coach, and teacher reports of teacher evaluation ratings and classroom implementation fidelity

paper_profiles.title: Project-based learning in a high school pre-engineering program: Findings on student achievement (RTP, Strand 3)
paper_profiles.venue: American Society for Engineering Education Annual Conference
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a high school pre-engineering academy used project-based learning and what students actually learned from it. The central question is whether students in an open-ended engineering course were gaining the intended knowledge and skills—especially math/science understanding, engineering practices, and critical thinking—or whether the model was producing mostly hands-on activity without deeper learning.

The study focuses on two junior-level sections of a pre-engineering course in a public STEM academy serving a diverse high school population (n=39 students in the course; smaller subsets participated in surveys and focus groups). The course project was the design and fabrication of full-scale hovercrafts, with students working in teams, doing prototypes, presenting progress, and receiving feedback. Data came from assignments, quizzes, grades, surveys, interviews, focus groups, and observations; the author used an ethnographic case study approach.

The main conclusion is that students and teachers often valued the freedom, teamwork, and hands-on nature of the class, but the course showed a weak connection between projects and disciplinary content. Students commonly relied on intuition and trial-and-error rather than explicit math/science reasoning, and many did not demonstrate strong understanding of underlying concepts. The paper argues that ambiguous learning goals, limited curriculum development time, and a tendency to prioritize engagement over rigor reduced opportunities for direct assessment and deeper knowledge construction. It recommends clearer goals, more explicit content integration, and stronger assessment of disciplinary reasoning and critical thinking.

finding.finding_summary: The study found weak math understanding and limited use of math in the engineering project. Students reported little use of math (17 of 19 focus group participants), and the three assignments requiring explicit math understanding showed poor grasp of concepts; the paper also notes that just 6% of the grade depended on math/science application. The sample included 39 students in the course, with 37 survey respondents and 19 focus group participants.
finding.measure: Math worksheets, formative assessments, course grades, surveys, focus groups

finding.finding_summary: Science content comprehension was limited and often disconnected from the hovercraft design work. Although some students could name a few concepts such as forces of flight, pressure, and center-of-mass, many reported little use of science (14 of 19 focus group participants), and the paper describes science lessons as largely tangential to the project. The course’s formative assessments and class work suggested only basic understanding of the science concepts presented.
finding.measure: Formative assessments, assignments, surveys, focus groups, presentations

finding.finding_summary: Students generally valued the course’s hands-on freedom and engagement, but many were frustrated by insufficient guidance and by content that felt disconnected from building. The paper reports that 12 of 19 focus group participants enjoyed classroom freedom and 14 of 19 wanted more guidance, while survey responses showed moderate agreement that STEM teachers provide enough guidance (M=3.38/5) and strong agreement that trial-and-error is the best way to learn (M=4.01/5).
finding.measure: Likert surveys, focus groups, interviews
finding.study_size: n=37 survey respondents; n=19 focus group participants

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively centers on durable skills, especially critical thinking, teamwork, creativity, and problem solving. Participants widely perceived gains in these areas, but the author argues the evidence was mostly indirect: critical thinking was inferred from product quality and presentations rather than directly measured. The study also reports that many students used guess-and-check or trial-and-error instead of mindful reasoning, and only 4 of 13 groups produced working hovercrafts.
finding.measure: Assignments, presentations, interviews, focus groups, observations, grades

finding.finding_summary: The course appears inefficient as a means of ensuring students learned the intended content and reasoning skills. The paper emphasizes that teachers spent more time on task directions than content, that only 6% of grades required explicit math/science application, and that direct assessment of individual understanding was difficult because each project group encountered different content. The author concludes that the open-ended model made assessment time-consuming and weakly informative about actual learning.
finding.measure: Classroom time allocation, grading structure, feasibility of assessment

paper_profiles.title: Defining Life Skills in health promotion at school: a scoping review
paper_profiles.population: School pupils and teacher training populations (school settings; review spans children/adolescents and pre-service/teacher education studies)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a conceptual problem in the school health-promotion literature: how 'Life Skills' are defined, what terms are used interchangeably with the construct, and whether a consensus definition exists. The authors note that Life Skills are frequently linked to critical thinking, problem solving, communication, and other personal/social competencies, but that definitions vary substantially across English- and French-language research.

To answer this, the authors conducted a scoping review across five databases (Google Scholar, ERIC, PubMed, ISIDORE, and HAL SHS) and screened peer-reviewed English and French publications focused on health promotion in schools, pupils, and teacher training, provided they included a definition of Life Skills. In total, 55 papers were included (48 English, 7 French), and the authors used NVivo to code terms, purposes, and taxonomies appearing in the conceptual definitions.

The review concludes that there is no consensual conceptual definition of Life Skills. Across the literature, the construct is described using many overlapping terms, is tied to several different purposes at school (e.g., coping with life, success, citizenship, health), and is organized into diverse taxonomies. The authors argue that this polysemic and cross-disciplinary nature helps explain why Life Skills are difficult to define and evaluate, and they call for further epistemological, ontological, and linguistic clarification.

finding.finding_summary: This scoping review does not test an intervention or estimate an effect on critical thinking, metacognition, or other durable skills; instead it synthesizes how Life Skills are defined in school health-promotion literature. The paper identifies critical thinking as one of the skills commonly bundled into Life Skills definitions, but reports no empirical outcome data, effect sizes, or measured student gains.
finding.measure: Conceptual definitions and taxonomies of Life Skills in the literature

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces VLM@school, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on German middle school content. The authors argue that many existing multimodal benchmarks are overly English-centric, often multiple-choice, and too easy or decontextualized to reflect real-world visual reasoning. To address this, they assemble 2,038 open-ended questions grounded in 486 images drawn from school textbooks and related educational materials across nine subjects, with a special emphasis on tasks that require combining image interpretation, subject knowledge, and reasoning.

The study evaluates 13 open-weight VLMs on this benchmark, including InternVL3, Ovis2, Qwen2.5-VL, Gemma 3, Llama 4 Scout, and Mistral Small 3.1. Models are scored using a panel-of-LLMs judging approach because answers are open-ended. The results show that even the best model reaches under 45% overall accuracy, with particularly weak performance in math, music, and adversarial questions that ask about objects or relations not actually present in the image. The authors conclude that middle-school German tasks are challenging for current VLMs and that benchmark performance on popular datasets does not necessarily transfer to this more realistic educational setting.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark included 308 math questions, and the best-performing models reached only about 34% accuracy on math (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL 32B at 34.09%; Mistral Small 3.1 at 29.06%). The paper reports that models were better at straightforward calculation than at counting, geometry, and reading coordinates, indicating limited mathematical reasoning on image-based tasks.
finding.measure: Accuracy on middle-school math questions involving geometry, counting, formulas, and simple calculations

finding.finding_summary: The science-relevant content appears primarily in biology and physics, where models struggled to explain relationships and interpret diagrams. For example, the authors report failures on questions requiring explanation of why yellow main-sequence stars become red giants and on identifying circuit explanations, despite some success with naming diagrams like Hertzsprung-Russell diagrams.
finding.measure: Accuracy and qualitative error patterns on biology and physics questions requiring diagram interpretation and explanation
finding.study_size: n=403 questions total across biology (169) and physics (234)

finding.finding_summary: Across non-math, non-science school subjects, the benchmark showed substantial but uneven performance. Best overall subject scores included history and religion at about 54%, while music was especially difficult with best scores around 31%; the paper also notes problems with art-style recognition, map reading in geography, and sports situation interpretation.
finding.measure: Accuracy on subject-specific VLM questions in arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports
finding.study_size: n=1,127 questions across arts (286), geography (251), history (264), music (166), religion (206), and sports (154)

finding.finding_summary: A central contribution of the paper is to test whether models can handle difficult visual reasoning, including adversarial questions and tasks requiring integration of image evidence with background knowledge. The authors conclude that VLMs often fail to say they do not know, fall for misleading prompts, and perform far worse on adversarial questions than on the full set, suggesting weak critical-thinking-like capability in this setting.
finding.measure: Accuracy on adversarial questions designed to be unanswerable from the image and require rejecting misleading semantic cues
finding.study_size: n=all adversarial questions; domain-level counts not fully reported in the paper text

paper_profiles.title: Developing Critical Thinking in Second Language Learners: Exploring Generative AI like ChatGPT as a tool for Argumentative Essay Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a structured ChatGPT-use guideline can improve second-language learners’ critical thinking and argumentative writing. The authors propose the ChatGPT Guideline for Critical Argumentative Writing (CGCAW), which combines the Paul-Elder Critical Thinking Model with Tan’s framework for argumentative essays and maps those ideas onto ChatGPT-assisted feedback prompts.

The study used a small experiment with 10 university students from a state university, randomly assigned to an experimental group that used the CGCAW prompts and a control group that used ChatGPT without specific guidance. Each participant wrote a short argumentative essay in 40 minutes on the prompt about whether social media is beneficial or harmful, and the essays were scored by Grammarly, ChatGPT, and a course instructor using different criteria. Results were mixed across raters: ChatGPT favored the CGCAW group on clarity, logical coherence, and evidence use, while Grammarly and the instructor rated the control group higher overall. The authors conclude that the framework may support specific critical-thinking-related writing subskills, but it needs refinement and further testing because results were inconsistent and the sample was very small.

finding.finding_summary: The study found mixed effects on argumentative writing quality in a sample of 10 undergraduate L2 learners (n=10). ChatGPT ratings favored the CGCAW group on clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence (experimental mean=74 vs control mean=72.2), but Grammarly (90.6 vs 92.2) and the course instructor (35 vs 56) rated the control group higher overall.
finding.measure: Argumentative essay quality scored by ChatGPT, Grammarly, and course instructor on criteria including clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, persuasiveness, grammar, and thesis quality
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT total SD=7.6 (Group 1) and 5.5 (Group 2); subscale SDs reported for clarity, evidence, and coherence

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly targets critical thinking development through the CGCAW framework, but the outcomes were mixed. The experimental group showed improvements in clarity, logical coherence, and evidence use on ChatGPT scoring, suggesting some gains in reasoning-related writing skills, while the control group performed better on other assessments, indicating the framework was not uniformly effective.
finding.measure: Critical-thinking-related components embedded in argumentative writing, especially clarity, logical coherence, evidence use, and argumentative structure
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT group SD=7.6 vs 5.5 total scores; item-level SDs reported for clarity, evidence, and coherence

finding.finding_summary: The paper briefly reports that the CGCAW framework was intended to support self-regulation and confidence through structured prompts and feedback, but the empirical evidence is limited. Two participants in the experimental group could not finish the task because they were unfamiliar with the framework, and the authors note that prior familiarity and the 40-minute limit affected performance.
finding.measure: Task completion within a 40-minute argumentative writing session; participant ability to complete the essay under the CGCAW framework

paper_profiles.title: When Scaffolding Breaks: Investigating Student Interaction with LLM-Based Writing Support in Real-Time K-12 EFL Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how an LLM-based writing support tool can function as real-time scaffolding in a K-12 English-as-a-Foreign-Language classroom. The authors address a practical gap in prior AI-for-education research: most LLM writing studies have focused on asynchronous or higher-education settings, while real classrooms involve time pressure, mixed proficiency levels, teacher orchestration, and peer interaction.

To study this, the authors designed WriteAid, a chat-based LLM writing support system with separate tabs for sentence construction, vocabulary/grammar explanations, and grammar checking. They deployed it for six weeks in a South Korean middle school with 157 eighth-grade students, analyzed 14,863 interaction messages, qualitatively coded a sampled subset of interactions, and conducted naturalistic classroom observations plus a teacher interview. The study also included a delayed written assessment 2–3 weeks after the classroom writing tasks to examine whether LLM-supported sentences were retained and transferred into independent writing.

The main findings are mixed. WriteAid improved grammatical accuracy during in-class writing, especially for higher-proficiency students, and many generated sentences were later reused in students’ final essays. However, the step-by-step scaffolding often demotivated lower-proficiency students and increased their dependence on the system, especially under time constraints. The tool also altered classroom dynamics: students asked fewer questions of the teacher, a few extroverted students dominated teacher attention, and teachers had more difficulty identifying common student difficulties. The authors conclude that real-time classroom LLMs need proficiency-aware scaffolding, clearer teacher/AI role division, and better teacher-facing monitoring to support equitable learning.

finding.finding_summary: WriteAid improved in-class writing accuracy and supported sentence construction for eighth-grade EFL students (n=157; analyzed consented data n=133). During the fall semester, students produced 632 LLM-assisted sentences, and 309 (48.9%) were copied verbatim into final essays; 82.3% of those reused sentences were grammatically correct. This indicates a positive effect on writing accuracy, although transfer to independent writing varied by proficiency group.
finding.measure: Grammar accuracy of LLM-assisted English sentences; incorporation of those sentences into delayed independent essays; analytic rubric language-use domain
finding.study_size: n=133 consented for analysis; 632 assisted sentences

finding.finding_summary: The intervention had mixed effects on motivation and engagement. Higher-proficiency students used the system efficiently, but lower-proficiency students were often demotivated or frustrated by step-by-step scaffolding; negative affective behaviors (confusion/annoyance) occurred 12.2 times per session for middle-performing students and 11.4 for low-performing students, versus 3.8 for high-performing students. The authors also report increased system reliance among lower-proficiency learners.
finding.measure: Observed affective behaviors during interaction (confusion, annoyance, gratitude, indifference) and engagement patterns in classroom use

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines higher-order task delegation, but the findings are mixed rather than clearly positive. Higher-performing students mostly used the LLM for lower-order tasks like vocabulary translation and validation, while lower-performing students outsourced core sentence-generation work, suggesting the system did not uniformly strengthen critical thinking or independent writing. The authors also note that step-by-step scaffolding could reduce students’ own problem-solving and increase dependence on the system.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of question types and interaction patterns, including vocabulary translation, validation seeking, sentence generation, and revision requests
finding.study_size: 1,386 coded queries from a 9.3% sample of the 14,863 utterances

finding.finding_summary: WriteAid reduced routine teacher burden by handling many simple spelling and grammar questions, giving the teacher more time to circulate and check student progress. In the follow-up interview, the teacher reported having more time to walk around the classroom because they no longer had to answer every simple question, although the tool also made it harder to identify common student difficulties.
finding.measure: Naturalistic classroom observations and teacher interview on question handling and time allocation

finding.finding_summary: At the classroom level, the intervention changed participation patterns and equity dynamics in ways that have institutional relevance. The tool helped more students complete tasks and reduced the gap between top and bottom students in task completion, but it also concentrated teacher attention among a few outspoken students and made it harder for teachers to detect shared difficulties across the class. These effects suggest both potential and risks for classroom governance and equitable instruction.
finding.measure: Classroom observation of participation/teacher attention patterns and teacher interview on equity and monitoring
finding.study_size: 3 observed class sessions; 157 students in deployment

paper_profiles.title: Discussion Tracker: Supporting Teacher Learning about Students’ Collaborative Argumentation in High School Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of helping high school teachers monitor and improve students’ collaborative argumentation during classroom discussions. The authors developed Discussion Tracker (DT), a classroom discussion analytics system that uses NLP classifiers to automatically code student talk along three dimensions: argument moves, specificity, and collaboration.

The system was designed to support teachers by generating visual analytics such as overview charts, annotated transcripts, collaboration maps, and strength/weakness summaries. In this study, DT was evaluated in real classrooms with 18 high school English Language Arts teachers from 4 schools. Teachers used a version of DT on transcripts of their own recorded literature discussions, first with manually coded data to isolate usability effects and then in cognitive interviews and surveys about usefulness.

Results show that teachers generally found the system helpful for understanding student discussion and for reflecting on their facilitation. The paper also reports moderate-to-substantial agreement between the automated classifiers and human annotations for argument move, specificity, and collaboration coding. However, the study does not test student learning outcomes directly; it primarily evaluates teacher usability perceptions and classifier performance, suggesting DT may be a useful support tool for classroom discussion analysis rather than demonstrating causal impact on instruction or students.

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies collaborative argumentation, which aligns with durable skills such as critical thinking and collaboration. In a deployment with 18 high school ELA teachers across 4 schools, teachers reported that DT was helpful for understanding student discussion strengths/weaknesses and for reflecting on facilitation, with mean ratings up to 4.89/5 on annotated transcripts and 4.72/5 overall helpfulness. The paper does not measure student critical-thinking gains directly; the main empirical evidence is teacher usability and perceived value of the discussion analytics.
finding.measure: Teacher usability/perceived helpfulness survey items about collaborative argumentation analytics; NLP coding agreement with human annotations
finding.study_size: n=18 teachers (usability evaluation); 1942 ADUs for argument move/specificity coding; 1467 turns for collaboration coding

paper_profiles.title: Using Transformers to Provide Teachers with Personalized Feedback on their Classroom Discourse: The TalkMoves Application
paper_profiles.population: K-12 mathematics teachers and their classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of giving K-12 mathematics teachers timely, scalable, and personalized feedback on their classroom discourse. The authors focus on “talk moves,” a set of discourse strategies used to support productive mathematical discussion, student participation, and reasoning, and argue that current human observation and transcript-coding approaches are too costly and slow to scale.

The study presents the TalkMoves application, an end-to-end system that ingests classroom video/audio, transcribes speech, classifies teacher utterances into six talk-move categories plus none, and generates teacher-facing feedback dashboards. The core technical contribution is a series of NLP model experiments, with transformer-based models outperforming earlier BiLSTM approaches; the best reported test performance was RoBERTa-Large with F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779 on the talk-move classification task.

The population/context is 21 pilot teachers in two midwestern U.S. school districts who taught grades 3–12 and used the application during the 2019–2020 academic year. Teachers recorded lessons, reviewed automated feedback, and participated in surveys/interviews. The paper concludes that the system can approximate expert human coding with useful reliability and has promise as a scalable tool for teacher professional learning, but it does not report direct student outcome impacts such as achievement or critical-thinking gains.

finding.finding_summary: The TalkMoves system substantially automates a labor-intensive teacher-observation workflow by transcribing lessons, classifying discourse moves, and generating feedback dashboards from classroom recordings. The best model achieved F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779 on the talk-move classification task, indicating the pipeline can support scalable, relatively reliable feedback generation compared with manual transcript coding.
finding.measure: Talk-move classification performance used as a proxy for automated feedback production efficiency and reliability
finding.study_size: n=176,757 sentences from 501 K-12 math lesson transcripts

finding.finding_summary: The paper is substantively about classroom discourse practices that support rigorous thinking, participation, and reasoning, but it does not directly measure student critical thinking or metacognition outcomes. Its closest substantive focus is on enabling teachers to prompt student reasoning through talk moves; however, the empirical results are limited to model performance rather than learner skill gains.
finding.measure: Classification of teacher talk moves associated with rigorous thinking and discourse quality
finding.study_size: n=176,757 sentences from 501 transcripts; 21 pilot teachers used the app
finding.effect_size: F1=79.33% for the best model; no learner effect size reported

paper_profiles.title: Celestial mechanics, from high-school to Newton’s Principia
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper uses a classic high-school physics contest problem about a spacecraft slowing from a circular orbit and entering an ellipse to illustrate how planetary motion can be understood through multiple levels of physics and mathematics. The central question is how much kinetic energy is lost when the orbit changes from circular to elliptical and touches the planet’s surface at the opposite point.

Rather than reporting an intervention study, the paper presents a sequence of ten derivations of the same result, ranging from elementary Kepler-law reasoning to more advanced tools such as conservation laws, the radial equation, Frenet formulas, the Runge-Lenz vector, the hodograph, Maxwell’s geometric method, and Newton’s Principia. The author frames the exercise as suitable for high-school students in its simplest form, while also showing how it connects to university-level mechanics and the history of celestial mechanics.

The main conclusion is that the relative kinetic-energy loss depends only on the geometry of the orbit and equals the numerical eccentricity of the new ellipse, with the given numerical example yielding 1/19. The paper’s educational value is conceptual and expository: it demonstrates how a contest-style problem can stimulate deeper physical insight and show links among geometry, mechanics, and classical astronomy, but it does not test any instructional intervention or measure student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper uses a high-school physics contest problem to illustrate scientific reasoning about orbital motion, showing that the spacecraft’s kinetic-energy loss can be derived from multiple physical principles. The worked example concludes that the relative loss is 1/19 for the given radii, but no student outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual derivation of orbital motion / kinetic-energy loss in a spacecraft landing problem

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly emphasizes imagination, creative thinking, and deeper insight as the goals of the high-school problem, rather than lexical knowledge or routine calculation. It argues that such problems can lead to genuine research, but it does not report any empirical measurement of critical thinking or metacognitive gains.
finding.measure: Reasoning about a contest physics problem; qualitative discussion of imagination/creative thinking

paper_profiles.title: Data Preservation in High-Energy Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a field-wide problem in high-energy physics: how to preserve experimental data, software, documentation, and analysis capabilities after experiments end, so that unique and expensive datasets remain usable for future scientific work. The document is an intermediate report from an international study group convened in 2008 and 2009 to examine the physics case, preservation models, technologies, and governance needed for long-term data preservation in HEP.

The report does not study an educational intervention or classroom AI system. Instead, it proposes a four-level preservation framework ranging from enhanced documentation only to full preservation of reconstruction and simulation software plus basic data. It also discusses the infrastructure, staffing, funding, validation, and governance required to support long-term re-analysis, open access, outreach, and cross-collaboration use of preserved HEP data.

The population is the high-energy physics research community, including experimental collaborations, laboratories, computing centers, and funding agencies. The paper concludes that data preservation is urgent, that higher levels of preservation better support future scientific reuse, and that institutions should create dedicated archival roles and internationally coherent policies to maintain access and scientific value over time.

finding.finding_summary: The report argues that HEP data preservation requires coordinated institutional action across collaborations, laboratories, computing centers, and funding agencies. It recommends an internationally coherent policy, dedicated data archivist roles, and an International Data Preservation Forum to oversee preservation, access, and re-use.
finding.measure: governance/policy recommendations and institutional organization for data preservation

paper_profiles.title: Cosmic rays studied with a hybrid high school detector array
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Cosmic Ray Conference (ICRC)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes a hybrid cosmic-ray detection pathfinder that combines a radio antenna array (LORUN) with a high-school particle detector network (HiSPARC/NAHSA). The central question is whether radio-detection hardware and school-based scintillator detectors can be combined to detect cosmic-ray air showers in coincidence and thereby support both research and education/outreach in high-school settings.

The system used two NAHSA scintillator detector stations and four radio antennae on the roof of the Radboud University Nijmegen building, with triggers generated by coincident particle detections and then matched offline to radio data. The setup was built largely with student participation and was designed as a prototype for extending high-school detector arrays; the paper emphasizes instrumentation, data acquisition, and signal-processing methods rather than an instructional intervention or student learning experiment.

Over the period reported, the authors found three candidate air-shower events between 2005-01-01 and 2005-08-01. These events were consistent with coincident detection by both the particle detectors and the radio antennae, with estimated primary energies above roughly 0.2-0.3 EeV. The main conclusion is that the hybrid approach is technically feasible and could be scaled to support further cosmic-ray research and educational outreach in high schools, but the paper does not report any student achievement, critical-thinking, or other learner-outcome measures.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that a hybrid radio-plus-particle detector array successfully identified three candidate cosmic-ray air-shower events over 2005-01-01 to 2005-08-01, supporting the scientific feasibility of the instrumented approach. These events were matched between HiSPARC/NAHSA and LORUN data and were estimated to have primary energies above 0.2-0.3 EeV, but the paper does not evaluate student scientific reasoning as an outcome.
finding.measure: Coincident cosmic-ray air-shower event detection and estimated primary energy from detector data

paper_profiles.title: Transforming High School Physics with Modeling and Computation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This thesis examines whether adding computational modeling to a ninth-grade Physics First classroom can help transform physics instruction toward authentic scientific practice. The broader problem is that traditional science classes often emphasize content acquisition over the practices of scientists, such as modeling, computation, and critical thinking. The author situates the work within the NRC Framework for K-12 Science Education, Modeling Instruction (MI), and prior physics education research to argue that computation should be integrated into high school physics.

The intervention was a set of scaffolded VPython/PhysUtil computational activities added to a Modeling Instruction physics course at a private co-educational K-12 day school in Georgia. Students used laptops to build and run computational models of force-and-motion topics, including constant velocity, constant acceleration, balanced forces, and unbalanced forces, following in-class experiments and problem-solving sessions. The thesis reports on several forms of evidence: a proctored programming assignment, written essay responses about how the iterative computational loop connects to physical models, think-aloud interviews, and survey information about students’ prior programming experience.

The main conclusion is that ninth-grade students with little prior programming experience were able to learn to use computation to model physics phenomena, and that the computational curriculum helped them connect scientific practice to the classroom. The work suggests that students' success depended not only on producing code that ran, but also on demonstrating conceptual understanding of how the code represented physical systems. The thesis is best read as an early-stage pilot study rather than a causal efficacy trial, and it emphasizes feasibility, student reasoning, and implementation issues rather than estimating a precise treatment effect.

finding.finding_summary: The thesis reports that ninth-grade students were able to use computational modeling to represent and reason about force-and-motion phenomena in physics. Evidence came from a proctored VPython programming task, essays, and think-aloud interviews; the author concludes that computation helped students connect scientific practice to mechanics and demonstrate understanding of the iterative model-update loop. Specific effect sizes were not reported.
finding.measure: VPython proctored programming assignment; written essay on iterative computational loop; think-aloud interviews
finding.study_size: n=36 (survey); n=32 (essay); proctored assignment sample size not explicitly reported in the excerpt, but within the same 36-student cohort

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines computational thinking and related critical-thinking processes, especially whether students could move beyond memorizing code to explain how a computational model corresponded to the underlying physics. Students were asked to describe how their code connected to the physical model through the iterative loop, and the author frames successful performance as evidence of deeper understanding rather than syntax alone. No effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Essay responses about computational thinking and model-physics connections; code analysis

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Three Pivotal Concepts in K-12 Science State Standards and Maps of Conceptual Growth to Research in Physics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks which physics concepts are most central to K-12 science standards, foundational for later learning, and especially difficult for students to learn. The authors analyze concept maps from Project 2061 and state science standards from four U.S. states (California, Colorado, Rhode Island, and Wisconsin), then connect those standards to prior research on student misconceptions and instructional approaches in physics.

The paper identifies three concepts that meet all three criteria: Newton’s laws, conservation of energy, and geometrical optics. It argues that these ideas appear prominently across standards, support many other science ideas, and are persistent sources of student difficulty. The article then reviews research on common misconceptions and discusses instructional strategies that have shown some success, such as prediction-based demonstrations, interactive lecture demonstrations, and research-based explorations.

Although the paper is not an intervention study and does not test AI-personalized feedback, it provides a conceptual framework for prioritizing topics in K-12 physics instruction and professional development. Its main contribution is synthesis: it explains why these physics ideas matter, how state standards treat them, and why students struggle with them across grade levels.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Newton’s laws, conservation of energy, and geometrical optics are foundational scientific concepts that support broader reasoning across the K-12 science curriculum. However, the paper is a conceptual synthesis rather than an intervention study, so it does not report a single causal effect size; instead it compiles evidence that these concepts are central but difficult for students to learn and apply.
finding.measure: State science standards analysis; synthesis of prior physics education research on misconceptions and conceptual understanding

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that students often fail to transfer deep principles to new situations, rely on surface features, and struggle with conceptual reasoning even after instruction. These difficulties are presented as persistent challenges in reasoning and problem-solving, but the paper does not provide a direct estimate of improvement from an intervention.
finding.measure: Students’ ability to recognize and apply conservation of energy / Newtonian reasoning across contexts

paper_profiles.title: Breakable Machine: A K–12 Classroom Game for Transformative AI Literacy Through Spoofing and eXplainable AI (XAI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents Breakable Machine, a classroom game designed to teach K–12 students critical and transformative AI literacy through adversarial play with an image classifier. The authors frame the activity as a way to help learners understand that AI systems are brittle, biased, and vulnerable to spoofing, and to use these failures as opportunities for inquiry rather than as mere technical glitches.

The resource is a browser-based game for students aged 10–15, intended for use in grade 4–9 classrooms. Students use a camera-equipped device to manipulate their appearance or surroundings so that a classifier produces a high-confidence misclassification for a chosen label; they can also inspect class activation maps (CAMs) and training data through an XAI view to reason about why the model responds as it does. A teacher dashboard supports whole-class coordination, shared leaderboards, and collective sensemaking.

This paper is explicitly non-empirical: it describes the game’s design, pedagogical rationale, interface, privacy features, and intended learning outcomes, but does not report learning outcome data. The main conclusion is that spoofing and explainability can be combined into a pedagogically rich AI-literacy activity that supports critical thinking, ethical reflection, data agency, and a more critical stance toward AI as a sociotechnical system. The authors note that empirical evaluation of learning outcomes is planned for future work.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is a design/resource paper and does not report empirical evidence of gains in critical thinking, metacognition, collaboration, or other durable skills. It argues that the game is intended to support critical inquiry and collective sensemaking, but these outcomes are described as learning goals rather than measured results.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The authors describe the game as potentially fostering engagement, inquiry, and agency through playful adversarial activity, but they do not present data measuring motivation, engagement, persistence, or self-regulation. No empirical effect on social-emotional outcomes is reported in the paper.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Identification of Books That are Suitable for Middle School Students Using Artificial Neural Networks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of identifying books that are suitable for middle school students without relying solely on subjective human judgment. The authors argue that book selection for school curricula and reading lists is time-consuming and can be biased, especially when reviewers or evaluators rely on personal opinions rather than the text itself.

To solve this, the paper proposes a natural-language-processing pipeline combined with an artificial neural network (ANN). The authors built a unique dataset of 416 books, labeled as suitable or unsuitable for middle school students, using sources such as Turkish Ministry of National Education-approved books, Oxford and Cambridge library books, Gutenberg Project texts, and books with R-ratings or Amazon age ratings. They extracted 14 features from each book, including positive/negative sentence and word counts, ratios, words per sentence, vocabulary-level ratios, and a custom coefficient of positivity derived from VADER sentiment analysis plus a manually created bad-words list.

The ANN was trained on these features to classify books as suitable or unsuitable. The paper reports that the model achieved 90.06% consistency on a test set of 83 books, with 91.2% accuracy for appropriate books and 80.7% for inappropriate books. The authors conclude that the system may help schools, teachers, parents, and education officials screen books more efficiently and objectively, though they also note limitations such as the small dataset and difficulty handling academically complex but age-appropriate texts.

finding.finding_summary: The ANN-based screening tool was designed to speed up and standardize the process of selecting books suitable for middle school students. Using a dataset of 416 books and 14 text-based features, the model reportedly achieved 90.06% consistency on 83 test books, suggesting the approach can reduce the time needed for preliminary book evaluation and curriculum screening.
finding.measure: Book suitability classification accuracy / consistency of ANN model

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly frames the model as a tool for Ministry of National Education officials, schools, teachers, parents, and students to support institutional book-selection decisions. The authors argue that the software could serve as a screening system for curriculum inclusion and potentially reduce personal and societal bias in evaluation processes.
finding.measure: Proposed institutional use of ANN screening system for curriculum/book selection

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how elementary school students and teachers perceived a generative AI-powered tool for creative mathematical writing. The authors were interested in both the educational benefits and the challenges of using GenAI to support students in understanding math problems, expressing mathematical ideas through stories, and revising AI-generated content.

The intervention involved a classroom implementation of a GenAI-supported learning platform built with GPT-4 and DALL·E 3. Across six classrooms in two U.S. elementary schools, 79 fifth-grade students and six teachers used a three-step process called Ask, Represent, and Transform. Students first analyzed a math story, then represented their understanding visually, and finally collaborated with GenAI to draft and revise culturally relevant math stories. The study used interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observation notes, analyzed through mixed inductive/deductive thematic analysis.

Findings suggest that students and teachers saw multiple benefits from the activity, including greater creativity in math, improved mathematical understanding, increased AI literacy, and stronger interest, curiosity, and ownership of learning. At the same time, they identified important challenges: students sometimes did not critically evaluate AI outputs, struggled to generate coherent stories, wanted more room to improve or work independently, and lacked social and communicative features in the system. The paper concludes that GenAI can support creative mathematical writing and related learning processes, but only when the technology and instruction are designed to preserve opportunities for critical thinking, feedback, autonomy, and social interaction.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers reported that the GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing activities helped students understand math problems, represent mathematical ideas, and uncover misconceptions. The paper’s qualitative evidence suggests the Ask, Represent, and Transform sequence supported mathematical understanding and problem solving, but no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Interview themes on mathematical understanding, mathematical knowledge representation, and misconception identification
finding.study_size: n=79 students; 6 teachers (with 10 students interviewed in focus groups)

finding.finding_summary: Participants described increased interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership in math learning when using the GenAI-supported story-writing tool. Students said the activity made math more fun and motivating, and teachers observed greater engagement and attention, but the study did not report quantitative outcome measures or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Interview themes on interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning
finding.study_size: n=79 students; 6 teachers (10 student focus-group interviewees)
