finding.finding_summary: The study reports gains in creativity-related thinking and AI literacy, including divergent and convergent thinking, originality, flexible thinking, and prompt engineering. However, it also found challenges in critical evaluation of AI outputs and story generation competence, so the durable-skills picture is mixed rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Interview themes on creativity, prompt engineering, critical evaluation of AI-generated content, and AI literacy
finding.study_size: n=79 students; 6 teachers (10 student focus-group interviewees)

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic review examines how artificial intelligence applications were being studied in higher education from 2007 to 2018, with a particular focus on where the research was coming from, how AI was being conceptualized, and what kinds of applications were represented. The authors screened 2,656 records and included 146 peer-reviewed journal articles for synthesis. They coded publication patterns, disciplinary affiliations, countries, research methods, ethical reflection, and AI application areas across the student life cycle.

The review finds that most publications came from computer science and STEM researchers, with very limited involvement from educators, and that the evidence base was dominated by quantitative studies. The four main application areas were profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems/personalisation. Across these areas, the reviewed studies generally reported positive or promising technical performance—such as accurate prediction, automated grading, and adaptive feedback—but the review notes that long-term educational evidence is limited and that critical reflection on ethics, privacy, and costs is rare.

The paper is not an intervention study of a single AI tool, but rather a synthesis of higher-education AI research. Its main conclusion is that AI in education research was growing rapidly, yet was weakly connected to pedagogy and underrepresented by educators. The authors argue for more theoretically grounded, ethically informed, and educator-driven research, especially around the educational use and consequences of AI systems.

finding.finding_summary: Across the review, AI applications in higher education generally showed promising technical performance for academic tasks such as admission prediction, course selection, grading, and content delivery, but the evidence was mostly short-term and often limited to pilot studies. The review included 146 studies and reports that many systems achieved high classification or agreement accuracy, but the authors caution that educational effectiveness and long-term learning impact were rarely established.
finding.measure: Prediction accuracy, grading agreement, and short-term learning-performance outcomes across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies used AI to model or respond to student engagement, motivation, and related learning behaviors, including systems that predicted student engagement or academic motivation from learning-platform data. The review suggests these applications can help identify low-engaged students and support intervention, but it does not report a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Student engagement and academic motivation outcomes inferred from VLE/LMS behavioral data

finding.finding_summary: The review includes AI-supported feedback and tutoring systems intended to support higher-order learning processes such as self-regulation, collaboration, and problem solving. Evidence was generally positive at the study level, but the authors note that these systems were usually evaluated over short periods and that one collaborative-learning study reported negative results relative to the control condition.
finding.measure: Self-regulation, collaboration, problem-solving, and related learning-process outcomes reported in ITS/adaptive-system studies

finding.finding_summary: A major theme in the review was that AI can automate or streamline educational and administrative work, including automated grading, feedback generation, student advising, course scheduling, and lecturer-performance evaluation. The reviewed studies generally reported high accuracy and efficiency, and the authors explicitly note that these tools could reduce workload for staff and scale to large enrollments.
finding.measure: Task automation, grading efficiency, workload reduction, and administrative decision-support performance

finding.finding_summary: The review found substantial use of AI for institutional and administrative purposes such as admissions prediction, retention modeling, course management, career services, and alignment of student credentials with industry needs. These applications were often framed as decision-support tools for universities and managers, though the authors emphasize that ethical, governance, and privacy concerns were rarely addressed in the literature.
finding.measure: Institutional decision-support and administrative prediction tasks

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: All levels of education (primary, secondary, tertiary, professional development); not an empirical K-12 sample
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper surveys the emerging opportunities and risks of large language models, especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than testing an intervention, it synthesizes early applications and argues that these systems could support content creation, personalized learning, assessment, tutoring, and feedback while also raising concerns about bias, privacy, plagiarism, overreliance, and inequitable access.

The paper discusses potential uses for learners and teachers across elementary school, middle/high school, university, and professional development contexts. For students, it highlights uses such as generating quizzes, explanations, summaries, prompts, and feedback; for teachers, it emphasizes lesson planning, adaptive feedback, grading support, and content generation. It also frames key challenges and mitigation strategies, especially the need for human oversight, fact-checking, and critical thinking instruction.

Because this is a conceptual position paper, it does not report original empirical data or a classroom intervention study. Its main contribution is a structured argument about how LLMs might be integrated responsibly into education and what governance, pedagogical, and ethical safeguards are needed before broad adoption.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models could support critical thinking, problem-solving, and fact-checking by generating prompts, explanations, and alternative perspectives, but it also warns that easy access to model-generated answers may weaken students’ independent reasoning if used uncritically. No empirical effect size is reported because this is a position paper rather than an intervention study.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, and fact-checking as conceptual educational outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly claims that LLMs could save teachers time by semi-automating feedback, grading, lesson planning, and the generation of quizzes, prompts, and learning materials. These are proposed benefits only; the paper does not present empirical measurements of workload reduction or productivity gains.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, and content-generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLMs may improve engagement and participation, for example by providing personalized guidance, discussion structure, and interactive prompts. However, these claims are conceptual and not based on direct outcome measurement in a study sample.
finding.measure: Student engagement and participation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can support reading and writing development through grammar and style corrections, summaries, explanations of complex texts, and writing assistance. It does not report original literacy outcome data; the discussion is aspirational and based on potential use cases across elementary through higher education.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension, writing quality, grammar, and writing style

paper_profiles.title: The cognitive paradox of AI in education: between enhancement and erosion
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This opinion paper argues that AI in education has a paradoxical role: it can enhance learning through personalization and efficiency, but it may also erode cognition by encouraging dependency and cognitive offloading. The authors frame the discussion using Cognitive Load Theory, Bloom’s Taxonomy, and Self-Determination Theory to examine how AI tools may influence retention, critical thinking, creativity, motivation, and deeper learning.

Rather than reporting a new empirical study, the article synthesizes prior literature and examples across educational contexts, including adaptive learning systems, chatbots, intelligent tutoring systems, and generative AI tools such as ChatGPT. The paper emphasizes that AI can support lower-order learning and accessibility, but overuse may weaken engagement, autonomy, and higher-order thinking if students passively accept AI-generated responses.

The paper concludes that AI should complement, not replace, human instruction. It recommends using AI in ways that preserve active cognition, including reflection prompts, AI-free practice, teacher-guided discussion, and balanced implementation in blended learning. The article also highlights the need for fairness, transparency, and ongoing monitoring when integrating AI into education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can support some elements of durable skills, especially problem-solving and higher-order thinking when used as a scaffold, but it may also erode independent critical thinking through cognitive offloading and passive reliance on AI-generated answers. No original effect size is reported because this is an opinion/synthesis paper rather than an empirical study.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, and higher-order thinking as discussed across cited studies

finding.finding_summary: The article claims that AI may improve competence through personalized learning but can reduce autonomy, intrinsic motivation, and relatedness if students become dependent on AI. It discusses motivation and engagement as theoretical concerns rather than reporting direct new measurement results.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, autonomy, and relatedness

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses AI’s effects on general learning outcomes such as retention, conceptual understanding, and creativity across STEM and language-learning examples. It cites prior studies suggesting improved performance on some procedural tasks and standardized tests, but weaker conceptual understanding and long-term retention with overreliance on AI.
finding.measure: Learning retention, conceptual understanding, creative thinking, and standardized test performance (as cited from prior studies)

paper_profiles.title: Online University Teaching During and After the Covid-19 Crisis: Refocusing Teacher Presence and Learning Activity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the sudden shift to online teaching during the Covid-19 crisis and asks what pedagogical knowledge non-expert university teachers need to design and deliver effective online learning. Rather than testing an intervention, the authors use expert interviews to synthesize practical guidance about online course design, communication, interaction, monitoring, and assessment.

The paper focuses on higher education instructors and online learning experts in Switzerland, Australia, Spain, and Canada, all of whom have long experience with online and distance education. Through five interview questions, the authors explore how online learning differs from face-to-face teaching, what makes online teaching successful, how to move beyond materials-based or tools-based approaches, and how to monitor engagement and learning in online courses.

The main conclusions emphasize that effective online teaching depends on careful learning design, student-centered activities, clear communication, and a blended conception of teacher presence that includes cognitive, social, and facilitatory dimensions. The authors also argue for continuous assessment, learner self-regulation, and the use of feedback, analytics, and portfolios to support learning. Because the paper is based on expert opinion and not empirical testing, it offers conceptual and practical guidance rather than evidence of measured student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that online teaching can improve instructional efficiency when teachers shift effort upstream into careful planning, chunking content, clarifying tasks, and using communication channels and analytics to monitor progress. No effect size or experimental estimate is reported because the article is an expert interview/synthesis rather than an outcome study.
finding.measure: Expert-reported guidance on planning, monitoring, and assessment practices in online teaching

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes learner autonomy, self-regulation, reduced anxiety, and engagement as central to successful online learning. Experts recommend clear expectations, pacing, and support to help students manage time and stay engaged, but no quantitative student data are reported.
finding.measure: Expert-reported discussion of autonomy, self-regulation, engagement, and anxiety in online learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively discusses collaboration, self-regulation, metacognition, and time management as key competencies in online courses. Experts describe peer collaboration, student co-design, reflection, and self-paced work as beneficial, but the paper does not measure these skills empirically.
finding.measure: Expert-reported discussion of collaboration, self-regulation, metacognition, and time management

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that institutions must support online teaching through infrastructure, assessment redesign, faculty development, and flexible policy responses. It presents online learning as an opportunity to improve institutional readiness and inclusiveness, but does not provide measured institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Expert-reported implications for institutional support, assessment policy, and digital infrastructure

paper_profiles.title: Ethical use of ChatGPT in education—Best practices to combat AI-induced plagiarism
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an opinion piece about the ethical risks of ChatGPT in education, especially AI-assisted plagiarism, and the need for institutional responses. It argues that generative AI can support personalized learning, immediate feedback, engagement, and creativity, but that its misuse can undermine academic integrity, distort assessment, and make student work harder to authenticate.

Rather than presenting an empirical study, the paper synthesizes prior literature and proposes best practices for reducing AI-induced plagiarism. Recommended responses include clear AI-use policies, improved plagiarism and AI-detection tools, adaptive and personalized assessments, oral exams, peer review, reflective writing, and multimodal tasks that are harder to outsource to AI.

The discussion is framed mainly for higher education and institutional educators, with some relevance to broader schooling contexts. The paper concludes that effective AI governance requires combining technological detection with pedagogical redesign and ethics education, while remaining alert to privacy, bias, false accusations, and the need for ongoing updates as AI systems evolve.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-detection tools, adaptive testing, learning analytics, oral exams, and continual monitoring may improve the efficiency of plagiarism detection and assessment management, but it also notes substantial implementation burdens. These include higher costs, privacy/data-security concerns, false positives, and increased teacher time for manual review and redesign of assessments.
finding.measure: reported considerations of plagiarism detection, adaptive testing, monitoring, and teacher workload

finding.finding_summary: The paper strongly emphasizes institutional strategies to address AI-induced plagiarism, including explicit AI-use policies, academic integrity campaigns, AI-recognition technologies, and curriculum redesign. Its claims are based on cited prior studies and policy-oriented argument rather than original data, but the central conclusion is that coordinated institutional action can reduce misuse and support ethical AI adoption.
finding.measure: institutional policy recommendations and synthesis of prior evidence on integrity interventions

finding.finding_summary: The article claims that personalized, reflective, oral, and critical-thinking-oriented assessments can foster deeper learning, originality, and critical thinking while reducing reliance on AI-generated text. However, it does not present direct outcome data from K-12 students; the support is conceptual and drawn from prior studies and examples.
finding.measure: critical thinking, originality, reflective learning, and problem-solving in assessment design

paper_profiles.title: Scaffolding in Teacher–Student Interaction: A Decade of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines a decade of research on scaffolding in teacher–student interaction, with a focus on how scaffolding is conceptualized, what forms it takes in classroom practice, and whether it is effective. The authors argue that scaffolding is commonly discussed too broadly and propose that it should be understood as an interactive process characterized by three core features: contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility.

The review synthesizes 66 English-language articles published from 1998 to 2009, most of which are descriptive and centered on literacy, with additional work in math and science. The authors also develop an analytical framework that distinguishes scaffolding intentions (metacognitive, cognitive, affective) from scaffolding means (e.g., questioning, modeling, hints, explaining, feedback) to better organize the literature and future studies.

Across the small set of effectiveness studies, the review concludes that scaffolding generally appears beneficial for student metacognitive and cognitive outcomes, and may also support student affect in some contexts. However, the authors emphasize that the evidence base is limited, often small-scale, and methodologically uneven, and that the major challenge for future work is developing valid ways to measure scaffolding as a dynamic interaction rather than a static teacher behavior.

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies literacy as the most common domain in the scaffolding literature, but the evidence is largely descriptive rather than experimental. Multiple classroom studies are summarized as showing that scaffolding in literacy lessons can support comprehension, conceptual understanding, and strategy use, though the review does not report a single pooled effect size for literacy outcomes.
finding.measure: Literacy outcomes such as text comprehension, conceptual understanding, strategy use, and classroom literacy performance

finding.finding_summary: Several effectiveness studies in mathematics showed benefits of contingent scaffolding. For example, in one-to-one long-division tutoring, students receiving contingent support solved significantly more problems than peers in other conditions (n=40 in the key comparison groups; 4 long-division problems), and another study of fifth and sixth grade mathematics classes found that teacher scaffolding of involvement was associated with higher student engagement.
finding.measure: Math problem-solving performance and mathematics involvement/engagement
finding.study_size: varies across included studies; not_reported for the review overall

finding.finding_summary: The review includes science studies showing positive effects of scaffolding on reasoning and conceptual learning. In one science-class intervention, students in the experimental condition were better able to use talk for reasoning and made greater gains on non-verbal reasoning measures than controls (N=109 vs. N=121), and other science studies are described as showing improved mental model construction and knowledge gains with scaffolding.
finding.measure: Scientific reasoning, conceptual change, and science knowledge/mental models
finding.study_size: varies across included studies; e.g., N=109 and N=121 in one study

finding.finding_summary: The review finds evidence that scaffolding can support student affect, motivation, and involvement, although this evidence is thinner than for cognitive outcomes. In one correlational study of 42 fifth- and sixth-grade students across 34 mathematics lessons, classes with higher involvement showed more intrinsic support strategies and transfer of responsibility; in another quasi-experimental study, students in no-support conditions reported lower enjoyment than those receiving scaffolding.
finding.measure: Student involvement, motivation, enjoyment, and affect
finding.study_size: n=42 in the correlational study; additional quasi-experimental study with small groups (N=8 per condition)

finding.finding_summary: A central conclusion of the review is that scaffolding supports metacognitive and cognitive processes that are closely aligned with durable skills such as reasoning, self-regulation, and transfer. The review summarizes multiple studies in which scaffolding improved students’ reasoning together, self-regulated learning behaviors, transfer of responsibility, and performance on transfer questions, although no single overall effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Metacognitive activity, self-regulated learning, reasoning, transfer, and responsibility for learning
finding.study_size: varies across studies; examples include N=109, N=38, N=41, N=20

finding.finding_summary: The review does not focus on operational efficiency as a primary outcome, but it does discuss measurement and implementation fidelity issues, including the need for manipulation checks and coding of tutor behavior to verify whether scaffolding was actually delivered. This is more a methodological consideration than an outcome result, so substantive evidence for efficiency effects is limited.
finding.measure: Intervention fidelity and coding of teacher/tutor behavior

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education from 2016 to 2022. Its purpose is to map the state of the field, identify where and how AIEd studies were conducted, and synthesize the main ways AI was being used in higher education settings.

Using PRISMA procedures, the authors screened 371 records and included 138 peer-reviewed journal articles. They coded studies for geography, author affiliation, academic level, subject domain, intended user, and AI use category. The review found a sharp increase in publications in 2021 and 2022, a shift in publication leadership from the US to China, and that most studies focused on undergraduate students, especially in language learning, computer science, and engineering.

For AI use, the review identified five major categories: assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistant, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. The paper highlights that AI is most often used for student support, prediction of academic outcomes, automated assessment, personalized feedback, and learning analytics. It concludes that the field is growing quickly but still has gaps, especially in graduate-level work, studies in low-income countries, and research on more novel uses of AI beyond efficiency and automation.

finding.finding_summary: The review found that AI was frequently used in language learning contexts, especially for writing, reading, and vocabulary acquisition. Across the 138 studies, language learning was the most common subject domain (17%), and several studies used AI for automated feedback and assessment of writing, including personalized feedback systems and automatic grading. Because the paper synthesizes multiple studies rather than reporting a single effect estimate, no pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Language learning applications, including writing, reading, vocabulary acquisition, and automated writing feedback/assessment
finding.study_size: n=138 studies in the review; language learning was 17% of studies

finding.finding_summary: The review found that AI was widely used across non-language academic domains, particularly computer science (16%) and engineering (12%). These studies included uses such as automated assessment, intelligent tutoring, and AI-supported laboratory/discipline-specific learning. The review does not report a single pooled effect size or standardized comparison across these subject areas.
finding.measure: Disciplinary applications in computer science and engineering, including tutoring, assessment, and domain-specific learning support

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies used AI to support student motivation, persistence, self-testing, and emotional or affective aspects of learning. For example, the review notes AI systems that provided diagnostic questions, goal support, and feedback intended to encourage persistence, as well as studies evaluating affect in assessment contexts. The evidence is descriptive and synthesized from included studies, so the review does not report a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Student persistence, self-testing opportunities, engagement, and affective responses in AI-supported learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that some AI applications were used to evaluate or support higher-order thinking, reflective activity, and personalized guidance that could support metacognition and critical thinking. One cited use of AI in the assessment/evaluation category included evaluating reflections, achievement goals, community identity, and higher-order thinking. The review is not a direct outcome study of critical thinking, so no effect size is available.
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking, reflections, and related metacognitive/reflective activities

finding.finding_summary: A major finding was that AI was commonly used to increase efficiency in assessment, prediction, and student management. The review describes automatic assessment, question generation, learning analytics, and curriculum sequencing as ways AI reduced instructor workload and helped manage large student datasets; for example, automatic grading reduced the time needed for instructors to grade. The review is qualitative/synthesized and does not provide pooled quantitative effects.
finding.measure: Instructor workload reduction, automated assessment, question generation, learning analytics, curriculum sequencing, and student data management

finding.finding_summary: The review found that AI was used at the institutional level for student management, admissions prediction, learning analytics, and quality assurance-related instructional design. These applications were described as supporting administrators and organizational tasks, such as tracking enrollment and analyzing large-scale student data for actionable insight. No quantitative institutional impact estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Admissions prediction, enrollment tracking, learning analytics, instructional design, and student data management

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the impact of artificial intelligence on teaching and learning in higher education
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emergence of artificial intelligence in higher education and asks how AI may change teaching, learning, student support, assessment, and institutional governance. Rather than testing a specific AI intervention, the authors provide a conceptual and literature-based analysis of the promises and limits of AI, including teacherbots, machine learning, personalized feedback, and brain-computer interfaces.

The paper argues that AI is already shaping higher education through automated support systems, personalized assistance, and data-driven tools, but it is not yet capable of replacing teachers or the broader human purposes of education. It emphasizes risks such as loss of transparency, bias, corporate control, workforce displacement, and a reduction of education to automation and efficiency. The authors conclude that universities should approach AI critically, preserve human-centered pedagogy, and further research the ethical and pedagogical implications of AI in teaching and learning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI systems can improve operational efficiency by automating routine teaching and administrative tasks, including student advice, content delivery, basic feedback, supervision, and support. Examples such as IBM Watson and the Jill Watson teacherbot are presented as evidence that AI can provide scalable, bespoke assistance and reduce staff workload, but no original empirical effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on institutional implications of AI for higher education, including workforce displacement, governance, privacy, transparency, and the role of universities in a technology-driven ecosystem. It argues that AI may restructure university administration and teaching labor, but also warns that corporate control and algorithmic opacity could undermine institutional autonomy and academic values. No original empirical study or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: A Systematic Assessment of OpenAI o1-Preview for Higher Order Thinking in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether OpenAI o1-preview can perform higher-order thinking tasks at or above human levels in education-relevant contexts. The authors evaluate the model across 14 cognitive domains, including critical thinking, systems thinking, computational thinking, design thinking, metacognition, data literacy, creative thinking, abstract reasoning, quantitative reasoning, logical reasoning, analogical reasoning, scientific reasoning, spatial reasoning, and collaborative thinking.

The study uses a broad set of established instruments and datasets, typically adapted into zero-shot or one-shot text prompts. Examples include the Ennis-Weir Critical Thinking Essay Test, biological systems thinking tests, the Village of Abeesee, the Lake Urmia vignette, Bebras problems, algorithmic thinking tests, and other benchmark tasks. The paper is not an intervention study with students; rather, it is a benchmark-style evaluation of an AI model against published human performance on those instruments.

Across domains, the authors report mixed results. o1-preview performs very strongly on several tasks, often exceeding reported human benchmarks in systems thinking, computational thinking, creative thinking, and scientific reasoning, while showing somewhat weaker performance on critical thinking, quantitative reasoning, logical reasoning, and abstract reasoning. The authors conclude that o1-preview has substantial promise for education-related reasoning tasks, but also important limitations, reinforcing the need for human oversight and careful curriculum design if such systems are used to support learning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally evaluates durable skills, especially critical thinking, systems thinking, computational thinking, design thinking, metacognition, creative thinking, abstract reasoning, logical reasoning, and analogical reasoning. On the Ennis-Weir Critical Thinking Essay Test, o1-preview scored a mean of 2.25/3 per paragraph (81.25% scaled), with SD=0.43, slightly below reported human posttest benchmarks in some comparisons but above many pretest human scores. Across other durable-skill benchmarks, the model often outperformed humans in systems/computational/creative reasoning but underperformed in abstract and some quantitative reasoning tasks.
finding.measure: Multiple higher-order thinking assessments, including Ennis-Weir Critical Thinking Essay Test and several systems/computational/creative reasoning benchmarks

finding.finding_summary: The paper assesses quantitative reasoning as one of its core domains, using benchmark items to compare o1-preview with human performance. The authors report that o1-preview performed below human expert benchmarks by roughly 15-20% on the FINAQ dataset, indicating a relative weakness compared with its stronger performance in other reasoning areas.
finding.measure: Quantitative reasoning benchmark performance (including FINAQ dataset)

finding.finding_summary: Scientific reasoning is a major focus of the study and is one of the areas where o1-preview is reported to outperform human benchmarks. The abstract states that o1-preview significantly outperformed humans by about 150% in scientific reasoning, and the paper frames this as evidence of strong scientific problem-solving capability.
finding.measure: Scientific reasoning tasks/benchmark performance

paper_profiles.title: Exploring LLM-Generated Feedback for Economics Essays: How Teaching Assistants Evaluate and Envision Its Use
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether AI-generated feedback can be used as suggestions to speed up and improve human instructors’ feedback on student writing, even when the AI feedback is imperfect. The authors focus on a college introductory economics course with frequent short essay assignments that are graded against detailed rubrics, and they build an LLM-powered feedback pipeline that first identifies relevant evidence in the essay, then makes a rubric-based judgment, and then generates feedback aligned to instructor expectations.

The study was conducted in Fall 2024 in ECON101 with 5 teaching assistants across 20 one-hour think-aloud sessions. After grading essays as usual, TAs reviewed AI-generated feedback embedded as in-text comments in Word, compared it with their own handwritten feedback, and discussed how they might use AI suggestions in their workflow. The paper reports that TAs found AI feedback more detailed, more rubric-aligned, and often more personalized than their own comments, especially because it included praise, explanations, and guiding questions.

At the same time, the study shows important limitations: AI could be overly rigid, miss holistic considerations, and make mistakes when rubrics were underspecified or when students expressed ideas in alternative ways. TAs emphasized that AI output should not replace human judgment, but could help them save time, improve consistency, and standardize grading if paired with highlights and intermediate outputs that made the AI reasoning easier to inspect. The authors conclude that detailed rubrics and transparent, decomposed AI assistance are key for using LLMs productively in feedback workflows.

finding.finding_summary: TAs reported that AI-generated feedback and sentence highlights could expedite grading, speed up reading, and reduce time spent constructing individualized comments. Across 5 TAs and 20 think-aloud sessions, participants said the system would help them identify key ideas faster and save time writing feedback, especially for guiding questions and positive comments.
finding.measure: TA think-aloud reports and qualitative judgments about grading speed, reading speed, and comment-writing time

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines how AI-generated feedback may support critical thinking and metacognitive evaluation in grading workflows, but only from the TA perspective rather than student outcomes. TAs used the AI feedback as a second opinion, compared it against their own judgments, and reflected on rubric interpretation and feedback quality, suggesting the tool could support more careful evaluation and self-monitoring during grading.
finding.measure: TA reflections on rubric interpretation, judgment verification, and comparison of AI vs. human feedback

paper_profiles.title: Using Transformers to Provide Teachers with Personalized Feedback on their Classroom Discourse: The TalkMoves Application
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers in mathematics classrooms (grades 3-12 in pilot use; model trained on K-12 math lesson transcripts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of giving K-12 mathematics teachers timely, individualized feedback on their classroom discourse without requiring labor-intensive human transcript coding. The authors focus on “talk moves” from the Accountable Talk framework—teacher discourse strategies intended to broaden student participation, strengthen mathematical reasoning, and support productive classroom discussion.

The study presents TalkMoves, an end-to-end system that uses automated speech recognition and transformer-based natural language processing to detect talk moves in classroom transcripts and generate teacher feedback dashboards. The core modeling task is a 7-way sentence classification problem over six talk-move categories plus a none label, trained on 501 K-12 math lesson transcripts comprising 176,757 sentences. The best model, RoBERTa-Large, achieved F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779 on the test set, substantially improving over a prior baseline (F1 = 65%).

Beyond model development, the paper describes the feedback interface and a pilot deployment with 21 teachers across two Midwestern U.S. school districts during the 2019-2020 academic year. Teachers reviewed automated feedback and participated in surveys and interviews, but the paper does not report student learning outcomes or an experimental evaluation of the feedback’s impact. The main conclusion is that modern transformer models can approximate expert coding of classroom discourse sufficiently well to support scalable, personalized teacher feedback, though technical challenges remain, especially noisy child speech recognition and class imbalance in talk-move labels.

finding.finding_summary: The TalkMoves system substantially automates the labor-intensive process of coding classroom discourse for accountable talk moves, reducing reliance on trained human observers. On the classification task using 501 transcripts (176,757 sentences), the best model (RoBERTa-Large) reached F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779, indicating it can provide scalable feedback generation for teachers more efficiently than manual coding.
finding.measure: Talk-move classification performance used to automate feedback generation; F1 and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC)

finding.finding_summary: The system is explicitly designed to support classroom discourse practices associated with students' reasoning, explanation, and participation, but the paper evaluates only detection of teacher talk moves rather than direct student critical-thinking outcomes. The relevant measured outcome is model accuracy for identifying talk moves such as press for reasoning, revoicing, and getting students to relate, with the best model achieving F1 = 79.33% across six labels.
finding.measure: Classification of accountable talk moves related to reasoning, explanation, and discourse quality

paper_profiles.title: Common Problems and Effects of Feedback on Fun When Programming Ozobots in Primary School
paper_profiles.venue: WiPSCE ’22 (Proceedings of the 17th Workshop in Primary and Secondary Computing Education)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates common problems primary school children encounter while programming Ozobot Evo robots and examines how different kinds of corrective feedback affect children’s fun during programming activities. The authors focus on a practical classroom problem: primary teachers often need to support students with robotics and programming, but may not know how to give effective, encouraging feedback when children get stuck.

The study consisted of seven workshops with 116 third- and fourth-grade students (ages 8–10) across seven Ozobot Evo activities. Students worked mostly in pairs and completed a sequence of pen-and-paper robot programming tasks followed by one block-based digital programming task. During the workshops, supervisors recorded students’ problems and the feedback they gave, while students reported fun after each activity using the Fun Toolkit (Smileyometer and Again Again Table).

The analysis identified eight recurring problem categories, including misunderstandings of the task, wrong color codes, Ozobot-specific concepts, reading directions, U-turns, directional movement, app use, and technical/organizational issues. Overall fun ratings were very high, but the paper found that some problems and feedback types were associated with lower enjoyment: urgent problems and issues that might threaten self-efficacy were linked to worse fun ratings, direct instruction tended to reduce fun, and hints tended to increase it. The authors conclude that teachers should prefer encouraging hints over direct instruction when possible, and that this introductory Ozobot course was enjoyable for both girls and boys.

finding.finding_summary: The workshop was rated very positively overall, with mean fun scores of 1.9/2 on the Again Again Table and 3.72/4 on the Smileyometer across 116 children. However, receiving corrective feedback on urgent problems or through direct instruction was associated with lower enjoyment, while hints were associated with higher enjoyment (Smileyometer rp_b = -0.17 for hints; direct instruction rp_b = 0.13).
finding.measure: Fun/enjoyment ratings using the Fun Toolkit (Smileyometer and Again Again Table)
finding.effect_size: rp_b=0.11 overall for having received feedback vs not on Smileyometer; rp_b=-0.17 for hints; rp_b=0.13 for direct instruction

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines children’s ability to handle programming problems, debug mistakes, and understand robot behavior in a primary school robotics context. It reports eight common problem types and shows that when task understanding or app use broke down, students’ ability to continue the task was hindered and fun ratings were significantly worse (e.g., task understanding p=.001, rp_b=0.18; app p=.022, rp_b=0.11).
finding.measure: Observed problem categories during programming activities and associated fun ratings as a proxy for engagement during problem solving
finding.effect_size: rp_b=0.18 for task understanding; rp_b=0.11 for app problems; Kruskal-Wallis η2=0.10 for directional movement differences across group constellations

paper_profiles.title: ClassMind: Scaling Classroom Observation and Instructional Feedback with Multimodal AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the long-standing challenge of scaling classroom observation and instructional coaching, which are widely viewed as effective but are expensive, time-intensive, and difficult to provide consistently across teachers. The authors ask what design features make AI systems effective for supporting classroom observation and how teachers perceive such systems when they are used for instructional feedback.

The paper presents ClassMind, an AI-enabled classroom observation and feedback system that combines multimodal learning, long-context video understanding, transcription, diarization, and rubric alignment to analyze classroom recordings. Its core agent, AVA-Align, processes full lesson videos and generates timestamped, rubric-grounded feedback intended to be specific, actionable, and tied to frameworks such as Danielson, Bloom’s taxonomy, and COPUS. The work is built from three formative studies: a literature review, an online survey of 75 PK–12 teachers, and interviews with six high school educators, followed by a simulated-user role-play study with six secondary teachers using ATLAS classroom videos.

Across the formative and user studies, teachers generally viewed the system as useful, easy to use, fair, and novel, especially for linking evidence to frameworks, navigating lessons efficiently, and surfacing concrete suggestions. Participants also valued the objectivity and time-saving potential of AI feedback, but raised concerns about privacy, accountability, explainability, cognitive load, and the limits of AI relative to human coaching. The paper concludes that multimodal AI can help scale expert-like instructional feedback, but should complement rather than replace human judgment and relationship-based coaching.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers rated ClassMind as highly usable (USE overall M=5.9/7, 95% CI [5.5, 6.4], n=6) and reported modest workload (NASA-TLX overall M=28.5/100, 95% CI [18.1, 38.9], n=6). Participants said the system was easy to learn and helped them navigate directly to salient classroom moments, suggesting it reduced time and effort for reviewing lessons and making sense of instructional feedback.
finding.measure: USE usability questionnaire; NASA-TLX workload; qualitative reports of navigation and reflection efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The system supported teachers’ reflection and metacognitive review of their own practice by making teaching behaviors visible through Bloom’s taxonomy distributions, transcripts, timestamps, and rubric-aligned feedback. In the simulated-user study (n=6), teachers said the tool helped them compare their intentions with what they were actually asking students to do and prompted them to think about how to act on the feedback in future lessons.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview themes; baseline reflection logs; reactions to Bloom’s taxonomy, transcript, and Danielson-coded feedback

finding.finding_summary: Teachers generally reported positive emotional responses to the AI feedback, with FATE outcome ratings for Emotion averaging M=6.0 and Satisfaction M=5.9 (n=6). In interviews, participants described the system as fair and non-biased toward their teaching style, though some expressed concern about trust, cognitive load, and whether AI could capture the relational side of coaching.
finding.measure: FATE questionnaire emotion and satisfaction subscales; semi-structured interviews

paper_profiles.title: SPHERE: Scaling Personalized Feedback in Programming Classrooms with Structured Review of LLM Outputs
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (conference proceedings; exact venue not specified in provided text)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of helping instructors provide timely, personalized feedback during live programming activities in large classrooms. The authors argue that while LLMs can generate feedback at scale, instructors still need support to identify which student issues are most important, tailor feedback appropriately, and verify that AI-generated feedback is accurate and aligned with learning goals.

To address this, the paper presents SPHERE, an interactive system for programming classrooms that combines real-time issue detection, structured feedback generation, and visual review support. SPHERE first analyzes student code submissions and group discussion messages to surface critical issues, then lets instructors choose a feedback strategy (Hint, Explanation, or Verification) and generate feedback from componentized templates, and finally supports rapid verification by showing linked code and conversation evidence.

The evaluation includes formative interviews with four university programming instructors and a between-subject lab study with 20 participants who had teaching and programming experience. In the lab study, participants reviewed real classroom data from an introductory university programming course with 111 students. Compared with a baseline prompt-editing workflow, SPHERE led to substantially more high-quality feedback and less incorrect feedback, without significantly increasing time spent. Qualitative results suggest the structured workflow helped instructors think more carefully about feedback content and made verification easier.

finding.finding_summary: SPHERE improved instructor efficiency in creating and reviewing personalized feedback for programming classrooms. In the between-subject study (n=20 participants), SPHERE enabled significantly more high-quality generated feedback (80.83% vs. 45.83%, p<0.01) and significantly less incorrect generated feedback (14.16% vs. 44.17%, p<0.05), while not significantly increasing time spent on the overall review process.
finding.measure: Feedback quality distribution, number of feedback items generated/sent, time spent on review process

paper_profiles.title: Evidence-Decision-Feedback: Theory-Driven Adaptive Scaffolding for LLM Agents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a central challenge in AI-powered educational agents: how to provide personalized feedback that is adaptive, pedagogically grounded, and interpretable, rather than offering one-size-fits-all responses. The authors propose Evidence-Decision-Feedback (EDF), a theory-driven framework for LLM-based adaptive scaffolding that structures agent behavior around three modules: evidence gathering from student actions, pedagogical decision-making, and feedback generation.

EDF is instantiated in Copa, a collaborative peer agent embedded in the C2STEM learning environment for STEM+C problem solving. Copa was deployed in an authentic high school science classroom with 33 sophomore dyads over six weeks as students learned 1- and 2-D kinematics through computational modeling. The system used log data and conversation data to adapt its dialogue policies as student mastery increased, shifting from probing understanding toward suggesting actions and pushing limits.

The study reports correlational evidence that Copa’s scaffolding became more advanced as task mastery increased, that students’ verbalized understanding was aligned with their task mastery, and that students relied less on the agent as mastery improved. The authors also find that Copa’s internal evidence-to-decision-to-feedback chain was interpretable and statistically non-random. However, the paper is not an experimental causal test of EDF; the results are observational and based on within-system relationships in a classroom deployment. The authors also note a tension between pedagogically principled scaffolding and students’ preference for direct answers.

finding.finding_summary: In an authentic high school physics/computing classroom, Copa supported students’ conceptual understanding and reasoning during kinematics model-building tasks. Student ability to verbally explain their code after probing questions increased with task mastery (Spearman’s ρ = 0.40, p = 0.014), and the share of DEMONSTRATES_UNDERSTANDING responses also rose as mastery increased (ρ = 0.34, p = 0.030), suggesting stronger reasoning as students progressed (n = 33 dyads).
finding.measure: Students’ demonstrated understanding / verbal explanations of code in response to agent probes; alignment of understanding with task mastery

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies critical thinking–related scaffolding and finds that the agent increasingly promoted deeper reasoning as mastery grew. Copa reduced probing questions and increased action-oriented and extension-oriented support (PROBE_UNDERSTANDING ρ = −0.34, p = 0.034; SUGGEST_ACTION ρ = 0.33, p = 0.039; PUSH_LIMIT ρ = 0.42, p = 0.007), while students’ need for support declined (ρ = −0.26, p < 0.001), indicating reduced reliance and greater independent problem solving (n = 33 dyads).
finding.measure: Dialogue policy frequencies across task mastery quintiles; student requests for agent support across mastery deciles

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that students increasingly used Copa less often as they achieved mastery, consistent with growing autonomy and self-regulation. Requests for agent support declined significantly with mastery (Spearman’s ρ = −0.26, p < 0.001), and the authors interpret this as evidence of developing self-efficacy and reduced overreliance, although student survey responses also show some frustration with the lack of direct answers (n = 33 dyads).
finding.measure: Student requests for agent support; self-report perceptions of questions, usefulness, and understanding

paper_profiles.title: Discussion Tracker: Supporting Teacher Learning about Students’ Collaborative Argumentation in High School Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that teaching collaborative argumentation in K-12 classrooms is difficult for many teachers because it is hard to track and reflect on students’ discussion moves in real time or after class. To support teacher learning, the authors developed Discussion Tracker (DT), a classroom discussion analytics system that automatically codes student talk along three dimensions: argument moves (claim/evidence/explanation), specificity, and collaboration (e.g., new, agree, extension, challenge/probe).

The system uses transformer-based NLP models trained on an existing corpus of collaborative argumentation to generate visual analytics such as pie charts, annotated transcripts, collaboration maps, and strength/weakness summaries for goal-setting. In the reported evaluation, 18 high school English Language Arts teachers from 4 schools used a desktop version of DT after leading and recording a literature discussion; experienced annotators manually coded the discussions, and teachers then completed surveys and 45-minute cognitive interviews while using the tool.

Results show that teachers perceived DT as useful for understanding their students’ collaborative argumentation, recognizing strengths and weaknesses, and planning future discussion instruction. On the technical side, the NLP classifiers achieved moderate-to-substantial agreement with human labels, with argument move classification (Kappa=0.574, macro F=0.730, micro F=0.789), specificity (Kappa=0.727, macro F=0.688, micro F=0.679), and collaboration (Kappa=0.566, macro F=0.439, micro F=0.775). The study is primarily a usability and model-evaluation paper rather than a student-outcome impact study, and it does not report direct effects on student critical-thinking performance.

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on collaborative argumentation, a durable skill closely related to critical thinking and collaboration. In a deployment with n=18 high school English Language Arts teachers, teachers reported that Discussion Tracker helped them recognize students’ strengths and weaknesses in discussion, gave them more insight into student learning, and supported goal-setting for facilitating collaborative argumentation. However, the evidence is teacher-perception based rather than a direct measure of student skill gains.
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings and cognitive interview feedback about student collaborative argumentation during classroom discussions

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education educators/students (examples span Grade 12 and undergraduate contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative/practical review of how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, can be used to support formative assessment and feedback. The authors frame the discussion around a formative assessment model: clarifying where learners are going, where they currently are, and how to move them forward. They argue that many current LLM uses in education emphasize technical output quality, but do not adequately align with the pedagogical goals of formative assessment.

The article does not report an intervention study or empirical evaluation. Instead, it synthesizes prior literature and provides concrete prompt examples and classroom-oriented guidance for educators, such as rewriting learning objectives into student-friendly language, generating questions to co-construct success criteria, creating sample work for critique, and producing feedback or questions that encourage revision. The paper repeatedly emphasizes that LLMs should augment, not replace, teacher expertise and that educators must review outputs for accuracy, appropriateness, and alignment with learning goals.

The context includes classroom and course examples ranging from Grade 12 biology to undergraduate fMRI instruction, but these are illustrative rather than study participants. The main conclusion is that LLMs can potentially scale formative assessment practices and reduce teacher workload, but their value depends on thoughtful prompting, pedagogical oversight, and the development of better evaluation criteria that capture formative-quality feedback rather than just surface-level correctness.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce educator workload by helping generate student-friendly learning objectives, sample work, formative questions, and feedback at scale. However, this is a conceptual claim rather than an empirically tested effect; no sample size, effect size, or outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests that AI-generated exemplars and prompts can be used to help students critique sample work, reflect on quality, and avoid over-reliance on LLM outputs, thereby supporting critical thinking and metacognitive reflection. No direct student outcome measurement is reported, and the paper provides no quantitative estimate of impact.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Listening with Language Models: Using LLMs to Collect and Interpret Classroom Feedback
paper_profiles.population: Graduate students (higher education); two graduate courses at UC Santa Cruz
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether LLM-powered conversational tools can improve how instructors collect and interpret classroom feedback. The authors argue that standard end-of-quarter surveys are often too late, too generic, and too low-response to support timely instructional improvement, so they designed a three-part system: PromptDesigner for instructor co-design of feedback prompts, FeedbackCollector for student chatbot-based feedback collection, and FeedbackAnalyzer for summarizing responses for instructors.

The system was piloted in two graduate courses at UC Santa Cruz, Game Data Science and Ethics in HCI, taught by the same instructor, with about 40 students total. Students provided feedback asynchronously through GPT-4-powered conversational sessions at two points in the quarter, and the researchers then interviewed six students and the instructor after the term. The study is qualitative and based on close reading of interview transcripts and reflections rather than experimental outcome measures.

Findings suggest that the LLM-based approach produced richer, more contextual, and more actionable feedback than traditional surveys. The instructor reported that the system surfaced specific issues such as misalignment between readings and lectures and enabled mid-course adjustments, while students generally found the conversational format more engaging and reflective. The paper concludes that AI-mediated feedback tools may support more responsive teaching, though the authors note the small sample and limited context mean the results are exploratory rather than broadly generalizable.

finding.finding_summary: The instructor reported that the chatbot was quick to use and elicited substantially more feedback than the standard end-of-quarter survey, improving the efficiency of collecting course feedback. The paper reports receiving 23 feedback responses in about five minutes and emphasizes that the system supported mid-course adjustments and reduced reliance on low-participation surveys.
finding.measure: Instructor-reported feedback collection efficiency and response volume compared with standard end-of-quarter surveys
finding.study_size: n=1 instructor; two graduate courses; total students n=40

finding.finding_summary: Students generally described the conversational chatbot as more reflective, meaningful, and engaging than conventional review forms, suggesting improved engagement with the feedback task. Interview comments indicate the dialogue format encouraged elaboration and made the process feel less like a chore, although some students remained concerned about anonymity and candor.
finding.measure: Student interview perceptions of engagement, reflection, and willingness to provide feedback

finding.finding_summary: The tool was reported to improve the responsiveness of classroom feedback processes by giving instructors actionable insights that supported changes during the quarter. Examples included identifying misalignment between readings and lectures and surfacing communication confusion early enough for the instructor to make mid-course corrections.
finding.measure: Qualitative evidence of instructional decision-making and course adjustments informed by feedback summaries

paper_profiles.title: Students’ Perceptions to a Large Language Model’s Generated Feedback and Scores of Argumentation Essays
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory study asks whether a large language model (GPT-4o) can generate useful feedback and scores for students’ written scientific argumentation in an introductory physics course. The motivation is that large-enrollment STEM courses make individualized feedback difficult, and the authors argue that argumentation can support critical thinking, metacognition, and expert-like problem solving.

Students in a first-semester calculus-based physics course wrote short scientific arguments on quiz bonus questions in the course’s last module. Their responses were scored and commented on by GPT-4o using a physics-focused prompt and rubric, and students later completed a delayed survey about the perceived usefulness and accuracy of the feedback. The paper compares LLM scores for students who answered the associated multiple-choice problems correctly versus incorrectly and reports student perceptions of the feedback.

The main findings are that GPT-4o’s scores differed as expected by problem difficulty and student correctness, suggesting the model could distinguish stronger from weaker arguments on these physics tasks. Students generally rated the feedback as mostly useful and mostly accurate, with no significant difference in perceptions between students who answered the physics question correctly and those who did not. The study concludes that LLM-generated feedback may be a viable tool for providing scalable formative feedback in large physics classes, while noting that the feedback was delayed and that future work should compare against human grading and move toward more timely feedback.

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4o was able to score students’ scientific argumentation essays in a way that aligned with underlying problem difficulty and performance on the associated multiple-choice physics question. For Quiz 08 (n=730), students who answered the MC item correctly received higher LLM scores than those who answered incorrectly (2.14 vs. 1.12 out of 5; d=0.87, p<0.001). For Quiz 09 (n=565), the same pattern held with a smaller difference (2.77 vs. 2.53; d=0.22, p=0.015).
finding.measure: LLM-generated scores of students’ written scientific argumentation essays on physics quiz items
finding.std_deviation: Quiz 08: 1.29 overall, 1.24 correct, 1.11 incorrect; Quiz 09: 1.08 overall, 1.08 correct, 1.04 incorrect

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that the LLM feedback on their argumentation essays was mostly useful and mostly accurate across both quizzes, indicating perceived support for metacognitive/critical-thinking-related skills. The paper reports no significant difference in usefulness or accuracy ratings between students who answered the MC question correctly versus incorrectly, suggesting broad acceptability of the feedback regardless of prior performance.
finding.measure: Student Likert-scale ratings of perceived usefulness and accuracy of GPT-4o feedback

finding.finding_summary: The study’s core claim is that GPT-4o could provide individualized feedback on argumentation essays in a setting where manual feedback would be difficult at scale. While the paper does not directly measure teacher workload reduction, it presents the model’s scoring/feedback pipeline as a potentially viable way to deliver timely feedback in large-enrollment physics courses.
finding.measure: Feasibility of automated feedback generation for large-enrollment quiz essays

paper_profiles.title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to scale expert guidance for novice tutors in live K-12 mathematics tutoring, especially in under-served communities where access to high-quality instructional support is limited. The authors argue that real-time expert feedback is expensive to provide through conventional professional development, and that generic large language model outputs are often poorly aligned with classroom teaching needs.

To address this, they introduce Tutor CoPilot, a human-AI system that generates expert-like, strategy-specific suggestions for tutors during live virtual tutoring sessions. The system is integrated into a tutoring platform and uses a method called Bridge to generate guidance based on de-identified conversation context, lesson topic, and a selected pedagogical strategy. The study is a preregistered randomized controlled trial involving 900 tutors and 1,800 K-12 students from Title I schools in a southern U.S. district, with analysis on 4,136 tutoring sessions and over 550,000 chat messages.

The main finding is that access to Tutor CoPilot improves students’ immediate math learning outcomes: students whose tutors had access to the system were 4 percentage points more likely to pass exit tickets, with larger gains for lower-rated tutors (+9 percentage points) and less-experienced tutors (+7 percentage points). The paper also finds that treatment tutors more often used pedagogical strategies associated with deeper understanding, such as asking guiding questions and prompting students to explain their reasoning, while control tutors more often gave away answers or relied on more passive support. The authors conclude that AI-supported real-time guidance can improve tutoring quality and proximal student learning at relatively low cost, though they note no statistically significant gains on end-of-year math test scores and some concerns about grade-level appropriateness of generated suggestions.

finding.finding_summary: In an intent-to-treat analysis of 4,136 tutoring sessions, students whose tutors had access to Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to pass their exit tickets than students in the control group (62% to 66%, p<0.01). The treatment effect was larger for lower-rated tutors (+9 percentage points; 56% to 65%) and less-experienced tutors (+7 percentage points; 61% to 68%), indicating stronger benefits for novices.
finding.measure: Exit ticket passing / math topic mastery during tutoring sessions
finding.study_size: n=4136 sessions; 1800 K-12 students; 900 tutors assigned initially

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines whether Tutor CoPilot changes tutoring language in ways that promote student understanding and critical thinking. Using classifiers on 550,000+ messages, the authors find treatment tutors were more likely to prompt students to explain their reasoning and ask questions that guide thinking, and less likely to give away answers or solution strategies; these shifts were reported as roughly 2 standard deviations more frequent on a log-odds scale for key constructive strategies.
finding.measure: Tutor message strategy use / pedagogical language classified from chat messages

finding.finding_summary: Student survey outcomes related to engagement, perceptions of tutor care, and attitudes toward math did not show statistically significant treatment effects. The paper reports mixed small positive and negative estimates across session rating and survey items, but none were significant.
finding.measure: Student post-session survey responses and session ratings (e.g., tutor cared about understanding, confidence about learning hard math)

paper_profiles.title: Is ChatGPT a Good Teacher Coach? Measuring Zero-Shot Performance For Scoring and Providing Actionable Insights on Classroom Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can serve as an automated teacher coach for classroom instruction. The authors frame three coaching tasks for generative AI: (1) scoring classroom transcript segments using established observation rubrics, (2) identifying highlights and missed opportunities in instructional practice, and (3) generating actionable suggestions to elicit more student mathematical reasoning.

The study uses the National Center for Teacher Effectiveness (NCTE) elementary mathematics transcript dataset, which contains 1,660 observation transcripts from 317 teachers across four school districts serving largely historically marginalized students. For the main evaluations, the authors sample 100 transcript segments for score prediction and 18 segments each for qualitative feedback tasks, then compare ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo, zero-shot) against expert human ratings and teacher judgments. The scoring tasks cover CLASS items related to classroom climate, behavior management, and instructional dialogue, plus MQI items related to mathematical explanations, remediation of errors, imprecision in language, and student mathematical questioning/reasoning.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT shows promise as a scalable feedback tool but performs poorly overall as a coach. Its score predictions have low Spearman correlations with human ratings across all items, and adding rubric descriptions or chain-of-thought reasoning does not reliably help. For qualitative feedback, teachers judged many outputs as not insightful, not relevant, or redundant; for suggestions, 82% of the model’s recommendations repeated something the teacher already did in the transcript. The paper concludes that current LLMs can sometimes generate actionable and contextually faithful feedback, but they are not yet reliable enough to replace expert coaching and require further work on insightfulness, novelty, and truthfulness.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test a student learning intervention; instead, it evaluates ChatGPT as a scorer/feedback generator for elementary mathematics classroom transcripts. On MQI scoring tasks, ChatGPT’s predictions showed very low correspondence with expert ratings (Spearman correlations ranged from -0.11 to 0.17 across prompting methods and items), indicating weak performance on mathematically oriented instructional assessment rather than evidence of improved math outcomes.
finding.measure: MQI rubric scores for elementary mathematics classroom transcript segments (EXPL, REMED, LANGIMP, SMQR) compared with human ratings
finding.study_size: n=100 scored transcript segments for Task A; MQI subset sampled from the NCTE dataset

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies critical-thinking-related teacher feedback by asking whether ChatGPT can generate suggestions for eliciting more student mathematical reasoning. In the suggestion task, teachers rated the model’s outputs as mostly faithful and actionable, but novelty was weak: 82% of suggestions were judged redundant because they described what the teacher already did in the transcript. This shows the model can sometimes surface reasoning-oriented prompts, but it does not reliably provide novel critical-thinking support.
finding.measure: Human teacher ratings of model-generated suggestions for eliciting student mathematical reasoning; novelty/redundancy judgments

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates ChatGPT as a potentially scalable substitute for some teacher-coaching labor, so operational efficiency is a central focus. The authors conclude that the system could provide low-cost, scalable feedback in principle, but current outputs are insufficiently accurate and insightful to replace human coaching; no formal productivity or time-savings effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Feasibility of automated classroom coaching via zero-shot transcript scoring and feedback generation

paper_profiles.title: An Interview Reflection on BIntelligent Tutoring Goes to School in the Big City^
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an interview-based reflection on the 1997 Cognitive Tutor Algebra study, written by the original authors as they look back on the study’s motivations, design choices, findings, and long-run influence. Rather than presenting a new intervention trial, it revisits why the team evaluated an intelligent tutoring system embedded in a full algebra curriculum and how they tried to measure outcomes using multiple assessments, including standardized tests and tasks aligned to curriculum goals.

The intervention discussed was the Algebra Cognitive Tutor, deployed in a year-long quasi-experimental classroom study in three urban Pittsburgh high schools during the 1993–94 school year. The interview emphasizes the importance of integrating the tutor into the broader instructional and social context of schooling, including teacher practices, curriculum materials, and scheduling of lab and classroom time.

The authors report that the original study found strong positive learning outcomes, with experimental classes outperforming comparison classes by about 15% on standardized tests and 100% on tests targeting course objectives. The paper also reflects on limitations: the nonrandomized design, the use of single standardized measures in later evaluations, challenges of implementation and adoption, and the need to study which tutor features are actually responsible for learning gains. Overall, the article argues that scientifically grounded intelligent tutoring systems can scale in school settings, but that effectiveness evidence must be considered alongside theory, implementation quality, and adoption context.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that in the original year-long quasi-experimental study, 470 high-school students in experimental classes outperformed comparison students by 15% on standardized tests and by 100% on tests targeting course objectives. The outcome was algebra learning, measured with standardized test items and curriculum-aligned problem-solving/representation items.
finding.measure: Algebra achievement on standardized tests and curriculum-aligned course-objective tests

finding.finding_summary: Beyond student learning, the interview argues that the study helped drive dissemination of Cognitive Tutor Algebra into schools and influenced broader adoption of intelligent tutoring systems. The authors describe the study as the 'initial snowball' for widespread uptake, eventually leading to use in thousands of schools, indicating important institutional and market-level impact.
finding.measure: Dissemination/adoption of Cognitive Tutor Algebra across schools

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses the study’s attention to complex problem solving, representations, and the relationship between isolated procedures and open-ended problem solving. It also notes that the project investigated students’ interest and motivation, but the concrete empirical results reported in this article are primarily about achievement rather than separate durable-skill outcomes.
finding.measure: Complex problem solving and use of representations

finding.finding_summary: The interview states that the broader project examined students’ interest in and motivation to learn math, but it does not report separate quantitative effect sizes for motivation or engagement in this article. Any such evidence is described only at a high level as part of the broader motivation for evaluating the tutor-curriculum package.
finding.measure: Student interest and motivation to learn math

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic review maps research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education from 2007 to 2018. The authors ask how the literature has developed, how AI is conceptualized and ethically discussed, and what kinds of AI applications are being studied across the student lifecycle. They screened 2,656 records and included 146 peer-reviewed journal articles for synthesis.

The review organizes the literature into four main application areas: profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalisation, and intelligent tutoring systems. Most studies came from Computer Science and STEM, used quantitative methods, and focused on undergraduate settings. Across the corpus, the authors found very limited critical reflection on ethics, challenges, and risks; privacy concerns and implementation costs were mentioned only rarely.

Substantively, the review reports that AI systems often achieved high prediction and classification accuracy for admissions, dropout, engagement, automated grading, and feedback tasks, and that many ITS/adaptive systems showed preliminary positive results in short-term pilots. However, the authors conclude that the field is dominated by technical work, with weak pedagogical grounding and little educator involvement, and they call for more attention to ethical governance, educational theory, and human-centered design.

finding.finding_summary: The review includes several studies of automated essay scoring and automated writing feedback. These systems often showed high agreement with human raters (e.g., 94.6% to 98.2% in one postgraduate medical essay study), but the authors also note concerns about feedback quality and limited usefulness for some learners, including beginning language students.
finding.measure: Automated essay scoring agreement; writing feedback quality and revision behavior

finding.finding_summary: A small set of studies in second-language learning examined intelligent tutoring and automated feedback for language tasks. The review characterizes these as generally positive pilot results, with AI used to emulate teacher support and provide prompts, hints, and feedback in language learning contexts.
finding.measure: Language learning tutor/feedback outcomes
