finding.finding_summary: The review includes intelligent tutoring studies in mathematics and statistics, including systems that taught mathematics content and provided adaptive feedback. These studies were generally reported as producing positive or satisfactory preliminary results in short-term implementations, though no longitudinal evidence was identified.
finding.measure: Performance in math/statistics tutoring systems

finding.finding_summary: Several intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning studies targeted STEM content such as computer science, engineering, medicine, and physics. The review reports that these systems typically produced positive preliminary outcomes, such as adaptive feedback and improved support for problem solving, although the synthesis does not report standardized effect sizes.
finding.measure: STEM learning outcomes in tutoring/adaptive systems

finding.finding_summary: The review covers AI applications in a range of non-STEM academic areas, including business statistics, accounting, reading comprehension strategies, and collaborative writing. Across these studies, AI tools were usually described as improving support for course content learning or providing helpful adaptive feedback, though evidence was typically preliminary and short-term.
finding.measure: Course content learning in non-STEM subjects

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of the review concerns student engagement, motivation, self-regulation, and academic support. The paper notes that machine learning systems were used to predict engagement and motivation, and that most studies reported positive or satisfactory preliminary results; however, some systems performed worse than controls on delayed post-tests, indicating that benefits were not universal.
finding.measure: Student engagement; academic motivation; self-regulatory support

finding.finding_summary: The synthesis includes studies on collaboration, metacognitive support, and learning strategies, such as systems facilitating collaborative writing and peer dialogue, and tools supporting self-regulated learning. Results were generally positive in short-term pilots, but the review also highlights at least one negative result and limited evidence of durable skill development over time.
finding.measure: Collaboration, self-regulation, metacognitive strategy support

finding.finding_summary: Operational efficiency is one of the paper’s central themes, especially in automated grading, feedback automation, administrative prediction, and teacher-facing support. The review reports high accuracy for automated grading and prediction systems, and argues that these tools can reduce teacher and staff workload by automating tasks such as grading, feedback, admissions prediction, and early warning identification.
finding.measure: Teacher workload reduction; automated grading; administrative prediction accuracy

finding.finding_summary: The review includes multiple studies at the institutional level, including dropout prediction, admissions, course scheduling, student advising, career services, and institutional decision support. The synthesis suggests that AI can support institutional planning and policy decisions with high predictive accuracy, although the authors caution that such systems require large data sets, calibration, and ethical oversight.
finding.measure: Admissions decisions, retention/attrition prediction, institutional decision support

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a benchmark dataset for evaluating vision-language models on German middle school curriculum content. The authors argue that existing multimodal benchmarks are often English-only, heavily multiple-choice, and sometimes solvable without genuine visual understanding, so they created a dataset grounded in real school materials from grades 8-10 across nine subjects.

The benchmark contains 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions spanning arts, biology, geography, history, math, music, physics, religion, and sports. Some questions are intentionally adversarial and cannot be answered from the image alone, in order to test whether models can refuse unanswerable prompts rather than hallucinate. The authors evaluate 13 open-weight VLMs using an LLM-as-a-judge / panel-of-LLMs scoring setup. Overall accuracy is low, with the best model reaching under 45%, and performance drops sharply on adversarial questions. The paper concludes that middle-school-level multimodal tasks are already highly challenging for current VLMs, especially in German, and that performance on popular public benchmarks does not necessarily predict performance on this more realistic dataset.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark includes 308 math questions, and models performed poorly relative to the task demands. The best model reached 34.09% accuracy on math (Qwen2.5VL 32B), while the overall best model did not exceed 45% accuracy, indicating substantial difficulty with geometry, counting, and formula application when visual information had to be integrated with background knowledge.
finding.measure: Accuracy on middle-school math benchmark questions

finding.finding_summary: The physics and biology sections required interpreting diagrams, identifying structures, and reasoning from visual cues plus domain knowledge. Performance was mixed but generally weak: the best physics score reported was 47.65% and biology scores were mostly below 50%, with the discussion noting frequent failures on explanation-based items and on identifying labeled structures in diagrams.
finding.measure: Accuracy on physics and biology benchmark questions involving diagrams, labels, and reasoning
finding.study_size: physics n=234 questions; biology n=169 questions

finding.finding_summary: Across arts, history, music, religion, and sports, models showed substantial difficulty with subject-specific visual questions. Best reported accuracies included 54.36% in history, 52.92% in religion, 49.34% in arts, 31.03% in music, and 43.84% in sports, with adversarial questions revealing especially poor refusal behavior and frequent hallucinated answers.
finding.measure: Accuracy on domain-specific benchmark questions in arts, history, music, religion, and sports
finding.study_size: arts n=286; history n=264; music n=166; religion n=206; sports n=154 questions

finding.finding_summary: Although not framed as a skills intervention study, the paper directly assesses reasoning behaviors such as visual integration, contextual inference, and the ability to recognize when a question is unanswerable. Adversarial questions show that models often hallucinate instead of declining to answer, suggesting weak metacognitive self-monitoring in multimodal settings.
finding.measure: Accuracy on adversarial questions requiring refusal or contextual reasoning
finding.study_size: overall adversarial set included across the benchmark; domain subset examples reported, exact total adversarial count not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper is primarily a benchmark paper, so it does not evaluate classroom efficiency directly. However, it does describe an automated evaluation pipeline using a panel of LLM judges to score more than 2,000 open-ended answers, showing that such methods can make large-scale evaluation feasible without manual scoring, though no direct productivity effect is measured.
finding.measure: Feasibility of automated scoring with LLM-as-a-judge / panel-of-LLMs

paper_profiles.title: Do intelligent tutoring systems benefit K-12 students? A meta-analysis and evaluation of heterogeneity of treatment effects in the U.S.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), an AI-powered form of personalized instructional feedback, improve learning outcomes for U.S. K-12 students and under what conditions those effects are strongest. The authors also examine whether study design features linked to internal validity and external validity explain heterogeneity in effects, using the MUTOS framework and What Works Clearinghouse standards.

The review identified 18 experimental studies published between 2011 and 2021, yielding 77 effect sizes across 11 ITS. The pooled estimate showed a statistically significant positive effect on student learning outcomes (Hedges’ g=0.271), indicating that ITS generally improved achievement relative to comparison conditions. Effects were similar across elementary and middle school students and across low-achieving and general-population samples, but were smaller in rural settings and in longer-duration interventions. MetaForest results suggested that treatment features mattered most: worked-out examples, intervention duration, intervention condition, and immediate measurement were the strongest moderators.

The study concludes that ITS can be beneficial in K-12 schools, but impact varies by implementation context and intervention design. The authors note that just-in-time hints were not statistically significant, while on-demand hints and worked-out examples were associated with positive effects. They also find that most included studies met strong experimental standards, but attrition reporting was incomplete, limiting certainty about internal validity in some cases. Overall, the paper supports thoughtful, context-sensitive use of ITS in schools rather than assuming uniform effects across settings or student groups.

finding.finding_summary: Across studies of reading and writing outcomes, ITS produced a statistically significant positive effect (g=0.323). The meta-analysis included 55 effect sizes for reading and writing outcomes, suggesting that personalized tutoring systems improved literacy-related achievement in K-12 settings.
finding.measure: Reading and writing achievement outcomes

finding.finding_summary: ITS had a statistically significant positive effect on mathematics outcomes (g=0.253). This analysis included 22 effect sizes and indicates that AI tutoring systems improved math achievement for K-12 students, though the effect was smaller than the reading/writing estimate.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper examined support types intended to affect engagement and motivation, including motivation support and just-in-time/on-demand help. Motivation support showed a statistically significant positive effect (g=0.265), while just-in-time hints were not statistically significant (g=0.337, p=0.108), indicating mixed evidence for affective/engagement-related benefits.
finding.measure: Motivation support / engagement-related instructional support type
finding.study_size: k=23 effect sizes for motivation support; k=18 for just-in-time hints
finding.effect_size: g=0.265 (motivation support); g=0.337 (just-in-time hints, not significant)

finding.finding_summary: The review treated worked-out examples, hints, and related support types as moderators of learning and concluded that worked-out examples were the most influential predictor in the MetaForest model. While the paper does not directly measure durable skills such as metacognition, its discussion links student choice and help-seeking features to self-regulated learning and productive problem solving, which are adjacent durable-skill constructs.
finding.measure: Worked-out examples and help-seeking support as moderators of learning effects
finding.study_size: k=59 effect sizes for worked-out examples

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Multimodal Feedback Using Multiple External Representations: Strategy Profiles and Learning in High School Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether students’ use of elaborated, personalized feedback in a high school physics learning platform is associated with better learning outcomes, and whether those associations depend on students’ representational competence. The authors frame the study around adaptive instruction, multiple external representations (MERs), and the emerging role of AI-enabled tutoring systems that can provide feedback in different formats.

The study used a custom web platform (KI4SCool) that gave all students verification feedback after each multiple-choice physics item and optional elaborated feedback in three formats: verbal, graphical/pictorial, and mathematical. Students in German high schools (10th–11th grade; 661 completers across 29 schools and 87 classes) worked through kinematics exercises over 16–24 weeks. The researchers analyzed platform logs and pre/post tests using linear mixed-effects models, correlations, and clustering of feedback-selection strategies.

Results showed a small positive association between more frequent use of elaborated feedback and higher post-test performance, after adjusting for prior knowledge, platform score, number of exercises, and confidence. The association was statistically significant in one cohort and positive but marginal in the other; no robust interaction effects were found between feedback use and prior knowledge, platform performance, or confidence. Cluster analyses suggested that students tended to either never open elaborated feedback, frequently open all three formats together, or prefer verbal feedback more than graphical/mathematical feedback. However, the authors found no clear evidence that these feedback-selection patterns were strongly linked to initial representational competence, and the time-resolved sequence analysis did not reveal distinct temporal strategy types beyond frequency of feedback use.

finding.finding_summary: Frequent use of elaborated multimodal feedback was associated with higher post-test physics scores in a 16–24 week observational study of high school students (Cohort 1 n=351; Cohort 2 n=310). In the mixed-effects models, feedback frequency had a small positive association with post-test performance (Cohort 1 standardized β=0.13, 95% CI [0.05, 0.22]; Cohort 2 β=0.08, 95% CI [0.00, 0.16], p=.054), controlling for pre-test score, platform score, exercises solved, and confidence.
finding.measure: Post-test score on kinematics/physics assessments
finding.study_size: n=661 total completers; n=351 Cohort 1; n=310 Cohort 2

finding.finding_summary: The paper examined whether students’ feedback-use patterns were related to initial representational competences and whether those competences moderated learning from feedback. In Cohort 1, the MANOVA found no significant differences in initial verbal, graphical, or mathematical competences across feedback-strategy clusters (Pillai’s trace=0.018, F=0.74, p=.67), suggesting limited evidence that baseline representational skill determined strategy choice. The authors also report no robust moderation overall, though one cluster showed a positive slope between feedback frequency and post-test score.
finding.measure: Initial representational competence (verbal, graphical, mathematical pre-test subscores) and moderation of post-test performance

finding.finding_summary: The study focused on how students selected among multiple external representations embedded in feedback, identifying distinct usage profiles but not strong evidence of time-based strategy differentiation. K-means clustering on aggregated feedback use yielded four groups: no feedback, high use of all three representations, verbal-dominant use, and balanced but non-simultaneous use; however, the time-resolved sequence analysis did not reveal meaningful temporal strategy types beyond frequency of use.
finding.measure: Feedback-selection patterns across verbal, graphical, and mathematical representations
finding.study_size: n=661 for aggregated clusters; n=192 for time-resolved sequence clustering

finding.finding_summary: The paper used average response confidence and response time as adjacent learner characteristics when testing associations with feedback use, but these variables were not strongly related to feedback frequency. Correlations between feedback frequency and average confidence were near zero in both cohorts (r=0.00 and r=0.10), and the authors concluded that confidence did not explain who used elaborated feedback more often.
finding.measure: Average response confidence; feedback frequency associations
finding.study_size: n=661 total; correlations reported by cohort

paper_profiles.title: Al científico que todo niño lleva dentro
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This document is a Spanish-language educational astronomy book for teachers and classroom use, published by CosmoAmautas as a second edition in 2022. It covers foundational astronomy and cosmology topics such as the sky, constellations, Earth’s motions, the atmosphere, the Moon, the solar system, stars, exoplanets, galaxies, and the expanding universe.

The book is organized as instructional content plus inquiry-based learning activities (Aprendizaje por Indagación, API) intended for educational use in classrooms. It does not present a research study, evaluation, or intervention trial of an AI system or personalized feedback; instead, it is curriculum-style instructional material. The text is aimed at teachers using science activities with children, likely in K-12 or elementary settings, but no empirical classroom outcomes are reported.

Because the provided text is pedagogical and descriptive rather than an empirical study, there are no measurable findings about learning, engagement, workload, or institutional impact to extract. The paper/book mainly serves as instructional content supporting astronomy education and inquiry-based classroom activities.

paper_profiles.title: Physics for the masses: teaching Einsteinian gravity in primary school
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether primary school students can learn core ideas from Einsteinian gravity and whether such instruction is engaging. The authors focus on two research questions: students’ understanding of gravity as curvature of spacetime, and students’ attitudes toward learning Einsteinian physics.

The intervention was a 15-hour teaching sequence delivered in three Italian primary school classes of 10- to 11-year-olds (n=58) in Turin. Instruction used language, models, and analogies rather than mathematics, especially a lycra-sheet “spacetime simulator” to visualize how mass curves space and affects motion. Students also worked with triangles on curved balloon surfaces to explore non-Euclidean geometry. Pre- and post-questionnaires were administered, with the post-test given one month later to probe retention.

Results indicate substantial gains in students’ explanations of gravity after the intervention. Before instruction, most students described gravity mainly by its everyday effects; afterward, many responses referred to interaction between bodies, mass, curvature, or Einsteinian ideas, and 70% of answers to the curved-surface geometry question were correct and motivated. The paper also reports very positive student attitudes, with 100% positive questionnaire responses about the activities. The authors conclude that Einsteinian physics can be taught fruitfully in primary school, that the approach appears robust across different socio-cultural contexts, and that students retained key ideas after a delay.

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved students’ understanding of gravity as a geometric phenomenon and their ability to reason about curved space. After the 15-hour lesson sequence (n=58), 70% of answers to the curved-surface question were correct and correctly motivated, and more than half of students’ explanations of gravity referenced modern-physics ideas such as curvature or black holes. The post-test was administered one month later, suggesting retention of the key concepts.
finding.measure: Open-ended questionnaire responses about gravity, spacetime curvature, and the behavior of parallel lines/triangle angles on curved surfaces

finding.finding_summary: Students reported very positive reactions to the Einsteinian gravity activities. The paper states that students enjoyed the activities a lot and that the questionnaire yielded 100% positive answers, indicating strong engagement and interest in the topic. No negative affective outcomes are reported.
finding.measure: Student attitude/engagement questionnaire items about the learning activities

paper_profiles.title: Common Problems and Effects of Feedback on Fun When Programming Ozobots in Primary School
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 17th Workshop in Primary and Secondary Computing Education (WiPSCE '22)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates which problems primary school children encounter while programming Ozobot Evo robots and how different kinds of corrective feedback affect children’s enjoyment of the activity. The authors were especially interested in whether feedback on common problems can unintentionally reduce fun, and whether girls and boys differ in the kinds of problems they experience or in how much they enjoy the activities.

The study was conducted as seven workshops with 116 third- and fourth-grade students (ages 8–10) in pairs or small groups. Across seven Ozobot activities, students first worked in pen-and-paper robot programming tasks and then one digital OzoBlockly debugging task. Supervisors documented the problems students raised and the feedback they provided, while students rated each activity using the Fun Toolkit (Smileyometer and Again Again Table). The authors used thematic analysis for the qualitative problem/feedback data and correlational/nonparametric analyses for fun and gender differences.

The paper identifies eight recurring problem types, including understanding the task, wrong color codes, Ozobot-specific concepts, reading directions, U-turns, directional movement, app use, and technical/organizational issues. The main conclusion is that corrective feedback can reduce fun when the problem is urgent or when it may threaten self-efficacy, and that direct instruction is associated with lower fun ratings, while hints are associated with higher fun ratings. Overall enjoyment was high, and the activity appeared similarly enjoyable for girls and boys, though mixed groups more often needed support with directional movement.

finding.finding_summary: The workshop was generally rated as highly enjoyable, with mean fun scores of 1.9/2 on the Again Again Table and 3.72/4 on the Smileyometer across 116 primary school students. However, fun ratings dropped when feedback was urgently needed or when it took the form of direct instruction (Smileyometer mean 3.37 for direct instruction vs. 3.90 for hints), while hints were associated with higher fun ratings.
finding.measure: Fun Toolkit ratings (Smileyometer; Again Again Table) after each activity

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines problem-solving and debugging during robotics activities, including how children dealt with task misunderstandings, incorrect color codes, directionality, and app use. These issues were analyzed as part of students’ learning processes, and the authors conclude that hints and guided feedback support children in solving problems more autonomously than direct instruction.
finding.measure: Observed problem categories and tutoring feedback during Ozobot programming and debugging tasks

finding.finding_summary: The study focuses on introductory programming with Ozobot Evo robots, including both pen-and-paper coding and block-based OzoBlockly debugging, which is best classified as an academic other domain rather than literacy, numeracy, or science. The paper reports that children were able to complete the activities successfully with support, and that the course was evaluated very positively overall, indicating positive learning engagement in introductory programming.
finding.measure: Completion of Ozobot programming activities and qualitative performance/problem observations

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of a STEM-based Entrepreneurship Program on the Entrepreneurial Intention of Secondary School Female Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a one-day, female-focused STEM-based entrepreneurship program increases secondary school girls’ entrepreneurial intention, and whether entrepreneurial inspiration, entrepreneurial learning, and entrepreneurial attitude help explain that change. The authors situate the study in a broader concern that entrepreneurship education research has focused mostly on university students, while evidence for secondary school students—especially girls in STEM-related contexts—remains limited.

The intervention, called the OzGirlsEntrepreneurship program, was a three-part workshop series for Year 10 girls in Victoria, Australia. The workshops combined role-model talks, mentoring by female STEM university students, collaborative ideation around real-world problems, micro:bit-based prototyping, and a final pitch. The study used pre- and post-workshop surveys from 193 valid respondents and analyzed relationships among attitude, intention, inspiration, and learning using PLS-SEM, along with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test for pre/post intention change.

The paper concludes that the program significantly increased entrepreneurial intention from pre to post workshop, and that entrepreneurial attitude strongly predicted intention. Inspiration and perceived learning both positively predicted entrepreneurial attitude, but their direct effects on intention were not significant; instead, attitude fully mediated both relationships. The authors also find that having a businessperson in the immediate family was associated with higher intention and stronger inspiration-to-attitude links, while prior entrepreneurship experience and having an entrepreneur in the family did not significantly moderate the model.

finding.finding_summary: The OzGirlsEntrepreneurship program significantly increased students’ entrepreneurial intention from pre to post workshop (time1 M=3.37, time2 M=3.77; Wilcoxon signed-rank p=0.000, r=0.413) among 193 Year 10 female students. Entrepreneurial attitude was also strongly associated with intention (β=0.638, t=12.932, p=0.000), and entrepreneurial inspiration and learning both improved attitude, with full mediation through attitude for their effects on intention.
finding.measure: Entrepreneurial intention (single-item Likert agreement with "I would like to start my own business one day"), plus entrepreneurial attitude, inspiration, and perceived entrepreneurial learning

finding.finding_summary: The study identifies entrepreneurial inspiration and entrepreneurial learning as significant contributors to entrepreneurial attitude, which the authors interpret as reflecting skills such as creative thinking, problem-solving, and real-world opportunity identification. Inspiration had a positive effect on attitude (β=0.317, t=3.414, p=0.001), and learning also had a positive effect on attitude (β=0.221, t=2.714, p=0.007), but neither had a significant direct effect on intention.
finding.measure: Entrepreneurial inspiration and entrepreneurial learning survey scales; entrepreneurial attitude as the proximal outcome
finding.std_deviation: inspiration construct item SDs reported in Table 2; overall construct SD not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Intelligent Tutors Beyond K-12: An Observational Study of Adult Learner Engagement and Academic Impact
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a K-12-oriented intelligent tutoring system can support adult learners when used voluntarily as a supplemental resource. The authors focus on Apprentice Tutors, a novel intelligent tutoring platform for College Algebra topics, and examine how adult students at a 2-year state technical college adopt and use the system, and whether use is associated with learning gains.

The intervention/approach is not an experimental treatment but an observational analysis of real-world usage data from a two-year deployment integrated into Blackboard and Canvas via LTI. The system provides Bayesian Knowledge Tracing-based problem selection, immediate correctness feedback, layered hints, progress tracking, and linked learning resources. The study combines tutor log data, institutional grades, and demographics for 3,510 enrolled students, with 520 using the tutors at least once and 214 using Unit 1 tutors. Usage patterns were analyzed by time, day, and demographics, and learning was examined both within the tutor (error-rate reductions across practice opportunities) and outside the tutor (Unit 1 grades).

The main conclusions are that adult learners used the tutors mostly during evenings and late nights, that tutor users were older and more likely to be female than non-users, and that error rates decreased with practice inside the tutor. The authors also report a small positive association between the number of tutor transactions and Unit 1 grades (linear regression coefficient = 0.26, p < 0.001), but they explicitly caution that causal inference is not possible because the study is observational and subject to selection effects. Overall, the paper concludes that intelligent tutors appear promising as voluntary supplementary tools for adult learners, while noting that stronger experimental evidence is still needed.

finding.finding_summary: The study found evidence of improved performance on College Algebra content through both in-tutor learning and course outcomes. In tutor logs, student error rates decreased with additional practice opportunities (p < 0.001), and on Unit 1 assessments tutor users earned slightly higher mean grades than non-users. A linear regression further showed a significant positive association between tutor transactions and Unit 1 grade (estimate = 0.26, p < 0.001), though the authors caution that causality cannot be inferred.
finding.measure: College Algebra tutor error rates; Unit 1 assessment grades
finding.study_size: n=3,510 enrolled students; n=520 tutor users; n=214 Unit 1 tutor users
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI reported for mean grades in Figure 9, but exact values not reported; regression CI not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines engagement and voluntary adoption patterns as indicators of how adult learners interact with the system. It reports that 14.81% of students used the tutors at least once, with usage concentrated in evenings, late nights, and Thursdays, suggesting the tool fit learners' schedules and supported persistence/engagement outside traditional hours. The study does not provide a causal estimate for motivation or persistence, but the engagement evidence is central to the analysis.
finding.measure: Tutor adoption rates, transaction timing, and usage patterns
finding.study_size: n=3,510 enrolled students; n=520 tutor users

finding.finding_summary: The authors analyze learning within the tutor as skill acquisition over repeated practice, which is closely tied to mastery and self-regulated practice behavior. Using an Additive Factors Model learning-curve analysis, they found error rates decreased as practice opportunities increased, indicating knowledge-component mastery growth over time. The paper frames this as evidence of learning and skill improvement, although specific effect sizes for the learning-curve slope are not reported.
finding.measure: Knowledge-component mastery / practice error rates in the tutor
finding.study_size: n=3,510 enrolled students; tutor-level learning curve analyzed on users who practiced in Unit 1
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI shown in Figure 8, exact values not_reported

paper_profiles.title: A cross-age study on secondary school students’ views of stars
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a gap in astronomy education research: how secondary school students’ ideas about stars develop across the secondary years, and which misconceptions remain widespread. The authors note that prior work has often focused on isolated astronomy topics, so they first develop and validate a new instrument to assess students’ views of stars across five domains: stars and the solar system, formation and evolution of stars, properties of stars, (sub-)stellar objects, and spectral aspects.

The study uses a cross-age, paper-pencil survey design with German secondary school students in grades 7-12 (N=366 in the main study), plus a pilot sample (N=390) used to refine the instrument. Responses are categorized as aligned with scientific views, opposing them, or abstentions. The authors analyze cohort differences using ANOVAs and post-hoc tests, finding a steady increase in scientifically aligned responses from lower to upper secondary school in all five domains, though progress is weakest for (sub-)stellar objects. They also identify persistent misconceptions, such as confusion about the solar system, the size and motion of stars, and the idea that stars twinkle because they change brightness.

Overall, the paper concludes that students’ views of stars become progressively more scientifically accurate across secondary school, but several misconceptions remain common and some topics receive little curricular attention. The authors argue that their instrument can be used in future astronomy education research to study learning trajectories and to examine how instructional materials or informal learning experiences support conceptual change.

finding.finding_summary: Students’ responses became progressively more aligned with scientific views from lower to upper secondary school across all five star-related domains. For example, the percentage of scientifically aligned responses increased from 48.4% to 72.6% in Domain 1, from 42.9% to 65.4% in Domain 2, and from 58.9% to 78.9% in Domain 5; all cohort differences were statistically significant in the ANOVAs.
finding.measure: Percentage of responses aligned with scientific views on a 55-item star-conceptions instrument across five domains
finding.effect_size: η2p=0.18 (Domain 1), 0.13 (Domain 2), 0.12 (Domain 3), 0.02 (Domain 4), 0.07 (Domain 5); pairwise Cohen’s d ranged from 0.31 to 1.20
finding.std_deviation: Domain-level SDs reported by cohort (e.g., Domain 1: 22.9, 18.6, 18.3; see paper tables)

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central non-cognitive contribution is the development and psychometric evaluation of a new instrument for assessing secondary students’ views of stars. After expert review and piloting, 55 items remained from an initial 82-item pool, and the authors report acceptable internal consistency across subscales (Cronbach’s alpha roughly 0.67-0.86 in the main sample).
finding.measure: Psychometric evaluation of a newly developed 55-item star-views instrument (item difficulty, discrimination, Cronbach’s alpha)

paper_profiles.title: Identification of Books That are Suitable for Middle School Students Using Artificial Neural Networks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to identify books that are suitable for middle school students by using automated text analysis rather than relying only on human reviewers. The authors argue that book selection for schools can be time-consuming and subjective, and that inappropriate content can negatively affect children. To reduce this burden, they propose an artificial neural network (ANN) that analyzes books themselves using natural language processing and sentiment analysis.

The system was built on a custom dataset of 416 books, labeled as suitable or unsuitable for middle school use. The authors extracted 14 features from each book, including counts and ratios of positive/negative sentences and words, words per sentence, vocabulary-level ratios, and a coefficient of positivity derived from VADER sentiment scores. They also created a bad-words list to force clearly inappropriate terms to negative sentiment values. The ANN was trained on these features and tested on 83 books, achieving 90.06% consistency overall, with reported accuracy of 91.2% for suitable books and 80.7% for unsuitable books.

The paper concludes that the coefficient of positivity can be a useful input feature for identifying age-appropriate books, but it is not sufficient on its own. The authors note that the model struggles with academically complex texts that may be appropriate for middle school readers, suggesting that additional academic-jargon features and a larger training set would improve performance. They propose the system as a screening tool for schools, teachers, parents, and education authorities to help speed up curriculum book selection.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed ANN was intended as a screening tool for book selection in schools and education authorities. On a custom dataset of 416 books, it achieved 90.06% overall consistency and was described as potentially useful for Ministry of Education and school curriculum review, with the authors arguing it could speed up and standardize suitability decisions.
finding.measure: Book suitability classification accuracy / consistency rate
finding.study_size: n=416 books (training dataset); n=83 books (test sample)

paper_profiles.title: Transforming High School Physics with Modeling and Computation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This thesis examines how to bring scientific computation into a ninth-grade Physics First classroom so that students practice physics more like professional scientists. The central problem is that traditional high school physics emphasizes content and formula use, while the NRC Framework and related reform reports call for more authentic engagement with scientific practices such as modeling and computational thinking.

The intervention introduced computational modeling activities, mainly in VPython with the PhysUtil module, into a Modeling Instruction physics course at a private co-educational K-12 school in Georgia. Students worked with scaffolded code and used computation to model force and motion topics, including constant velocity, constant acceleration, balanced forces, and unbalanced forces. These activities followed in-class experiments and problem-solving sessions and were assessed through a proctored programming task, written essay questions, and interviews.

The study population was 9th-grade high school physics students, most of whom reported little to no prior programming experience. The thesis reports that students were able to use computation to connect physics models to numerical simulations and that their responses suggested some understanding of the iterative loop linking force, velocity, and position. The author concludes that computation can successfully support authentic scientific practice in the high school physics classroom, though the evidence presented is exploratory and based on a small pilot implementation.

finding.finding_summary: The pilot suggests students could use computation to build and reason about physics models in a high school setting. The thesis reports that ninth-grade students with little prior coding experience successfully completed scaffolded computational modeling tasks and demonstrated understanding of how iterative numerical updates connect force, velocity, and position, based on a proctored assignment and follow-up essay/interview data (n=36 in the class; n=32 essay responses).
finding.measure: Proctored VPython programming assignment; essay responses about the iterative computational model; think-aloud interviews

finding.finding_summary: The paper also examines whether students could apply computational thinking and connect code to physical reasoning, which is a durable-skill-like outcome. Evidence from the essay and interview analyses indicates that students who were successful on the coding task more often displayed force-causal and iterative reasoning, suggesting gains in computational thinking and model-based problem solving rather than mere memorization of code.
finding.measure: Essay-coded views of computational reasoning; interview responses; relationship between reasoning views and proctored success
finding.study_size: n=32 essays; n=29 for coded-view/proctored comparison

finding.finding_summary: The thesis primarily concerns programming/computing as part of physics instruction, so it also substantively studies students' ability to write and use code in a physics context. Students generally could complete scaffolded VPython code tasks, and the author uses this as evidence that computational assignments can be integrated into high school physics even when most students begin with little programming background.
finding.measure: VPython coding performance on proctored assignment

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how elementary school students and their teachers perceived a GenAI-powered learning tool designed to support creative mathematical writing. The authors were motivated by a practical classroom problem: many young students struggle to generate rich, original math stories and to connect math concepts to narrative writing, while AI systems may be able to scaffold ideation, representation, and revision.

The intervention was a three-step classroom activity: Ask, Represent, and Transform. In the Ask step, students unpacked the math story and identified the underlying mathematics; in Represent, they used visual tools to model ideas; and in Transform, they supplied story elements and a math goal to a GenAI system (using GPT-4 and DALL·E 3) that generated a story draft and image support. The study took place in six fifth-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools (n=79 students, six teachers). Data came from focus-group interviews with 10 students, one-on-one teacher interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations, analyzed thematically.

The main findings were mixed but overall positive for learning processes and classroom experience. Participants reported benefits for creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and affective engagement: students tried multiple ideas, refined prompts, better understood the math in stories, and felt more interested, curious, and ownership over learning. At the same time, they identified important limitations and unintended harms, including weak critical evaluation of AI outputs, difficulty generating coherent stories, AI being "too perfect" and reducing opportunities to revise, limited adaptive feedback, reduced autonomy, weaker social connection, and limited accessibility/communication modes. The paper concludes that GenAI can support elementary mathematical writing, but only when carefully designed to preserve student agency, provide pedagogical feedback, and allow room for productive imperfection.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers perceived that GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing improved mathematical understanding, including breaking down word problems, representing mathematical ideas visually, and uncovering misconceptions. The study is qualitative and does not report test-score gains, but it provides consistent interview evidence from 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers that the Ask/Represent/Transform workflow helped students engage with fraction concepts more deeply.
finding.measure: Perceived mathematical understanding, problem decomposition, knowledge representation, and misconception identification from interviews, survey responses, and observations
finding.study_size: n=79 students; 6 teachers; 10 student interview participants

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies creative mathematical writing, a writing task supported by GenAI story generation and revision. Participants reported that AI helped them draft, expand, and refine stories, and that students could produce more original and coherent math narratives with support from the system.
finding.measure: Perceived writing support and quality of student-generated math stories

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers reported increased interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership in learning math through GenAI-supported creative writing. The qualitative findings suggest improved engagement and motivation, but no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership in learning from interviews and open-ended responses

finding.finding_summary: The system was perceived to support divergent and convergent thinking, flexible thinking, prompt engineering, and critical evaluation of AI outputs. However, students also showed gaps in critically evaluating AI-generated content and in generating coherent original ideas, so the durable-skills impact was beneficial but uneven.
finding.measure: Perceived creativity, critical evaluation, prompt refinement, and problem formulation skills

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the GenAI tool could provide draft stories and preliminary support more quickly than humans alone, which may reduce some time spent on initial story creation. At the same time, they emphasized that the system still lacked adaptive, formative feedback, so efficiency benefits were partial rather than complete.
finding.measure: Perceived drafting speed and support efficiency from teacher and student interviews

paper_profiles.title: Students' Perceived Roles, Opportunities, and Challenges of a Generative AI-powered Teachable Agent: A Case of Middle School Math Class
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle school students perceive a generative AI-powered teachable agent (TA) used in a mathematics classroom. The authors ask what roles students assign to the TA, what benefits they perceive from learning with it, and what challenges they encounter when interacting with it. The work is motivated by growing interest in using generative AI to support learning-by-teaching, while also surfacing student perspectives on the design and classroom use of such systems.

The study involved 108 sixth-grade students from a public laboratory middle school in the southeastern United States. Students interacted with a GenAI-powered TA during two 47-50 minute class periods on rate-and-ratio problems; the system used GPT-4-Turbo, a knowledge graph built from math Q&A data, personalization features, gamification, and retrieval-augmented generation. Data came from classroom observation, open-ended surveys, and focus-group interviews with 14 students, and were analyzed thematically.

Students described the TA as a learning companion, learning facilitator, and collaborative problem-solver. They reported perceived benefits including a more student-centered learning climate, increased autonomy, stronger cognitive/social/emotional capacities, improved math understanding and transfer, greater enjoyment and self-efficacy, and more positive attitudes toward AI. They also identified barriers such as weak problem-presentation skills, surface-level questioning, inability to match learning styles, poor sequencing, limited social-emotional fluency, their own lack of domain and pedagogical knowledge, technical glitches, interface issues, lack of multimodal input, lack of interoperability, and the need for teacher facilitation. Overall, the paper concludes that GenAI-powered TAs may support learning-by-teaching in K-12 settings, but effective classroom use requires careful design, better multimodal and adaptive features, and human teacher involvement.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that interacting with the GenAI-powered teachable agent improved their understanding of middle-school rate and ratio content. They described clearer grasp of concepts, better ability to apply knowledge in new contexts, and correction of misconceptions, but the paper is qualitative and does not report standardized learning gains or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of math understanding, application of knowledge, and concept clarity in rate and ratio tasks

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived improvements in enjoyment of math, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, engagement, and positive attitudes toward AI. They said the TA made math feel more fun and dynamic and helped them persist when problems were difficult, but these outcomes were based on self-reports rather than measured changes.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of enjoyment, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, engagement, and attitude toward AI

finding.finding_summary: Students said the TA fostered cognitive, social, and collaborative capacities, including reasoning, elaboration, perspective-taking, communication, and problem-solving with a partner. The study also reports that students saw the TA as a collaborative problem-solver, but the evidence is qualitative and does not include direct skill assessments.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of reasoning, elaboration, communication, perspective-taking, and collaboration

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 (Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This participatory design study asks how middle school students perceive an AI peer during collaborative mathematical problem solving, and what behaviors and controls they want from such a system. The paper is motivated by a gap in AI-in-education research: most systems frame AI as a tutor or teacher aide, while this work explores AI positioned as a fellow student collaborator in group math work.

The authors ran a five-day summer camp with 24 rising grades 6-8 students at a U.S. university. Students completed human-only collaborative math tasks and comparable tasks with two AI peers through a sandboxed technology probe, then reviewed dialogue excerpts, co-designed ideal AI peer behaviors, and completed preference surveys. The tasks focused on middle-school mathematics topics such as ratio/proportional reasoning, expressions and equations, and early functions/geometry.

Findings show that students wanted an AI peer that was competent but deferential: it should give hints, checks, and concept refreshers, not immediate answers; use a friendly expert tone; and remain clearly under student control. The study also found important unintended harms and tradeoffs: AI peers reduced temporal demand, but increased physical/operational load, lowered group cohesion, and sometimes felt overly didactic, rude, unresponsive, or emotionally unsupportive. Overall, the paper concludes that AI peers for K-12 collaboration should scaffold rather than direct, and should support co-agency, social attunement, and emotional responsiveness.

finding.finding_summary: Students completed middle-school math collaborative problem-solving tasks with and without AI peers. The paper reports that AI peers reduced perceived temporal demand (M=5.67, SD=4.38) compared with human-only CPS (M=9.62, SD=4.13), but the study did not measure math achievement gains; instead, it found that the AI peer design changed how students experienced mathematical work and collaboration.
finding.measure: Middle-school mathematics collaborative problem-solving tasks; NASA-TLX temporal demand during math task sessions
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired quantitative comparisons; N=24 enrolled

finding.finding_summary: The study found both beneficial and harmful effects on students’ experience. Students reported lower temporal demand with AI peers (M=5.67 vs. 9.62, d=1.15), but qualitative data showed frustration, self-blame, and reduced trust when the AI was emotionally unresponsive or seemed not to recognize struggle. The paper emphasizes the need for emotional scaffolding, not just correctness-oriented help.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand; interview/reflection themes about frustration, self-blame, trust, and emotional attunement
finding.study_size: n=22 for survey comparisons; N=18 individual interviews and 5 whole-class reflection sessions

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies collaboration and co-agency in small-group math problem solving. Compared with human-only CPS, AI peers lowered Group Integration-Task (M=4.76, SD=1.58 vs. 5.54, SD=1.52; d=0.81) and Group Environment Questionnaire social attraction scores (M=5.21, SD=1.81 vs. 6.50, SD=2.05; d=0.94), indicating weaker perceived coordination and group cohesion. Qualitative findings further show students wanted an AI peer that negotiates methods, listens, and supports shared problem solving rather than taking over.
finding.measure: GEQ Group Integration-Task; GEQ Attractions to Group-Social; interview and reflection themes about co-agency and collaboration
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired survey comparisons; N=24 enrolled
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.58 vs. 1.52 for GIT; SD=1.81 vs. 2.05 for ATGS

finding.finding_summary: AI peers improved perceived efficiency by reducing temporal demand, suggesting less time pressure during task completion. However, they also increased physical demand because students had to type, navigate the interface, and interpret AI outputs, indicating that the system made collaboration more operationally burdensome even as it sped up the work.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand and physical demand
finding.std_deviation: Temporal demand SD=4.38 vs. 4.13; physical demand SD=4.65 vs. 2.41

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not report a direct academic outcome in a non-math subject, but it does involve general AI literacy and design-oriented reflection activities (e.g., card sorting about when to use AI and poster co-design). These activities informed students’ judgments about AI, yet the paper does not provide a substantive measured academic outcome beyond mathematics and collaboration-related dimensions.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
paper_profiles.population: Middle School (7th grade mathematics teachers and students)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether teachers should remain in the loop when using generative AI to personalize instructional tasks, and what the tradeoffs are between personalization quality, student preference, and teacher efficiency. The authors focus on context personalization in middle school mathematics, where ChatGPT/GPT-4o is used to adapt existing Illustrative Mathematics problems to students’ interests.

Seven 7th-grade math teachers from six U.S. schools participated. They first received training on personalization and prompting, then used ChatGPT to modify 143 mathematics problems for 521 students across two curriculum units (Unit 4: proportional relationships and percentages; Unit 6: expressions, equations, and inequalities). The study analyzed teacher prompt logs, video/audio of problem-posing sessions, time spent per problem, and student survey responses (closed- and open-ended) about interest, relevance, and realism.

The main findings were that teachers primarily used ChatGPT to swap in broad or specific popular-culture references, but spent substantial effort correcting realism, age appropriateness, and numerical plausibility. Students generally preferred smaller-grain, specific cultural references over broad categories, yet also focused more on surface-level interest than on realism or depth. Personalizing a problem took about 4 minutes on average, which the authors argue is not time-efficient enough to scale to multiple versions per student. Teacher prompting showed a nonlinear pattern: 3–5 prompts per problem was associated with higher student ratings, but more prompts did not improve outcomes. Teachers used more prompts and more time in Unit 6 than Unit 4, and student ratings were higher in Unit 6, suggesting iterative improvement but not increasing efficiency. The paper concludes that teacher-in-the-loop personalization may support teacher learning and monitoring, but it is time-consuming and struggles to match the fine-grained personalization that students appear to want.

finding.finding_summary: The study did not measure math learning or achievement directly, but it did examine how teachers used generative AI to personalize middle school math problems and how students rated those problems. Teachers spent an average of 246 seconds per problem (SD=165.7; n=143 problems) and the authors conclude that this process was not time-efficient enough to scale well; student ratings of interestingness and closeness were modest (means around 2.5/5), and the paper reports that 3–5 prompts per problem was associated with higher student ratings by about 0.24 points on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073).
finding.measure: Student ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to interests; teacher time creating personalized math problems
finding.std_deviation: SD=165.7 seconds (time per problem); SD=1.24 interestingness, SD=1.28 closeness

finding.finding_summary: Students generally responded positively to personalized tasks when the problems matched their interests, especially when specific popular-culture references aligned with their preferences. Across 53 problems with closed-ended ratings, the average interestingness rating was 2.46/5 (SD=1.24) and the average closeness rating was 2.53/5 (SD=1.28); in Unit 6, these rose to 2.56 and 2.66 respectively, and the increase from Unit 4 to Unit 6 was statistically significant (B=0.33, SE=0.095, t=3.49, p=0.0012).
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests; open-ended feedback about whether problems were interesting
finding.study_size: n=52-53 problems with closed-ended ratings; n=454-449 open-ended responses; n=521 students

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that teacher-in-the-loop personalization was not especially efficient. Teachers used 558 prompts to create 143 problems, averaging 3.2 prompts per problem (SD=2.6), and each problem took about 246 seconds (roughly 4 minutes; SD=165.7 seconds) to pose. Efficiency did not improve over time; in fact, Unit 6 required more prompts and more time than Unit 4, with increases of 1.26 prompts per problem (B=1.26, SE=0.41, t=3.08, p=0.0025) and 70.4 seconds per problem (B=70.4, SE=29.6, t=2.38, p=0.0189).
finding.measure: Teacher prompts per problem and time spent creating each personalized problem
finding.effect_size: B=1.26 (prompts per problem increase from Unit 4 to 6); B=70.4 seconds (time increase from Unit 4 to 6); B=0.240 for 3–5 prompts vs. other ranges on student ratings
finding.std_deviation: SD=2.6 prompts per problem; SD=165.7 seconds per problem; Unit 4 SD=2.6 prompts, Unit 6 SD=2.6 prompts

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that teachers iteratively refined their prompting practices and improved their ability to craft interesting problems with generative AI, which the authors frame as professional learning and reflective practice. However, this outcome is indirect and not measured as a student durable-skill outcome; the evidence comes from teacher prompting behavior and qualitative interpretation of how prompting evolved across Units 4 and 6.
finding.measure: Teacher prompting strategies, iteration, and reflection while using ChatGPT

paper_profiles.title: Do intelligent tutoring systems benefit K-12 students? A meta-analysis and evaluation of heterogeneity of treatment effects in the U.S.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) improve K-12 students’ academic achievement in U.S. school settings, and under what conditions those effects are stronger or weaker. The authors frame ITS as AI-driven software that personalizes instruction turn-by-turn through feedback, hints, worked examples, and other supports, and they focus on whether these systems deliver reliable learning gains across different study designs and implementation contexts.

The study is a meta-analysis of 18 experimental studies from U.S. elementary, middle, and high school contexts, yielding 77 effect sizes across 11 ITS. The authors used a multivariate multilevel meta-regression with fixed effects for ITS names, then examined heterogeneity across internal-validity features and across moderators in the MUTOS framework (units, treatments, observing operations, and setting). They also used MetaForest to identify the most important moderators of effect size.

Overall, ITS had a statistically significant positive effect on learning outcomes (g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). Effects were fairly similar for elementary and middle school students and for disadvantaged subgroups such as low achievers, English learners, and students in poverty, but smaller in rural settings. Moderator analyses suggested that worked-out examples, intervention duration, intervention condition, and immediate measurement were among the most influential factors; just-in-time hints were not statistically significant, and effects tended to decline as interventions became longer. The authors conclude that ITS can benefit K-12 learners, but implementation details and measurement choices matter, and evidence for some hypothesized internal-validity differences was mixed or weak.

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis found positive effects for reading/writing outcomes in ITS studies. For reading and writing, the pooled effect size was g=0.323 across 55 effect sizes, with a statistically significant positive confidence interval, indicating improved literacy-related achievement relative to control conditions.
finding.measure: Reading and writing outcomes; literacy achievement measures (standardized and researcher-developed tests across studies)

finding.finding_summary: ITS showed a positive effect on mathematics outcomes across the included K-12 studies. The pooled effect size for mathematics was g=0.253 across 22 effect sizes, and the estimate was statistically significant, suggesting a modest improvement in math achievement from ITS use.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement tests

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively discusses motivational and engagement-related supports as moderators of achievement effects, but these were not measured as standalone social-emotional outcomes. Motivation support as an ITS feature was associated with a positive achievement effect (g=0.265 across 23 effect sizes), suggesting that systems including motivational scaffolds tended to perform better than controls.
finding.measure: Not direct social-emotional outcome; ITS support type 'motivation support' as moderator of achievement effects

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Multimodal Feedback Using Multiple External Representations: Strategy Profiles and Learning in High School Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether students’ voluntary use of elaborated, personalized feedback in a high school physics platform is associated with better learning outcomes, and whether those associations depend on students’ representational competence. The authors focus on feedback delivered after multiple-choice kinematics exercises, comparing simple verification feedback (correct/incorrect) with optional elaborated feedback available in three external representations: verbal, graphical/pictorial, and mathematical.

The study used a custom web platform (KI4SCool) in German high schools over 16–24 weeks with 661 students in grades 10–11 who completed pre- and post-tests and at least one exercise. Because the design was observational rather than randomized, the analysis examined associations using linear mixed-effects models, correlations, clustering of feedback-use patterns, and ANCOVA-based group comparisons. The paper reports a small positive association between more frequent use of elaborated feedback and higher post-test scores, even after adjusting for prior knowledge, platform performance, and confidence, but it explicitly cautions that causality cannot be inferred.

The authors also identified distinct feedback-use profiles: some students rarely opened elaborated feedback, some used all three representations frequently, and others favored verbal feedback more heavily. Time-resolved clustering did not reveal meaningful temporal strategy differences beyond frequency of use. Overall, the paper concludes that elaborated multimodal feedback is associated with modest gains in post-test performance in this physics context, and that adaptive tutoring systems should consider both feedback elaboration and representational format when tailoring instruction. However, the evidence remains correlational, and the observed benefits are small.

finding.finding_summary: Elaborated multirepresentational feedback was associated with higher post-test physics performance. In linear mixed-effects models, feedback frequency predicted post-test score with a standardized β=0.13 (95% CI [0.05, 0.22]) in Cohort 1 (n=351) and β=0.08 (95% CI [0.00, 0.16], p=.054) in Cohort 2 (n=310), after adjusting for pre-test score, platform score, exercises solved, and confidence. The outcome measure was post-test score on kinematics tests.
finding.measure: Physics kinematics post-test score (% correct)

finding.finding_summary: The paper measured students’ average response confidence and examined whether it related to feedback use and post-test performance. Average confidence was not a significant predictor of post-test score in either cohort (Cohort 1: β=0.07, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.17]; Cohort 2: β=0.09, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.18]), but it was used as an individual-difference covariate in the models and as a potential confounder for feedback use.
finding.measure: Average response confidence on a 1-5 scale

paper_profiles.title: The Illusion of Understanding: How Middle-Schoolers Fail to Regulate Inquiry with ChatGPT in a Science Task
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle-school students use ChatGPT during science inquiry tasks, with a particular focus on whether they can conduct meaningful question-asking (QA) cycles. The authors frame the problem as one of AI-mediated inquiry quality: students may be able to access answers from GenAI, but still fail to formulate effective prompts, evaluate response quality, or regulate their search by asking follow-up questions.

The study involved 63 French middle school students aged 14–15 who completed six science investigation tasks in school. Students were shown either efficient or inefficient prompt suggestions, could choose to use them or write their own prompts, and had to rate every ChatGPT response they received. Researchers analyzed prompt discrimination, answer evaluation, follow-up behavior, and final task explanations, along with relations to self-reported prior knowledge, AI attitudes, and metacognitive skills.

Results showed substantial over-reliance and weak calibration. Students were near chance at distinguishing efficient from inefficient prompts, frequently rated low-quality AI answers as useful, and rarely asked follow-up questions even after unsatisfactory responses. Final task success was only moderate (mean success rate 0.51), and better outcomes were associated with receiving more high-level AI answers, being more sensitive to answer quality, and asking follow-up questions. Positive AI attitudes and higher self-reported prior knowledge were linked to poorer judgment, while metacognitive regulation and more skeptical views of AI were associated with better interaction quality. The paper concludes that students need explicit AI literacy and metacognitive scaffolding, not just technical familiarity with GenAI.

finding.finding_summary: Students used ChatGPT during six science investigation tasks, but their science-task performance remained only moderate despite unrestricted access. Final written explanations were scored for conceptual understanding; the average success rate was 0.51 (SD=0.25), indicating that GenAI-supported inquiry did not reliably produce strong scientific understanding.
finding.measure: Binary-coded correctness/depth of final written science explanations across six science investigation tasks

finding.finding_summary: The central finding is that middle-school students struggled to regulate inquiry with ChatGPT: they were near chance in distinguishing efficient from inefficient prompts (Md'=0.19, SD=0.8; t=1.77, p=0.08) and near chance in evaluating AI answer quality (Md'=0.07, SD=1.2; t=-0.45, p=0.65). Only 14 students asked follow-up questions (22 total across six tasks), showing weak metacognitive monitoring and regulation in GenAI-mediated learning.
finding.measure: Prompt discrimination sensitivity (d′), answer evaluation sensitivity (d′), and follow-up-question behavior

finding.finding_summary: The study found patterns consistent with over-reliance and premature termination of inquiry, suggesting reduced persistence and self-regulation in the AI-supported task. Students often accepted inefficient prompts, frequently judged low-level answers as useful, and rarely continued questioning after receiving unsatisfactory responses.
finding.measure: Prompt use behavior, acceptance of AI responses, and frequency of follow-up questions

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Usage of Generative AI for Group Project-Based Offline Art Courses in Elementary Schools
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2025 ACM SIGCHI Conference on Computer-Supported Cooperative Work & Social Computing (CSCW '25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI can support elementary school students during group project-based learning in offline art classes. The authors focus on the problem that young students often struggle to seek information, generate ideas, and translate those ideas into tangible project outcomes during classroom art projects, while teachers cannot always provide timely one-on-one support.

Across a four-phase field study in Chinese elementary classrooms, the researchers first observed students using DALL-E and GPT through a standard chat interface, then built and evaluated a custom interface called AskArt. AskArt adds project-specific introductions, audio-to-text input, suggested follow-up prompts, and a select-and-generate workflow that links GPT outputs to DALL-E image generation. The study involved 132 students and two experienced art teachers across several offline class sessions.

The main findings were that GenAI helped students brainstorm project ideas, gather background information, and get personalized implementation guidance; however, students also struggled with query formulation, typing, and sometimes misunderstanding which model to use. AskArt reduced incorrect use of the tools, improved students’ understanding of how to use GenAI, and increased overall satisfaction in the intervention groups, but it did not significantly improve perceived challenge, creativity expression, or team collaboration. Teachers reported that GenAI increased engagement but raised concerns about misuse and interface suitability.

finding.finding_summary: GenAI was helpful for art project ideation and implementation in elementary school PBL art classes. In Phase 2, six students rated the statement that generated content helped their group come up with more ideas at M=5.67 (SD=0.82 on a 7-point scale), and students reported that GPT and DALL-E helped with background knowledge, design choices, and visualization of final artifacts.
finding.measure: Student ratings of ideation assistance; interviews and observed project work in art classes
finding.study_size: n=6 respondents for the rating; overall field study n=132 students

finding.finding_summary: AskArt users reported higher overall satisfaction with the class than students in the baseline condition without AskArt. In Phase 4, satisfaction was significantly higher for the experimental group (M=6.64, SD=0.12) than the baseline group (M=5.46, SD=0.27), t=3.62, p=0.0005, indicating a positive impact on students’ classroom experience and engagement-related attitudes.
finding.measure: Overall satisfaction with the class (7-point questionnaire)
finding.study_size: n=97 valid respondents for the compared groups (43 AskArt, 54 baseline)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved collaboration-related processes but no measurable gain in team collaboration ratings. Students used GenAI in different group strategies for brainstorming and task division, but the experimental group did not differ significantly from the baseline on team collaboration (M=5.59, SD=0.24 vs. M=5.31, SD=0.30; t=0.70, p=0.48). Teachers also observed both collective brainstorming and individual task balancing, suggesting process-level collaboration support without a clear outcome advantage.
finding.measure: Team collaboration participation ratings; interview and observation of group collaboration strategies
finding.study_size: n=97 valid respondents for the compared groups (43 AskArt, 54 baseline)

finding.finding_summary: AskArt streamlined student interactions with GenAI by reducing incorrect usage and making prompting easier, especially through project-specific introductions, suggested follow-ups, and select-and-generate features. The paper reports that incorrect GPT/DALL-E use disappeared in Phases 3 and 4, and the audio-to-text feature helped reduce typing burden, though the generated voice input was sometimes disorganized or incomplete.
finding.measure: Observed prompt accuracy / incorrect usage counts; qualitative usability feedback on input workflow
finding.study_size: Phases 2-4 classroom sessions with students (n=132 total across the study)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived that GenAI increased student engagement during the art courses, but they also expressed concerns about misuse and interface suitability. This suggests a beneficial engagement effect accompanied by implementation concerns rather than a uniformly positive experience.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about student engagement and concerns

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Design Features of an Intelligent Tutoring System for Advanced Mathematics Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates two design features in an intelligent tutoring system (ITS) called Xiaomai for advanced mathematics: free-response questions with automatic feedback/self-evaluation, and an error-reflection prompt that asks learners to explain why they made mistakes. The authors ask whether these design choices improve learning and practice performance compared with more conventional multiple-choice questions and with no reflection.

The study recruited 129 university students in central China who had taken advanced mathematics; 120 remained in the final sample (n=120, mean age 20.13). Participants were randomly assigned to a 2x2 factorial experiment crossing item format (multiple-choice vs. free-response) and reflection (reflection vs. no reflection), completed a pretest, practiced for 40 minutes in Xiaomai on three knowledge components, and then completed a posttest. Practice data included number of attempts, correctness, and time per item.

Results showed that multiple-choice practice outperformed free-response practice on several measures. Students in the multiple-choice conditions had significantly better practice performance, attempted more items, spent less time per item, and achieved higher posttest scores than students in the free-response conditions; the item-format effect on posttest was marginal after controlling for pretest, and the paper reports larger pre-post effect sizes for multiple-choice groups than free-response groups. In contrast, error reflection did not significantly improve practice performance, correctness, time, or posttest learning gains, and no interaction with prior knowledge was detected. The authors conclude that the current implementation of free-response and reflection in Xiaomai does not improve advanced mathematics learning and suggest redesigning the system, such as adding incorrect examples/misconceptions and revising or better instrumenting the reflection feature.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students practicing with multiple-choice items learned more than those using free-response items. After controlling for pretest scores, the multiple-choice conditions had higher posttest scores (estimated marginal means 9.21 vs. 7.94; n=120), and the authors reported larger pre-post effect sizes for multiple-choice groups than free-response groups, while the item-format main effect was only marginally significant (F(1,115)=3.72, p=0.06).
finding.measure: Pretest and posttest mathematics scores; pretest-to-posttest learning gain in advanced mathematics

finding.finding_summary: The error-reflection feature did not improve learning or practice outcomes, indicating no measurable benefit for metacognitive reflection in this implementation. Reflection had no significant effect on posttest scores (F(1,115)=0.07, p=0.79), and it was not related to learning gain even when prior knowledge was split into high/low groups; the prior-knowledge-by-reflection interaction was also not significant.
finding.measure: Reflection prompt requiring students to report reasons for errors; posttest scores and pretest-to-posttest learning gain

finding.finding_summary: Free-response questions were less efficient than multiple-choice questions during practice. Students in multiple-choice conditions attempted more questions (M=21.98, SD=8.11) than students in free-response conditions (M=15.41, SD=8.61; t(118)=4.29, p<.001), and they spent less time per question (item-format effect on time: B=46.26, SE=8.92, p<.001).
finding.measure: Number of attempts during practice; time per question

finding.finding_summary: The paper tested whether error reflection improved students’ practice behavior, but it did not. Reflection had no significant effect on number of attempts (M=18.53 with reflection vs. M=19.30 without reflection; t(118)=0.47, p=0.64), suggesting no observable benefit for persistence or engagement in the session.
finding.measure: Number of practice attempts as a behavioral proxy for engagement/persistence

paper_profiles.title: How Students Use AI Feedback Matters: Experimental Evidence on Physics Achievement and Autonomy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether the way students use generative AI feedback changes its effects on learning and autonomy. The authors argue that prior AI-in-education research often focuses on the content or accuracy of feedback, while paying less attention to usage patterns such as compulsory exposure versus student-initiated on-demand help. They test whether personalized AI feedback helps or harms students differently depending on baseline achievement level and control structure.

The study reports two sequential randomized controlled trials in a naturalistic high school physics setting in southwest China. Experiment 1 compared compulsory personalized recommendation with GAI-generated heuristic hints against conventional workbook answers/explanations and a no-recommendation control; Experiment 2 compared fully learner-controlled on-demand help against shared-control on-demand help and control. Across both experiments, students completed physics exams and autonomy/SRL questionnaires before and after five-week interventions, with subgroup analyses by prior achievement.

The main findings are heterogeneous.
