In Experiment 1, low-achieving students improved on physics achievement when receiving AI-generated heuristic hints, while medium-achieving students declined when given conventional workbook answers/explanations, and high-achieving students showed no achievement gain but a decline in self-regulated learning. In Experiment 2, fully learner-controlled on-demand AI help improved achievement for high-achieving students without reducing autonomy, whereas lower-achieving students experienced declines in autonomy, especially in technical-psychological self-regulation-like dimensions. Overall, the paper concludes that AI feedback is not uniformly beneficial; its effects depend strongly on usage pattern and learner achievement level.

finding.finding_summary: Across the two RCTs, the AI-feedback interventions produced heterogeneous effects on physics exam performance. In Experiment 1 (n=121 valid cases), low-achieving students improved substantially with AI-generated heuristic solution hints (d=0.673, p<0.05), while medium-achieving students declined when given conventional workbook answers/explanations (d=-0.539, p<0.05); the full sample showed no significant overall effect. In Experiment 2 (n=266 valid cases), fully learner-controlled on-demand AI help improved performance for high-achieving students (d=0.378, p<0.05), with no overall effect across the full sample.
finding.measure: Physics exam scores (pre/post standardized z-scores)

finding.finding_summary: The study directly measured learner autonomy/self-regulated learning using questionnaire instruments and found both benefits and harms depending on condition and achievement level. In Experiment 1, high-achieving students experienced a significant decline in SRL under compulsory AI-powered personalized recommendation (d=-0.477, p<0.05) with no achievement gain. In Experiment 2, autonomy did not decline for high-achieving students under fully learner-controlled on-demand help, but lower-achieving students showed a significant autonomy drop (d=-0.383, p<0.05), especially on the technical-psychological dimension (d=-0.549, p<0.05).
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning / learner autonomy questionnaire scores

paper_profiles.title: Learning About Algorithm Auditing in Five Steps: Scaffolding How High School Youth Can Systematically and Critically Evaluate Machine Learning Applications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to help high school students systematically and critically evaluate machine learning applications, especially when the systems are opaque and may behave in biased or harmful ways. The authors argue that prior K-12 AI learning activities often emphasize discussion or one-off observations rather than a structured method for investigating how AI systems behave in practice.

To address this, the paper proposes a five-step algorithm-auditing process for youth learning activities: developing a hypothesis, generating systematic inputs, running tests, analyzing data, and reporting results. The authors designed and iteratively refined workshop activities in an after-school science program, then present a detailed case study of two high school students auditing peer-designed TikTok filters. The students used the scaffolded process to test a filter and concluded that it systematically altered people toward female-presenting appearances, with additional changes involving hair, skin tone, blush, and other features.

The study is primarily qualitative and focuses on how scaffolds supported youth participation in each auditing step, including hypothesis generation, input selection, recording test results, and communicating findings. The main conclusion is that algorithm auditing can be adapted for high school learning, but students need substantial scaffolding to move beyond casual observations toward systematic evaluation. The authors also note practical challenges for classroom adoption, including time, tool access, input generation, and the need for teacher support.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that a five-step algorithm-auditing scaffold helped high school youth engage in systematic, critical evaluation of an ML-powered TikTok filter. In the featured case study (n=2 focal students; 14 youth in the workshop), students generated hypotheses, constructed a 33-image test set, analyzed input-output pairs, and drew evidence-based conclusions about gendered bias in the filter’s behavior.
finding.measure: Youth participation in algorithm-auditing steps, quality of hypotheses, input generation, test documentation, data analysis, and evidence-based reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that algorithm auditing can be integrated into K-12 learning contexts and identifies implementation considerations for classrooms, including tool access, collaboration structures, and teacher professional development. While not an outcome evaluation of policy change, it provides evidence that audit-based learning activities are institutionally feasible and highlights constraints that schools would need to address.
finding.measure: Feasibility and classroom-implementation considerations for integrating algorithm auditing in school settings

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in K-12 Education: The CyberScholar Initiative
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether CyberScholar, a generative AI writing assistant, can support K-12 students’ writing through formative feedback aligned to teacher rubrics, classroom materials, and subject-specific expectations. The central problem is how to provide timely, detailed, and pedagogically grounded feedback in middle and high school writing instruction, while also considering AI literacy and the changing role of teachers in AI-supported feedback loops.

The study used a qualitative multiple case study design across four public schools in the United States, including one middle school and three high schools in diverse socioeconomic contexts. Data came from observations, surveys, and interviews with 121 students and 4 teachers, with 54 students and 3 teachers completing post-surveys and 8 students plus 1 teacher interviewed. CyberScholar was piloted in grades 7, 8, 10, and 11 in English Language Arts, Social Studies, and Modern World History classes; the system was customized using retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering to align feedback with teachers’ rubrics and instructional materials.

Findings were based on thematic analysis of participant perceptions rather than outcome testing. Students generally described the tool as useful for detailed and specific feedback, interactive clarification, rubric-based scoring, and helping them perceive improvements in writing quality; some also reported improved grammar, transitions, and sentence clarity after revision. At the same time, some students found the rating displays inconsistent when the same paper received different scores on repeated submissions. The authors conclude that CyberScholar shows promise for supporting formative writing feedback and student revision, but it should complement rather than replace teacher feedback and requires further development and evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students perceived CyberScholar as helpful for improving writing, especially through detailed, specific, and rubric-aligned feedback. Across the 121 participating students, 36 said they would like to use the tool again, while 11 were hesitant; students reported improvements in grammar, transitions, sentence clarity, and overall writing quality after revising with AI feedback, but the evidence is qualitative and perception-based rather than a controlled outcome measure.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of writing support; thematic analysis of surveys and interviews; rubric score changes reported in examples
finding.study_size: n=121 students, n=4 teachers; post-survey n=54 students, n=3 teachers; interviews n=8 students, n=1 teacher

finding.finding_summary: Students described the tool as engaging, motivating, and supportive of self-directed revision, with some saying it made feedback more interactive and helped them feel they could improve their writing. The paper also reports that 36 students wanted to use CyberScholar again, suggesting positive acceptance and engagement, though this was not measured with a standardized scale.
finding.measure: Student willingness to reuse the tool; survey and interview themes about engagement, motivation, and self-directed learning
finding.study_size: n=121 students, n=4 teachers; post-survey n=54 students, n=3 teachers; interviews n=8 students, n=1 teacher

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that CyberScholar supported self-regulation, metacognition, and critical thinking by prompting students to revise drafts, ask follow-up questions, and reflect on rubric-based feedback. The authors explicitly frame the tool as supporting a dialogic feedback process and note that students used repeated submissions to examine changes in rubric scores, but no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Thematic evidence of self-regulation, metacognition, and critical thinking during revision cycles
finding.study_size: n=121 students, n=4 teachers; post-survey n=54 students, n=3 teachers; interviews n=8 students, n=1 teacher

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests CyberScholar may save time by providing quick, detailed feedback and reducing the need for peer or self-analysis, with some students describing it as faster and easier to use than other feedback sources. The paper also suggests that it could support teacher workload by shifting teachers toward managing AI feedback loops, but this is an interpretation rather than a measured efficiency outcome.
finding.measure: Student and teacher perceptions of speed, ease of use, and workload implications
finding.study_size: n=121 students, n=4 teachers; post-survey n=54 students, n=3 teachers; interviews n=8 students, n=1 teacher

paper_profiles.title: Using Transformers to Provide Teachers with Personalized Feedback on their Classroom Discourse: The TalkMoves Application
paper_profiles.population: K-12 mathematics teachers (grades 3-12; pilot users in two U.S. midwestern school districts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of giving K-12 mathematics teachers timely, scalable, and individualized feedback on their classroom discourse. The authors focus on “talk moves,” a set of instructional discourse strategies associated with productive mathematics discussions, and argue that current human-observation approaches are too costly and time-intensive to scale across many teachers.

To support this goal, the paper presents the TalkMoves application, an end-to-end system that uses automated speech recognition and transformer-based natural language processing to analyze classroom transcripts and classify teacher utterances into six accountable-talk categories plus a none label. The model is trained and evaluated on 501 transcript files from K-12 math lessons (176,757 total sentences) and achieves best test performance with RoBERTa-Large (F1 = 79.33%, MCC = 0.7779). The system then turns these predictions into a teacher-facing dashboard showing talk-move frequencies, teacher/student talk balance, wait time, and related discourse indicators.

The paper is primarily a technical system-development and model-evaluation study, not an impact study of student learning outcomes. It reports that the model performance is substantially better than the authors’ earlier baseline (F1 = 65%) and that the application was piloted by 21 teachers in grades 3-12 across two districts during the 2019-2020 academic year, with teachers viewing feedback, completing surveys, and participating in interviews. The main conclusion is that transformer-based models can produce reliable automated feedback for teachers, but the paper also notes technical limitations, especially errors in recognizing children’s speech and underestimation of student talk by the ASR system.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that a transformer-based classifier can automate teacher-feedback generation for classroom discourse analysis, reducing reliance on highly trained human coders. The best model (RoBERTa-Large) achieved F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779 on the held-out test set, compared with the prior baseline F1 = 65%, suggesting improved feasibility and scalability for producing feedback on teachers’ talk moves.
finding.measure: Model classification performance for talk-move labeling used to generate automated teacher feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper is situated in K-12 mathematics classrooms and aims to support discourse practices tied to mathematical learning, but it does not report student achievement outcomes, test scores, or any direct change in mathematical numeracy from using the system. The evidence presented is limited to model-performance metrics and teacher-feedback functionality rather than learning gains.
finding.measure: Student mathematical achievement or numeracy outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The system is intended to promote productive classroom discourse and engagement, and the pilot involved teacher surveys and interviews about the feedback interface. However, the paper does not report quantitative changes in student engagement, motivation, or self-regulation, so no direct social-emotional impact can be inferred from the reported evidence.
finding.measure: Student engagement or related social-emotional outcomes
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers in pilot use; student outcomes not reported

paper_profiles.title: Excited, Skeptical, or Worried? A Multi-Institutional Study of Student Views on Generative AI in Computing Education
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 25th Koli Calling International Conference on Computing Education Research
paper_profiles.population: High School; Undergraduate; Master’s students in computing programs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how students in different educational contexts use and perceive generative AI (GenAI) in computing education, with a particular focus on high schools, vocational colleges, and research universities. The authors note that most prior work centered on university students, leaving high school and vocational contexts underexplored. To address this gap, they conducted a multi-institutional survey of 410 students from 23 institutions in the Netherlands.

The survey examined GenAI use frequency, attitudes, perceived ethics, policy awareness, help-seeking behavior, and perceived effects on learning. It was adapted from prior GenAI education surveys and included both closed and open-ended questions. Students responded about general GenAI use and, for the second part, a specific computing course or informatics class. The analysis used non-parametric group comparisons, correlation analyses, and qualitative coding of open responses.

The main finding is that students across all groups use GenAI frequently for learning and text tasks, while higher-education students use it more for programming and code debugging. High school students expressed more trust and fewer negative emotions toward GenAI, but also reported more perceived misuse and more permissive ethical views in some cases. Across groups, most students saw GenAI as helpful for learning but not appropriate for exams or graded assignments. The authors conclude that GenAI has different meanings and roles across educational levels, and that educators should clearly communicate boundaries and strengthen GenAI literacy, especially for high school students transitioning into higher education.

finding.finding_summary: Students across all three educational levels reported frequent GenAI use for learning, and the study found that higher use was generally associated with more positive attitudes and less concern about learning impacts. However, qualitative responses also described worry, skepticism, overreliance, and occasional feelings of reduced thinking effort, suggesting both supportive and potentially undermining effects on motivation and self-regulation. The study is based on 410 students (n=410) and reports several significant group differences, but no single intervention effect size.
finding.measure: Self-reported GenAI use frequency, perceived learning impact, and attitudes toward GenAI

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examined beliefs about whether GenAI hinders learning, whether it can guide students as effectively as teachers, and whether it affects critical thinking and self-sufficiency. Students often said GenAI can help with explanations and practice, but many also warned it can reduce independent problem solving, debugging practice, and critical thinking; higher-education students were more likely to agree that frequent GenAI use can hinder learning, while high school students were more trusting. Sample size was n=410, with additional open-ended responses from 318 students about attitude change and 242 about learning effects.
finding.measure: Likert-scale perceptions of learning hindrance, trust in guidance, overreliance, and open-ended reports of learning process effects

finding.finding_summary: The study substantively examined institutional GenAI policy clarity, perceived allowance, and ethical norms across high school, vocational college, and university settings. College students reported clearer and more permissive policies, while high school students reported more confusion about rules; across all groups, most students believed GenAI should be allowed only under certain conditions and not for exams or graded tasks. The study surveyed 410 students from 23 institutions and found significant between-group differences in policy perception and ethics.
finding.measure: Perceived institutional GenAI policy clarity, allowance spectrum, and ethical judgments about GenAI use in assignments/exams

paper_profiles.title: App Planner: Utilizing Generative AI in K-12 Mobile App Development Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces App Planner, a generative-AI-supported scaffolding tool for K-12 mobile app development education. The system is designed to help students move through early-stage app ideation and design by prompting them to define a problem, identify users, brainstorm features, and reflect on both positive and negative societal impacts of their proposed app.

The authors report a small pilot usability study with five high-school seniors who completed two app-design tasks, with App Planner used for one task and not the other in a counterbalanced manner. Data came from observations and semi-structured interviews after the tasks. Students generally said the tool made it easier to brainstorm, proceed more quickly, and think more deeply about user needs and unintended consequences, though some also preferred to rely on their own ideas first and worried about overreliance on AI.

Overall, the paper concludes that App Planner can support creative ideation, human-centered thinking, and ethical reflection in early app development. At the same time, the authors explicitly note a possible unintended harm: if AI-generated suggestions are too repetitive or generic, the tool could eventually plateau creativity or encourage dependency, motivating longer-term studies.

finding.finding_summary: In a pilot usability study with five high-school students (n=5), App Planner was reported to improve brainstorming, ideation, and reflection during app design. Participants said it helped them think more broadly about users and consequences, with one student noting it made brainstorming easier and allowed them to create things more quickly; however, the evidence is qualitative and based on interviews/observations rather than a quantified learning outcome.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interviews and observations of app-design tasks; reported changes in brainstorming, ideation, user-centered thinking, and ethical reflection

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that App Planner made the app-planning process more efficient and easier to navigate, especially when they were stuck and needed guidance. The paper describes perceived gains in speed and ease of proceeding through design steps, but no timing or productivity metrics were reported.
finding.measure: Perceived efficiency and ease of progressing through app-design tasks

finding.finding_summary: The tool was intended to expand ethics and societal-impact considerations in K-12 computing education, and participants reported that reflecting on positive and negative app impacts was a novel and helpful prompt. At the same time, the paper raises an institutional concern that generative-AI scaffolds may foster creative stagnation or dependency over time, indicating both a positive educational contribution and a potential longer-term harm.
finding.measure: Participant reflections on ethical/societal consideration in app design; authors' discussion of potential long-term educational dependence on AI

paper_profiles.title: Children’s Overtrust and Shifting Perspectives of Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how middle school girls understand and evaluate generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, and how exposure to AI mistakes changes those understandings. The authors were interested in children’s initial trust in genAI, their reasoning about its capabilities and limitations, and their views on whether and how genAI should be used in school settings.

The study used two educational workshop sessions with 26 middle school girls in university-based STEM outreach programs. Participants first discussed perceived benefits and drawbacks of ChatGPT, then completed a guessing-game activity in which they judged whether several ChatGPT outputs were correct or incorrect, including deliberately wrong answers about math, research papers, and procedural help. One of the two workshop groups also ideated future genAI applications, and both groups discussed fairness, cheating, access, and school policy.

The main finding was that the girls initially overtrusted ChatGPT, often judging incorrect outputs as correct because of visual presentation, seemingly transparent reasoning, or their assumption that an AI should handle computational tasks well. After seeing erroneous examples, many shifted toward a more skeptical and nuanced view, recognizing that genAI can be wrong and should not be trusted in high-stakes contexts such as medical advice. At the same time, they remained optimistic about future uses, including homework help and other school applications, while expressing concerns about cheating, unequal access, and policy fairness.

finding.finding_summary: The workshop prompted a substantial change in students’ critical evaluation of ChatGPT. Initially, 59% of assessments of incorrect outputs were wrong, reflecting overtrust; after exposure to erroneous examples, students became more skeptical and better able to question genAI’s shortcomings and decide when it should not be used, especially in high-stakes situations.
finding.measure: Qualitative judgments of ChatGPT output correctness during the guessing-game activity and post-discussion reasoning about limitations

finding.finding_summary: Students discussed school policy, fairness, cheating, and access issues around genAI in classrooms. Many saw educational benefits such as homework help, but they also worried about cheating, negative grade effects, and inequitable access if ChatGPT were paid, and some supported school bans while others argued for limited, allowed use.
finding.measure: Open-ended group discussion on school policies, cheating, and paid access to ChatGPT Plus

finding.finding_summary: Participants viewed genAI as potentially useful for homework help and improving school learning, but they also recognized that incorrect outputs could harm schoolwork. In discussion, they suggested ChatGPT might help students understand material or support lower-resourced schools, yet could also negatively affect grades if trusted without verification.
finding.measure: Discussion of schoolwork/homework use cases and perceived effects on classroom learning

finding.finding_summary: Students expected ChatGPT to handle arithmetic correctly, but the deliberately incorrect multiplication example surprised many and revealed that genAI is not reliable for math. In the combined workshop data, many participants incorrectly judged the wrong multiplication output as correct; specifically, 59% of incorrect-output judgments across the targeted items were erroneous, and the multiplication item was one of the clearest cases of overtrust.
finding.measure: Judgments of ChatGPT’s multiplication answer in the guessing game

paper_profiles.title: A systematic review of AI-driven intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) in K-12 education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic review examines the evidence on AI-driven intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) in K-12 education, focusing on two questions: what experimental designs are used to evaluate ITSs, and what effects ITSs have on students’ learning and performance. The authors note that prior ITS research often mixes school-age and adult populations or blends school and professional settings, making K-12-specific evidence difficult to interpret.

The review synthesizes 28 studies involving 4,597 students across elementary, middle, and high school settings, most of which used quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test designs. The interventions were mainly in STEM subjects, with some language and literacy studies, and compared ITSs against teachers, non-intelligent tutoring systems, modified ITS versions, or no control. Across the included studies, ITSs generally produced positive learning and performance effects, especially when compared with traditional teacher-led instruction; however, effects were less consistent when ITSs were compared with non-intelligent or modified digital systems.

The review concludes that ITSs can support K-12 learning, particularly when they include personalization, adaptivity, immediate feedback, and are used under suitable instructional conditions. At the same time, the authors emphasize that many interventions were short, sample sizes and study diversity remain limited, and ethical implications were largely absent from the reviewed literature. Overall, the paper argues that ITSs are promising but that stronger, longer-term, and more diverse K-12 studies are still needed.

finding.finding_summary: Across the review, math-focused ITS studies were generally positive, especially when compared with teacher-led instruction, but results were mixed when ITSs were compared with non-intelligent or modified digital systems. Reported examples included medium-to-large gains such as Hedges’s g=0.68 for 8th-grade Pythagorean theorem learning (n=163; experimental n=90, control n=73), d=0.77 for planning skills in grade 5 writing-related instruction, d=0.99 and d=1.30 against national test benchmarks, and d=0.31 to 0.87 in several quasi-experimental math studies.
finding.measure: Pre/post tests of math learning, algebra exams, placement exams, problem-solving and fraction tasks
finding.study_size: n=4597 (review total); math studies varied by study
finding.effect_size: mixed; examples include g=0.68, d=0.77, d=0.99, d=1.30, d=0.31, d=0.87

finding.finding_summary: The review includes multiple K-12 literacy and writing studies showing positive effects of ITS use. For example, Writing Pal users (n=113) had significantly improved essay scores from November to May with d=0.71, and a 5th-grade We Write study reported a medium effect on planning skills (d=0.77) while writing quality gains were smaller and not significant. The review also includes first- and second-language studies where ITS-supported learners generally outperformed controls or showed improved language-related performance.
finding.measure: Essay scores, planning skills, writing quality, first-language and second-language learning outcomes
finding.study_size: varies by study; e.g. n=113 for Writing Pal, n=299/165 for We Write (pre/post subsets varied)
finding.effect_size: d=0.71; d=0.77; other study-specific effects not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review includes English as a foreign language and second-language ITS studies that generally favored the ITS condition. For instance, Choi’s EFL study reported significant pre/post gains with a strong effect for both middle- and high-school students, and Cui et al.’s language-learning condition showed larger gains for the ITS group than the comparison app. The paper does not isolate speaking/listening outcomes, but it substantively treats language learning outcomes as part of its K-12 ITS evidence base.
finding.measure: Second-language / foreign-language learning gains on pre/post tests

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies targeted science- or physics-related learning and generally found positive effects, though not always versus all controls. Examples include a physics study where the ITS condition outperformed the control with significantly higher gains, and another science/physics-related line of evidence where the review notes overall positive performance effects for ITSs in STEM contexts. The paper’s emphasis is broader than scientific reasoning alone, so this outcome is included with moderate confidence.
finding.measure: Physics/science post-tests and learning gains

finding.finding_summary: The review substantively addresses durable skills such as self-regulation, metacognition, planning, and critical thinking when these were measured as outcomes of ITS use. For example, students using ITS-supported planning tools improved planning skills (d=0.77), and several studies reported benefits from self-assessment, progress information, or goal-setting supports. The review also includes a no-control study where 300 high school students improved in problem-solving, critical thinking, and logical reasoning after an ITS-integrated math intervention.
finding.measure: Planning skills, self-regulated learning supports, self-assessment, problem-solving, critical thinking, logical reasoning
finding.study_size: varies by study; e.g. n=300 for one no-control study, n=299/165 in We Write subsets

finding.finding_summary: The review includes some evidence related to engagement, independent learning, and student perception of support, especially in studies of personalized and adaptive ITSs. For example, interviewed students in one study reported that learning was facilitated and that they could complete assignments without teacher assistance, suggesting improved learner independence and perceived support. However, these outcomes are secondary to the review’s main focus on learning/performance, so confidence is moderate.
finding.measure: Student interview responses on facilitation, independence, and perceived support; engagement-related observations

finding.finding_summary: The review makes an institutional-level contribution by mapping the K-12 ITS evidence base and identifying patterns relevant to implementation, such as reliance on quasi-experimental designs, short interventions, concentration in STEM, and the need for longer, more diverse studies. It also highlights that ethical considerations were absent in the included studies, implying a governance and policy gap rather than a measured intervention effect.
finding.measure: Review synthesis of study designs, locations, durations, and ethics reporting

paper_profiles.title: An Interview Reflection on elligent Tutoring Goes to School in the Big City
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an interview-based retrospective reflection on the 1997 Cognitive Tutor Algebra I study, rather than a new classroom intervention study. The article asks what the original study was trying to demonstrate, how the curriculum-plus-intelligent-tutoring-system package was implemented in real school settings, what the major limitations were, and how the work influenced later research, product development, and dissemination of Cognitive Tutor Algebra.

The approach discussed was a full-year algebra curriculum that integrated the Algebra Cognitive Tutor into urban high school instruction in Pittsburgh. The authors describe the original 1993–94 quasi-experimental field study in three city schools serving many low-income and low-performing students, with multiple assessments including standardized test items and curriculum-aligned problem-solving tasks. Although the article is not itself an outcome study, it reports the original finding that experimental classes outperformed comparison classes on standardized tests and on course-objective tests, and it uses that result to discuss scale-up, social context, adoption, and the need for multiple forms of assessment.

The main conclusions are reflective and field-building rather than experimental: intelligent tutoring systems can have real educational impact when embedded in a curriculum and school context; evaluation should distinguish between efficacy under intended use and policy-level adoption effects; and future work should focus on open-ended problem solving, theory-driven design, and stronger integration into classroom practice. The paper also argues that the original study helped catalyze dissemination of Cognitive Tutor Algebra and influenced the broader AI in Education community to value large-scale classroom evidence.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports the results of the original 1993–94 quasi-experimental high-school algebra study: on average, 470 students in experimental classes outperformed comparison students by 15% on standardized tests and 100% on tests targeting course objectives. The measures included standardized algebra test items and curriculum-aligned assessments of problem solving and representations.
finding.measure: Standardized algebra tests and course-objective tests assessing problem solving and representations

finding.finding_summary: The interview emphasizes that the original study also examined more complex mathematical competencies beyond routine procedures, including representations and problem solving. The reported gains on course-objective tests indicate improved performance on these deeper skills, though no separate effect size is given for this outcome.
finding.measure: Tests targeting course objectives, including complex problem solving and use of representations

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the study had substantial dissemination and institutional impact: it was described as the initial snowball for Cognitive Tutor Algebra adoption, contributing to growth from 3 schools to 75 schools and eventually to about 3000 schools. The authors link the evidence of learning gains and the integration of the tutor into classroom practice to broader uptake, commercialization, and influence on how AI in Education evaluations were conducted.
finding.measure: School adoption/dissemination of Cognitive Tutor Algebra; scale-up of use across schools

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses the practical school implementation of the tutor as part of a curriculum and notes that the system was designed to support teachers rather than replace them. However, it does not report direct quantitative evidence on teacher workload or operational efficiency, so the finding is limited to implementation-related claims about practical use in schools.
finding.measure: Implementation and integration of the tutor into classroom instruction

paper_profiles.title: Do intelligent tutoring systems benefit K-12 students? A meta-analysis and evaluation of heterogeneity of treatment effects in the U.S.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) improve learning outcomes for K-12 students in U.S. schools, and under what conditions the effects are strongest. The authors frame ITS as AI-based software that personalizes instruction turn-by-turn using learner models, including hints, feedback, worked-out examples, motivation support, reading materials, and other supports.

To answer these questions, they conducted a meta-analysis of 18 experimental studies published between 2011 and 2021, yielding 77 effect sizes across 11 ITS used in elementary, middle, and high school contexts. They focused specifically on studies that met What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations or with reservations, and they analyzed heterogeneity using the MUTOS framework to examine internal validity (methods) and external validity (units, treatments, observations, settings).

The overall effect of ITS on K-12 learning outcomes was positive and statistically significant (g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). Effects were similar across elementary and middle school and across several student subgroups, but were smaller in rural settings and declined as intervention duration increased. MetaForest results suggested that the most important moderators were worked-out examples, outcome type, intervention duration, intervention condition, and immediate measurement, with worked-out examples emerging as the single most influential moderator. The authors conclude that ITS can benefit K-12 students, but effectiveness depends on design features, implementation duration, and context.

finding.finding_summary: Across 18 experimental studies and 77 effect sizes, ITS produced a statistically significant positive effect on student learning outcomes in U.S. K-12 schools (g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). The outcome was broadly student academic achievement, with effect sizes estimated from standardized mean differences across multiple ITS and contexts.
finding.measure: Student learning outcomes / academic achievement

finding.finding_summary: For reading and writing outcomes, the meta-analysis found a significant positive effect of ITS (g=0.323, SE=0.039, 95% CI [0.218, 0.428], p<0.001). The paper also reports that reading outcomes had a larger effect than mathematics outcomes in the O-dimension analyses.
finding.measure: Reading and writing outcomes

finding.finding_summary: For mathematics outcomes, ITS showed a significant positive effect (g=0.253, SE=0.007, 95% CI [0.224, 0.281], p<0.001). Mathematics was also one of the moderators highlighted in the MetaForest analysis, where math ITS had lower importance than worked-out examples but still contributed to prediction of effect size.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement

finding.finding_summary: The paper coded several affective/support features of ITS, including motivation support, but its main outcome was achievement rather than a direct social-emotional endpoint. Within the T-dimension, motivation support was associated with a significant positive effect size (g=0.265, SE=0.027, 95% CI [0.102, 0.428], p=0.024), indicating that ITS designs including motivational features were beneficial for learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes in studies where ITS provided motivation support

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly measure durable skills as an endpoint, but it does analyze worked-out examples, hints, and other features that may support metacognitive regulation and productive help-seeking. Worked-out examples were associated with a positive and statistically significant effect (g=0.324, SE=0.020, 95% CI [0.176, 0.472], p=0.018) and were ranked as the most influential moderator in the MetaForest analysis, suggesting that structured support can aid learning processes linked to durable skills.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes in studies with worked-out examples

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s core contribution is to inform K-12 implementation and scaling decisions by identifying when ITS are most effective across school settings, student groups, and intervention conditions. It finds smaller effects in rural schools (g=0.146, SE=0.012, 95% CI [0.053, 0.239], p=0.029) than in urban or suburban settings, which has direct implications for institutional adoption and equitable deployment.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes by school location (urban, suburban, rural)
finding.study_size: k=43 to 51 effect sizes depending on location

paper_profiles.title: AI Instructional Agent Improves Student’s Perceived Learner Control and Learning Outcome: Empirical Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether an AI instructional agent can improve students’ perceived learner control and learning outcomes compared with a human teacher and a self-paced MOOC-style condition. The authors frame the problem around a persistent tension in lecture-based instruction: how to preserve structured content delivery while giving learners more autonomy and responsive interaction.

The intervention was an AI instructional agent embedded in the MAIC system, which delivered lecture content in real time and responded to student questions during instruction. The study compared three conditions: an in-person human teacher, a MOOC-style video lecture with chatbot support, and the AI instructional agent. All conditions used the same instructional content from a general education course on artificial intelligence, and the sample was 140 university students in Beijing, with 125 valid cases analyzed.

Results showed that the AI instructional agent condition produced significantly higher perceived learner control than both comparison groups, along with more interaction and shorter learning time. Students in the AI condition also scored higher on the post-test than those in the human-teacher and MOOC conditions. Regression analyses further indicated that perceived learner control positively predicted post-test performance, suggesting that the sense of control was not only subjective but also associated with better academic outcomes. The paper concludes that AI instructional agents can enhance both learning experience and learning performance when they combine structured lecture delivery with real-time, learner-initiated interaction.

finding.finding_summary: Students in the AI instructional agent condition reported significantly higher perceived learner control than those taught by a human teacher or using MOOC-style videos with chatbot support. The ANOVA showed a significant group effect on perceived learner control, F(2,122)=12.155, p<.001; Tukey comparisons favored AI over human teacher (M difference=0.732, p<.001) and AI over MOOC (M difference=0.416, p<.05).
finding.measure: Perceived learner control scale (4-item scale; Cronbach’s alpha=0.823)

finding.finding_summary: Perceived learner control was positively associated with post-test performance and negatively associated with learning duration, indicating more self-directed and efficient learning behavior. Across participants, PLC correlated with post-test scores (r=0.23, p<.01) and learning duration (r=-0.30, p<.001), and PLC significantly predicted post-test scores in regression (β=0.055, p<.05) after controlling for gender, age, self-regulated learning, and pre-test score.
finding.measure: Correlation/regression analyses involving perceived learner control, learning duration, and post-test performance

finding.finding_summary: The AI instructional agent improved learning efficiency by reducing completion time relative to the human-teacher condition. The ANOVA on duration was significant, F(2,122)=265.168, p<.001, with both the AI and MOOC groups showing shorter learning durations than the human-teacher group by approximately 30 minutes; the AI-human mean difference was -1.860 (p<.001).
finding.measure: Learning duration / task completion time

finding.finding_summary: Students in the AI instructional agent group achieved significantly higher post-test scores than students in both the human-teacher and MOOC conditions. The group effect on post-test performance was significant, F(2,122)=7.673, p<.01, with AI outperforming human teacher (M difference=0.128, p<.01) and MOOC (M difference=0.112, p<.01).
finding.measure: Post-test score on a 16-item multiple-choice assessment (proportion correct)

paper_profiles.title: Investigating Students’ Preferences for AI Roles in Mathematical Modelling: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how students perceive different AI roles during mathematical modelling tasks and how baseline learner characteristics relate to those preferences. The authors focus on an unresolved question in AI-supported mathematics education: whether AI should behave like a tutor, teaching assistant, peer student, struggling student, or excellent student when helping learners work through the iterative modelling process.

The experiment used a within-subjects randomized, counterbalanced design with 26 university students who had not taken university-level mathematics courses, making them comparable to high school graduates in mathematical preparation. Participants completed one baseline modelling task without assistance and five additional modelling tasks, each with a different GPT-based AI role. Before the tasks, participants completed scales measuring mathematical modelling self-efficacy, computational thinking, and design thinking; after each task they rated confidence, helpfulness, and ease of interaction, and they also ranked their preferred AI roles overall.

Results showed that students strongly preferred competent and supportive AI roles over the struggling-student role. The tutor role was rated most favorably overall, but the tutor, teaching assistant, peer, and excellent-student roles did not differ significantly from one another on preference rankings or user-experience measures, suggesting that learners mainly valued AI competence and supportiveness rather than a specific pedagogical persona. Baseline computational thinking did not predict role preferences, while higher design thinking was associated with a more favorable view of the teaching assistant role. The paper concludes that AI role design matters in mathematical modelling and that adaptive systems should align support style with learner needs and expectations.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students strongly preferred competent AI support during mathematical modelling tasks. In a within-subjects RCT with n=26, the tutor role received the best overall ranking (M=2.35, SD=1.02), while the struggling-student role was rated worst (M=4.42, SD=1.17); the Friedman test showed a significant effect of AI role on preference, χ2(4, N=26)=28.83, p<.001. This outcome reflects students’ responses to AI-supported mathematical modelling performance and role-based scaffolding rather than direct test-score gains.
finding.measure: AI role preference rankings and modelling-task experience ratings during mathematical modelling tasks

finding.finding_summary: AI role significantly affected task confidence, perceived helpfulness, and ease of interaction across the modelling activities. In the n=26 within-subjects experiment, the tutor role produced the highest helpfulness (M=4.12, SD=0.91) and ease of interaction (M=4.08, SD=0.93), while the struggling-student role produced the lowest confidence (M=1.88, SD=1.24), helpfulness (M=1.92, SD=1.23), and ease of interaction (M=1.81, SD=1.17); all Friedman tests were significant at p<.001. These results indicate that more competent AI personas supported students’ affective experience and perceived task confidence during modelling.
finding.measure: Task confidence, perceived AI helpfulness, and ease of interaction ratings

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studied durable skills in the form of computational thinking and design thinking, and found both were positively associated with mathematical modelling self-efficacy. In the PLS-SEM model, design thinking predicted MMSE with β=0.730 (p<.001) and computational thinking with β=0.300 (p<.001), explaining 80.8% of the variance in MMSE (R²=0.808, adjusted R²=0.791). At the subdimension level, several CT and all DT subscales were positively correlated with MMSE, although not all correlations were significant.
finding.measure: Computational thinking scale, design thinking scale, and mathematical modelling self-efficacy scale

paper_profiles.title: Perspectives on astronomy: probing Norwegian pre-service teachers and middle school students
paper_profiles.population: Middle school students and pre-service teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces and pilots the Norwegian Introductory Astronomy Questionnaire (NIAQ), an adapted and translated version of an existing astronomy instrument. The authors used it to probe astronomy knowledge, views, and explanation patterns among two groups in Norway: pre-service teachers enrolled in teacher education and middle school students in grades 8 and 10, before and after astronomy instruction.

The study combines multiple-choice, ranking, and free-response items, with qualitative coding of written responses and simple quantitative comparisons of pre/post patterns. The main purpose was not to test an AI intervention but to understand students’ and future teachers’ astronomy conceptions, including how they explain astronomical phenomena and how their views change after instruction.

The paper reports preliminary findings that pre-service teachers improved in explaining astronomical objects and concepts after instruction, but many shifted from pedagogical to more authoritative responses when addressing hypothetical students. For middle school students, the authors found persistent misconceptions about size and distance in the universe and little or no improvement from year 8 to year 10 on the relevant items, with notable gender stratification. Overall, the paper concludes that the NIAQ can reveal rich diagnostic information about astronomy understanding and pedagogical reasoning, but the results are preliminary and further analysis is needed.

finding.finding_summary: The study found pre-service teachers improved pre- to post-instruction in explaining astronomical objects and in giving more detailed explanations of complex concepts such as Earth's stable orbit around the Sun, but middle school students showed little or no gain on the relevant astronomy explanation and ranking items. For the middle school sample, scores on all aspects of questions 5a and 5b were statistically identical or slightly lower in year 10 than in year 8 (n=535 year 8; n=387 year 10).
finding.measure: Free-response explanations of astronomical objects and concepts; ranking tasks on size and distance in the universe
finding.study_size: n=40 pre-service teachers pre-test; n=38 post-test; n=535 year 8; n=387 year 10

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports a striking decline in pre-service teachers’ pedagogical responses when asked what they would say to hypothetical year 10 students about controversial astronomy topics. Pre-instruction, more than one-third of responses were categorized as pedagogical, but post-instruction fewer than 10% retained these features, indicating a shift away from attention to students’ learning needs.
finding.measure: Coding of free-response explanations as pedagogical vs. authoritative

finding.finding_summary: The authors discuss the development of explanatory reasoning and the ability to justify answers using scientific evidence, particularly in the pre-service teachers’ free responses. While the paper does not directly measure general critical thinking or metacognition, it does substantively analyze the quality of students’ explanations, categorizing them as scientifically compatible or not, and as brief vs. detailed.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of explanation quality in free-response items
finding.study_size: n=40 pre-service teachers pre-test; n=38 post-test; n=535 year 8; n=387 year 10

paper_profiles.title: Surveying Turkish high school and university students’ attitudes and approaches to physics problem solving
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines Turkish students’ attitudes and approaches to physics problem solving using a translated version of the Attitudes and Approaches to Problem Solving (AAPS) survey. The authors aimed to validate the Turkish instrument and then compare responses across grade level, school type, and gender, as well as against previously collected U.S. university student data. The study is motivated by the idea that students’ epistemological beliefs and problem-solving approaches affect physics learning and success.

The Turkish AAPS was translated, reviewed by bilingual science and English faculty, refined through expert feedback, and cognitively tested with four high school students before large-scale administration. The survey was given to 528 students in Turkey: 10th- and 11th-grade students from regular, science, and vocational high schools, plus first-year university science-education majors taking algebra-based physics. The researchers analyzed the data using chi-square tests, ANOVA/t-tests for group comparisons, and exploratory factor analysis. Reliability of the Turkish survey was strong (Cronbach α = 0.817–0.897 across groups).

Overall, the study found no statistically significant differences in total survey means by gender or between 10th and 11th grade, but it did find item-level differences across groups. University students were more expert-like than vocational high school students on the survey overall, though not consistently across items. Compared with U.S. algebra-based university students, Turkish university students were less expert-like on average on the full survey, with statistically significant differences on many items. The factor analysis suggested 10 underlying factors, including metacognition and novice-like problem-solving approaches. The paper is primarily a validation and comparative survey study, not an intervention study.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly assessed metacognition and problem-solving approaches with the 33-item AAPS survey in n=528 Turkish high school and university students. Overall scores did not differ significantly by gender or between 10th and 11th grade, but item-level results showed meaningful differences in expert-like versus novice-like problem-solving behaviors, and factor analysis identified a metacognition-related factor.
finding.measure: Attitudes and Approaches to Problem Solving (AAPS) survey; item-level normalized response scores and exploratory factor analysis

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on physics problem solving attitudes, including use of equations, identifying principles, checking reasonableness of answers, and applying principles across contexts. Turkish university students were more expert-like than vocational high school students overall, but U.S. university students were more expert-like than Turkish university students on the overall survey (mean normalized score +0.38 vs +0.21), with significant item-level differences on many scientific problem-solving questions.
finding.measure: AAPS survey responses about physics problem solving and epistemological beliefs
finding.study_size: n=528 in Turkey; comparison group n=397 U.S. algebra-based university students from prior study

finding.finding_summary: Several AAPS items probed handling mathematics in physics problem solving, symbolic versus numerical solution strategies, and whether equations are intuitive tools or merely calculation devices. Results showed persistent novice-like views on some mathematics-related items, such as treating equations as applying primarily to specific situations, but also more expert-like responses on some items for university students and on item 9 for 11th graders.
finding.measure: AAPS survey items concerning equations, symbolic solution strategies, and mathematical handling in physics problems

finding.finding_summary: The survey included items related to persistence, confidence in checking answers, and willingness to continue working when a solution seems unreasonable. Some groups showed more expert-like persistence—for example, many students reported tracing back solutions when answers seemed wrong—while other items reflected less favorable beliefs, such as feeling stuck without external help. The paper reports statistically significant item-level differences but no overall group differences in total means for gender or grade level.
finding.measure: AAPS survey items on persistence, self-checking, and willingness to continue problem solving

paper_profiles.title: When Scaffolding Breaks: Investigating Student Interaction with LLM-Based Writing Support in Real-Time K-12 EFL Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether LLM-based writing support can function effectively in real-time K-12 classrooms, where students have limited time, varied proficiency levels, and teacher-led instruction. The authors argue that much of the prior LLM-writing literature is based on adults, higher education, or self-study, and does not capture the constraints of live classroom use.

To study this gap, the authors developed WriteAid, a chat-based LLM scaffold for English writing that offered step-by-step help for sentence construction, vocabulary/grammar questions, and grammar revision. They deployed the tool for six weeks in a South Korean middle school EFL classroom with 157 eighth-grade students (133 consented for analysis), collected 14,863 query-response pairs, and combined log analysis with qualitative coding and naturalistic classroom observation. They also assessed later written work to examine whether students retained and transferred AI-supported sentences.

The findings are mixed. WriteAid improved grammatical accuracy and helped some students complete writing tasks, but the step-by-step scaffolding also demotivated lower-proficiency students, increased reliance on the system, and sometimes produced unnatural or misleading guidance when Korean-English structural differences were involved. Classroom observations showed that LLM support changed teacher-student and peer interactions: it reduced some repetitive teacher workload, but it also made it harder for teachers to identify common struggles and may have weakened peer learning. The authors conclude that real-time classroom LLMs need proficiency-aware, syntax-aware, and teacher-integrated design to support equitable learning.

finding.finding_summary: WriteAid improved students' grammatical accuracy during in-class writing, but effects on retention and transfer varied by proficiency group. In the fall semester, students constructed 632 sentences with the LLM; 309 (48.9%) were copied verbatim into final essays, and 82.3% of those copied sentences were grammatically correct. High-performing students incorporated 65.8% of LLM-constructed sentences into final assessments, compared with 37.8% for middle-performing and 14.0% for low-performing students.
finding.measure: English writing quality, grammatical correctness, and transfer of LLM-generated sentences into final essays
finding.study_size: n=133 consented students; 632 sentences analyzed in fall semester

finding.finding_summary: The LLM scaffold had divergent motivational effects by proficiency. Lower-proficiency students were more likely to become demotivated, confused, annoyed, or dependent on the system, especially under time pressure and step-by-step prompting, while higher-proficiency students tended to use the tool more efficiently and with less negative affect. The authors report average negative affective behaviors of 3.8 per session for the high-performing group versus 12.2 and 11.4 for the middle- and low-performing groups.
finding.measure: Affective responses (gratitude, annoyance, confusion, indifference), motivation, and reliance/dependence behaviors during writing sessions
finding.study_size: n=133 consented students; affective coding on sampled interaction data

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that LLM scaffolding can support some higher-order writing processes but may also displace independent problem-solving and peer collaboration. High-performing students tended to delegate lower-order tasks such as vocabulary translation and validation, while lower-performing students outsourced core sentence generation, and classroom observations indicated that students increasingly turned to the LLM instead of peers or the teacher. This points to a mixed effect on collaboration and metacognitive engagement.
finding.measure: Question-type coding, interaction patterns, and classroom observations of peer/teacher interaction
finding.study_size: n=133 consented students; 14,863 messages; qualitative coding on 1,386 sampled queries

finding.finding_summary: The LLM reduced teacher burden by handling repetitive low-level questions and allowed the teacher to spend more time circulating and monitoring students. The teacher explicitly reported having more time to walk around the classroom because they no longer needed to answer every simple question, although the system also introduced new coordination costs because students still asked the teacher many questions and the teacher had to redirect them to the model.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, time spent responding to repetitive questions, and classroom orchestration/monitoring
finding.study_size: n=1 teacher plus 6 classes of eighth-grade students

finding.finding_summary: At the classroom level, the system changed how instructional attention and participation were distributed, improving access for some lower-proficiency students but also making it harder for teachers to identify common student difficulties and potentially amplifying inequities in who received attention. The study frames these effects as institutional/classroom coordination issues, including fairness, teacher-student dynamics, and the need for real-time teacher dashboards.
finding.measure: Classroom equity, teacher-student dynamics, and visibility of student difficulties
finding.study_size: n=133 consented students; observational classroom study across 3 sessions

paper_profiles.title: ExpTrialMng: A Universal Experiment Trial Manager for AR/VR/MR Experiments Based on Unity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint describes a software tool rather than an empirical study. The authors identify a practical barrier for researchers running VR/AR/MR experiments in Unity: setting up randomized trial flow, saving data reliably, and recovering from unexpected interruptions such as headset tracking loss or battery problems.

To address this, they developed ExpTrialMng, a Unity library that uses a pre-generated CSV file to manage trials, deliver trial settings to an experiment manager, save results after each trial, and resume the experiment from a specified trial number after an interruption. The paper explains the library’s design, workflow, and implementation details, and argues that minimizing boilerplate and failure recovery burden can make VR/AR experimentation easier for researchers who are not expert Unity programmers.

The context is general VR/AR/HCI experimentation, not a K-12 classroom or educational intervention. The paper does not report a participant study, comparison condition, or outcome evaluation; its conclusion is primarily that the library should reduce technical overhead and data loss in future experiments.

paper_profiles.title: Machine Learning Algorithms for Detecting Mental Stress in College Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of identifying stress among college students using machine learning rather than physiological sensing. The authors argue that stress is common in higher education and that a questionnaire-based approach can be a lower-cost, easier-to-deploy alternative to sensor-based stress detection.

The study reports a workshop-based survey of approximately 843 college students aged 18 to 21 in Chhattisgarh, India. Students completed a 28-item questionnaire covering emotional well-being, physical health, academic performance, relationships, and leisure, and the resulting dataset was used to train and compare seven classifiers: Decision Tree, Random Forest, SVM, AdaBoost, Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, and k-NN.

Using a 75/25 train-test split and 5-fold cross-validation, the authors report that Support Vector Machines achieved the best performance, with 95% accuracy, 93% precision, 97% recall, and 94% F1-score, and an ROC AUC of 0.98. The paper concludes that questionnaire-based machine learning can help identify student stress and may support future stress-mitigation and mental-health interventions in college settings, though the work is limited to prediction/classification rather than testing an educational intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that questionnaire-based machine learning could classify college students into stress vs. non-stress categories with high performance, suggesting the collected stress-related indicators were predictive of students' mental state. The best model, SVM, reached 95% accuracy, 93% precision, 97% recall, 94% F1-score, and an ROC AUC of 0.98 on the reported evaluation.
finding.measure: Stress vs. non-stress classification accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC curve/AUC

paper_profiles.title: The Most Considered Type of Student Characteristics by Primary School Teachers
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal on Integrating Technology in Education (IJITE)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks which student characteristic primary school teachers consider most important when planning instruction, and whether attending to that characteristic is associated with better student learning outcomes. The authors frame the study around individualized instruction and argue that teachers often cannot assess every possible learner characteristic in depth, so identifying the most salient one could help with classroom decision-making.

The study surveyed 37 grade 4-6 class teachers from seven primary schools in Indonesia. Teachers completed a questionnaire about the student characteristics they usually identify and the one they most consider; instructional planning documents were also reviewed, and midterm exam scores were compared between learning that did and did not incorporate information about student characteristics.

The main finding is that teachers most often prioritize student intelligence level over motivation, cognitive style, learning style, prior knowledge, and socio-cultural factors. Intelligence level was also the highest-rated characteristic in planning documents (mean 3.65/5, categorized as high), while socio-cultural conditions were lowest (mean 2.55/5, low). A comparison of midterm exam scores showed higher average performance in classes where instruction was developed based on student intelligence level (average 72.67 vs. 68.20; gain reported as 6% overall, with subject-level gains of 3% to 10%), suggesting a positive association between intelligence-level-informed instruction and achievement.

finding.finding_summary: Instruction developed based on students' intelligence level was associated with better midterm exam performance across subjects. The comparison reported higher average scores for classes using intelligence-level information (72.67) than for classes not using it (68.20), with subject-level gains ranging from 3% to 10% and the largest differences in Indonesian language and mathematics.
finding.measure: Midterm exam scores in Indonesian language, math, social science, natural science, and art-culture-craft

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies how teachers identify learner characteristics such as intelligence level, cognitive style, learning style, prior knowledge, and motivation, all of which are treated as inputs for instructional adaptation. It reports that intelligence level was most considered (54% of teachers selecting it as the main characteristic; mean identification score 3.65/5), with the implication that these learner factors guide classroom decision-making and individualized support.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire on identifying and using student characteristics in instruction; observation of lesson planning documents

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Recommendations in EdTech: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether personalized content recommendations increase engagement in a children’s educational app. The authors study a key implementation question in edtech personalization: can a recommender system improve usage when it replaces an editorial curation system, and does it benefit some students more than others?

The intervention is a personalized recommender deployed in the “Recommended Story” section of Freadom, a mobile/web reading app for Indian children aged 3 to 12. The system was developed using historical interaction logs and matrix factorization, then evaluated in a two-week randomized controlled trial. Only users with at least 60 prior story interactions were eligible, and 7,750 users were randomized to receive either personalized recommendations or the existing editorial-based story selection. The study focuses on engagement outcomes, not learning outcomes.

The main finding is that personalization substantially increased engagement. Relative to the editorial baseline, the personalized section saw about a 60% increase in total story engagement, 78% more completed stories, and 87% more reading time; across the whole app, engagement increased by about 14%, 19% more completed stories, and 20% more reading time. Effects were larger for heavier users, users with longer histories, and users with niche content preferences. The authors conclude that personalized recommendations can meaningfully increase app usage in a children’s educational setting, though they do not measure direct learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: Personalized recommendations substantially increased student engagement with the educational app. In the randomized experiment (n=7,750 randomized; n=3,023 launched the app; n=525 viewed at least one Recommended Story), total story engagement in the personalized section increased by 60% (S.E. 17%), with 78% more completed stories and 87% more reading time.
finding.measure: Total Story Engagement, number of completed stories, and reading time in the Recommended Story section
finding.study_size: n=7750 randomized; n=3023 launched app during experiment
finding.effect_size: 60% increase in Total Story Engagement; 78% more completed stories; 87% more reading time

finding.finding_summary: The personalized recommender improved how efficiently the app delivered content that users engaged with, compared with editorial curation. While the paper’s primary emphasis is on user engagement rather than labor productivity, it directly evaluates a system-level content selection process and shows the personalized model outperformed the baseline in predictive accuracy (MSE 0.0962 vs. 0.1022 for TWFE and 0.1309 for a mean model).
finding.measure: Mean Squared Error of recommendation/outcome models; app content consumption outcomes under alternative recommendation systems
finding.effect_size: MSE 0.0962 vs. 0.1022 vs. 0.1309; 60% engagement lift in deployed section

paper_profiles.title: AI-Driven Interface Design for Intelligent Tutoring System Improves Student Engagement
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Symposium on Neural Gaze Detection (Woodstock '18 proceedings as provided in text)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether changing the user interface of an intelligent tutoring system can improve student engagement by making the system’s AI analysis more visible, explainable, and motivating. The authors argue that most ITS research focuses on knowledge modeling and recommendation, while comparatively little work has tested interface designs that use AI outputs to encourage continued study.

The intervention is a set of AI-driven diagnostic-page designs in Santa, a mobile self-study tutoring service for TOEIC preparation. The interface variants include features such as estimated score, skill/proficiency displays, comparison to similar users, tutor comments, problem-solving analysis, recommended lectures, adaptive curricula, and “Santa Labs” explanations of how AI predictions are computed. The study was conducted in the wild with new users of Santa, using controlled A/B tests that randomly assigned users to different interface versions.

The population is not K-12 students in a school setting; it is adult learners using a commercial TOEIC preparation platform in South Korea. The paper reports that more informative and explainable AI-driven interfaces increased engagement outcomes such as conversion rate, ARPU, total profit, and free-question consumption. The strongest reported gain was up to 25.13% improvement in total profit in one A/B test, with page design B outperforming page design A on all engagement metrics in a later test.

Overall, the study concludes that better presentation of AI-generated diagnostic feedback can meaningfully improve engagement with an intelligent tutoring system. Because the outcomes are behavioral engagement metrics rather than learning achievement, the paper is most directly evidence about social-emotional engagement and secondarily about the system’s commercial/operational performance.

finding.finding_summary: Across controlled A/B tests in Santa, AI-driven diagnostic page designs increased student engagement. In one experiment (w/o radar chart n=1,391; w/ radar chart n=1,486), the radar-chart version increased conversion rate from 5.25% to 6.26%, ARPU from $5.92 to $6.94, total profit from $8,236.01 to $10,305.58, and free-question consumption from 14.77 to 16.51, with total profit up by 25.13%.
finding.measure: Conversion rate, Average Revenue Per User (ARPU), total profit, and number of free questions consumed as engagement indicators

finding.finding_summary: The paper also evaluates outcomes tied to platform performance and user monetization, which function as operational indicators for the ITS service. In the A/B comparison of page design A versus B (n=9,442 vs n=9,722), design B improved conversion rate (5.60% to 6.22%), ARPU ($5.54 to $6.11), total profit ($83,335.76 to $93,807.27), and free-question consumption (15.15 to 16.24).
finding.measure: Conversion rate, ARPU, total profit, and free-question consumption on the Santa platform

paper_profiles.title: Brazilian National High School Examination: assessing student’s learning in Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines what can be inferred about Brazilian high school students’ learning in Physics from the national high-stakes exam ENEM (Natural Sciences section) across 2009–2014. The authors ask whether the exam’s item content and students’ response patterns reveal genuine learning outcomes, and whether the test functions as intended under item response theory (IRT).

The study does not evaluate an AI system or personalized feedback intervention; instead, it combines psychometric analysis (3PL IRT, item characteristic curves, test information curves) with content analysis of Physics items. The population is students concluding high school in Brazil who took ENEM, with analyses focusing on millions of examinees and a filtered subset of graduating students with valid test records.

The authors report that average Physics/Natural Sciences performance is low, with students answering only about one-third of items correctly on average and performing worse on items requiring disciplinary knowledge, quantitative reasoning, problem solving, or practical laboratory knowledge. They also find notable performance gaps by gender and school type, with male students and students from federal/private schools scoring higher than female students and state-school students. Overall, the paper argues that ENEM reveals substantial inequities and suggests a gap between the exam’s intended construct and actual student learning in Physics at the end of high school.

finding.finding_summary: Across ENEM Natural Sciences/Physics items from 2009–2014, students showed low performance on items requiring disciplinary Physics knowledge, basic mathematical reasoning, problem solving, and laboratory/practical understanding. The paper reports that the mean number of correct answers on the 45-item Natural Sciences test was only about one-third of the total (e.g., 3.0–3.4 on a 0–10 normalized scale), and that items demanding more complex reasoning or conceptual understanding were especially difficult.
finding.measure: ENEM Natural Sciences / Physics item performance; Classical Test Theory correct-answer totals; item characteristic curves
finding.study_size: millions_of_candidates; analyzed subset of graduating high school participants not_reported exactly per item

finding.finding_summary: The paper uses ENEM results to diagnose system-level inequities and to argue that the exam functions as a high-stakes selection mechanism for Brazilian higher education. It reports persistent gaps by gender and school type, with female students and state-school students scoring lower on average than male students and federal/private-school students, suggesting broader institutional inequality in access and preparation.
finding.measure: ENEM score distributions by gender and school type; participation rates by school type
finding.std_deviation: reported in tables, but not consolidated as a single study-wide value

finding.finding_summary: The authors infer weaknesses in durable cognitive skills such as problem solving and handling multi-step reasoning from item analyses of Physics questions. They state that items requiring multiple cognitive steps and higher-level reasoning had relatively low correct-answer rates, indicating limited development of these skills at the end of high school.
finding.measure: Physics item content analysis and student response patterns on multi-step/reasoning items

paper_profiles.title: Inverted Classroom an der Hochschule Karlsruhe - ein nicht quantisierter Flip
paper_profiles.venue: Das Inverted Classroom Model: Begleitband zur ersten deutschen ICM-Konferenz
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter describes the introduction and evaluation planning for an Inverted Classroom Model (ICM) initiative at Hochschule Karlsruhe within the SKATING project. The paper is motivated by common problems in German engineering and mathematics higher education, including heterogeneous entry skills, high workload at the end of semesters, and dropout risk. The authors argue that flipped and video-supported instruction may better support semester-long learning and create more time in class for active problem solving, feedback, and discussion.

The paper is not a controlled effectiveness study; instead, it presents a practitioner-oriented account of several pilot implementations and the evaluation framework used to judge them. It outlines multiple variants of ICM, from minimally inverted lecture summaries to partially or fully inverted topics in higher mathematics, and discusses the technical and pedagogical setup, including videos hosted on YouTube/ILIAS, online questionnaires, classroom observations, and follow-up surveys. The context is an undergraduate engineering and mathematics setting at a university of applied sciences, with an emphasis on adapting the method to instructor preferences, course content, and student needs.

Main conclusions are cautious and procedural rather than causal.
