The authors conclude that ICM is promising for increasing interaction, supporting self-paced preparation, and potentially improving motivation and understanding, but they stress that success depends on careful adaptation, process monitoring, and multi-method evaluation. They recommend measuring not only student learning outcomes but also acceptance, usage patterns, and unintended effects such as increased student or instructor workload.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports a pilot implementation of inverted classroom methods in an undergraduate higher mathematics course (Höhere Mathematik 3) with about 20 motivated students. The chapter does not provide quantitative pre/post learning gains, but it states that the inverted topic was completed successfully enough to justify planned continuation and that follow-up evaluation would include exam results and comparisons with the prior year.
finding.measure: Course participation, in-class problem solving, student understanding of differential equation systems and planned exam performance
finding.study_size: n=20 (pilot course); exact evaluative sample not fully reported

finding.finding_summary: The chapter reports that student reactions to the inverted classroom pilots were mostly positive, with interest, engagement, and curiosity explicitly treated as important success criteria. The instructor's stated goals included a bilateral 'flow' experience and awakening student curiosity, and the author notes that students generally accepted the videos and the restructured class, although some concerns about missing opportunities to ask questions and perceived extra time investment were raised.
finding.measure: Student feedback, acceptance, satisfaction, motivation/curiosity, perceived usefulness

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes collaborative and active learning during class, including self-directed preparation, partner work, discussion, and problem solving. Although it does not report a causal estimate, the chapter frames ICM as supporting deeper understanding, self-regulated semester-long learning, and cooperative learning processes, and it notes that students could participate more actively in class ('Man kann jetzt in der Vorlesung mitreden').
finding.measure: Observed collaboration, student participation in partner/problem-solving work, self-directed preparation, and perceived deeper understanding
finding.study_size: n=20 (pilot course); other process observations not fully quantified

finding.finding_summary: A central focus of the chapter is the workload and implementation effort for instructors and support staff. The authors report that producing a video segment took about 1 hour total, with the instructor spending roughly 30 minutes setting up and 30 minutes on organizational tasks per recording session, while the SKATING staff handled post-production; at the same time, they argue that effort may decrease in later semesters after initial setup.
finding.measure: Instructor and support-staff time required for video creation, recording setup, editing, and organization
finding.study_size: 1 pilot implementation context; time estimates reported narratively

finding.finding_summary: The chapter presents ICM as part of a broader institutional reform effort under the German 'Qualitätspakt Lehre' project SKATING, aimed at improving study conditions and teaching quality in engineering programs. It concludes that, if pilot projects are positively evaluated and sufficient experience is accumulated, the approach could become a more permanent part of the university's teaching repertoire and inform future comparative studies.
finding.measure: Institutional implementation and adoption potential; pilot-project continuation and dissemination plans

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces VLM@school, a German-language benchmark for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on middle school curriculum content. The authors argue that existing multimodal benchmarks are often English-only, heavily multiple-choice, and contain decontextualized or artificially difficult items that do not reflect real classroom-style reasoning. Their goal is to create a more realistic test set grounded in authentic subject matter from German school textbooks and related educational materials.

The benchmark contains 486 images and 2,038 open-ended questions across nine school subjects: arts, biology, geography, history, math, music, physics, religion, and sports. Questions were created in German by native speakers, and some items are deliberately adversarial, requiring models to recognize when an answer cannot be inferred from the image. The paper evaluates 13 open-weight VLMs using LLM-as-a-judge style scoring, reporting that even the best systems reach under 45% overall accuracy, with especially weak performance on math, music, and adversarial items.

The study is not an intervention with students or teachers; it is a benchmark evaluation of AI models. The main conclusion is that middle school-level multimodal tasks remain challenging for current VLMs, especially in non-English settings and when visual evidence must be integrated with background knowledge. The authors also find that strong performance on public multimodal benchmarks does not necessarily transfer to this more realistic German school-content benchmark, suggesting that benchmark selection strongly shapes conclusions about model capability.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark shows that VLMs struggled substantially on math items grounded in middle school content. The best model reached only about 34.09% accuracy on math overall, and the paper notes that the strongest models performed especially poorly on counting, geometry, and formula assignment tasks.
finding.measure: Accuracy on middle school math benchmark questions

finding.finding_summary: Models had difficulty with science-oriented visual reasoning, especially in biology and physics tasks that required combining image interpretation with factual knowledge. The best model scores were 48.53% on biology and 47.65% on physics, and the discussion describes frequent failures on explanation-based questions, diagram interpretation, and technical term identification.
finding.measure: Accuracy on biology and physics benchmark questions
finding.study_size: biology n=169 questions; physics n=234 questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates performance on non-core school subjects including arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports. Results were mixed across these domains but generally modest, with the best model reaching 54.36% in history and 52.92% in religion, while music was particularly difficult at 31.03% best accuracy.
finding.measure: Accuracy on arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports benchmark questions
finding.study_size: arts n=286; geography n=251; history n=264; music n=166; religion n=206; sports n=154 questions

finding.finding_summary: Although not a student-skill intervention study, the benchmark explicitly tests visual reasoning, inference, and the ability to combine clues across modalities, which are durable skills in the broad sense. The authors report that even strong models often failed when tasks required multi-step reasoning, reverse lookup from maps/legends, or deciding that a question was unanswerable from the image alone.
finding.measure: Performance on open-ended multimodal reasoning and adversarial unanswerable questions
finding.study_size: overall n=2,038 questions; adversarial subset included within the benchmark

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s core contribution is institutional/benchmark infrastructure: it creates a publicly available German school-content benchmark intended to better measure VLM capabilities than existing English-language or multiple-choice-heavy datasets. The authors argue that benchmark choice changes model rankings and that their dataset exposes shortcomings not visible on popular public benchmarks such as MMMU.
finding.measure: Creation and comparative evaluation of a new benchmark dataset

paper_profiles.title: Impact of ChatGPT on ESL students’ academic writing skills: a mixed methods intervention study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed methods intervention study examines whether ChatGPT can function as a formative feedback tool to improve undergraduate ESL students’ academic writing. The paper addresses a practical problem in large writing classes: providing timely, individualized feedback on content, organization, and grammar. The author argues that AI-generated feedback may help students receive more immediate and tailored support than is feasible with traditional instructor-only feedback.

The intervention was conducted with first-year science and engineering undergraduates at a private university in India. An intact class was split into experimental and comparison groups; 35 students in the experimental group and 37 in the comparison group completed the full study. Both groups completed pre-, post-, and delayed post-tests on process, comparison, and cause-effect paragraph writing; the experimental group also received one hour of training and used ChatGPT for self-assessment and peer assessment during six hours of instruction. Qualitative data came from focus group discussions with five experimental-group students.

Quantitatively, the experimental group improved substantially over time and outperformed the comparison group on both post-test and delayed post-test writing scores. The reported effects were very large, with repeated-measures results showing strong gains and pairwise comparisons such as pre-test to post-test d=-3.300 and pre-test to delayed post-test d=-3.898. Qualitative findings were strongly positive as well: students said ChatGPT helped them generate ideas, stay on topic, organize paragraphs, improve grammar, and collaborate with peers, though a few noted risks of overdependence and reduced creativity. Overall, the study concludes that ChatGPT can be an effective feedback tool in tertiary-level writing instruction when students are properly trained.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT use as a formative feedback tool significantly improved undergraduate ESL students’ academic writing performance. In the experimental group (n=37), mean writing scores increased from 12.581 on the pre-test to 19.216 on the post-test and 20.419 on the delayed post-test; the repeated-measures ANOVA showed a strong effect (F(2,72)=330.704, p=5.146e−37, η2=0.902). The experimental group also outperformed the comparison group on post-test (t(70)=-5.643, p=3.297e−7) and delayed post-test (t(70)=-9.371, p=5.544e−14).
finding.measure: Academic writing test scores on process, comparison, and cause-effect paragraph tasks (content, organization, grammar, vocabulary rubric)
finding.study_size: n=72 analyzed quantitatively (EG n=37, CG n=35)
finding.std_deviation: Pre-test SD=0.833; Post-test SD=2.485; Delayed post-test SD=2.575

finding.finding_summary: Students reported overwhelmingly positive perceptions of ChatGPT’s support, describing it as helpful for autonomy, confidence, and reduced anxiety about asking for feedback. In focus group discussions (five students), they emphasized that ChatGPT made feedback feel immediate, personalized, and less intimidating, though a few negative comments noted possible dependence and reduced motivation to think independently.
finding.measure: Focus group discussion themes on perceptions of feedback, autonomy, motivation, and dependence

finding.finding_summary: The intervention supported collaboration and metacognitive/self-regulatory writing behaviors, especially in idea generation, organization, and peer feedback. Students reported that ChatGPT helped them focus on controlling ideas, connect supporting details, use signposts, and discuss writing decisions with peers, although a small number of comments suggested it could impose a fixed pattern and hinder creativity.
finding.measure: Focus group themes on collaboration, organization, focus, and self/peer assessment practices

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was perceived to improve writing efficiency by reducing brainstorming time and speeding task completion. Students said it provided quick, specific feedback on content and grammar, made it easier to stay on task, and helped complete collaborative writing activities more quickly, suggesting workflow benefits in a crowded classroom setting.
finding.measure: Focus group themes on faster writing, brainstorming time, and task completion efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how elementary school students and their teachers perceived a GenAI-powered tool designed to support creative mathematical writing. The authors were motivated by the idea that mathematical story writing can deepen understanding and creativity, but young learners often need scaffolding to begin, revise, and connect their ideas to math concepts.

The intervention, [ANONYMOUS], used a three-step workflow—Ask, Represent, and Transform—to help students analyze math stories, model their thinking visually, and then co-create culturally relevant math stories with GPT-4 and DALL·E 3. The study was implemented in six fifth-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools with 79 students and six teachers. Data came from student focus groups, teacher interviews, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observations, and were analyzed thematically.

The paper concludes that students and teachers saw several benefits of GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing: it fostered creativity, improved mathematical understanding, promoted AI literacy, and increased interest, curiosity, and ownership in learning. At the same time, participants identified important challenges, including students’ limited ability to critically evaluate AI output, the risk that AI stories were "too perfect," the lack of adaptive pedagogical feedback, reduced autonomy, limited social connection, and accessibility barriers such as the absence of speech-to-text. The authors argue that GenAI can support K-12 learning, but only when deliberately designed to preserve meaningful human learning, feedback, and social interaction.

finding.finding_summary: In six 5th-grade classrooms (n=79 students), students and teachers reported that GenAI-supported creative mathematical writing improved understanding of math problems, helped students represent mathematical ideas visually, and surfaced misconceptions. The evidence is qualitative and interview-based rather than test-based, so no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Interviews, open-ended surveys, and classroom observations about mathematical understanding/problem representation

finding.finding_summary: The study focused on creative mathematical writing, and students reported that GenAI helped them draft, revise, and make their stories more original, interesting, and coherent. Because the writing task was embedded in mathematics and outcomes were perceived rather than scored, no quantitative writing effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions of writing quality, drafting, revising, and storytelling in math-story creation

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers described stronger interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership of learning when working with GenAI-supported math stories. The study is qualitative and reports themes from interviews/observations, so no effect size or standardized measure was reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions of interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership in learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that GenAI-supported writing promoted divergent/convergent thinking, flexible thinking, prompt engineering, and evaluation of AI strengths and weaknesses. However, it also noted weaker critical evaluation skills among some students, indicating a mix of benefits and remaining skill gaps; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions and observed evidence of critical thinking, prompt engineering, and problem formulation during story creation

finding.finding_summary: A secondary focus of the study was AI literacy: students learned that prompt specificity matters and that AI has strengths and limitations. This was based on qualitative perceptions from the classroom implementation rather than a direct AI-literacy assessment.
finding.measure: Perceptions of AI literacy and prompt engineering during GenAI use

paper_profiles.title: Automated Personalized Feedback Improves Learning Gains in an Intelligent Tutoring System
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether automatically generated, data-driven personalized feedback improves learning outcomes in a large-scale intelligent tutoring system (ITS). The authors focus on the challenge of generating scalable personalized hints, explanations, Wikipedia-based explanations, and mathematical hints without hand-crafted rules or expert intervention.

The system studied is Korbit, a dialogue-based ITS used for online instruction in machine learning, data science, and artificial intelligence. The paper describes machine-learning and NLP pipelines for producing personalized feedback and ranking feedback quality using historical student-system interaction data. The main evaluation uses 796 annotated interactions from 183 students in a free machine learning course on Korbit (collected Jan–Feb 2020), comparing baseline, shallow personalization, and deep personalization models.

The main outcome is student learning gain, defined as the proportion of cases where a student answered correctly after receiving feedback. Deep personalization achieved the highest gains overall, and the difference between deep personalization and baseline was statistically significant before the second attempt (60.47% vs. 37.93%, p=0.03005). The paper also reports that Wikipedia-based explanations were rated helpful in 83.33% of cases and that over 90% of mathematical hints were judged by domain experts as very useful or somewhat useful. Overall, the study concludes that automated personalized feedback can improve learning outcomes in this ITS context, while remaining fully automated and scalable.

finding.finding_summary: Automated personalized feedback in the Korbit ITS was associated with improved learning gains on machine learning course problems. In 796 annotated student-system interactions from 183 students, deep personalization produced the highest correct-after-feedback rate, especially before the second attempt (60.47%) compared with the baseline no-personalization model (37.93%); this difference was statistically significant (p=0.03005).
finding.measure: Learning gain, operationalized as the proportion of instances where a student provided a correct solution after receiving a personalized hint or explanation
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CIs reported for model means: baseline [20.69%,57.74%] before second attempt; shallow [33.99%,68.62%]; deep [44.41%,75.02%]

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved subjective evaluations of feedback alongside learning gains. Students rated the generated explanations as helpful 83.33% of the time, suggesting a positive effect on perceived usefulness/engagement with the tutoring feedback, though no standardized engagement or motivation scale was used.
finding.measure: Subjective helpfulness ratings of explanations/feedback

paper_profiles.title: When Scaffolding Breaks: Investigating Student Interaction with LLM-Based Writing Support in Real-Time K-12 EFL Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how large language models can function as real-time writing support in K-12 English-as-a-Foreign-Language classrooms. The authors focus on a core tension in AI tutoring: step-by-step scaffolding may improve immediate task performance, but in a live classroom it may also create dependency, demotivation, and new classroom-management challenges.

To study this, the authors developed WriteAid, an LLM-based chat tool for sentence construction, vocabulary/grammar explanations, and grammar checking. They deployed it over six weeks in a South Korean public middle school with 157 eighth-grade students, collecting 14,863 query-response pairs and conducting naturalistic observations during three class sessions. They also analyzed a delayed written assessment completed without AI support to examine whether students retained and transferred what they produced with the system.

The study finds that WriteAid improved students’ grammatical accuracy during in-class writing, but its effects were uneven. Higher-proficiency students tended to use the LLM for lower-level help such as vocabulary and validation, while lower-proficiency students more often relied on it for sentence generation and revision, and were more likely to become frustrated or over-dependent when the system withheld direct answers. Classroom observations suggested that the LLM reduced teacher burden on routine questions, but also made it harder for teachers to detect struggling students and shifted participation patterns in ways that could reduce peer interaction and exacerbate inequities.

Overall, the paper argues that LLM scaffolding in real-time K-12 classrooms should be proficiency-aware, syntax-aware, and designed to support teacher oversight rather than replace it. The authors propose classroom design guidelines emphasizing clearer role division between teacher and AI, real-time teacher dashboards, and mechanisms to prevent over-reliance while preserving equitable access to support.

finding.finding_summary: In a six-week deployment with 157 eighth-grade students, WriteAid improved in-class grammatical accuracy for sentence construction, but transfer to final essays varied by proficiency. Of 632 AI-assisted sentences produced in the fall semester, 309 (48.9%) were incorporated verbatim into final essays, and 82.3% of those incorporated sentences were grammatically correct; however, high-performing students reused 65.8% of sentences in their final work versus 37.8% and 14.0% for middle- and low-performing students, respectively.
finding.measure: Grammar accuracy of AI-assisted sentences and transfer into final written essays; analytic rubric for written essays (content, organization, vocabulary, language use)
finding.study_size: n=133 consenting students; 632 AI-assisted sentences analyzed in fall semester

finding.finding_summary: The system had differential affective effects across proficiency levels. Higher-performing students generally showed fewer negative affective behaviors (3.8 instances per writing session on average) than middle- and low-performing students (12.2 and 11.4, respectively), while lower-proficiency students were more likely to become demotivated, confused, or annoyed by step-by-step feedback and repeated non-disclosure of direct answers.
finding.measure: Affective responses during LLM interaction coded as gratitude, annoyance, confusion, and indifference
finding.study_size: n=133 consenting students; affective coding drawn from 1,386 sampled queries across 15 students

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that LLM use reshaped students' help-seeking, revision behavior, and interaction patterns, but not always in ways that supported independent problem-solving. Lower-proficiency students more often outsourced core sentence generation and relied on iterative revision, whereas higher-performing students delegated lower-order tasks such as vocabulary translation and validation, suggesting more efficient task management and higher-order focus for the latter group.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of query types and interaction patterns (e.g., sentence revision, paragraph revision, validation seeking, vocabulary translation, full/partial sentence generation)
finding.study_size: n=133 consenting students; 1,386 queries qualitatively coded from a 9.3% sample

finding.finding_summary: WriteAid reduced teacher burden on repetitive low-level questions and allowed the teacher to spend more time circulating and monitoring students. The teacher reported having more time to walk around the classroom and check progress because the LLM handled many routine spelling and grammar questions, though the system also created new coordination demands because students were not always clear about when to ask the AI versus the teacher.
finding.measure: Classroom observation and follow-up teacher interview about question handling and teacher time allocation
finding.study_size: 6 classes; 3 observed sessions; teacher interview not further quantified

finding.finding_summary: The intervention changed classroom participation and equity dynamics. It widened access to support for students who might otherwise struggle to complete tasks, but it also shifted questions away from the teacher, made it harder to identify common misconceptions, and concentrated teacher attention on a few extroverted students while quieter students increasingly relied on the AI.
finding.measure: Naturalistic classroom observations and teacher interview focusing on classroom participation, equity, and teacher-student interaction patterns

paper_profiles.title: eRevise: Using Natural Language Processing to Provide Formative Feedback on Text Evidence Usage in Student Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents eRevise, a web-based automated writing evaluation (AWE) system that uses natural language processing to provide formative feedback on students’ use of text evidence in response-to-text writing. The core problem is that students often need more than a score; they need targeted guidance to revise drafts in ways that improve evidence use, specificity, and elaboration.

The system was built for upper-elementary students writing essays in response to a common source text task. After a first draft is submitted, eRevise analyzes the essay with rubric-aligned NLP features and selects two prewritten feedback messages tailored to the detected evidence weaknesses. In a pilot deployment across 7 classrooms in two rural Louisiana parishes, 143 fifth- and sixth-grade students used the system across two class periods: first to draft, then to revise after receiving feedback.

The evaluation focused on whether student writing improved after feedback and revision. Human scoring showed a small but statistically trending increase in the RTA Evidence rubric score from first to second drafts (M=2.62 to 2.72, SD=0.95 to 0.92, n=143, p≤0.08). NLP-based measures also improved significantly: number of pieces of evidence (NPE) increased from 2.61 to 2.81 (SD=1.27 to 1.08, p≤0.003) and the merged specific-evidence count increased from 9.65 to 11.15 (SD=4.94 to 5.39, p≤0.001). The paper concludes that eRevise shows promise for supporting revision in K-5/6 classrooms, especially for students with weaker initial evidence use, but it is a first deployment without a control group and the findings are limited to short-term revision outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: In a pilot deployment with 143 fifth- and sixth-grade students across 7 classrooms, writing quality on the RTA Evidence rubric improved from first to second drafts after students received eRevise feedback and revised their essays. The human-scored Evidence score increased from M=2.62 (SD=0.95) to M=2.72 (SD=0.92), a small improvement with trending statistical significance (p≤0.08).
finding.measure: Human-scored RTA Evidence rubric score for response-to-text writing

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that eRevise can reduce teacher effort by automatically selecting formative feedback messages based on NLP analysis of student drafts. However, this is presented as a system rationale rather than directly measured with a workload outcome, so the evidence is indirect.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / feedback automation (not directly quantified in the study)

paper_profiles.title: Do intelligent tutoring systems benefit K-12 students? A meta-analysis and evaluation of heterogeneity of treatment effects in the U.S.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) improve learning outcomes for U.S. K-12 students and under what conditions their effects are strongest. The authors position ITS as AI-based systems that personalize instruction turn-by-turn using learner models, hints, feedback, worked examples, and related supports.

To answer the question, the authors conducted a meta-analysis of 18 experimental studies published between 2011 and 2021, yielding 77 effect sizes across 11 ITS used in elementary, middle, and high school settings in the U.S. The review was restricted to studies meeting What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations or, when applicable, with reservations; however, no quasi-experimental studies met inclusion criteria. The analysis used multilevel meta-regression and MetaForest to examine heterogeneity across internal-validity factors and external-validity moderators within the MUTOS framework.

The main finding is that ITS had a statistically significant positive effect on student learning outcomes overall (g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). Effects were similar across elementary and middle school samples and across some student subgroups, but were smaller in rural settings. Moderator analyses suggested that worked-out examples, intervention duration, intervention condition, and immediate measurement were among the most important predictors of variation in effects. The paper concludes that ITS can benefit K-12 students, but impact depends on implementation conditions and study design features.

finding.finding_summary: Across 18 experimental studies in U.S. K-12 schools (77 effect sizes from 11 ITS), the overall effect of intelligent tutoring systems on student learning outcomes was positive and statistically significant. The meta-analytic estimate was g=0.271 (SE=0.011, p=0.001), indicating a medium-sized benefit on academic achievement measures.
finding.measure: Student learning outcomes / academic achievement

finding.finding_summary: For reading and writing outcomes, ITS produced a statistically significant positive effect. The meta-analysis reported g=0.323 for reading/writing outcomes across 55 effect sizes, which was larger than the mathematics estimate.
finding.measure: Reading and writing outcomes

finding.finding_summary: For mathematics outcomes, ITS showed a statistically significant positive effect, though smaller than the reading/writing estimate. The pooled effect size was g=0.253 across 22 effect sizes.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively analyzed ITS features related to motivation support, hints, and student engagement through treatment moderators, but it did not report a standalone social-emotional outcome as the primary endpoint. The closest direct empirical evidence was for motivation support as a treatment feature, which had a positive significant effect on learning outcomes (g=0.265 across 23 effect sizes), suggesting that support features tied to engagement/motivation were beneficial.
finding.measure: Motivation-support feature as a moderator of learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper examined worked-out examples and other support types that may foster problem-solving and self-regulation, but it did not directly measure durable skills with a dedicated instrument. The strongest related moderator was worked-out examples, which was associated with a significant positive effect on learning outcomes (g=0.324 across 59 effect sizes) and was the top predictor in the MetaForest model, implying potential support for deeper problem-solving processes.
finding.measure: Worked-out example support as a moderator of learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The study addressed school-level implementation conditions such as assignment level, clustering, intervention condition, and location, which are relevant to institutional deployment rather than a direct institutional outcome measure. However, it did not directly measure policy, governance, or organizational outcomes, so evidence here is indirect; the clearest institutional implementation signal was that rural studies had smaller effects (g=0.146) than urban (g=0.298) and suburban (g=0.260) studies.
finding.measure: Study setting / location as a moderator of ITS effects

paper_profiles.title: Deep Discourse Analysis for Generating Personalized Feedback in Intelligent Tutor Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of generating automated, personalized feedback in an intelligent tutoring system (ITS). The authors argue that existing feedback systems can tell students that an answer is wrong or suggest broad improvements, but often cannot explicitly identify which concepts are correct, incorrect, missing, or how the student’s reasoning should be revised.

To solve this, the paper proposes a multi-stage neural pipeline that segments student responses into elementary discourse units (EDUs), predicts discourse relations between adjacent EDUs, clusters semantically similar EDUs with SBERT embeddings, and uses an exercise-specific relational graph plus a triplet classifier to search for the best correction path. The feedback mechanism is tested in the Korbit dialogue-based ITS, where students watch STEM lectures and answer short-form exercises. The paper also reports separate intrinsic evaluations for discourse segmentation and discourse relation classification on standard NLP datasets (RST-DT and PDTB 2.0), showing strong performance improvements over prior models.

The main application evaluation is on 247 student interactions in Korbit, where the system’s feedback is compared with a minimal feedback baseline and a cluster-based feedback baseline. The full model produces better second-attempt learning outcomes and is judged more helpful by human experts, suggesting that discourse-aware structure improves automated feedback quality. However, the study is not a K-12 classroom study; it is an ITS study with STEM exercises, and the paper does not provide evidence about school-aged students in classroom settings.

finding.finding_summary: In the Korbit ITS, the full discourse-aware feedback model improved student performance on STEM exercise follow-up attempts. Across 247 student interactions, the average learning gain was 51.11% ± 14.61 for all attempts and 75.00% ± 18.98 before the second attempt, compared with 23.53% ± 13.25 and 20.00% ± 10.08 for the cluster-based baseline, respectively. The paper interprets this as evidence that personalized feedback helps students correct reasoning and solution structure in STEM tasks.
finding.measure: Second-attempt correctness / learning gain on STEM exercise responses in an intelligent tutoring system

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to support students’ ability to identify missing concepts, correct relations, and reasoning gaps in their own answers, which aligns most closely with feedback on metacognitive and problem-solving processes. Human judges ranked the full feedback as the best option in 65.93% ± 9.73 of 91 incorrect attempts, indicating that the model’s feedback was usually judged most helpful for guiding revision. No direct standardized durable-skill measure was reported, but the study substantively evaluates feedback quality for reasoning support.
finding.measure: Expert ranking of feedback helpfulness on incorrect student attempts

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies a fully automated feedback mechanism intended to reduce reliance on human-generated tutoring feedback and to scale personalized support inside an ITS. While no teacher workload metric is reported, the system automates segmentation, discourse analysis, candidate generation, and feedback assembly, demonstrating a workflow that can provide immediate feedback without manual authoring. The study’s evidence is therefore indirect but substantively focused on automation and efficiency of tutoring feedback delivery.
finding.measure: Automated generation of personalized feedback in an ITS

paper_profiles.title: Students' Perceived Roles, Opportunities, and Challenges of a Generative AI-powered Teachable Agent: A Case of Middle School Math Class
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle school students perceive the roles, benefits, and challenges of a Generative AI-powered teachable agent (TA) used in a math classroom. The authors are motivated by the gap between prior TA research in higher education and the need for evidence from authentic K-12 settings, especially as generative AI becomes more common in education.

The study reports on a classroom implementation of a GenAI-powered TA for 108 sixth-grade students in a public laboratory middle school affiliated with a Research 1 university in the southeastern United States. Students interacted with the TA across two class periods while learning rate and ratio content. The system used GPT-4-Turbo, a knowledge graph built from K-12 math Q&A data, personalization features, gamification, and retrieval-augmented generation to simulate a less knowledgeable peer and prompt learning-by-teaching interactions.

Using classroom observations, focus-group interviews, and open-ended survey responses, the authors conducted thematic analysis of students' perceptions. Students saw the TA as a learning companion, learning facilitator, and collaborative problem-solver. They also reported benefits such as a more student-centered learning climate, greater autonomy, improved cognitive/social/emotional capacities, deeper math knowledge, stronger motivation and self-efficacy, and more positive attitudes toward AI. Challenges included weak problem presentation, shallow questioning, poor fit to learning styles, disorganized sequencing, technical issues, lack of multimodal input, and the need for teacher facilitation. The paper concludes that GenAI may expand the traditional teachable-agent model in K-12 math, but effective design still requires stronger pedagogy, multimodal interaction, and teacher support.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that the GenAI-powered teachable agent helped them improve understanding of rate-and-ratio math, especially by forcing deeper explanation, multiple representations, and revisiting misconceptions. However, the paper is qualitative and does not report test score gains or other quantitative achievement effects, so the evidence is based on perceived learning rather than measured performance.
finding.measure: Students' perceptions of math learning, especially understanding rate and ratio concepts and applying knowledge in different contexts
finding.study_size: n=108 (with 14 interview participants and open-ended survey/observation data from all students)

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived the TA as increasing enjoyment of math, motivation, self-efficacy, confidence, and resilience. They described the experience as fun and engaging and said the TA's encouraging responses helped them persist when frustrated, but these are self-reported perceptions rather than experimentally estimated effects.
finding.measure: Perceived enjoyment of math, intrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, confidence, resilience, and engagement

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students believed the GenAI-powered TA fostered cognitive, social, and metacognitive capacities, including elaboration, reflective analysis, communication skills, perspective-taking, and collaborative problem-solving. Students described having to explain their reasoning more clearly and think about the AI's perspective, suggesting perceived gains in higher-order skills, but no direct performance measures were reported.
finding.measure: Perceived cognitive, social, and metacognitive capacities (e.g., reasoning, elaboration, perspective-taking, collaboration)

finding.finding_summary: Students reported an interdisciplinary learning opportunity, noting that they were engaging with computer science concepts while doing math. This outcome is substantively present but secondary to the paper's main focus on mathematics and students' perceptions of GenAI-powered tutoring interactions.
finding.measure: Perceived interdisciplinary learning connecting computer science and mathematics

paper_profiles.title: Using Transformers to Provide Teachers with Personalized Feedback on their Classroom Discourse: The TalkMoves Application
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of giving K-12 mathematics teachers timely, scalable, and personalized feedback on their classroom discourse practices, particularly their use of “talk moves” that support student participation and mathematical reasoning. The authors frame this as a major instructional-coaching challenge because existing human observation and transcript coding is expensive, slow, and difficult to scale across many teachers.

To address this, the paper presents TalkMoves, an end-to-end system that uses automatic speech recognition and transformer-based natural language processing to classify teacher utterances from classroom transcripts into six accountable-talk categories plus a none label. The system was trained and evaluated on 501 K-12 math lesson transcripts, with 176,757 sentence examples, manually coded by trained annotators with high inter-rater agreement. The best model, RoBERTa-Large, achieved F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779 on the test set, which the authors argue is roughly comparable to expert human reliability for this coding task.

The paper also describes the feedback interface and pilot deployment of the application with 21 teachers in two Midwestern school districts, grades 3–12, during the 2019–2020 academic year. Teachers used the system to review lesson-level dashboards showing talk-move frequencies, teacher-versus-student talk, and related discourse metrics, and then provided feedback through surveys and interviews. The main conclusion is that transformer-based NLP can substantially improve automated detection of teacher discourse strategies and can support a practical feedback workflow for K-12 teacher professional learning, though the paper emphasizes technical limitations such as noisy classroom speech and weak ASR performance on children’s speech.

finding.finding_summary: The system is designed to support mathematics instruction by identifying accountable talk moves in K-12 math lessons, which the authors argue are linked to richer mathematical discussion and learning. The strongest empirical result reported is model performance for classifying teacher discourse in math classrooms, with the best model (RoBERTa-Large) reaching F1 = 79.33% and MCC = 0.7779 on the test set (n=176,757 sentence instances from 501 transcripts).
finding.measure: Classification of teacher utterances into six accountable talk move categories plus none in K-12 mathematics lesson transcripts

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central contribution is an automated pipeline intended to replace or reduce the need for time-consuming human transcript coding and to provide teachers with scalable, prompt feedback. Compared with the earlier baseline model (F1=65%), the transformer-based approach improved automated classification performance to F1=79.33%, supporting the claim that the system can more efficiently generate feedback for teacher reflection.
finding.measure: Automated transcript coding / model performance for generating teacher feedback
finding.study_size: n=176,757 sentence instances from 501 transcripts; pilot use by 21 teachers
finding.effect_size: F1 improved from 65% baseline to 79.33%; MCC=0.7779

finding.finding_summary: The application was piloted as a scalable professional-learning tool for 21 teachers in two Midwestern school districts, indicating potential institutional use for teacher development at district scale. The paper reports that teachers used the system throughout the 2019–2020 academic year and provided survey and interview feedback, but it does not report student-learning or district-level outcome effects.
finding.measure: Pilot deployment/adoption of the TalkMoves feedback system in school districts
finding.study_size: 21 teachers in two Midwestern school districts

paper_profiles.title: Vocalnayno: Designing a Game-Based Intervention to Support Reading Development in Primary Schools
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 6th European Conference on Games-Based Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of supporting early reading development in primary schools, especially where teachers rely on teaching assistants and parent volunteers to provide one-on-one reading support. The author argues that current paper-based records and informal feedback systems are too slow, qualitative, and fragmented to help teachers quickly identify pupils’ specific phonics and reading needs.

To address this, the paper proposes Vocalnayno, a game-based reading assessment tool designed to fit into the existing culture of a primary school. The proposed system would ask pupils to read letters and words aloud while playing a game, with results stored in a database accessible to parents, teachers, and teaching assistants; the intended benefit is more immediate, objective assessment and better tailoring of support.

The paper is primarily a design and requirements-oriented work-in-progress rather than an evaluation study. It describes an early prototype built in Multimedia Fusion Developer 2 and reports a very small pilot test involving the author and one primary school pupil, which revealed limitations in the platform’s speech recognition. It also reports informal discussions with teaching assistants, parents, and children about current practice and acceptance concerns. The paper concludes that the system needs further development, especially in speech recognition, and that no classroom deployment had yet been conducted.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not report a demonstrated literacy intervention effect; it presents a proposed game-based reading assessment tool intended to support phonics and word reading development. The only empirical testing described is a very small pilot with the author and one primary school pupil, which found that the prototype’s native voice recognition was not sufficient for intended use.
finding.measure: Reading aloud of phonics, letters, numbers, and words; prototype speech-recognition feasibility
finding.study_size: n=2 (author and one primary school pupil)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports informal stakeholder feedback suggesting that participants were generally receptive to the design discussions, but it also notes concerns about misuse and detrimental impact. It does not provide a formal measure of engagement or motivation, only qualitative observations about acceptance and convenience.
finding.measure: Informal stakeholder acceptance/discussion of the proposed classroom technology

finding.finding_summary: The proposed system is explicitly intended to improve the efficiency of reading assessment and feedback by replacing fragmented paper records with a database-accessible, more immediate reporting process. The paper argues that this could help teaching assistants and teachers identify individual needs faster, automatically flag concerns, and reduce the time required to interpret progress records, but these benefits are proposed rather than demonstrated.
finding.measure: Assessment/feedback workflow for reading support; teacher and assistant access to pupil progress data

finding.finding_summary: A central concern of the paper is whether the game-based tool can integrate into the existing teaching culture of a primary school and align with school accountability and parent/governor expectations. The paper’s main conclusion is that design acceptance and fit with school culture are necessary for adoption, but no institutional outcome is measured empirically.
finding.measure: Informal consultation on classroom adoption, school culture fit, and stakeholder acceptance

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '26 Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how middle school students want AI to function as a peer collaborator during collaborative mathematical problem solving, rather than as a tutor or teacher aide. The authors argue that most prior AI-in-education work has focused on individualized tutoring, leaving a gap in understanding how AI should participate in small-group classroom problem solving where students are expected to co-construct solutions.

To investigate this, the researchers ran a five-day participatory design summer camp with 24 rising grades 6-8 students. Students completed human-only collaborative math tasks and then worked with a sandboxed AI peer technology probe built around two AI peers (Alice and Bob) that differed in proficiency and conversational style; they also reviewed dialogue excerpts, co-designed ideal AI peer behaviors, and completed preference surveys and interviews. The study combined quantitative measures (GEQ and NASA-TLX, paired t-tests) with qualitative thematic analysis of interviews, reflections, and design artifacts.

The main finding is that students preferred an AI peer that provides scaffold-first help: hints, checks, error detection, concept refreshers, and clear student control over when and how much the AI speaks. Students rejected overly didactic, answer-giving, or socially insensitive behaviors, and instead wanted an AI peer with friendly expertise, peer-like tone, and emotional attunement. Quantitatively, AI peers reduced temporal demand but increased physical demand and lowered some aspects of group cohesion/coordination, suggesting a tradeoff between procedural efficiency and the lived experience of collaboration. Overall, the paper offers youth-grounded design recommendations for AI peers in middle-school mathematics CPS.

finding.finding_summary: The study centers on middle-school mathematics collaborative problem solving and shows that students want AI peers to support mathematical reasoning with hints, checks, error detection, concept refreshers, and follow-up practice rather than provide direct answers. The paper does not report learning gains in mathematics achievement, but it does report that AI peers helped reduce temporal demand during math tasks (M=5.67, SD=4.38 vs. M=9.62, SD=4.13; p=0.002, d=1.15), while also creating some friction in collaboration.
finding.measure: Math collaborative problem-solving task performance context; NASA-TLX temporal demand during mathematics tasks
finding.study_size: n=22 paired comparisons for quantitative condition analyses; n=24 enrolled
finding.std_deviation: SD=4.38 (AI peers temporal demand), SD=4.13 (human-only temporal demand)

finding.finding_summary: Students’ reactions indicate that social-emotional support mattered alongside correctness: they preferred AI peers that were encouraging, listened, and acknowledged frustration or uncertainty. Qualitatively, students said the AI felt less trustworthy or even self-blame-inducing when it failed to respond affectively; quantitatively, group social attraction declined in the AI condition (ATGS M=5.21, SD=1.81 vs. M=6.50, SD=2.05; p=0.029, d=0.94).
finding.measure: GEQ Attractions to Group-Social; interview/reflection themes about emotional scaffolding and trust
finding.study_size: n=22 paired comparisons; interviews n=18; whole-class reflections n=5 sessions

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies collaboration, co-agency, turn-taking, and coordination in small-group math problem solving. Students wanted AI peers to negotiate methods, ask what the group should do next, and contribute as a collaborator rather than a teacher; however, group coordination scores were lower with AI peers (GIT M=4.76, SD=1.58 vs. M=5.54, SD=1.52; p=0.047, d=0.81), suggesting a weaker collaboration experience even though the AI made the process more procedurally efficient.
finding.measure: GEQ Group Integration-Task; qualitative accounts of collaboration, co-agency, and turn-taking
finding.study_size: n=22 paired comparisons; interviews n=18; whole-class reflections n=5 sessions

finding.finding_summary: The AI peers improved perceived time efficiency but increased physical/interactional burden. Students reported significantly lower NASA-TLX temporal demand in the AI condition (M=5.67, SD=4.38) than in human-only CPS (M=9.62, SD=4.13; p=0.002, d=1.15), indicating faster or less time-pressured work; however, physical demand rose (M=8.48, SD=4.65 vs. M=4.90, SD=2.41; p=0.014, d=1.14), reflecting extra typing and interface management.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand and physical demand during collaborative problem solving
finding.std_deviation: SD=4.38 vs. 4.13 (temporal demand); SD=4.65 vs. 2.41 (physical demand)

finding.finding_summary: The study also touches a broader educational design outcome: students’ preferences for AI-generated instructional style and classroom fit. They strongly preferred scaffold-first help, clear control over AI speaking, and a friendly-expert tone rather than exaggerated personas or direct-answer tutoring, but this was framed as design preference rather than an achievement outcome.
finding.measure: Day 5 feature-preference survey; participatory design artifacts and interviews
finding.study_size: n=24 enrolled; preference survey based on 20 items derived from Day 4 posters

paper_profiles.title: Tinkering in Primary School: From Episode to Science Practice
paper_profiles.venue: The Primary School as a Playful Space
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how tinkering, understood as a constructionist and open-ended making practice, can be integrated into primary school classrooms as a bridge between playful exploration and formal science learning. The authors propose the TIDE model (Tinkering, Ideas generation, Disciplinary connection, Exploration) to help teachers connect tinkering episodes to curricular learning without losing the exploratory character of the practice.

The main empirical material comes from an implementation of the “Oﬃcina della Luce” project in four primary schools in Bologna, involving 13 classrooms, 24 teachers, and approximately 300 students. Teachers received professional development, access to a digital resource library, and documentation tools; classroom sessions centered on light and color. Data included a questionnaire completed by 20 teachers and analysis of a fishbowl documentation protocol, along with qualitative teacher comments and classroom observations.

Findings suggest that tinkering can improve classroom dynamics, student engagement, collaboration, and access to knowledge, especially for students who are often less successful in conventional school settings. The study also shows that tinkering surfaces authentic scientific questions, but many teachers feel underprepared to pursue those questions in depth, particularly in physics. Rather than producing a definitive curricular model, the paper argues for further co-design and for additional disciplinary support so teachers can better sustain science-oriented inquiry emerging from tinkering activities.

finding.finding_summary: Tinkering sessions generated authentic scientific questions about light and color, including a classroom-wide question about producing white light with colored filters. In the fishbowl analysis, teachers recognized that these questions reflected real inquiry, but also reported that they were not yet prepared to address them disciplinarily, especially in physics.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported analysis of fishbowl documentation and classroom discussion of student research questions

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported unexpectedly high engagement, participation, and enthusiasm during tinkering, particularly among students who struggle in traditional settings. In the questionnaire, 70% of teachers said tinkering revealed unexpected or partially expected behavior, including increased motivation, sustained attention, and enjoyment of group work.
finding.measure: Teacher questionnaire on student engagement, participation, motivation, and behavior during tinkering

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that tinkering supported collaboration, idea-sharing, self-reflection, and the ability to persist through frustration and failure. Teachers noted that students learned to manage frustration, work in pairs and groups, and take on protagonist/leadership roles in the workshop context.
finding.measure: Teacher descriptions coded from open-ended questionnaire responses

finding.finding_summary: The project showed that primary schools can embed tinkering into classroom life through co-design, documentation, and teacher professional development, but implementation was constrained by pandemic disruptions and by teacher uncertainty about disciplinary follow-up. The authors conclude that future adoption requires additional support for disciplinary preparation and more intentional integration with school routines.
finding.measure: Project implementation experience across 13 primary classrooms, teacher feedback, and documentation protocol analysis

paper_profiles.title: Kanji Workbook: A Writing-Based Intelligent Tutoring System for Learning Proper Japanese Kanji Writing Technique with Instructor-Emulated Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of teaching and assessing Japanese kanji writing for novice foreign-language learners, especially when instructors have limited time to provide individualized feedback on handwriting technique, structure, and precision. The authors argue that existing educational software lacks the richer, instructor-like assessment needed for meaningful practice outside class.

To address this, they developed Kanji Workbook, a writing-based intelligent tutoring system that captures students’ handwritten kanji on digital devices and provides automated, instructor-emulated feedback using ten assessment metrics. The system was designed from instructor interviews and classroom observations, and it supports practice and quiz modes, tracing aids, stroke-by-stroke animations, and scoring feedback for stroke order, direction, structure, and precision.

The system was deployed over an academic year in first- and second-year university Japanese courses at Texas A&M University. In the classroom study, 94 students were split into case and control groups; the case group used Kanji Workbook in addition to normal coursework, while the control group used conventional paper-based study and optional online resources. Students using the system achieved higher average course test scores, with statistically significant gains reported overall (case mean 92.70 vs. control mean 86.48, p=.046) and for first-year students (p=.048). Student feedback was generally positive, especially regarding usefulness, intuitiveness, and the motivational value of the feedback animations, although some found the three-star ratings overly strict or less intuitive.

finding.finding_summary: Students using Kanji Workbook in first- and second-year university Japanese courses scored higher on course tests focused on kanji writing, vocabulary, and sentence writing. Across all participants, the case group (n=44) outperformed the control group (n=50) on averaged test scores (M=92.70 vs. 86.48), with a statistically significant difference (p=.046); the first-year case group also scored higher than the first-year control group (p=.048).
finding.measure: Five semester tests on vocabulary and sentence writing with emphasis on recently introduced kanji characters; averaged test scores on a 100-point scale

finding.finding_summary: In the interaction study, students reported that the interface felt intuitive, useful, rewarding, and supportive of self-improvement while practicing kanji writing. Most Likert-scale responses were Agree or Strongly Agree for intuitiveness and usefulness of buttons, ratings, and animations, though the ratings feature was viewed as less intuitive by some students.
finding.measure: Likert-scale responses and freeform feedback on intuitiveness and usefulness of interface features

paper_profiles.title: The Chemistry Between High School Students and Computer Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports a five-year high school outreach effort that integrated computer science concepts into required chemistry classes using interactive Molecular Workbench worksheets. The authors aimed to increase students’ awareness and understanding of computer science by embedding CS-related ideas and examples into chemistry topics such as evaporation, precipitation, parallelization, and real-world contexts like the Gulf oil spill and mobile devices.

The intervention was implemented with high school chemistry students in Poudre School District and supported by high school teachers, university researchers, and NSF funding. Students completed surveys over multiple years to assess attitudes toward computer science, understanding of the field, and misconceptions, while teachers also completed a follow-up survey about feasibility and classroom use. The paper additionally reflects on workshop-based teacher professional learning and the practical challenges of deploying technology reliably in K-12 classrooms.

Overall, the authors conclude that the worksheets can improve awareness of computer science and reduce some misconceptions, but the effects on student interest are mixed and often negative in the most reliable analyses. A major limiting factor was system reliability: hardware and network problems significantly affected classroom implementation, student experience, and the validity of some survey results. The teacher workshop was viewed positively, and teachers reported willingness to use the materials, suggesting the approach is feasible but operationally fragile.

finding.finding_summary: Across the student surveys, the intervention had mixed effects on attitudes toward computer science. In the 2011-2012 paired pre/post analysis of 101 students, overall interest decreased slightly (interest construct mean Δ=-0.0644, p=0.0525), while one misconception item improved and another understanding item changed in opposite directions; the most reliable AP subgroup (n=29) showed a slight increase in interest on some items but also a decrease in one item across the full dataset.
finding.measure: Student attitudes toward computer science, including interest and perceived usefulness/understanding, measured with Likert-scale survey constructs and paired pre/post tests
finding.study_size: n=101 overall; subgroup analyses included n=26 (MYP), n=17 (General Chemistry), n=29 (AP)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students appeared to gain some understanding of scientific/CS concepts through the interactive worksheets, particularly in the AP subgroup. In the 2011-2012 survey, question 14 (computer science skills in daily life) and the overall understanding construct showed significant positive change for AP students (n=29), although the construct-level change was not reported with an effect size.
finding.measure: Survey items and construct scores assessing understanding of computer science concepts and misconceptions in the context of chemistry learning

finding.finding_summary: The authors repeatedly note that hardware and network unreliability made implementation difficult for teachers and reduced the quality of the student experience. In the teacher workshop follow-up, all 7 respondents found the balance and length acceptable and said they would use the worksheets, but during classroom deployment the lack of dependable computers and network access caused protocol deviations, team-based survey completion, and technical frustrations.
finding.measure: Teacher feasibility survey and qualitative reports of classroom implementation constraints, including access to machines and network reliability
finding.study_size: n=7 teacher survey respondents; classroom implementation across multiple student cohorts

finding.finding_summary: The project had institutional impact in the form of teacher professional learning and reported readiness to adopt the materials. After the 3-day summer workshop, all 7 survey respondents said they would attend a similar workshop again, and most indicated they would use the worksheets in their classrooms at least once per year; 2 said they would use them weekly.
finding.measure: Teacher workshop feedback and stated intentions for classroom adoption

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Design Features of an Intelligent Tutoring System for Advanced Mathematics Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates two design features of Xiaomai, an intelligent tutoring system (ITS) created to support Chinese college students in advanced mathematics and graduate entrance exam preparation. The authors focus on whether free-response questions with automatic feedback and self-evaluation improve learning compared with multiple-choice questions, and whether an added error-reflection prompt improves practice and posttest performance.

The study used a 2x2 randomized experiment with 120 university students in central China who had taken advanced mathematics courses. Participants completed a pretest, 40 minutes of practice in Xiaomai under one of four conditions, and then a posttest. The free-response version required students to upload step-by-step work and self-rate their answers after seeing solutions; the reflection condition additionally asked students to identify the reason for errors.

Results showed that multiple-choice conditions outperformed free-response conditions on practice performance and learning gains, while reflection had no significant effect on either practice or posttest outcomes. The authors conclude that the current free-response and error-reflection designs in Xiaomai do not improve effectiveness and may need redesign, such as adding worked incorrect examples or better support for meaningful reflection.

finding.finding_summary: The experiment found that students in the multiple-choice conditions achieved better mathematics practice performance and higher posttest learning gains than students in the free-response conditions. Posttest ANCOVA showed a marginal main effect of item format (F(1,115)=3.72, p=0.06), with adjusted means of 9.21 for multiple-choice versus 7.94 for free-response; the authors also report larger pretest-to-posttest effect sizes for the multiple-choice groups than the free-response groups.
finding.measure: Pretest and posttest mathematics scores; practice correctness/performance in an intelligent tutoring system

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly tested whether error reflection improved metacognitive learning support in Xiaomai, but found no statistically significant effect on posttest scores, practice performance, number of attempts, item correctness, or time per item. Reflection also did not interact with prior knowledge in the follow-up analysis, suggesting the reflection prompt as implemented did not measurably improve students’ metacognitive learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Reflection on errors; pretest-to-posttest gain; practice attempts, correctness, and response time

paper_profiles.title: Исследовательские задачи и Московская математическая конференция школьников
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a reflective, practice-oriented discussion of the Moscow Mathematical Conference for School Students (ММКШ) and the authors’ approach to supporting student mathematical research. The central question is how to help school students produce genuinely independent, meaningful, and sufficiently reliable mathematical work, while distinguishing between informal exploratory work, completed educational research, and work that meets higher standards of scientific research.

Rather than evaluating a technical intervention or algorithm, the paper proposes and explains a conference ecosystem: short-form submission and revision, detailed referee feedback, consultant support, transparent peer review, and explicit nomination categories (research, educational research, research development, visual/experimental materials). The authors argue that these structures help students learn to formulate precise claims, write complete proofs, check results more carefully, and gradually move from “work in progress” toward reliable, user-facing mathematical texts.

The context is a long-running Russian extracurricular mathematics culture centered on circles, olympiads, and student conferences. The paper illustrates the system with many concrete examples of student works, revisions, referee interactions, and cases where students developed from short, partially complete submissions into award-winning or even publishable research. Its main conclusion is normative: for school mathematics research, transparency, careful review, and explicit distinctions between levels of completion and novelty are essential, and these practices support both student development and institutional integrity.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that participation in the conference helps students learn to formulate precise mathematical statements and write complete proofs, but it does not report experimental effect sizes. The evidence is illustrative and anecdotal, based on multiple student examples (e.g., works [AB], [Ko], [Ne], [Ni08], [Ru10]) rather than quantitative outcome measurement.
finding.measure: Quality/completeness of mathematical formulations and proofs; student mathematical research products

finding.finding_summary: A central claim is that the process develops students’ ability to think independently, refine intuition, revise work based on feedback, and collaborate with consultants and referees. The paper describes this as a gradual movement from exploratory problem solving toward more mature research practice, but does not provide quantitative estimates.
finding.measure: Independent problem solving, revision ability, reasoning quality, and collaboration in research writing

finding.finding_summary: The authors present a conference workflow intended to improve the efficiency and quality of student submissions through short initial formulations, transparent refereeing, consultant feedback, and iterative revision. The paper claims this reduces wasted effort and makes the process more productive, but gives no numerical productivity outcomes.
finding.measure: Revision cycle efficiency, referee/consultant workflow, and submission-to-acceptance process

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main institutional argument is that transparent peer review, explicit nomination categories, archival availability, and public accountability improve the integrity of school mathematics conferences. The paper is policy- and governance-focused, using many concrete conference examples to argue that these procedures prevent misrepresentation, encourage fairness, and better align awards with work quality.
finding.measure: Conference governance practices, transparency of review, nomination rules, and award decisions

paper_profiles.title: Surveying Turkish high school and university students’ attitudes and approaches to physics problem solving
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines students’ attitudes and approaches to physics problem solving using a Turkish translation of the Attitudes and Approaches to Problem Solving (AAPS) survey. The authors ask whether Turkish high school and university students differ by grade level, school type, and gender, and whether Turkish university students in algebra-based physics courses differ from comparable U.S. university students.

The study is not an intervention study; it focuses on translation, validation, and survey administration of the AAPS instrument. The survey was translated into Turkish, reviewed by experts, cognitively tested with a small number of high school students, and then administered to 528 Turkish students from grade 10, grade 11, and university science-education programs across six high schools and one university. Internal consistency was strong (Cronbach’s alpha 0.817-0.897 across groups), and exploratory factor analysis identified 10 factors explaining 51.86% of variance.

Overall, no statistically significant differences were found in the total survey means across Turkish gender or grade groups, but university students were somewhat more expert-like than vocational high school students on average. Item-level analyses showed several significant differences by gender and school type, and Turkish university students were generally less expert-like than U.S. students on the same AAPS survey, with statistically significant differences on 18 items. The authors conclude that the Turkish AAPS appears reliable and valid for studying students’ physics problem-solving attitudes, but the study is descriptive and correlational rather than an AI-personalized feedback or classroom intervention study.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly measures students’ attitudes and approaches to physics problem solving using the 33-item AAPS survey, which is closely tied to scientific reasoning in physics. Across 528 Turkish students (10th grade, 11th grade, vocational/regular/science high school, and university), overall mean differences were not statistically significant, but item-level differences showed that university students were somewhat more expert-like than vocational high school students, and Turkish university students were generally less expert-like than U.S. students on many items.
finding.measure: Attitudes and Approaches to Problem Solving (AAPS) survey; item-level favorable/unfavorable/neutral responses and normalized scores
finding.study_size: n=528 (Turkish sample); n=43 Turkish university subset; n=397 U.S. comparison subset

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines metacognition, self-monitoring, persistence, and strategy use during physics problem solving, all of which fall under durable skills. Item-level results indicate that many students reported novice-like tendencies such as feeling stuck without help or relying on equations mechanically, while expert-like responses were more common on metacognitive items such as checking whether an answer is reasonable and tracing back solutions when needed.
finding.measure: AAPS survey items related to metacognition, strategy selection, and self-monitoring in problem solving

paper_profiles.title: (Science) Teacher Education in the Knowledge Society: Good Practice at the University of Geneva
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a reflective, practice-oriented essay about teacher education at the University of Geneva, with a particular emphasis on science teacher education. It argues that university-based Professional Schools of Education provide an effective structural model because they integrate research, academic teaching, and school practice, and because they support both initial and continuing teacher education within a coherent institutional framework.

The paper uses the Geneva Institute of Teacher Education as a case example of this model. It describes structural features such as dual affiliation with disciplinary faculties, coordination between educational sciences and discipline-based education research, and close links to primary and secondary schooling. It also highlights out-of-school science learning resources (e.g., Scienscope, Bioutils, Stellarium Gornergrat, experiment@l) as part of teacher education and professional development.

A second major focus is evidence-based education in science teacher education. Rather than testing a new intervention, the paper synthesizes existing research and meta-analytic findings to argue that effective science teaching and teacher preparation should rely on systematic evidence about formative assessment, collaborative learning, inquiry with teacher guidance, motivation, and measurement. The conclusion is that the Geneva model represents a strong example of good practice, but not an ideal or exclusive solution; the author presents it as a potentially transferable institutional approach for other contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that science teacher education should be grounded in evidence-based science education, especially for improving understanding of scientific concepts and inquiry. It cites prior studies showing that guided inquiry outperforms unguided inquiry (d=0.65 vs. d=0.25) and that active/collaborative learning improves science achievement, but these are reported as background evidence rather than new results from this paper.
finding.measure: Science achievement and conceptual understanding in cited prior studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes motivation, interest, enjoyment, and self-efficacy as important outcomes in science education and teacher education. It reports previously published evidence that hands-on activities, out-of-school learning, and astronomy topics can strongly increase interest and enjoyment, including a large-sample study (N≈8000) where hands-on activities were among the most interesting learning activities for ages 11-16.
finding.measure: Interest, enjoyment, motivation, self-efficacy in science learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses collaborative learning and inquiry practices as ways to develop higher-order learning behaviors in science education, and it highlights the role of teachers in diagnosing misconceptions and using measurement to improve instruction. The evidence cited suggests collaborative learning has substantial positive effects on achievement (d=0.64 across disciplines; d=0.95 in science), though these are synthesized findings from prior research rather than direct results from the paper itself.
finding.measure: Collaborative learning effects on science achievement and related learning processes

finding.finding_summary: The core argument of the paper is institutional: university-based Professional Schools of Education, such as Geneva's IUTE, are presented as a strong structure for integrating research, teacher education, and practice. The paper reports favorable institutional indicators in Geneva, including good to very good evaluations of initial science teacher education courses, low non-completion among science teacher students, strong continuing professional education participation, and productive links between in-service teachers and teacher education/research.
finding.measure: Institutional organization, course evaluations, completion, participation, and program integration

paper_profiles.title: The Effectiveness of a Proposed Strategy for Teaching Geography through Artificial Intelligence Applications in Developing Secondary School Students’ Higher-Order Thinking Skills and Achievement
paper_profiles.venue: Pegem Journal of Education and Instruction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This quasi-experimental study examined whether a proposed geography teaching strategy supported by artificial intelligence applications could improve secondary school students’ higher-order thinking skills and academic achievement.
