The paper was motivated by the author’s view that geography instruction in secondary school should better develop thinking skills, and that AI tools may provide more interactive, supportive learning environments.

The intervention used three AI-related applications: Nearpod, Teachmint, and Renderforest. The content focused on three geography units for second-year secondary female students in Saudi Arabia (lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere), delivered over 12 class sessions. Two groups of 30 students each were compared: a control group taught traditionally and an experimental group taught with the proposed AI-based strategy. Pretest results showed the groups were equivalent on both higher-order thinking and achievement.

Posttest results favored the experimental group on both outcomes. Higher-order thinking skills increased substantially (total mean 52.30 vs 29.00, p<.001, eta-squared=.940, described as a high effect), and geography achievement also improved (mean 21.53 vs 13.47, p<.001, eta-squared=.613, described as a high effect). The author concludes that AI-supported geography instruction was effective for improving both higher-order thinking and achievement, and recommends broader use of AI applications in secondary geography teaching.

finding.finding_summary: The AI-based geography strategy significantly improved students’ higher-order thinking skills compared with traditional instruction. On the posttest assessment card, the experimental group scored much higher than the control group (total mean 52.30 vs 29.00, n=60, p<.001), with a reported high effect size (eta-squared=.940).
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking skills assessment card

finding.finding_summary: The proposed AI-supported teaching strategy also improved geography achievement. On the posttest achievement test, the experimental group outperformed the control group (mean 21.53 vs 13.47, n=60, p<.001), and the paper reports a high effect size (eta-squared=.613).
finding.measure: Geography achievement test

paper_profiles.title: The cognitive paradox of AI in education: between enhancement and erosion
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an opinion/review-style discussion of the cognitive promise and risks of artificial intelligence in education. It asks whether AI acts primarily as a learning enhancer—through personalization, efficiency, and individualized feedback—or whether it can erode cognition by encouraging dependency, cognitive offloading, and reduced deep processing.

The authors frame the discussion using Cognitive Load Theory, Bloom’s Taxonomy, and Self-Determination Theory. They synthesize previously published studies and examples spanning memory retention, critical thinking/problem-solving, creativity, language learning, and STEM tutoring, including work with undergraduate and vocational students and a reported high-school example from prior studies cited in the discussion.

The main conclusion is that AI should complement rather than replace human instruction. The paper argues that AI can help lower-order learning and access, but overreliance may weaken retention, critical thinking, motivation, autonomy, and conceptual understanding unless instructional designs deliberately preserve effortful engagement, reflection, and teacher-guided discussion. No original empirical study is reported in the paper itself; it is primarily a conceptual/opinion synthesis of prior evidence.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI has a dual relationship with critical thinking and problem-solving: it can support learning efficiency, but overreliance may reduce independent reasoning and lead to cognitive offloading. This is supported only by cited prior studies rather than original data in the paper itself; one cited study of 206 vocational education students reported that AI posed significant perceived threats to retention and critical thinking, with male students showing more concern than female peers.
finding.measure: Perceived challenges to retention and critical thinking; discussion of critical thinking/problem-solving
finding.study_size: n=206 (cited study); paper itself reports no original sample

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that excessive dependence on AI may lower motivation and intrinsic engagement, while carefully designed AI could support autonomy and competence. This is a conceptual synthesis grounded in cited prior literature; no original outcome data are reported in the paper itself. The discussion emphasizes preserving student agency, engagement, and relatedness in AI-supported learning.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, autonomy-related learning processes

finding.finding_summary: Across cited examples, the paper portrays AI as improving some academic performance outcomes while potentially undermining deeper conceptual understanding. For instance, it cites prior work suggesting AI tutoring can increase standardized test performance, but also notes a cited study of Turkish high school students where ChatGPT-assisted practice led to 48% more correctly solved problems but a 17% lower concept-understanding test score.
finding.measure: Standardized test performance; concept understanding; procedural problem solving
finding.study_size: not_reported (paper cites external studies; one cited high-school study sample size not provided in the paper text)

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education (broad, not empirically sampled)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the promise and risks of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it synthesizes early examples and proposes how LLMs could be used to create educational content, support personalized learning, improve feedback, aid assessment, and stimulate critical thinking across learner age groups.

The paper discusses applications for elementary, middle/high school, university, remote/group learning, learners with disabilities, and teacher workflows such as lesson planning, feedback, grading, and professional development. It also surveys then-current research examples involving quiz generation, curiosity prompts, code explanations, adaptive feedback, and automated scoring. The authors argue that LLMs can be educationally useful if integrated with strong human oversight, fact-checking, and curriculum design.

A major focus of the paper is the set of ethical, practical, and institutional challenges that LLMs introduce, including bias, privacy, copyright, academic integrity, cost, sustainability, and the difficulty of distinguishing machine-generated from human-generated work. The paper concludes that LLMs are promising but require careful governance, teacher preparation, and further research before they can be used responsibly at scale in education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can support critical thinking by generating questions, prompts, explanations, and alternative perspectives, but also warns that overreliance on effortless model-generated answers may weaken learners’ independent reasoning and problem-solving. This is a conceptual claim grounded in examples and prior work rather than a new empirical test; no study size, effect size, or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking and problem-solving opportunities/risks discussed conceptually

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims LLMs can save teacher time by semi-automating grading, generating feedback, creating quizzes, and producing lesson materials. It cites prior work indicating grading effort could be reduced by up to 85% with NLP-based feedback systems, but the position paper itself does not report a new empirical estimate.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, feedback generation efficiency (discussed via cited studies)

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that adopting LLMs in education raises institutional issues around privacy, copyright, bias, sustainability, fairness, and academic integrity, and recommends governance, policy, and human-oversight strategies. These are framed as anticipated system-level impacts and mitigation needs rather than results from an empirical study.
finding.measure: Policy/governance and institutional adoption considerations

paper_profiles.title: Shaping integrity: why generative artificial intelligence does not have to undermine education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and broader education (general education context; not an empirical sample study)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This opinion paper argues that generative AI (GAI) does not inherently undermine education or academic integrity. Instead, the authors contend that when GAI is used responsibly, it can support authentic learning, improve digital literacy, and foster intrinsic motivation, thereby reducing dishonest behavior rather than encouraging it.

The paper is not an empirical intervention study; it is a conceptual and normative discussion grounded in ethical frameworks (deontological ethics and consequentialism), constructivist learning theory, and self-determination theory. The authors use illustrative classroom examples across history, language arts, science, and business to show how AI tools might provide personalized feedback, interactive simulations, and collaborative support that align with learning goals.

The main conclusion is that educators and administrators should emphasize transparency, ethical instruction, professional development, and iterative evaluation when integrating AI. The paper recommends making AI use explicit in learning outcomes and using AI as a supplement to human teaching, with the goal of preserving academic integrity while leveraging AI’s potential to enhance engagement and learning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GAI can improve writing through real-time feedback on grammar, tone, narrative structure, and revision support. This is presented as a conceptual claim rather than an empirical result; no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Writing quality, grammar, tone, and narrative structure feedback

finding.finding_summary: The authors describe AI-powered lab assistants and virtual experiments as supporting hypothesis generation, data analysis, and drawing conclusions in science learning. These claims are illustrative and theoretical, with no reported empirical sample, effect size, or confidence interval.
finding.measure: Scientific inquiry and virtual experiment participation

finding.finding_summary: Across history, business, and other classroom examples, the paper claims GAI can support authentic learning via simulations, timelines, market analyses, and project-based tasks. The paper does not report empirical outcomes; instead it argues that these uses may deepen understanding and reduce reliance on rote work.
finding.measure: Authentic learning in history, business, and other non-core subject tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally argues that GAI can foster intrinsic motivation by supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness. It claims personalized feedback and self-directed learning can increase engagement and reduce cheating, but provides no empirical effect estimates or sample data.
finding.measure: Intrinsic motivation, autonomy, competence, relatedness, engagement

finding.finding_summary: A major theme is that GAI can support critical thinking, metacognition, collaboration, and problem-solving through interactive simulations, feedback, and project-based learning. The paper presents these as theoretical benefits and does not report empirical measures such as critical-thinking tests or collaboration scores.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognition, collaboration, and problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper recommends institutional policies for transparent AI use, educator professional development, ethical guidelines, and iterative evaluation of AI tools in schools. These are policy-oriented arguments rather than measured institutional outcomes, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: AI governance, policy guidance, educator training, and institutional implementation

paper_profiles.title: AI in the Classroom: A Boon or a Threat to Pedagogical Practices?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI in education is primarily beneficial or harmful for pedagogical practice, with a particular focus on student engagement, critical thinking, retention, and the risk of over-reliance on AI tools. The authors frame AI as a potentially useful source of personalized feedback and content support, but also as a possible threat to independent thought and traditional learning processes.

The study combines a brief literature review, a teacher survey from schools in Almaty, and an experiment with 6th-grade students. In the experiment, students used AI tools to write a short story, were asked to customize the AI-generated content, and were later tested on recall after one week. Teacher survey responses were mixed: some teachers saw AI as helpful for engagement and academic progress, while others worried it reduced independence. The student activity showed moderate retention, low customization, and generally low engagement, though students were interested in the novelty of AI-assisted storytelling.

Overall, the paper concludes that AI can increase initial interest and support learning, but may also encourage dependency and surface-level engagement if not carefully guided. The authors argue for a balanced approach in which AI supplements rather than replaces traditional pedagogy, especially for younger learners, and call for more research on long-term effects.

finding.finding_summary: Teacher survey results suggested mixed views on whether AI improved student engagement and motivation. In the student experiment, AI-assisted storytelling was described as interesting and sparked initial interest, but engagement was generally low and several students did not complete the task.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of engagement and motivation; student participation/interest in AI-assisted storytelling task

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines critical thinking, independence, and problem-solving as outcomes of AI use. Teachers were divided on whether AI improved or hindered independent assignment completion, and the authors argue that students' minimal customization of AI-generated stories suggests over-reliance that could weaken critical thinking and independent thought.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of independence; observed customization of AI-generated stories; qualitative discussion of critical thinking and problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: The experiment involved writing a short story with AI support and then retelling it one week later, so the paper substantively engages with writing and recall of written text. About half of the students could retell the story with reasonable accuracy, but customization of the writing was minimal, suggesting only moderate comprehension and retention of the AI-generated narrative.
finding.measure: Story writing, retelling after one week, and brief interview discussion of the story

paper_profiles.title: Learn to Machine Learn via Games in the Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the deployment and use of ArtBot, a serious game designed to teach children and adolescents foundational concepts in artificial intelligence and machine learning. The authors are especially interested in whether a game-based approach can support AI literacy and prompt critical thinking about supervised learning, reinforcement learning, algorithmic behavior, and bias. They also explore usability, engagement, and how learners interact with game features such as informational help screens, parameter settings, and repeated play.

ArtBot was developed as part of the EU-funded LearnML project and released on web, Windows, and Android platforms. The paper combines anonymous in-game analytics collected from more than 2,000 users with survey responses from 130 students and 35 educators who played the game during dissemination and training events. The sample included primary and secondary education stakeholders, with the survey respondents reporting generally positive attitudes toward the game’s usability and educational value.

The main findings are that players meaningfully engaged with the AI/ML mechanics, experimented with settings, and reported that the game helped them understand how AI and machine learning work. However, the paper also finds clear design limitations: many users skipped informational panels, manual image labeling was repetitive, later reinforcement-learning levels did not retain many players, and some levels likely need tuning for difficulty and clarity. Overall, the study concludes that game-based AI instruction can be promising in K-12 settings, but the learning materials and mechanics need refinement to better sustain engagement and deepen conceptual understanding.

finding.finding_summary: The game was intended to promote critical thinking about AI/ML and the authors report evidence that players explored algorithm settings, reflected on labeling quality, and experimented with parameters to change outcomes. However, the evidence is observational and indirect: the paper infers critical thinking from player actions rather than measuring it with a dedicated assessment.
finding.measure: In-game behavior indicating experimentation with supervised-learning and reinforcement-learning parameters, plus survey/open-response reflections
finding.study_size: n=2222 unique users for log data; n=130 students and n=35 educators for surveys

finding.finding_summary: Engagement and enjoyment were generally high, with students and teachers reporting that the game was easy to use, fun, and worth playing again. Survey means were high for usability/enjoyment items (e.g., students: understand how to play M=4.2, fun M=4.0; teachers: would play again M=4.0, help understand AI M=4.2), suggesting positive motivational responses, although later RL levels showed drop-off and some boredom/complexity concerns.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey responses on ease of use, fun, boredom, recommendation, and willingness to replay; usage/completion data across game levels
finding.study_size: n=130 students; n=35 educators; n=2222 unique users in analytics
finding.std_deviation: students SDs reported as 0.8-1.4; teachers SDs reported as 0.7-1.2

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly targets understanding of machine learning concepts, including supervised learning, reinforcement learning, training/testing data, rewards, penalties, exploration, and algorithmic bias. Both groups reported that the game helped them understand AI/ML (students M=4.0, teachers M=4.2 for understanding how AI works), and the authors argue that players’ interactions show conceptual engagement, though no pre/post test was conducted.
finding.measure: Survey items on understanding AI/ML; gameplay patterns involving supervised-learning classification accuracy, training/test split comprehension, and RL parameter manipulation
finding.study_size: n=130 students; n=35 educators; n=2222 unique users in analytics
finding.std_deviation: students SD about 1.0; teachers SD about 0.9-1.0

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emergence of ChatGPT and asks what it may mean for higher education, especially assessment, learning, and teaching. The authors combine a literature review with hands-on experimentation using ChatGPT, positioning the tool within the broader history of AI in education and comparing it to earlier AI-powered writing tools such as Grammarly and Wordtune.

The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it analyzes ChatGPT’s capabilities and limitations through example prompts and a desktop review of early ChatGPT-related publications. The context is higher education, with a focus on student writing, automated feedback, and assessment integrity. The authors argue that ChatGPT is capable of producing fluent text, conceptual explanations, and some basic problem-solving, but struggles with higher-order critical and analytical writing, citation accuracy, and some non-English language tasks.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is unlikely to eliminate traditional assessment outright, but it does create both challenges and opportunities for educators. The paper recommends adapting assessment practices, using AI more thoughtfully in teaching, and preparing institutions to manage plagiarism, feedback, and policy issues in a changing AI landscape.

finding.finding_summary: In the authors' hands-on tests, ChatGPT could generate short essays quickly, but the output lacked breadth, depth, and reliable referencing. When asked for a 2000-word essay with citations, it produced only about 500 words with five end-of-text references and was described as generic, descriptive, and sometimes bogus in its citations.
finding.measure: Essay quality, coherence, analytical depth, and citation accuracy in generated writing

finding.finding_summary: The paper concludes that ChatGPT is less competent with content requiring higher-order thinking, specifically critical and analytical thinking. In the examples provided, the authors judged the model to be useful for conceptual explanation but weak for tasks requiring evaluation, reasoning, and depth.
finding.measure: Ability of ChatGPT to produce critical and analytical written responses

finding.finding_summary: When prompted to explain mean, standard deviation, z-scores, and a real-world application with step-by-step calculations, ChatGPT provided clear and sensible explanations within about 60-120 seconds. The paper treats this as evidence that the tool can support basic mathematical concept explanation, although no quantitative evaluation was conducted.
finding.measure: Quality of explanations for mean, standard deviation, z-scores, and example calculations

finding.finding_summary: The authors emphasize that ChatGPT can rapidly generate explanations and draft text within seconds to about two minutes, suggesting potential efficiency gains for drafting, brainstorming, and response generation. However, they also note interruptions from network errors, character limits, and the need for eventual monetization because of compute costs.
finding.measure: Speed and ease of generating responses and drafts

paper_profiles.title: Blue Sky Ideas in Artificial Intelligence Education from the EAAI 2017 New and Future AI Educator Program
paper_profiles.venue: EAAI 2017 (Symposium on Educational Advances in Artificial Intelligence)
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school, early undergraduate, and university faculty/future educators
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a collection of short position-style essays written for the EAAI 2017 New and Future AI Educator Program. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, it asks “blue sky” questions about how AI education should evolve, including how to teach AI at secondary-school or early-undergraduate levels, how to incorporate ethics throughout the AI curriculum, and how to make AI education more interdisciplinary.

The contributions propose a range of pedagogical ideas: peer-learning across disciplines, Montessori-inspired student-centric discovery, early introduction of AI concepts through games and puzzles, real-world problem-based instruction, and blending AI ethics into search, planning, machine learning, robotics, and project-based courses. Several essays explicitly target secondary-school students or early undergraduates, but they are conceptual proposals rather than evaluated interventions.

Overall, the paper concludes that AI education should be more accessible, interdisciplinary, ethically integrated, and grounded in meaningful real-world or hands-on learning experiences. However, it does not present experimental evidence, outcome data, or measured effects of any specific instructional approach.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is not an empirical evaluation of a policy or institutional reform; it is a set of proposals about how AI education should be structured. It argues for curricular changes such as ethics codes, IRB-like risk assessment, interdisciplinary teaching, and more accessible AI instruction, but provides no measured institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly discusses critical thinking, reasoning, collaboration, and independent thinking as desired educational goals, especially in the Montessori-inspired and interdisciplinary sections. However, these are aspirations and design ideas rather than measured student outcomes, so no empirical effect can be extracted.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Systems that Augment Human Performed vs. Demonstrated Critical Thinking
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2025 ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable / no direct study population
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses a conceptual problem in current generative AI research: studies of AI and critical thinking often conflate the critical thinking people do independently with the critical thinking they appear to demonstrate while using AI. The authors argue that this distinction matters because systems can make outputs look better without improving a person’s underlying reasoning ability.

The paper does not test an intervention. Instead, it synthesizes prior work from psychology, education, and human-AI interaction to define two categories: performed critical thinking (independent cognitive work) and demonstrated critical thinking (thinking expressed through AI-assisted outputs). It also discusses how existing assessments and AI tools tend to measure the latter, and it recommends future study designs that separately evaluate both forms, including before/after interventions and longitudinal methods.

The context is broad generative AI use, with examples from writing, coding, and decision-making rather than a specific K-12 classroom sample. The main conclusion is that AI systems may improve demonstrated critical thinking and task outputs without necessarily strengthening performed critical thinking, so educational and product design should explicitly support independent reasoning practice rather than only better AI-assisted answers.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not present new empirical results; it is a conceptual position paper arguing that current GenAI systems may improve demonstrated critical thinking while not necessarily improving performed critical thinking. The authors synthesize prior studies and conclude that existing evaluations often measure AI-assisted outputs rather than independent reasoning, so the evidence base is mixed and currently methodologically misaligned with the construct of interest.
finding.measure: conceptual distinction and review of prior critical-thinking assessments and GenAI studies

paper_profiles.title: Enterprise AI Canvas: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Business
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes the Enterprise AI Canvas, a structured framework for planning and evaluating artificial intelligence projects in businesses. The core question is how organizations can identify AI use cases that create value while also accounting for the technical, organizational, and operational changes required to implement them responsibly.

The canvas is divided into two parts: a business view and a model/data view. The business view covers value, success metrics, decision optimization, organizational change, sponsorship, and domain expertise; the model/data view covers prediction targets, features, data sources, constraints, domain/data quality, and evaluation/monitoring. The paper is conceptual and illustrative rather than empirical, using a supermarket replenishment example to show how the canvas can be applied to an AI-driven ordering system.

The paper’s main conclusion is that successful AI adoption requires joint planning by business experts and data scientists, because prediction quality alone does not guarantee good operational decisions. It argues that organizations should explicitly define KPIs, decision rules, data requirements, and change-management implications before deploying AI systems.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can improve operational efficiency by optimizing decisions such as replenishment/order quantities, reducing waste and stock-outs in the supermarket example. However, this is a conceptual claim illustrated with a fictitious example, not an empirical result; no effect size, sample size, or statistical test is reported.
finding.measure: Operational KPIs discussed conceptually, including stock-out rate, waste of perishable goods, overall inventory, and order-quantity optimization

finding.finding_summary: A central contribution of the paper is the Enterprise AI Canvas itself, which is intended to improve organizational planning, governance, and cross-functional coordination for AI adoption. The paper discusses sponsorship, role changes, change management, and how human and AI decision-making should be integrated, but it does not report empirical evidence of institutional effects.
finding.measure: Conceptual framework for organizational governance and change management in AI projects

paper_profiles.title: Gathering Strength, Gathering Storms: The One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence (AI100) 2021 Study Panel Report
paper_profiles.venue: Stanford University / AI100 Study Panel Report
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (multi-domain report; not a K-12 sample)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report is the second major installment in the One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence (AI100), a long-term expert review of the state of AI and its societal influences. Rather than evaluating a single intervention or educational program, it synthesizes recent developments in AI across technical and social domains, including language processing, computer vision, robotics, mobility, health, finance, recommender systems, governance, and the broader societal implications of AI.

The report was produced by a multidisciplinary Study Panel and is structured around 12 standing questions and 2 workshop questions. Its purpose is to assess how AI has advanced since the 2016 report, identify opportunities and risks, and provide expert-informed guidance for future AI research, deployment, and policy. The report discusses AI applications in high-stakes contexts such as education, but only at a general policy-and-governance level; it does not study K-12 AI-personalized feedback, student outcomes, or critical-thinking interventions.

Overall, the report concludes that AI has made major progress in many subfields and is increasingly embedded in everyday life, but it also emphasizes persistent limitations, including bias, transparency, overreliance, misuse, and the need for human-centered design and governance. For education specifically, the paper mentions predictive systems and public-sector AI as part of broader high-stakes decision-making, but it does not present empirical educational evidence or a school-based evaluation.

paper_profiles.title: Natural Language Query Engine for Relational Databases using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of making relational databases accessible to non-technical users who do not know SQL. It argues that current natural-language-to-SQL systems often fail to validate generated queries, do not handle business rules well, and do not return usable natural-language answers.

The paper proposes a generative-AI-based assistant that scans database schemas, stores schema information and business rules in a vector database, retrieves relevant context from user queries, generates SQL with an LLM, and then validates and iteratively refines the query before producing a natural-language response. The prototype is built with IBM watsonx.data, watsonx.ai, and Milvus, and is evaluated on the BIRD-SQL benchmark. The evaluation is not a study of learners or schools; it is a technical database-interface prototype assessed on SQL accuracy and response quality. The reported results suggest the approach can improve query generation and produce understandable responses, but the work remains a prototype with limited evaluation and no K-12 educational context.

finding.finding_summary: The prototype is designed to reduce user effort and improve efficiency in querying relational databases for non-technical users. In initial tests on BIRD Bench, over 50% of queries were correctly translated into SQL on the first attempt (over 58% for simple queries), and iterative refinement improved success rates further. The paper also reports that 90% of natural-language responses were rated excellent by a dozen nontechnical users, suggesting improved usability and task efficiency.
finding.measure: SQL translation accuracy; natural-language response quality ratings
finding.study_size: BIRD Bench evaluation size not_reported; 12 nontechnical users for response-quality rating

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI Toolkit - A Framework for Increasing the Quality of LLM-based Applications over Their Whole Life Cycle
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint presents the Generative AI Toolkit, a software framework intended to automate development, testing, deployment, and monitoring workflows for LLM-based applications across their full life cycle. The paper argues that current LLM application development is often manual, slow, and trial-and-error driven, and proposes a toolkit that supports prompt/model permutation testing, custom metrics, trace logging, CI/CD integration, and post-deployment monitoring.

The paper is not an education study; its setting is software engineering and product development at BMW Group and Amazon Web Services. The authors illustrate the toolkit through representative use cases such as text-to-SQL, a restaurant RAG agent, an in-vehicle assistant, and model comparison for tool-using agents. These examples are presented as demonstrations of functionality rather than controlled empirical evaluations with statistical analysis.

The main conclusion is that the toolkit can improve development efficiency, increase test coverage, and help identify optimization opportunities for LLM applications. However, the paper explicitly notes that generic quantitative claims are difficult to make, and it does not report rigorous experimental evidence of impact in educational settings or on student outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Making AI-Enhanced Videos: Analyzing Generative AI Use Cases in YouTube Content Creation
paper_profiles.venue: Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI EA ’25)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how YouTube content creators use generative AI tools across the video production pipeline. The authors ask what specific use cases GenAI serves in planning, production, editing, and uploading, addressing a gap in understanding how these tools are actually used in creator workflows.

The study analyzes 274 YouTube how-to videos collected via the YouTube Data API. The authors used thematic analysis and multi-researcher annotation to code GenAI use cases across four phases of creation: planning, production, editing, and uploading. They identify common uses such as topic ideation, script generation, prompt refinement, image/video generation, avatar creation, voiceover generation, lip-syncing, resolution enhancement, subtitle generation, and title generation.

The paper is situated in the adult creator community rather than an educational or K-12 setting. Its main contribution is a conceptual framework of GenAI use in video creation and a discussion of design implications for prompt support, creator workflows, authenticity, transparency, and accessibility. It does not evaluate educational outcomes or AI-personalized feedback for students; instead, it is a descriptive HCI study of creator practices and future research opportunities.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that creators use GenAI to streamline many time-consuming steps in video production, including scripting, prompt refinement, image/video generation, voiceover creation, lip-syncing, editing, subtitles, and title generation. Across 274 analyzed how-to videos, the most common use case was prompting for images/videos (n=167, 60.9%), followed by scripting/storytelling (n=85, 31%) and creating AI voiceovers (n=93, 33.9%).
finding.measure: Observed GenAI use cases in YouTube how-to videos across the video production workflow

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses GenAI as support for ideation, creativity, and prompt creation, but does not directly measure improvements in critical thinking or other durable skills. It argues that prompt crafting may become a critical skill for creators and raises concerns about over-reliance on AI potentially reducing originality and creativity.
finding.measure: Thematic identification of ideation- and prompt-related GenAI use cases

paper_profiles.title: Provocation: Who benefits from “inclusion” in Generative AI?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This provocation paper asks who actually benefits when marginalized communities are invited to participate in generative AI development and evaluation. The authors argue that dominant forms of “participatory AI” often assume community inclusion will improve models and produce downstream benefits, but these claims are under-theorized and may ignore extractive labor, limited ownership, paywalls, inaccessible interfaces, and other structural barriers.

Rather than reporting an empirical intervention study, the paper uses a speculative case study centered on a hypothetical Vietnamese community member invited to help enrich and evaluate a text-to-image system. Through this scenario, the authors trace potential benefits and harms for community members as end-users and non-end-users, and discuss how improved representation may also enable misuse, further marginalization, or reduced compensation and control.

The main conclusion is normative: participatory engagements in GenAI should be more transparent about who benefits, under what conditions, and what protections or ownership structures are in place. The paper highlights alternative models such as community authorship, community-owned models, restrictive licensing, royalties, and community-led harm assessment, but it does not test these approaches empirically.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that current participatory AI structures can both enable improved representation and reproduce extractive, inequitable power relations. Using a speculative case study rather than empirical data, it shows that one-time consultation without ownership, compensation, or governance can leave community members sold back improved models while institutions retain control and profit.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of participatory AI structures, stakeholder dependency mapping, and speculative case study

paper_profiles.title: Making Physical Objects with Generative AI and Robotic Assembly: Considering Fabrication Constraints, Sustainability, Time, Functionality and Accessibility
paper_profiles.venue: GenAICHI: CHI 2025 Workshop on Generative AI and HCI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This workshop paper examines how 3D generative AI can be paired with physical fabrication methods to turn text-prompted digital designs into real objects. The authors argue that although text-to-3D models can create meshes quickly, existing fabrication pipelines—especially 3D printing—do not adequately address physical-world constraints, production speed, sustainability, usability, or access to fabrication equipment.

As a case study, the paper presents a system that combines 3D generative AI (Meshy.AI) with discrete robotic assembly using a UR10 robotic arm. The system converts AI-generated shapes into modular components via voxelization and then applies geometric checks such as overhang detection, connectivity analysis, and robot reachability to make assembly feasible. The paper frames the work around five design considerations: fabrication constraints, time, sustainability, functionality, and accessibility.

The study reports a proof-of-concept evaluation showing that the approach can assemble several prompt-generated objects in under five minutes, reuse 40 modular components to create seven distinct objects, and produce objects that visually resemble the prompts. However, some assembled objects were not functional as furniture, and accessibility remains limited because industrial robotic equipment is expensive. The authors conclude that discrete robotic assembly may better align with the speed and scalability of generative AI than 3D printing, but that more work is needed to improve structural integrity and broaden access.

finding.finding_summary: The system enabled prompt-to-physical fabrication in under five minutes for nearly all assembled objects, with average object volume around 7500 cm3. The paper argues this is a promising match for generative AI because it reduces fabrication time relative to conventional methods, though the result is a case study rather than a controlled comparison.
finding.measure: Assembly / fabrication time from user prompt to completed physical object

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that discrete robotic assembly can support reuse of the same 40 modular components to create seven distinct objects, which the authors frame as a more sustainable and responsible fabrication workflow. This finding is presented as a systems-level argument about material reuse and reduced waste rather than as a causal impact estimate.
finding.measure: Number of distinct objects assembled from a fixed set of 40 modular components; reuse/disassembly capability

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on AI-assisted making and fabrication as a design/engineering workflow, not on student learning. Its core conclusion is that generative AI outputs can be translated into physical artifacts when paired with robotic assembly and feasibility checks, but the work does not evaluate educational outcomes.
finding.measure: Prompt-to-object fabrication feasibility and object resemblance/functionality

paper_profiles.title: A Survey on the Integration of Generative AI for Critical Thinking in Mobile Networks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper surveys recent research on generative AI (GenAI) methods for critical thinking tasks, with a focus on reasoning and planning in mobile and telecom networks. It asks how current GenAI approaches—especially large language models, but also GANs, VAEs/CVAEs, and diffusion models—can support reasoning-like behavior such as deduction, abduction, analogical reasoning, decomposition, conflict detection, and plan generation.

The paper is a conceptual survey rather than an intervention study. It organizes the literature into a taxonomy of reasoning tasks and reasoning types, then maps GenAI approaches to telecom use cases across business management, service management, network lifecycle management, and infrastructure management. The context is telecom/5G/6G network operations, not K-12 education; the discussion emphasizes how reasoning techniques might assist human operators, automate configuration and planning, and improve explainability.

The paper concludes that GenAI is promising for translating natural language to symbolic forms, generating candidate plans, and supporting decision-making in complex network environments, but that true reasoning remains uncertain and verification is still needed. It highlights challenges such as hallucinations, limited plan-execution fidelity, scalability, and the need for generate-and-verify or neuro-symbolic methods. Overall, it is a broad survey and future-research agenda for telecom AI rather than an empirical evaluation of educational outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively discusses critical thinking, reasoning, planning, and related cognitive capabilities as the central focus of GenAI methods. However, it does not evaluate these skills in an educational setting or report learner outcome data; instead it surveys prior technical work and argues that CoT, self-consistency, ReAct, and hybrid methods can exhibit reasoning-like behavior in tasks such as math, commonsense QA, and symbolic problem solving.
finding.measure: Reasoning capability / critical thinking performance in reviewed GenAI methods

paper_profiles.title: Combining exploratory learning with structured practice educational technologies to foster both conceptual and procedural fractions knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether combining two types of educational technology can better support fractions learning than structured practice alone: an exploratory learning environment (ELE) intended to build conceptual understanding, and an intelligent tutoring system (ITS) intended to build procedural skill. The authors frame the work around the idea that robust mathematics learning requires both conceptual and procedural knowledge, and that most existing systems emphasize only one of these two outcomes.

The study used the iTalk2Learn platform, which sequenced activities from an ELE (Fractions Lab) and an ITS (Maths Whizz in the UK; Fractions Tutor in Germany) using adaptive support based on student interactions and affect. Two quasi-experimental studies were run in school settings: 121 students aged 8-10 in the UK and 151 students aged 10-12 in Germany, all learning equivalent fractions. Students were assigned to either a combined ITS+ELE condition or an ITS-only condition, with pre/post fractions tests measuring procedural and conceptual knowledge.

Across both countries, students in both conditions improved, but the combined condition produced larger gains in conceptual knowledge without harming procedural learning. The strongest and most consistent effect was on conceptual scores: the ITS+ELE condition showed medium gains, while ITS-only showed no reliable conceptual improvement. The authors conclude that combining exploratory learning with structured practice can produce a beneficial "combination effect" for fractions learning and argue that AI-supported exploratory environments may complement, rather than replace, structured tutoring systems.

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved fractions learning overall, with the combined ITS+ELE condition producing larger gains than ITS-only. In the UK sample (n=121), conceptual scores increased from M=1.00 to 1.52 in ITS+ELE (d=0.58, 95% CI [0.22, 0.94]) and from M=0.88 to 0.70 in ITS-only (d=-0.21, 95% CI [-0.57, 0.15]); procedural scores also improved in both conditions, with ITS+ELE showing d=0.65 [0.28, 1.01] and ITS-only d=0.38 [0.02, 0.74]. In Germany (n=151), the pattern was similar: conceptual gains were stronger in ITS+ELE (d=0.59 [0.30, 0.87]) than ITS-only (d=-0.32 [-0.71, 0.07]), while procedural gains were positive in both conditions.
finding.measure: Online fractions knowledge test with separate conceptual and procedural subscales
finding.study_size: n=272 total; Germany n=151, UK n=121
finding.effect_size: d=0.59 conceptual (Germany ITS+ELE), d=0.58 conceptual (UK ITS+ELE), d=0.54 procedural (Germany ITS+ELE), d=0.65 procedural (UK ITS+ELE)
finding.confidence_interval: Germany conceptual [0.30, 0.87]; UK conceptual [0.22, 0.94]; Germany procedural [0.26, 0.82]; UK procedural [0.28, 1.01]

paper_profiles.title: A Scoping Survey of ChatGPT in Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a scoping survey of research on ChatGPT in mathematics education, conducted to map the emerging literature and identify the benefits and challenges reported in studies published from November 2022 to May 2024. The review was motivated by the rapid diffusion of ChatGPT and the need to clarify what kinds of educational uses had already been studied, especially in relation to teaching and learning mathematics.

The authors searched Google Scholar, Web of Science, arXiv, HAL, and conference proceedings, using keywords related to ChatGPT, GPT, mathematics, teaching, and learning. After screening about 200 records, they retained 50 publications and synthesized them thematically. The review organized findings into seven categories, including mathematical content use, teacher lesson planning, assessment and task design, personalized learning, critical thinking concerns, collaborative learning, and attitudes/outcomes.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT shows promise as a support tool for explanations, personalized learning, real-time feedback, lesson planning, and some forms of assessment and reasoning support. At the same time, it highlights important limitations such as inaccuracies, hallucinations, over-reliance, and the need for human oversight. Because it is a scoping review, the paper does not estimate a single causal effect, but instead provides a structured overview of the early evidence base and its practical implications for mathematics education.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, ChatGPT was often reported as useful for explaining mathematical concepts, supporting problem solving, and providing step-by-step assistance. However, the review also found substantial limitations in correctness and reliability, especially for more complex mathematics, graduate-level tasks, and abstract reasoning. Because this is a scoping review, the paper synthesizes patterns from multiple studies rather than reporting one pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning, problem solving, conceptual understanding, correctness of mathematical responses
finding.study_size: n=50 studies in the review (approximately 200 records screened)

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that ChatGPT was associated in several studies with improved self-regulated learning, motivation, confidence, and more positive attitudes toward mathematics or statistics. For example, studies summarized in the review described students gaining motivation and feeling more engaged when ChatGPT provided feedback and guidance, though the paper does not pool these outcomes into a single quantitative estimate.
finding.measure: Motivation, attitudes, engagement, self-regulated learning, confidence

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies critical thinking as a major theme, with several studies suggesting that ChatGPT can prompt reflective thinking, especially when used as a dialogic assistant or with chain-of-thought prompting. At the same time, other studies warn that heavy reliance on ChatGPT may reduce critical thinking because students may accept generated answers without sufficient questioning or deep understanding.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, reasoning, reflection, collaboration

finding.finding_summary: The review found recurring evidence that ChatGPT can reduce teacher workload by assisting with lesson planning, generating instructional materials, creating quizzes, and supporting feedback and assessment tasks. Several studies noted immediate feedback and faster production of lesson plans or grading support, although the quality of outputs varied and human oversight remained necessary.
finding.measure: Lesson planning efficiency, assessment support, feedback generation, instructional material creation

paper_profiles.title: Students’ perceptions and outcome of teacher feedback: a systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic review examines empirical research on teacher feedback for students aged 10–16 in elementary and lower secondary education. The authors ask what student outcomes have been measured, what factors moderate those outcomes, and which feedback characteristics appear most important. They followed PRISMA and PICO procedures, screened literature from 1991 to November 2022, and included 96 empirical studies after full-text review and extraction.

Across intervention, observational, and small-scale qualitative studies, the review finds that feedback is most effective when it is high-quality, tailored, specific, timely, and action-oriented. Such feedback is associated with better achievement, stronger motivation and engagement, and improved self-efficacy, interest, and self-regulation; vague, overly evaluative, or purely judgmental feedback tends to be less effective or even demotivating. The review also emphasizes that students’ interpretation of feedback, trust in the teacher-student relationship, and individual differences shape whether feedback is taken up and acted on.

The review is not about AI-personalized feedback itself, but it does note the potential future role of integrating AI with human feedback systems. Its evidence base is mainly teacher feedback research in K-12 settings, with many studies focused on achievement and motivational outcomes rather than on technology-mediated personalization. Overall, the paper supports a student-centered, adaptive feedback approach and highlights that feedback effectiveness depends on both message quality and learner context.

finding.finding_summary: Teacher feedback was repeatedly linked to improved writing and reading outcomes when it was specific, actionable, and tailored. In intervention and small-scale studies, examples included better writing achievement, grammar accuracy, reading accuracy, and revision quality; in one study, direct and indirect written corrective feedback together were reported as the best option for improving writing achievement.
finding.measure: Writing achievement, reading accuracy, grammar accuracy, revision quality
finding.study_size: multiple studies; e.g., n=5, n=12, n=26, n=44, n=97 across included studies

finding.finding_summary: In science-related contexts, feedback was sometimes associated with gains in achievement and understanding, especially when feedback was informative and actionable. However, some studies found no academic gains even when feedback improved motivation or engagement, and peer-collaborative feedback sometimes outperformed teacher-directed feedback for critical thinking in a virtual reality science task.
finding.measure: Science achievement, science understanding, critical thinking in science contexts
finding.study_size: multiple studies; e.g., n=51, n=165, n=277, n=9,841

finding.finding_summary: In mathematics, tailored and process-oriented feedback was often associated with better achievement and reasoning, but not uniformly. Some studies reported improved math achievement or mathematical reasoning, while others found no change in achievement despite improvements in self-efficacy, interest, or perceived usefulness.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement, mathematical reasoning, math engagement and self-efficacy
finding.study_size: multiple studies; e.g., n=426, n=620, n=1,261, n=823

finding.finding_summary: Across non-core-subject contexts such as physical education, vocational learning, and mixed subject settings, feedback often improved subject-specific performance and related learning outcomes. Examples include better motor-skill learning and welding performance, improved experiment planning, and more favorable attitudes toward social science when feedback was goal-focused and individualized.
finding.measure: Motor-skill learning, welding product quality, experiment planning, subject attitudes
finding.study_size: multiple studies; e.g., n=41, n=45, n=108, n=120, n=296

finding.finding_summary: This was one of the paper’s central focus areas. Feedback was associated with gains in motivation, interest, engagement, self-efficacy, control beliefs, mastery goals, enjoyment, and reduced frustration or anxiety when it was specific, supportive, and personalized; negative or vague feedback often produced the opposite pattern. The review repeatedly reports that feedback quality and student-teacher trust shape whether students feel motivated to use feedback.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, interest, self-efficacy, control beliefs, mastery goals, enjoyment, frustration, anxiety
finding.study_size: 96 studies overall; many intervention studies with samples ranging from n=26 to n≈6,500

finding.finding_summary: The review substantively covers critical thinking, metacognition, self-regulated learning, and strategy use as feedback outcomes. Several studies found that process-oriented, explanatory, or action-oriented feedback supported self-regulation, strategy use, and critical thinking; however, some students also reported over-reliance on teacher feedback could weaken independent critical thinking.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognitive reflection, self-regulated learning, strategy use, self-reported processing of feedback
finding.study_size: multiple studies; e.g., n=26, n=45, n=44, n=108

finding.finding_summary: A smaller subset of studies examined feedback systems intended to improve classroom efficiency or implementation, such as handheld devices for immediate feedback and rubric-based supports. These tools were generally positively received, but some did not produce clear academic gains; the paper does not frame operational efficiency as a primary outcome, so evidence here is limited.
finding.measure: Use of feedback tools, classroom feedback processes, implementation of immediate-feedback systems
finding.study_size: multiple studies; e.g., n≈6,500 in one large trial

paper_profiles.title: The Effectiveness of Online and Blended Learning from Schools: A Scoping Review
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School, High School, Kindergarten
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This scoping review asks whether online learning, blended learning, educational games, computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL), and computer-assisted instruction (CAI) used with school students are effective compared with traditional classroom instruction. The authors were motivated by the COVID-19 disruption to schooling and by the practical need to identify evidence-based guidance for teachers and schools as remote and blended approaches expanded.

The review searched eight databases and screened titles/abstracts of studies from 2000 onward, ultimately including 1,540 studies. The paper is not a full meta-analysis; it is an abstract-level scoping review that classifies studies by intervention, school sector, subject, subgroup, and outcome. The sample spans primary, secondary, early years/kindergarten, and mixed school settings across many countries.

Overall, the authors conclude that digital technology in schools was usually reported as better than traditional instruction, with 61% of studies finding better outcomes and only 2% reporting worse outcomes. By intervention, CAI, blended learning, and games looked strongest in the abstract evidence, while online learning and CSCL were somewhat less clear; by sector, primary and secondary settings were most positive. They also report generally positive findings for socio-emotional functioning and many subgroup areas, and note that design/pedagogy lessons were frequently reported, but they caution that the review is limited to abstracts and likely affected by publication bias.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports many school-based studies on reading, writing, English, and EFL within online, blended, games, and CAI categories. Across the full set of 1,540 studies, digital technology was more often better than traditional instruction, and literacy-related subjects were repeatedly listed as positive in primary and secondary settings, though the paper does not provide a single pooled effect size for literacy outcomes.
finding.measure: Reading, writing, English, and English as a Foreign Language outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Math was one of the most common subjects across the review, especially in games, CAI, online, and blended learning. The abstract-level synthesis states that Maths showed generally positive outcomes in primary and secondary sectors, but no pooled estimate or consistent effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement and math learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Science was repeatedly identified as a common and often successful subject, particularly in blended learning, online learning, and CAI. The review summarizes science outcomes as largely positive in primary and secondary school studies, but does not report pooled statistics or a unified effect size.
finding.measure: Science/STEM learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Beyond literacy, math, and science, the review explicitly notes positive findings for a wide range of subjects including history, geography, humanities, arts, music, and health. The evidence is summary-level only, but the authors state that these subjects also showed positive results in school-based digital learning studies.
finding.measure: Humanities, arts/music, health, and other non-core subject learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Socio-emotional functioning was a substantive focus of the review. The authors report that 247 studies (16% of the total) found improvement, while only 18 studies (1%) found deterioration and 8 found no difference; much of the improvement was in self-efficacy rather than broader social functioning.
finding.measure: Socio-emotional functioning, self-efficacy, social interaction, psychological well-being
finding.study_size: n=1540 studies total; 247 positive for socio-emotional functioning, 18 negative

finding.finding_summary: The review explicitly includes critical thinking and related 'thinking' outcomes among its subject categories and research questions about design/pedagogy. It concludes that digital learning studies reported positive results for critical thinking and other durable skills, but the evidence is summarized narratively and not pooled into a single effect estimate.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognition, and related thinking/collaboration outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses design principles and digital pedagogy, and many included studies were coded as having implications for intervention design. However, the review does not present direct quantitative outcomes on workload or productivity; the closest finding is that 410 studies (27%) had design/pedagogy implications, suggesting operational relevance rather than direct measurement of efficiency.
finding.measure: Design/pedagogy implications and implementation considerations
finding.study_size: n=1540 studies total; 410 coded as having design/pedagogy implications

finding.finding_summary: The review has clear institutional relevance because it synthesizes evidence intended to guide school practice, policy, and post-pandemic implementation. It reports broad positive effects across sectors and countries, but does not measure policy or governance outcomes directly; the main finding is that schools can likely use online/blended approaches effectively if access and design are addressed.
finding.measure: Practice, policy, and implementation implications for schools and educational systems

paper_profiles.title: The impact of AI integration in project preparation in education course on pre-service teachers’ innovativeness, AI anxiety, attitudes, and acceptance
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examined whether embedding AI tools into a Project Preparation in Education course changes pre-service teachers’ psychological readiness to use AI. The authors focused on four constructs tied to AI adoption: individual innovativeness, AI anxiety, AI attitudes, and AI acceptance.

Using a single-group pre-test/post-test design, the study followed 34 fourth-year pre-service teachers at a public university in Türkiye during a 14-week elective course. Students used AI tools such as ChatGPT Plus, Elicit, Consensus, Gemini, NotebookLM, and Perplexity to support research-question development, literature review, methodology, data analysis, and manuscript writing, while receiving instruction on ethical and critical use of AI.

Results showed significant gains in AI attitudes and AI acceptance, with medium effects (AI attitudes g_av = 0.64; AI acceptance g_av = 0.70), but no reliable change in AI anxiety. Individual innovativeness increased slightly, especially opinion leadership, but these effects did not survive Holm–Bonferroni correction and were not robust across nonparametric tests. Overall, the paper suggests that course-embedded AI use can improve pre-service teachers’ attitudes toward and acceptance of AI, but it provides little evidence of change in anxiety or broader innovativeness.

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that integrating AI tools into a university teacher-education course can improve pre-service teachers’ readiness for AI adoption, with significant gains in AI attitudes and AI acceptance after a 14-week intervention. However, because the design lacked a control group, the authors interpret the findings as associational rather than causal evidence of institutional-level impact.
finding.measure: AI attitudes and AI acceptance scales
finding.std_deviation: AI attitudes pre SD=0.85, post SD=0.68; AI acceptance SD not fully reported in provided text

finding.finding_summary: Participants showed a significant improvement in AI attitudes from pre-test to post-test, indicating more favorable cognitive, affective, and behavioral responses toward AI after the course. AI anxiety did not change significantly (total AI anxiety g_av≈0.05), suggesting the intervention improved positive orientation to AI without reducing apprehension.
finding.measure: AI attitudes scale; Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale
finding.std_deviation: AI attitudes pre SD=0.85, post SD=0.68; AI anxiety pre SD=1.27, post SD=1.24

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was explicitly designed around an AI-assisted Project Preparation in Education course and focused on students’ ability to use AI for academic writing and project development. Although the paper did not analyze rubric-based project quality scores, it reports that students used AI to support research-question generation, literature review, methods, data analysis, and manuscript drafting, and that their readiness to use AI in these academic tasks improved.
finding.measure: AI acceptance and attitudes toward AI in academic project work

finding.finding_summary: The study directly assessed individual innovativeness, a durable-skill proxy related to openness to new ideas and influence on others. Individual innovativeness increased slightly from M=3.30 to 3.41 (t(33)=-2.05, p=0.048; Hedges’ g_av=0.44 in the table, though the narrative describes the change as small), and opinion leadership also increased (g_av=0.35), but these results did not remain significant after Holm–Bonferroni correction and were not robust in the nonparametric tests for the overall scale.
finding.measure: Individual Innovativeness Scale and subdimensions
finding.std_deviation: Pre SD=0.26, post SD=0.24 for total innovativeness

finding.finding_summary: The course used AI tools to support literature review, academic writing, reporting, and manuscript drafting, making academic literacy a substantive component of the intervention. The paper does not report a direct literacy outcome such as writing quality scores, but it indicates that students gained experience using AI to produce and refine academic texts within the project-preparation course.
finding.measure: AI-supported academic writing and manuscript development processes

finding.finding_summary: Scientific research processes were central to the intervention, including research-question development, methodology selection, data collection, data analysis, and reporting. The study does not provide a direct scientific reasoning score, but it reports that students used AI to work through authentic research tasks over 14 weeks, which improved their attitudes and acceptance toward AI-supported research work.
finding.measure: AI-supported scientific project development and research-process engagement

paper_profiles.title: The impact of using ChatGPT for feedback in EFL writing: a systematic review
paper_profiles.venue: Revista Internacional de Lenguas Extranjeras / International Journal of Foreign Languages
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what empirical evidence exists on the impact of ChatGPT as a feedback tool for EFL/ESL writing. The authors conduct a systematic review of 30 empirical studies published from 2023 to 2025, screening records from Scopus, Web of Science, and Ebsco Host and excluding studies that did not measure writing performance, did not use ChatGPT for feedback, or were not accessible in full text.

Across the included studies, ChatGPT was used in a range of writing-instruction contexts, mostly with university learners and a small number of upper secondary students. The review synthesizes findings across dimensions of writing performance such as linguistic accuracy, overall writing quality, organization, content development, and vocabulary. Most studies reported positive effects, especially for surface-level accuracy, but also for broader writing quality when AI feedback was paired with teacher mediation, prompt training, or structured revision activities.

The review concludes that ChatGPT can improve EFL writing outcomes, but its effectiveness depends heavily on how learners engage with the tool. The strongest pattern is gains in grammar and other surface-level features; higher-order improvements in organization and content are more variable and appear to require more specific prompting and pedagogical scaffolding. The authors also highlight risks of overreliance and reduced learner agency, arguing that ChatGPT should supplement rather than replace teacher input and critical student engagement.

finding.finding_summary: Across 30 empirical studies, the review found that ChatGPT-supported feedback generally improved EFL/ESL writing performance, with the clearest gains in linguistic accuracy, overall writing quality, organization, content development, and vocabulary. The strongest pattern was for surface-level accuracy (e.g., grammar, spelling, syntax), though broader writing quality also improved when AI feedback was embedded in structured instruction and revision cycles.
finding.measure: Writing performance outcomes in EFL/ESL writing tasks; dimensions included linguistic accuracy, overall writing quality, organization, content development, and vocabulary

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that some studies found increased motivation, engagement, and affective involvement when students used ChatGPT for writing feedback, but it also notes risks such as overreliance, reduced creativity, and diminished ownership of the writing process. These motivational and engagement effects were not quantified in the review, but they were a recurring theme in the included studies.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, affective engagement, and learner agency/self-concept reported across included studies

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly emphasizes critical engagement with AI feedback, prompt literacy, metacognition, and autonomous revision as necessary for stronger writing gains. Studies summarized in the review suggest that learners who critically examined ChatGPT suggestions and prompted more specifically achieved better outcomes, while passive acceptance or vague prompting led to weaker higher-order improvements.
finding.measure: Critical engagement with AI feedback, prompt specificity/literacy, metacognitive reflection, and revision autonomy

finding.finding_summary: The review indicates that ChatGPT can provide immediate, personalized feedback that may reduce teacher workload and support faster revision cycles, especially for surface-level corrections. However, the paper does not quantify workload reduction; it mainly synthesizes prior studies and argues that ChatGPT can help automate parts of the feedback process when combined with teacher oversight.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / feedback efficiency as discussed in the reviewed literature

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Learning Performance in Primary Education: The Roles of Problem Solving and Creative Thinking Challenges
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Elementary Education (Revija za elementarno izobraževanje)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether integrating structured problem-solving and creative-thinking activities into primary science lessons improves student academic performance compared with traditional teacher-directed instruction. The authors frame the work as addressing a gap in primary-school evidence, especially in the Vietnamese context, where science is often taught through memorization and direct instruction.

The intervention consisted of two carefully designed science lessons for grade 3 and grade 5 students in southern Vietnam: one on the Earth’s movement and one on solar-powered vehicles. Students in the experimental groups engaged in hands-on, collaborative, and imaginative tasks intended to promote problem solving and creativity, while control groups received conventional instruction on the same content. Academic performance was measured with pre- and post-tests based on Bloom’s taxonomy.

Results showed statistically significant gains for the experimental groups on both topics, including higher post-test scores than control groups and large pre-to-post improvements within the experimental groups. The authors conclude that structured problem-solving and creative-thinking support can substantially improve primary students’ science learning, while noting that success depends on thoughtful scaffolding, teacher readiness, and supportive classroom conditions.

finding.finding_summary: Primary students who received structured problem-solving and creative-thinking science lessons outperformed those in traditional instruction on both science topics. For “The Movement of the Earth,” the experimental group improved from M=3.4 (SD=1.4) to M=8.8 (SD=2.1), and its post-test score exceeded the control group’s M=6.2 (SD=1.9), with t(31)=5.2, p<.001. For “Solar-Powered Vehicles,” scores rose from M=4.9 (SD=1.6) to M=9.4 (SD=1.4), also significantly above control (M=5.5, SD=1.5), t(30)=9.1, p<.001.
finding.measure: Structured science test based on Bloom’s taxonomy (knowledge, comprehension, application)

finding.finding_summary: The lessons explicitly embedded problem-solving and creative-thinking tasks, and the authors report that students demonstrated stronger problem-solving and creative outputs during the intervention. However, the study did not measure these skills with a separate validated instrument; evidence is inferred from task performance and teacher-scored participation within the science lessons.
finding.measure: Task performance / participation during problem-solving and creative-thinking lesson activities

paper_profiles.title: A Systematic Assessment of OpenAI o1-Preview for Higher Order Thinking in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates OpenAI o1-preview as a text-based reasoning system across 14 higher-order thinking domains, including critical thinking, systems thinking, computational thinking, design thinking, metacognition, data literacy, creative thinking, abstract reasoning, spatial reasoning, quantitative reasoning, logical reasoning, analogical reasoning, and scientific reasoning. The central question is whether a frontier LLM can demonstrate performance comparable to or better than humans on established instruments designed to measure these cognitive skills.

The authors use a largely zero-shot prompt strategy and benchmark o1-preview against published human performance on a range of existing instruments, such as the Ennis-Weir Critical Thinking Essay Test, systems-thinking assessments, Bebras-style computational thinking tasks, and other reasoning measures. The sample is not a participant sample in the usual educational sense; rather, the paper evaluates the model on test items and compares its scores to prior human norms, typically drawn from middle school through graduate-level populations depending on the instrument.

The main conclusion is that o1-preview performs strongly on many higher-order thinking tasks, often matching or exceeding human benchmarks in critical thinking, systems thinking, computational thinking, creative thinking, and scientific reasoning, while showing weaker performance on abstract reasoning and some quantitative reasoning tasks. The paper argues that these results suggest substantial educational potential for AI support, but also emphasize that human oversight remains important, especially for tasks requiring abstraction, nuanced judgment, or context-sensitive reasoning. Because the study is a benchmark-style evaluation of model outputs rather than an intervention with learners, it provides evidence about AI capability rather than direct educational impact.

finding.finding_summary: Across several benchmarked reasoning tasks, o1-preview generally performed strongly on durable skills, especially critical thinking. On the Ennis-Weir Critical Thinking Essay Test, the model scored a mean of 81.25% (M=2.25, SD=0.43; 8 paragraphs scored), which was slightly below some post-intervention human means but above the cited human benchmark range of 37.5% to 62.5%. The paper also reports strong performance on systems thinking, computational thinking, creative thinking, and analogical reasoning, though not uniformly superior across all subskills.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, systems thinking, computational thinking, creative thinking, metacognition, abstract reasoning, logical reasoning, analogical reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that o1-preview outperformed humans on scientific reasoning tasks, as part of its broader higher-order thinking evaluation. The abstract states that o1-preview significantly outperformed humans by about 150% on scientific reasoning, and the discussion summarizes scientific reasoning as one of the categories where the model exceeded human performance.
finding.measure: Scientific reasoning benchmark tasks

finding.finding_summary: Quantitative reasoning was evaluated with benchmark tasks and the model performed well overall, but below expert human performance. The paper states that o1-preview’s mean performance exceeded the general crowd but remained about 15-20% lower than human experts on the FINAQ dataset, indicating partial but not top-tier quantitative competence.
finding.measure: Quantitative reasoning / FINAQ dataset

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Systems that Augment Human Performed vs. Demonstrated Critical Thinking
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position paper that examines how generative AI changes the meaning and evaluation of critical thinking. The authors argue that research in this area often conflates two different constructs: performed critical thinking, which refers to independent cognitive work done without AI assistance, and demonstrated critical thinking, which refers to critical thinking expressed in AI-assisted outputs.
