Rather than evaluating a specific intervention, the paper synthesizes prior work and proposes a conceptual framework for distinguishing these two forms. It discusses how current AI systems may improve the quality of final outputs or collaborative reasoning while not necessarily improving users’ independent reasoning ability. The paper also suggests that future AI systems intended to augment critical thinking should scaffold the reasoning process itself, drawing on educational strategies such as questioning, debate, and guided support.

The paper does not study a K-12 sample directly and does not report original empirical results. Its main contribution is theoretical and methodological: it calls for future studies to measure performed critical thinking separately from demonstrated critical thinking, especially when assessing the impact of generative AI in education and other settings.

finding.finding_summary: This position paper argues that generative AI may improve demonstrated critical thinking in AI-assisted tasks without necessarily improving performed critical thinking, the independent cognitive ability. The paper synthesizes prior studies and notes mixed findings in the literature, but it reports no original effect size, sample size, or outcome measurement of its own.
finding.measure: Critical thinking conceptualization and evaluation methods

paper_profiles.title: Developing Critical Thinking in Second Language Learners: Exploring Generative AI like ChatGPT as a tool for Argumentative Essay Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether using ChatGPT in a structured way can help second-language learners develop critical thinking and improve argumentative essay writing. The authors propose the ChatGPT Guideline for Critical Argumentative Writing (CGCAW), which combines the Paul-Elder Critical Thinking Model, Tan’s argumentative writing framework, and the Hattie & Timperley feedback model to give learners structured prompts for using ChatGPT while composing essays.

The study used a small experiment with 10 university students from a state university, randomly assigned to an experimental group using the CGCAW framework and a control group using ChatGPT without specific guidelines. All participants wrote a short argumentative essay in 40 minutes on a social-media prompt, and essays were evaluated by Grammarly, ChatGPT, and a course instructor. Results were mixed: the experimental group did better on ChatGPT’s ratings for clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence, but the control group scored higher on Grammarly and instructor assessments, especially for grammar, thesis clarity, and overall essay quality.

The main conclusion is that the CGCAW framework shows some promise for supporting specific aspects of critical/argumentative writing, but it is not yet clearly superior across evaluators and may require refinement. The authors emphasize limitations including the very small sample, the short task duration, and variability in participants’ prior ChatGPT experience, and they recommend further research before treating the framework as effective or scalable.

finding.finding_summary: The study focused on argumentative essay writing and found mixed effects of the CGCAW framework. ChatGPT-rated scores favored the experimental group on clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence (mean total 74 vs. 72.2; SD=7.6 vs. 5.5), but Grammarly and the course instructor rated the control group higher (Grammarly mean 92.2 vs. 90.6; instructor mean 56 vs. 35).
finding.measure: Argumentative essay quality, including clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, persuasiveness, grammar, and thesis quality
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT total SD=7.6 (G1) and 5.5 (G2); Grammarly and instructor SD not reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally investigated critical thinking development through structured ChatGPT use. The experimental group reportedly improved in clarity, logical coherence, and evidence use, which the authors interpret as evidence of stronger critical thinking in argumentative writing, but other assessors found the control group stronger on some dimensions, so the overall finding is mixed rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Critical thinking as reflected in argumentative writing features (clarity, logical coherence, evidence use, reasoning)
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT-rated group SDs reported for total scores: 7.6 and 5.5

finding.finding_summary: The study discusses self-monitoring and self-regulation as part of the feedback framework, but these were not directly measured with a dedicated instrument. Evidence is indirect: the authors claim ChatGPT feedback may encourage reflection and self-regulation, yet no standalone self-regulation outcome scores are reported.
finding.measure: Indirect references to self-regulation and reflection during writing

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Critical Thinking with AI: A Tailored Warning System for RAG Models
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether tailored warning messages can help users critically evaluate hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. The authors frame the work as addressing a gap between technical hallucination reduction and user-facing support for reflective reasoning, especially in educational question-answering contexts. They argue that warnings should do more than issue generic disclaimers: they should be context-specific and explain why a response may be unreliable, thereby supporting critical thinking rather than passive acceptance.

The study describes an ongoing design of a tailored warning system that injects fact-checking at both retrieval and generation stages and then presents a context-specific warning in the interface. In a pilot study, participants answered multiple-choice questions based on an AP U.S. history textbook using an LLM-powered QA system. Eighteen participants were split across no-warning, standard-warning, and tailored-warning conditions, and the task included genuine, low-level hallucination, and high-level hallucination responses. Participants also completed a trust survey and short interview.

Results from the pilot suggest that tailored warnings improved accuracy in detecting hallucinations, especially for more difficult cases, and increased trust relative to the other warning conditions. The authors report 100%, 89%, and 81% accuracy for tailored warnings across no-, low-, and high-hallucination items, compared with 97%, 81%, and 69% for standard warnings and 100%, 64%, and 56% for no warnings. An ANOVA test yielded p=0.006162, indicating statistically significant differences among conditions. At the same time, qualitative feedback suggests a tradeoff: some users found warnings confusing or felt they reduced usability, indicating that context-specific warnings may support critical thinking but can also introduce cognitive friction if not designed carefully.

finding.finding_summary: Tailored warning messages improved participants’ ability to detect hallucinations and supported more reflective evaluation of AI-generated answers in a history quiz setting. In the pilot (n=18), accuracy in the tailored-warning group was 100% for no-hallucination items, 89% for low-level hallucinations, and 81% for high-level hallucinations, outperforming standard-warning and no-warning conditions; the authors report ANOVA p=0.006162.
finding.measure: Accuracy on multiple-choice question-answering task under no-warning, standard-warning, and tailored-warning conditions

finding.finding_summary: The warnings affected trust and ease of use in different directions. Tailored warnings were associated with higher trust than the other conditions by 0.67 points on a 5-point Likert scale, but participants in the no-warning condition rated the interface as easiest to use, and qualitative comments indicated that some warnings caused confusion and cognitive friction.
finding.measure: Trust survey and interface ease/usability ratings on 5-point Likert scales; interview feedback

paper_profiles.title: Cognitive Dissonance Artificial Intelligence (CD-AI): The Mind at War with Itself. Harnessing Discomfort to Sharpen Critical Thinking
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2025 ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper argues that most AI systems are optimized to reduce uncertainty and cognitive effort, which may inadvertently encourage passive acceptance, confirmation bias, and shallow reasoning. In response, the author proposes Cognitive Dissonance AI (CD-AI), a conceptual framework for AI that deliberately sustains uncertainty and presents well-supported contradictory viewpoints rather than quickly resolving them.

The paper is theoretical rather than empirical. It outlines how CD-AI would work through delayed closure, structured contradiction, self-reflection prompts, and adaptive difficulty to support critical thinking, epistemic humility, and dialectical reasoning. The paper situates this idea across several domains, including ethics, politics, law, science, and education, and discusses ethical risks such as decision paralysis, manipulation, autonomy loss, and bias.

The context is human-AI interaction broadly, not a specific classroom or K-12 intervention. Although the author suggests possible use in education and STEM learning, no student sample, school implementation, or outcome evaluation is reported. The main conclusion is normative and conceptual: AI should be designed to provoke productive cognitive struggle rather than provide only efficient answers, but empirical validation is explicitly left for future research.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that structured cognitive dissonance in AI interactions would strengthen critical thinking, reflective reasoning, epistemic humility, adaptability, and dialectical thinking. No empirical test is reported; the claim is supported only by theory and citations to prior literature, with no sample size or effect estimate provided.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, reflective reasoning, epistemic humility, adaptability

paper_profiles.title: Shots and Boosters: Exploring the Use of Combined Prebunking Interventions to Raise Critical Thinking and Create Long-Term Protection Against Misinformation
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses the problem of misinformation resilience and asks how human-AI systems might better support people’s critical thinking when encountering online content. The authors argue that debunking alone is insufficient because misinformation spreads quickly and can have lasting effects, so they propose combining short-term nudges with longer-term inoculation-style educational interventions.

The paper does not report an empirical study of students or other participants. Instead, it synthesizes prior work on critical thinking, media literacy, AI-based tutoring, and serious games, then proposes a design concept for an AI-driven interactive training game. In the proposed system, users first complete an inoculation stage where an AI tutor evaluates and corrects their reasoning about misleading posts, and then receive personalized reinforcement nudges over time to preserve and generalize these skills.

The paper’s main contribution is conceptual: it argues that AI can support both personalized feedback and reinforcement for media-literacy training by adapting to a user’s reasoning style, strengths, and weaknesses. The intended use context is everyday online media consumption, not a specific classroom or K-12 setting. Because the paper is a design concept and literature synthesis rather than a results paper, it does not provide empirical evidence about effects on critical thinking or misinformation discernment.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not report original empirical results; it proposes an AI-driven prebunking design intended to raise critical thinking and media literacy through inoculation and reinforcement nudges. The paper argues conceptually that personalized feedback, repeated interaction, and booster prompts may help users build and retain critical reasoning skills, but it presents no measured effect sizes, samples, or outcome data.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Navigating the State of Cognitive Flow: Context-Aware AI Interventions for Effective Reasoning Support
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that AI reasoning assistants can inadvertently disrupt users’ cognitive flow if they deliver support at the wrong time, in the wrong form, or at the wrong level of intensity. The authors frame the problem through Flow Theory, proposing that effective AI-augmented reasoning should preserve a state of deep focus and intrinsic motivation while still providing helpful cognitive support.

The proposed approach is a context-aware cognitive augmentation framework that adapts interventions based on three factors: type, timing, and scale. Rather than using a static, one-size-fits-all feedback style, the paper suggests that multimodal behavioral cues such as gaze behavior, typing hesitation, interaction speed, and other engagement signals could be used to infer when a user is stuck or under-challenged and to personalize interventions accordingly.

The paper is conceptual and forward-looking rather than empirical: it does not report a study with participants, a classroom deployment, or outcome measurements. Its main conclusion is that AI systems for reasoning support should be evaluated not only on performance or engagement, but on their ability to maintain or restore cognitive flow in a minimally intrusive, personalized way.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not report empirical evidence about critical thinking or other durable skills; instead, it argues conceptually that context-aware AI interventions could support deeper reasoning and critical thinking in future systems. No sample, effect size, or measured outcome is reported because the paper is a position/concept paper rather than an evaluation study.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on cognitive flow, engagement, and intrinsic motivation as theoretical goals of intervention design, but it does not present empirical measurement of these constructs. It proposes that adaptive timing and intervention scale may help sustain engagement and reduce disruption, yet no participant data or quantified results are provided.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Combining Design Thinking and Software Requirements Engineering to create Human-centered Software-intensive Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter addresses a conceptual and practical question in software and systems development: how Design Thinking and Requirements Engineering can be combined to better create human-centered software-intensive systems. The authors argue that Requirements Engineering is often insufficiently human-centered and too solution-oriented, while Design Thinking offers complementary strengths in empathy, problem exploration, rapid prototyping, and interdisciplinary collaboration.

The chapter develops artifact-based models for Design Thinking, Requirements Engineering, and an integrated combined model. It draws on prior literature, practitioner compendia, Delphi study evidence, multiple-case studies, and expert interviews with Design Thinking specialists to infer the artifacts produced by each approach and organize them across context, requirements, and system layers. The paper is primarily methodological and conceptual rather than an empirical evaluation of an educational intervention or AI system.

The context is software-intensive product development in industry and academia, not K-12 education. The main conclusion is that integrating Design Thinking and Requirements Engineering through an artifact-centric reference model can clarify synergies, support tailoring to project contexts, and improve the creation of human-centered systems. It does not study AI-personalized feedback, student learning, or critical thinking outcomes in schools.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that an integrated artifact model can improve the efficiency and reproducibility of requirements/design work by clarifying what artifacts need to be produced, how they relate, and how they can be tailored to project contexts. However, this is a conceptual claim supported by expert feedback and prior literature rather than a direct efficiency experiment; no effect sizes or experimental sample sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Artifact model clarity, process integration, and projected development efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Thinking in Space: How Multimodal Large Language Models See, Remember, and Recall Spaces
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can reason about spatial information from video, focusing on how they perceive, remember, and recall indoor spaces. The authors introduce VSI-Bench, a video-based benchmark of over 5,000 question-answer pairs derived from 288 indoor-scene videos sourced from ScanNet, ScanNet++, and ARKitScenes, covering tasks such as object counting, relative distance, relative direction, route planning, object size, room size, and appearance order.

The study evaluates 15 MLLMs in zero-shot settings and compares them with human performance on a 400-question subset. Results show that MLLMs achieve competitive but substantially subhuman performance overall, with strong local spatial awareness but weak global spatial models. The authors find that spatial reasoning is the main bottleneck, that chain-of-thought-style linguistic prompting does not improve and can even hurt performance, and that explicitly generating cognitive maps improves relative-distance reasoning. The paper’s contributions are benchmark creation and diagnostic analysis rather than an educational intervention.

Although the work is not about K-12 instruction or AI-personalized feedback, it is relevant to broader AI spatial reasoning research because it tests whether MLLMs can build internal representations of spaces from video. The paper does not study students, classrooms, or educational outcomes directly; its population is adult-level model evaluation and human annotators/evaluators for benchmark validation.

paper_profiles.title: The Shifting Sands of Creative Thinking: Connections to Dual Process Theory
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews how dual-process theories of cognition relate to theories of creative thinking. The authors focus on the distinction between generative and evaluative phases of creativity and argue that creative thought likely depends on shifting between associative, idea-generating processes and analytic, idea-evaluating processes, rather than on a single mechanism.

The paper synthesizes prior theoretical and empirical work on divergent/convergent thinking, ideation-evaluation cycles, blind variation and selective retention, Genoplore, Honing Theory, and the dual-pathway model of creativity. It does not test a new intervention or conduct a primary experiment; instead, it proposes an integrative framework and discusses possible mechanisms, including cognitive control, attentional focus, and brain networks (e.g., salience network, DMN, CEN) that may support switching between modes.

The intended context is general cognitive/creative thinking research rather than a specific K-12 or education intervention study. The authors conclude that existing models converge on the importance of interaction between generation and evaluation, but that the timing, control, and trainability of shifting remain open questions. They suggest that chronometric and neuroimaging methods could help clarify these processes and inform future creativity interventions, including classroom-relevant ones, but no such intervention is evaluated in this paper.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that creativity depends on shifting between associative/generative and analytic/evaluative modes of thought, which closely overlaps with critical thinking and metacognition. However, this is a theoretical synthesis rather than a primary empirical test, so no effect size or sample-based result is reported.
finding.measure: Theoretical review of dual-process models, shifting between idea generation and evaluation, and links to creative thinking/critical thinking

paper_profiles.title: Thinking-while-Generating: Interleaving Textual Reasoning throughout Visual Generation
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (computer vision / generative AI model study; no K-12 human population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes Thinking-while-Generating (TWIG), a framework for interleaving textual reasoning throughout the process of visual generation. The authors argue that prior approaches either think before generation (pre-planning) or after generation (post-refinement), but do not provide on-the-fly reasoning during synthesis. TWIG instead inserts textual reasoning steps during generation so the model can guide upcoming regions of the image and reflect on previously generated content.

The paper explores three implementation routes: zero-shot prompting, supervised fine-tuning on a curated TWIG-50K dataset, and reinforcement learning with a customized GRPO strategy. The experiments are conducted on text-to-image generation benchmarks using unified multimodal language models such as Janus-Pro, not on human learners or educational settings. Across benchmark results, TWIG improves compositional fidelity, attribute binding, and spatial reasoning in generated images, with the largest gains coming from reinforcement learning.

This is a technical AI generation paper rather than an education study. It does not investigate K-12 students, teachers, classrooms, or educational outcomes such as critical thinking in learners. Any relevance to the retrieval question is only indirect: the paper concerns interleaved reasoning in an AI system, not AI-personalized feedback for K-12 education.

paper_profiles.title: Thinking Twice: Clinical-Inspired Thyroid Ultrasound Lesion Detection Based on Feature Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of improving thyroid ultrasound lesion detection, where ultrasound image noise, blur, and low resolution make accurate detection difficult. The authors argue that standard one-stage detectors rely on a single feature extraction pass and can be vulnerable to noisy background patterns in ultrasound imagery.

To address this, they propose a clinically inspired "feature feedback" mechanism that mimics how radiologists first make a coarse observation and then focus on details. The method combines a feedback feature selection module, a feature feedback pyramid, an improved ConvNeXt backbone, and an adaptive detection head with deformable surround convolution to better handle multi-scale lesion shapes and adjacent weak features.

The study evaluates the detector on a thyroid ultrasound dataset of 1,023 annotated images from an affiliated hospital and also tests generalization on the BUSI breast ultrasound dataset. The proposed model reports improved detection accuracy over several baselines, reaching AP=70.3% and AP50=99.0% on thyroid ultrasound, with ablation results suggesting that feedback features, ConvNeXt, and the adaptive head each contribute to performance gains. The paper concludes that the feedback-based design improves lesion localization and can run in real time, but it remains challenged by small or low-contrast lesions and sample-imbalanced datasets.

paper_profiles.title: The Zero-Step Thinking: An Empirical Study of Mode Selection as Harder Early Exit in Reasoning Models
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (large language models; not a human K-12 population study)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates a computation-efficiency question in large reasoning models: whether methods originally developed for Early Exit can be repurposed to decide, before reasoning begins, whether a model should use long chain-of-thought or a short/no-thinking mode. The authors frame this as a harder problem called Mode Selection or zero-step thinking, because the decision must be made without an explicit reasoning trajectory.

The study evaluates nine baselines spanning prompt-based methods and internal-state methods on four reasoning benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME 2025, and GPQA Diamond, using DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen models at 1.5B, 7B, and 32B scales. They compare final accuracy, token usage, and NOTHINKING selection rates, and also analyze threshold dynamics, ROC-AUC, calibration error, and Brier score. Across benchmarks, prompt-based methods often fail under limited information, while internal-state methods generally perform better but remain unstable and highly sensitive to dataset and model scale.

The main conclusion is that Mode Selection is substantially harder than conventional Early Exit, and that neither prompt-only nor internal-state-only approaches are consistently reliable across settings. The paper is about adaptive reasoning efficiency in foundation models, not student learning, instructional feedback, or classroom use, so it does not provide K-12 educational evidence.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that some Mode Selection methods can reduce token usage substantially while maintaining or occasionally improving accuracy relative to full thinking. For example, on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, PROBECONF reduced GSM8K token usage from 2,455 to 2,299 and DEER from 2,455 to 2,276; on 7B and 32B models, several internal-state methods also lowered token usage while preserving accuracy, indicating improved inference efficiency.
finding.measure: Average generation length / token count and final answer accuracy on reasoning benchmarks
finding.study_size: n=4 benchmarks across 3 model sizes; exact total sample count not reported

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education; broad education stakeholders
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper asks how large language models such as ChatGPT could be used in education and what risks and constraints must be addressed for responsible adoption. It is not an empirical intervention study; instead, it synthesizes emerging examples and argues for potential uses in learning, teaching, assessment, and educational technology design.

The paper discusses opportunities for students and teachers, including personalized learning support, automated feedback, generation of exercises and quizzes, assistance with writing and research, and support for remote or group learning. It also highlights challenges such as bias, privacy, plagiarism, overreliance, lack of transparency, and difficulty distinguishing AI-generated from human-generated text. The authors emphasize that effective integration requires human oversight, critical thinking, fact-checking, and governance frameworks.

Although the paper references elementary, middle school, high school, university, and teacher-education contexts, its scope is broad and conceptual rather than centered on one population. The conclusions are normative: large language models may be beneficial in education if used as supplements to human teaching and embedded in responsible, ethically governed practices.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models could support critical thinking by generating prompts, questions, explanations, and multiple perspectives, but also warns that easy answer generation may weaken students' critical thinking and problem-solving if overused. No empirical effect size is reported because this is a position paper rather than a study.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, fact-checking, and related 21st-century skills

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that large language models can reduce teacher workload by helping create personalized learning materials, lesson plans, quizzes, feedback, and assessments, and by semi-automating grading and feedback for student work. No empirical effect size is reported; the paper cites prior examples suggesting potential grading-effort reductions but does not itself test them.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, and time spent creating instructional/assessment materials

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is institutional governance around privacy, bias, fairness, copyright, sustainability, and policies for responsible use of large language models in education. The paper argues that these systems can create opportunities for broader access and innovation, but also introduce significant risks that require oversight, regulation, and ethical frameworks. No empirical effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy/security, fairness, and institutional adoption considerations

paper_profiles.title: AI in the Classroom: A Boon or a Threat to Pedagogical Practices?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI in education is a pedagogical boon or threat, with particular attention to personalized feedback, student independence, critical thinking, and retention. The authors frame AI tools as potentially useful for individualized support and engagement, but also worry that students may become dependent on machine-generated answers and bypass deeper thinking and skill development.

The study combines a literature review, a teacher survey in Almaty schools, and a small classroom experiment with 6th-grade students. Teachers rated AI as having mixed effects on student engagement and independence, and the experiment asked students to use AI to write a short story, customize it, and retell it one week later. Students showed some initial interest and moderate retention, but customization was limited and many students engaged only superficially with the AI-generated content.

Overall, the paper concludes that AI can increase interest and support learning when used as a supplement, but it should not replace traditional pedagogy. The authors argue for guided, balanced use of AI to avoid over-reliance and to preserve critical thinking, creativity, and independent learning, especially for younger secondary students.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported mixed perceptions of AI’s effect on student engagement and motivation. In the survey, 41.7% of teachers rated engagement at level 3 on a 1-5 scale, 33.3% at level 4, 16.7% at level 2, and 8.3% at level 5, suggesting moderate but uneven engagement gains. The paper also reports that students found the AI-assisted storytelling task interesting, but overall engagement with the assignment was low.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of student engagement/motivation on 1-5 Likert scales; student interview feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally focuses on critical thinking, independent problem-solving, and metacognitive engagement, arguing that AI may both support and weaken these skills depending on use. In the experiment, many students minimally customized the AI-generated stories, and about half could retell the story one week later, indicating only moderate comprehension/retention and limited evidence of deep engagement. No effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Student customization of AI-generated stories; one-week story retell/recall; brief interviews about understanding and modification

finding.finding_summary: The classroom experiment involved AI-assisted story writing, which directly engaged writing and narrative composition. Students were asked to write a short story with AI, customize setting/characters/plot, and retell it after one week; the paper reports limited customization and only moderate retention, with approximately half of students able to recall and retell the story accurately. No standardized literacy outcome or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: AI-assisted story writing and one-week story retell/recall

finding.finding_summary: Beyond literacy and durable skills, the paper also addresses general academic progress and assignment completion using AI tools. Teacher survey results were mixed: 25% rated AI as significantly hindering independence, 25% as significantly improving it, and responses on motivation/academic progress leaned neutral-to-positive. The evidence is descriptive and based on teacher perception rather than a direct academic achievement measure.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of students' academic progress and independence with AI tools

paper_profiles.title: Learning design to support student-AI collaboration: perspectives of leading teachers for AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 learning should be designed when AI is introduced as a collaborative partner in classrooms, rather than only as a tool for individualized instruction. The authors ask what curriculum, interaction supports, learning environments, and developmental stages are needed for student-AI collaboration (SAC), motivated by the rapid expansion of AI in Korean schools and the lack of design guidance for teachers.

The study uses in-depth semi-structured interviews with 10 Korean leading teachers in AI in education: five primary school teachers and five secondary school teachers working in AI pilot schools, SW leading schools, or AI-convergence high schools. Using a hybrid inductive/deductive thematic analysis, the authors developed a student-AI collaboration model and identified themes about learning goals, content, assessment, interaction, environment, and SAC co-evolution over time.

Teachers emphasized that SAC should support capacity building, especially higher-order thinking, collaboration, and digital literacy, alongside subject-matter knowledge building. They also argued for interdisciplinary, authentic, and creative tasks; process-oriented and collaboration-oriented assessment; teacher support for AI principles, data literacy, debugging, and AI ethics; intuitive interfaces and digital tools; flexible classroom and digital infrastructure; systemic AIED policy; a collaborative school culture; and a safe-to-fail environment. The paper concludes that SAC should evolve through three stages—learn about AI, learn from AI, and learn together—and provides design implications for curriculum, AI systems, schools, and policy makers.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers argued that student-AI collaboration should intentionally build higher-order thinking, especially critical thinking, creativity, analytical thinking, problem-solving, and collaboration. The study does not test effects experimentally, but the interviews consistently frame SAC as a means to develop these durable skills through authentic tasks, reflection, debugging, and co-assessment.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about intended student learning goals and SAC design

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described SAC as supporting students’ engagement, persistence, motivation, and willingness to try again, especially when AI is designed to scaffold failure recovery and provide meaningful socio-emotional interaction. The study is qualitative and reports perceived benefits rather than measured student outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on motivation, engagement, persistence, and affective interaction with AI

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is the institutional and policy conditions needed for SAC, including systematic AIED policy, governance coordination, teacher capacity building, flexible school systems, collaborative school culture, and safe-to-fail environments. The findings are based on teacher perspectives and do not quantify institutional effects, but they strongly indicate that implementation depends on policy and organizational support.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on policy, governance, school system, and culture requirements for AIED

paper_profiles.title: A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a tertiary review (review of reviews) that maps the scope, methods, quality, and thematic findings of AI in higher education research published between January 2018 and July 2023. The authors screened 5,609 records and included 66 evidence syntheses focused solely on higher education or continuing education, coding each review for type, focus area, geography, collaboration patterns, tools used, and methodological quality.

Rather than evaluating a single AI intervention, the paper synthesizes secondary studies on applications such as adaptive systems and personalization, profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, and intelligent tutoring systems. Most included reviews were systematic reviews, and the corpus was dominated by general AIEd and personalization-related topics. The authors conclude that the field is growing quickly but is uneven in quality and reporting rigor, with common gaps including incomplete search reporting, limited inter-rater reliability reporting, infrequent quality appraisal, and weak reflection on limitations.

The paper also highlights that AIHEd evidence synthesis is highly collaborative, often domestically co-authored, and largely produced by STEM-affiliated researchers. Key findings across the reviewed literature suggest the strongest emphasis is on adaptive systems/personalization and profiling/prediction, while intelligent tutoring systems and assessment/evaluation are less frequently the primary focus. The article calls for greater ethical, methodological, and interdisciplinary rigor in future AIHEd reviews and primary studies.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed higher-education AI literature, chatbots and other adaptive systems were reported to affect critical thinking, but the paper does not synthesize a pooled effect. The review notes that studies measured outcomes such as student learning outcomes, critical thinking, empathy, communication skills, and satisfaction, and that evidence for adaptive learning research remains nascent and methodologically uneven.
finding.measure: Critical thinking and related learner outcomes reported in included reviews

paper_profiles.title: Interacting with educational chatbots: A systematic review
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education (mixed educational contexts; includes some K-12-relevant studies but predominantly broader education)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a gap in the educational chatbot literature by systematically reviewing how chatbots have been designed, deployed, and evaluated in education. The authors argue that prior reviews emphasized learning outcomes and general benefits, but paid less attention to interaction styles, chatbot roles, design principles, and the empirical evidence supporting chatbot effectiveness.

Using a systematic review process, the paper screened literature from 2011 to 2021 across ACM Digital Library, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and SpringerLink, ultimately retaining 36 studies. The review maps the selected papers across seven dimensions: educational field, platform, chatbot role, interaction style, design principles, evaluation methods, and limitations. Most chatbots were web-based, most often used as teaching agents, and commonly followed chatbot-driven, flow-based interaction patterns; personalized learning was the most frequent design principle.

The review’s evidence synthesis suggests that educational chatbots generally show positive effects on learning, engagement, and subjective satisfaction, though results depend on design and context. Experimental studies in the reviewed corpus often reported improved learning or engagement relative to traditional settings, while some studies found no sustained engagement or only context-specific benefits. The authors conclude that educational chatbots can be promising learning supports, but future work should improve dataset quality, usability, and design rigor, and further examine factors such as chatbot personality and localization.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed educational chatbot literature, the dominant academic effects were on subject-matter learning rather than one specific literacy, numeracy, or science domain. The review reports that experimental studies often found improved learning outcomes, including better performance on programming and other course tasks, with several studies showing statistically significant gains (e.g., p<0.05 to p<0.001) in the underlying articles.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes, course-task performance, post-tests, and subject-specific achievement measures across the reviewed studies
finding.study_size: 36 studies reviewed; individual empirical studies varied (e.g., n=28 to n=1000 in experiments)

finding.finding_summary: The review finds consistent positive evidence for engagement, interest in learning, subjective satisfaction, and motivation when students interacted with educational chatbots. For example, the reviewed experimental studies reported improved engagement and subjective satisfaction, although one longitudinal study found that interest in communicating with the chatbot declined over time.
finding.measure: Engagement, interest in learning, subjective satisfaction, motivation, and sustained interaction
finding.study_size: 36 studies reviewed; individual studies included samples such as n=34, n=56, n=122, n=182, n=1000

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes evidence that some chatbot designs supported deeper reasoning-related outcomes such as critical thinking, argumentation quality, reflection, and collaborative discussion. The review specifically notes that collaborative learning approaches have been shown to improve students’ critical thinking and argumentation, and one experiment reported better formal argumentation quality in writing.
finding.measure: Argumentation quality, critical thinking-related collaborative tasks, reflection prompts, and discussion quality
finding.study_size: 36 studies reviewed; individual studies varied (e.g., n=55, n=56, n=182)

finding.finding_summary: A subset of the reviewed chatbot studies focused on language learning and conversational practice, with generally positive effects on learning and feedback quality. The review notes improved learning for language-related chatbot uses and reports one user-driven language-learning chatbot that provided constructive feedback on transcribed speech/text.
finding.measure: Language learning outcomes, conversational practice, and feedback quality in language-learning chatbots

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the potential of artificial intelligence tools in educational measurement and assessment
paper_profiles.venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article examines how artificial intelligence tools can be used across the educational measurement and assessment process. The paper asks how AI—especially large language models such as ChatGPT—might support test development, administration, scoring, interpretation, reporting, and related classroom assessment tasks, while also considering the limitations and risks of AI use in education.

Rather than reporting a primary empirical study, the article synthesizes examples and prior literature to describe potential applications of AI in assessment. It discusses AI use for personalized feedback, test blueprints, item generation, automated grading, item analysis, and reporting, and argues that teachers remain essential for assessment design, interpretation, ethical oversight, and individualized instruction. The paper also outlines concerns such as bias, transparency, privacy, limited understanding among educators, and reduced human interaction.

The context is broad educational assessment, with examples that include classroom assessment and K-12 settings, but the paper is not an intervention study and does not evaluate a specific AI system in a sample of students. Its main conclusion is that AI can improve efficiency and provide personalized support in assessment, but human teachers must remain central to ensure fairness, validity, and ethical use.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools can automate and accelerate multiple assessment tasks, including test item generation, scoring, item analysis, and reporting. It does not report a primary effect size, but repeatedly claims that AI can save teachers time and reduce workload by streamlining assessment workflows.
finding.measure: Assessment task automation and teacher workload

finding.finding_summary: The article states that AI tools can support critical thinking by generating personalized feedback and by helping learners analyze and reflect on responses, but it also warns that AI assessment tools may be poorly suited to measuring critical thinking directly. No empirical effect size is reported because this is a review article.
finding.measure: Critical thinking support and assessment feasibility

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI-based personalized feedback and immediate responses can increase student engagement and motivation, and that AI tutoring/assessment systems may reduce anxiety. These statements are descriptive and literature-based rather than primary empirical findings, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, and anxiety

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Systems that Augment Human Performed vs. Demonstrated Critical Thinking
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines how generative AI systems should be evaluated and designed when the target capability is critical thinking. The authors argue that current research often conflates two different constructs: performed critical thinking, meaning independent reasoning done without AI assistance, and demonstrated critical thinking, meaning reasoning products or processes produced with AI collaboration.

Rather than testing a specific intervention, the paper proposes a conceptual framework grounded in prior work on critical thinking, Bloom’s taxonomy, and Engelbart’s intellect augmentation framework. It reviews how existing studies have evaluated AI’s effects on critical thinking, notes that many measure only the final AI-assisted output, and argues that this may overstate whether users’ independent critical thinking has improved.

The paper is not an empirical study of a K-12 intervention, but a theory and design paper. Its main conclusion is that AI systems can augment demonstrated critical thinking without necessarily improving performed critical thinking, and that future research should use study designs that separately assess independent reasoning over time, especially in educational settings. It recommends scaffolding questions, structured frameworks, and other supports that help users practice critical thinking themselves rather than simply generating better answers.

finding.finding_summary: This paper argues conceptually that generative AI may improve demonstrated critical thinking while leaving performed critical thinking unchanged or even weakened through overreliance. It does not report original empirical effect sizes, sample sizes, or statistical estimates; instead it synthesizes prior studies and calls for separate measurement of independent reasoning.
finding.measure: Critical thinking (performed vs. demonstrated), conceptual analysis of prior studies

paper_profiles.title: Cognitive Dissonance Artificial Intelligence (CD-AI): The Mind at War with Itself. Harnessing Discomfort to Sharpen Critical Thinking
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2025 ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable / unspecified (theoretical, not an empirical K-12 study)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper proposes Cognitive Dissonance AI (CD-AI), a human-AI interaction framework designed to enhance critical thinking by deliberately sustaining uncertainty and presenting users with strongly argued opposing viewpoints. Rather than optimizing for fast, coherent answers, the system is intended to create productive cognitive discomfort, prompting reflection, synthesis, and epistemic humility.

The paper is conceptual and theoretical rather than empirical. It draws on cognitive dissonance theory, argumentation, neuroscience, and critical thinking literature to argue that AI should function as a dialectical reasoning partner. The author discusses potential applications in education, ethics, law, politics, and science, and also outlines ethical risks such as decision paralysis, manipulation, and bias.

No K-12 population is studied, and no intervention is tested with learners. The paper instead calls for future research to evaluate whether AI-induced cognitive dissonance improves critical thinking, resilience against misinformation, and adaptive reasoning, including in educational settings. Its main conclusion is that AI systems could be redesigned to support deeper reasoning by preserving contradiction rather than resolving it immediately.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that CD-AI would strengthen critical thinking, metacognitive reflection, epistemic humility, and adaptive reasoning by sustaining cognitive dissonance instead of resolving it immediately. However, this is a conceptual proposal only; no empirical sample, comparator, or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognition, epistemic humility, adaptive reasoning (proposed outcomes)

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes a new design and governance model for AI-augmented reasoning, with implications for education, AI governance, and decision-making systems. It suggests future research and institutional safeguards, but provides no empirical evaluation of policy, governance, or institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: AI governance and design implications for educational/decision systems

paper_profiles.title: Navigating the State of Cognitive Flow: Context-Aware AI Interventions for Effective Reasoning Support
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that AI systems designed to support human reasoning can unintentionally harm performance when they interrupt a user at the wrong time, with the wrong kind of feedback, or at the wrong intensity. Drawing on flow theory, the authors introduce the concept of "cognitive flow" to describe an optimal state in which reasoning support should help users maintain deep engagement rather than disrupt it.

The paper proposes a context-aware cognitive augmentation framework that uses multimodal behavioral cues such as gaze behavior, typing hesitation, interaction speed, and other engagement signals to infer when and how to intervene. The core idea is that AI reasoning assistants should personalize the type, timing, and scale of feedback—such as direct corrections versus Socratic prompts—so that support is minimally intrusive and better aligned to the user's cognitive state.

This is a conceptual workshop paper rather than an empirical study. It does not report a participant sample, comparator condition, or outcome data; instead, it offers a theory-driven argument and a call for future evaluation using mixed-method approaches that combine behavioral analytics with subjective feedback. The main conclusion is that context-aware, personalized interventions are likely to support reasoning and critical thinking more effectively than static one-size-fits-all AI feedback, but this claim is presented as a proposal rather than evidence from a study.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that context-aware AI interventions can better support critical thinking and deliberate reasoning by adapting the type, timing, and scale of feedback to a user's cognitive state. No empirical effect size is reported; the claim is conceptual and framed as a theory-driven expectation rather than a measured outcome.
finding.measure: critical thinking / reasoning support / cognitive flow (conceptual framework)

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes that minimally intrusive, context-aware interventions can help maintain engagement, autonomy, and intrinsic motivation by preserving cognitive flow. This is presented as a conceptual argument about engagement and flow rather than an empirical result.
finding.measure: cognitive flow / engagement / autonomy (conceptual framework)

paper_profiles.title: Blue Sky Ideas in Artificial Intelligence Education from the EAAI 2017 New and Future AI Educator Program
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a collection of short position pieces from the EAAI 2017 New and Future AI Educator Program rather than an empirical study. The contributors respond to three broad questions about AI education: how to incorporate ethics into AI curricula, how to teach AI topics at early undergraduate or secondary school level, and how to make AI education more interdisciplinary so it benefits non-engineering fields.

The individual essays propose a range of pedagogical ideas, including peer-learning across disciplines, student-centric discovery inspired by Montessori, early introduction of AI concepts in K-12, ethics threaded throughout AI topics, real-world problem framing, and game-based or project-based learning. The contexts discussed span secondary school, early undergraduate, and teacher/faculty preparation, but the paper does not report any controlled evaluation, student outcome data, or comparative evidence.

Overall, the paper’s main contribution is conceptual: it surfaces design ideas, motivations, and cautionary arguments for future AI education practice. For the K-12-related portions, it argues that AI concepts can be taught in accessible ways using games, visualization, and conceptual activities, but it provides no empirical evidence about student learning, critical thinking, or the effect of personalized feedback.

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Critical Thinking with AI: A Tailored Warning System for RAG Models
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether tailored warning messages can help users critically evaluate hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems used for educational question answering. The authors frame the problem as one of AI-augmented reasoning: rather than merely improving model accuracy, they ask how user-facing explanations of retrieval and generation problems affect reasoning, trust, and decision-making.

The study proposes a warning system that adds fact-checking at both the retrieval and LLM output layers, then presents context-specific warnings in the interface. In a pilot study, 18 participants completed an AP U.S. history textbook-based multiple-choice quiz under one of three conditions: no warning, a standard generic warning, or a tailored warning generated from the specific output problem. The same questions and responses were used across conditions, with only the warning type changing.

Results suggest that tailored warnings improved participants’ accuracy, especially on hallucinated items, and were associated with higher reported trust than the other warning conditions. The tailored-warning group achieved 100% accuracy on non-hallucinated items, 89% on low-level hallucinations, and 81% on high-level hallucinations, compared with 97%/81%/69% for the standard-warning group and 100%/64%/56% for the no-warning group. An ANOVA reported a statistically significant difference in accuracy across groups (p=0.006162). Qualitative comments also indicate a tradeoff: some participants found the warnings confusing or felt they interfered with getting the correct answer. Overall, the paper argues that context-specific warnings can support critical thinking, but that their design needs refinement to avoid cognitive friction.

finding.finding_summary: Tailored warnings improved participants’ ability to detect hallucinations and answer questions more accurately in a critical-evaluation task. In the pilot study (n=18), the tailored-warning group reached 100% accuracy on non-hallucinated items, 89% on low-level hallucinations, and 81% on high-level hallucinations, outperforming the standard-warning group (97%, 81%, 69%) and the no-warning group (100%, 64%, 56%); ANOVA across groups was significant (p=0.006162).
finding.measure: Accuracy on multiple-choice question answering under no-warning, standard-warning, and tailored-warning conditions

finding.finding_summary: The tailored-warning condition was associated with higher self-reported trust in the system, with a reported difference of 0.67 on a 5-point Likert scale relative to the other groups. However, qualitative feedback indicated some cognitive friction: participants said the warnings were confusing and that they wanted the correct answer rather than prompts to think critically.
finding.measure: Self-reported trust and interface usability/ease ratings; qualitative interview feedback

paper_profiles.title: Developing Critical Thinking in Second Language Learners: Exploring Generative AI like ChatGPT as a tool for Argumentative Essay Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a structured ChatGPT use guideline can improve second-language learners’ critical thinking and argumentative writing. The authors develop the ChatGPT Guideline for Critical Argumentative Writing (CGCAW), which combines the Paul-Elder Critical Thinking Model with Tan’s framework for argumentative writing and adds feedback prompts aligned to Hattie & Timperley’s feedback model.

The study used a small quantitative experiment with 10 university students at a state university, randomly assigned to an experimental group that used CGCAW with ChatGPT and a control group that used ChatGPT without the structured prompts. All participants wrote a short argumentative essay in 40 minutes on the same social-media topic. Essays were scored by Grammarly, ChatGPT, and the course instructor using different criteria. Results were mixed: ChatGPT ratings favored the CGCAW group on clarity, logical coherence, and evidence use, but Grammarly and the instructor favored the control group on overall writing quality and language mechanics.

The authors conclude that ChatGPT-guided feedback may help students strengthen some higher-order aspects of argumentative writing, especially clarity, coherence, and evidence integration, but that the framework needs refinement. They also note important limitations, including the very small sample, short writing window, differences among scoring tools, and uncertain prior familiarity with ChatGPT. Overall, the paper presents CGCAW as a promising but preliminary approach for supporting critical thinking through AI-assisted writing in higher education second-language contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The study’s main writing outcome was argumentative essay quality. ChatGPT-rated results favored the CGCAW group on clarity (G1 mean 20.3 vs G2 19.4), logical coherence (18.4 vs 18.0), and use of evidence (17.7 vs 17.0), but Grammarly and the course instructor scored the control group higher overall (Grammarly means 92.2 vs 90.6; instructor means 56 vs 35). With n=10 and very small group sizes, the evidence suggests selective writing benefits rather than a uniform improvement.
finding.measure: Argumentative essay quality ratings (clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, persuasiveness; Grammarly and instructor writing scores)
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT assessment SDs reported: G1 total SD=7.6, G2 total SD=5.5; clarity SDs 2.4 vs 1.8, evidence SDs 1.7 vs 1.2, coherence SDs 1.9 vs 1.5

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly investigates critical thinking development through ChatGPT-guided argumentative writing. The CGCAW framework was associated with better performance on critical-thinking-related writing dimensions such as clarity, logical coherence, and evidence use according to ChatGPT, but the control group performed better on overall mechanics and some instructor-scored argumentative features. Given the small sample (n=10) and mixed outcomes across raters, the finding is promising but inconclusive.
finding.measure: Critical-thinking-related argumentative writing performance (clarity, logical coherence, evidence use, persuasiveness) as a proxy for critical thinking
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT assessment SDs reported: G1 total SD=7.6, G2 total SD=5.5

paper_profiles.title: Investigating Students’ Preferences for AI Roles in Mathematical Modelling: Evidence from a Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students’ baseline competencies and preferences relate to different AI roles in mathematical modelling tasks. The authors focus on a practical question in AI-supported mathematics education: whether an AI should act as a tutor, teaching assistant, peer student, struggling student, or excellent student when supporting modelling work that requires abstraction, representation, and iterative reasoning.

The study used a within-subjects, counterbalanced randomized controlled trial with 26 university students in non-STEM majors who had not taken university-level mathematics courses, making them roughly comparable to high school graduates in mathematical preparation. Each participant completed one baseline modelling task without assistance and five additional modelling tasks, each with a different GPT-based AI role. Participants also completed pre-task questionnaires on computational thinking, design thinking, and mathematical modelling self-efficacy, plus post-task ratings, rankings, and open-ended feedback.

Results showed that design thinking and computational thinking were positively associated with mathematical modelling self-efficacy, with design thinking a particularly strong predictor (β = 0.730, p < .001; CT β = 0.300, p < .001; R² = 0.808). For AI roles, students strongly preferred competent/supportive roles over the struggling student role. The tutor role was most preferred overall, while the struggling student role was rated least favorably across preference, task confidence, helpfulness, and ease of interaction. Among the constructive roles (tutor, TA, peer, excellent student), differences were generally small, though students with higher design thinking slightly preferred the teaching assistant role more than those with lower design thinking. The authors conclude that AI support in modelling should emphasize competence and adaptive scaffolding, and that students’ dispositions can shape how they value specific AI personas.

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that students preferred competent AI roles for mathematical modelling tasks and that AI role significantly affected modelling-related user experience. In the within-subjects RCT with N=26, the Tutor role was ranked most preferred overall (M=2.35, SD=1.02), while the Struggling Student role was ranked least preferred (M=4.42, SD=1.17); Friedman test χ2(4)=28.83, p<.001. This is an attitudinal and process-focused finding rather than a direct achievement effect, but it indicates that supportive AI personas were perceived as more effective for mathematical modelling.
finding.measure: AI role preference rankings for mathematical modelling tasks; task confidence; perceived helpfulness; ease of interaction
finding.effect_size: r=0.85 (largest pairwise preference difference for Struggling Student vs Tutor); beta coefficients for related competency model: DT β=0.730, CT β=0.300
finding.std_deviation: Tutor ranking SD=1.02; Struggling Student ranking SD=1.17

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studied computational thinking, design thinking, and their relationship to mathematical modelling self-efficacy. In the sample of N=26, design thinking and computational thinking both positively predicted modelling self-efficacy (DT β=0.730, p<.001; CT β=0.300, p<.001), explaining 80.8% of variance (R²=0.808). Several CT and DT subdimensions were positively correlated with modelling self-efficacy, indicating that higher-order thinking dispositions were closely linked to confidence in modelling.
finding.measure: Computational thinking scale, design thinking scale, mathematical modelling self-efficacy scale; Pearson correlations and PLS-SEM

finding.finding_summary: The study found that AI role significantly affected task confidence, perceived helpfulness, and ease of interaction. Across N=26 participants, the Tutor and Excellent Student roles produced the highest confidence and helpfulness ratings, while the Struggling Student role produced the lowest (task confidence M=1.88, SD=1.24; helpfulness M=1.92, SD=1.23; ease of interaction M=1.81, SD=1.17). The pattern suggests that supportive AI personas improve learners’ immediate motivational and affective experience during modelling.
finding.measure: Post-task Likert ratings of task confidence, perceived AI helpfulness, and ease of interaction
finding.effect_size: Friedman χ2(4)=24.85 for task confidence; χ2(4)=32.63 for helpfulness; χ2(4)=36.43 for ease of interaction; several pairwise Wilcoxon tests significant with large effects
finding.std_deviation: Task confidence SD=1.24 for Struggling Student; helpfulness SD=1.23; ease of interaction SD=1.17

finding.finding_summary: The paper offers design implications for adaptive, learner-centered AI systems in mathematical modelling, arguing that AI roles should vary by support level and pedagogical function. This is not a policy study, but it substantively contributes to institutional/system design by specifying which AI personas learners prefer and how those preferences vary by learner profile.
finding.measure: Participant rankings and qualitative feedback on AI role personas

paper_profiles.title: Study on the Helpfulness of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to evaluate the helpfulness of explainable AI (XAI) methods in a human-centered way. The authors argue that common XAI evaluations rely too heavily on subjective judgments such as satisfaction or perceived usefulness, and they propose an objective proxy-task methodology in which users judge whether an AI model’s prediction is correct based on the input, ground truth, and an explanation.

To demonstrate the approach, the authors ran a user study with 139 participants using image classification tasks on ImageNetV2 images and two pretrained CNNs (AlexNet and VGG16). Participants saw explanations from six XAI methods: LRP, Grad-CAM, LIME, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, and confidence scores. Their responses were scored for accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity as indicators of whether the explanation helped users judge, trust, or question the AI decision.

The study found that all methods performed above chance for overall accuracy, but confidence scores produced the best accuracy, while Grad-CAM and LRP performed best for trust-related judgments and SHAP performed best for questioning incorrect decisions. The authors conclude that no single explanation method works best across all goals and recommend using diverse, task-focused explanation frameworks rather than relying on one monolithic XAI approach.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly evaluated whether XAI methods help users perform a proxy task requiring judgment, trust, and questioning of AI decisions, which the authors frame as human-centered decision-making performance. Across 139 participants, all methods beat the 0.5 random baseline for accuracy, with confidence scores highest (mean accuracy ≈0.698, d=0.84), while Grad-CAM and LRP were strongest for trust-related judgments and SHAP was strongest for questioning incorrect decisions.
finding.measure: Accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity in judging whether an AI image-classification prediction was correct
finding.effect_size: varies_by_method (e.g., d=0.84 for confidence scores accuracy)

paper_profiles.title: Linking Artificial Intelligence Principles
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Workshop on Artificial Intelligence Safety (AAAI-Safe AI 2019)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that existing Artificial Intelligence (AI) principle statements are fragmented, use different terminology, and emphasize different ethical and governance concerns. The authors propose Linking Artificial Intelligence Principles (LAIP), a platform for semantically linking and comparing 27 AI principle proposals from academia, nonprofits, governments, and industry.

The approach is not an intervention study with human participants; rather, it is a text-analysis and knowledge-linking framework. The authors manually define 10 general topics (e.g., humanity, collaboration, fairness, transparency, privacy, security, safety, accountability, AGI/ASI) and then expand keyword sets using word2vec similarity to detect topic coverage in the principles. They compare principles by topic and keyword coverage, and also examine differences by publisher type.

The paper’s main conclusion is that AI principles share overlapping concerns but vary in emphasis and completeness, so no single principle set should be treated as sufficient on its own. The authors argue for integrating multiple principles into a comprehensive framework and highlight gaps such as limited attention to safety in academia and industry, and limited coverage of AGI/ASI. Because the paper studies governance texts rather than educational outcomes, it does not provide evidence about K-12 learning effects.

finding.finding_summary: The paper qualitatively analyzes 27 AI principle proposals and finds substantial variation in topic coverage across academia, government, and industry. It concludes that no single proposal is comprehensive; instead, different proposals are complementary and should be linked into a broader framework for AI governance.
finding.measure: Topic and keyword coverage of AI principles across 10 manually defined topics

paper_profiles.title: AI for Proactive Mental Health: A Multi-Institutional, Longitudinal, Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a generative AI-powered mobile app can provide proactive, strengths-based mental health support at scale for college students. The authors argue that most AI mental health tools are deficit-oriented and reactive, and they test whether a personalized, interactive app can instead boost well-being before distress escalates.

The intervention was Flourish, a mobile app with an AI chatbot (“Sunnie”), personalized recommendations, gamified activities, and weekly insights designed around science-based, timely, action-oriented, real-life-focused support. In a six-week randomized controlled trial across three U.S. institutions, 486 undergraduate students were assigned either to app access or to a waitlist control group with usual school supports. Outcomes were measured with validated self-report instruments across emotional, social, and overall well-being domains.

The app produced significant benefits for positive affect, loneliness, belonging, resilience, mindfulness, and flourishing, with effects typically small in magnitude. The treatment group was also buffered against declines in some outcomes over the semester. Negative affect and deficit-oriented outcomes such as depression, anxiety, stress, and academic self-efficacy did not significantly change. The authors conclude that a purpose-built generative AI system can deliver measurable preventive well-being benefits for college students, but they caution that effects may partly reflect general engagement because the study used a waitlist rather than an active control.

finding.finding_summary: In a 6-week multi-institutional RCT with undergraduate students (n=486), access to the Flourish app significantly improved several well-being outcomes relative to waitlist control. Positive affect increased (Week 6: d=0.33; Week 4: d=0.23), and resilience, mindfulness, and flourishing also showed significant Condition × Time effects (b=0.11 to 0.19, p=.047 to .032), indicating small but meaningful gains in emotional regulation and overall well-being.
finding.measure: Subcomponents of Affect Scale positive affect; Brief Resilience Scale; Mindful Attention Awareness Scale; Flourishing Scale
finding.effect_size: d=0.23 to 0.33 for positive affect; b=0.11 to 0.19 for other outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The intervention targeted and improved social connection-related skills and outcomes, including loneliness, belonging, and closeness to the university. In the RCT (n=486), loneliness decreased more in the treatment group than control (b=-0.05, p=.038; roughly a small effect), while belonging improved (b=0.06, p=.030) and closeness to school was marginal (b=0.04, p=.070). The paper frames these as gains in social connection and adaptive coping rather than academic performance.
finding.measure: UCLA 3-item Loneliness Scale; campus belonging single item; closeness to school IOS item
finding.effect_size: b=-0.05 for loneliness; b=0.06 for belonging; b=0.04 for closeness to school

finding.finding_summary: Academic self-efficacy was included as an additional outcome but did not show a statistically significant Condition × Time effect. The authors report p≥.462 for the set of deficit-oriented and academic measures, suggesting no detectable academic benefit over the six-week period in this nonclinical undergraduate sample (n=486).
finding.measure: Academic self-efficacy

paper_profiles.title: Promoting Real-Time Reflection in Synchronous Communication with Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: AIREASONING-2025-01 workshop (ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper asks how generative AI can support real-time reflection during synchronous communication. The authors argue that reflection is often treated as a post-hoc activity, whereas many important communication contexts require people to notice issues and adapt while they are still speaking or interacting.

The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it reviews 11 recent systems for reflection support in synchronous settings such as online meetings, live lectures, presentations, and practice talks. The authors compare design patterns for supporting reflection, including increasing contextual awareness, aggregating audience status, summarizing ongoing conversation, and providing expert suggestions. They also analyze interaction paradigms such as user-initiated, system-initiated, and continuous display, and discuss where generative AI adds value by producing nuanced summaries, role-playing audiences, and giving personalized feedback.

The main conclusion is that generative AI can expand real-time reflection beyond simple statistics and surface-level cues, but effective designs must address interpretability, timing/proactiveness, and the limitations of role-play agents. Because the paper is a conceptual review and design-implications article rather than an empirical evaluation, it does not report effect sizes or causal evidence of impact.

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively discusses real-time feedback in synchronous communication contexts such as lectures, presentations, meetings, and practice talks, which involves speaking and listening performance. However, it is a review/position paper and does not present original outcome data; the only evidence is qualitative synthesis of prior systems and design implications, with no reported effect sizes or sample-based language-fluency outcomes.
finding.measure: Real-time communication performance, spoken interaction quality, and feedback during synchronous speaking/listening tasks

finding.finding_summary: A central focus of the paper is real-time reflection as a way to improve communication strategy, self-monitoring, and adaptive performance, which aligns closely with durable skills such as critical thinking and metacognition. The paper synthesizes prior systems suggesting that AI-generated summaries, audience feedback, and expert-style suggestions can help users evaluate their own communication in the moment, but it also notes risks such as poor persona grounding and superficial responses.
finding.measure: Real-time reflection, self-monitoring, adaptive communication strategy, and perceived ability to re-evaluate ongoing performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can reduce user workload by proactively delivering summaries, agenda tracking, and timely feedback during synchronous communication. It synthesizes prior systems and design patterns showing that proactive assistance and continuous display can help users avoid manual searching and stay on task, but it does not evaluate productivity gains empirically.
finding.measure: User workload, need for manual information seeking, and efficiency of interacting with reflection-support systems

paper_profiles.title: Shots and Boosters: Exploring the Use of Combined Prebunking Interventions to Raise Critical Thinking and Create Long-Term Protection Against Misinformation
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses the problem of misinformation mitigation and argues that debunking alone is insufficient because misinformation spreads quickly and can have lasting effects. The authors review prior work on interventions that encourage critical thinking, especially nudging and inoculation, and frame these as complementary approaches rather than alternatives.

The paper proposes a design concept for an AI-driven prebunking intervention that combines two stages. Stage 1 is an inoculation-style training game in which users evaluate potentially misleading posts, explain their reasoning to an AI tutor, receive corrective and structural feedback, and build a personalized profile of strengths and weaknesses. Stage 2 is a booster phase in which the AI delivers brief, personalized nudges in everyday fact-checking contexts to reinforce previously learned strategies and reduce cognitive load.

The paper is not an empirical evaluation of the intervention and does not study a K-12 population. Instead, it synthesizes related research from HCI, media literacy, and AI-supported learning to motivate the design. Its main conclusion is that AI may be useful for personalization, immediate feedback, and adaptive reinforcement in prebunking systems, but the paper remains a conceptual proposal rather than tested evidence.
