finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of implications for assessment policy, plagiarism detection, and institutional response

paper_profiles.title: Shaping integrity: why generative artificial intelligence does not have to undermine education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education (examples across high school, language arts, science, and business classes)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This opinion piece argues that generative AI in education need not undermine academic integrity if it is integrated responsibly and ethically. The authors frame the issue around concerns about cheating, plagiarism, privacy, bias, and over-reliance on AI, and counter these concerns by drawing on deontological ethics, consequentialism, constructivist learning theory, and self-determination theory (SDT).

Rather than reporting a primary empirical study, the paper synthesizes prior literature and uses classroom examples to show how AI could support authentic learning, personalized feedback, digital literacy, and intrinsic motivation. Examples include high school history, language arts, science, and business settings, where AI-generated timelines, writing feedback, lab assistance, and planning tools are described as ways to promote deeper engagement and higher-order thinking.

The paper’s main conclusion is normative: AI can be used to strengthen rather than weaken academic integrity when educators set clear ethical boundaries, teach digital literacy, emphasize authentic assessment, and use AI to support autonomy, competence, and relatedness. It also recommends educator professional development, transparent institutional policies, and iterative evaluation of AI use in schools.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can support writing development through real-time feedback on grammar, tone, narrative structure, and revision. No primary study is reported, but the authors use language arts classroom examples to claim AI-assisted writing can improve academic writing skills and motivation.
finding.measure: Writing quality / academic writing skills (illustrative, not empirically tested in this paper)

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on self-determination theory and repeatedly claims that AI can foster intrinsic motivation by supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness. These claims are presented conceptually rather than as results from a new empirical study.
finding.measure: Intrinsic motivation, engagement, autonomy, competence, relatedness (conceptual/theoretical)

finding.finding_summary: A major theme is that AI can support critical thinking, metacognition, collaboration, and knowledge construction through interactive timelines, simulations, personalized feedback, and collaborative projects. The paper does not report new data; instead, it argues that these uses of AI encourage higher-order thinking and authentic learning.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognition, collaboration, and knowledge construction (conceptual/theoretical)

finding.finding_summary: The paper recommends institutional and policy changes such as transparent AI-use guidelines, educator professional development, and iterative monitoring of AI implementation. These are normative recommendations rather than measured outcomes, aimed at preserving academic integrity and aligning AI adoption with educational goals.
finding.measure: Institutional policy guidance, educator training, transparency, and monitoring (conceptual/recommended)

paper_profiles.title: The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the question of how artificial intelligence (AI) has been applied in STEM education and what effects those applications have had across the empirical literature from 2011 to 2021. Using a general system theory lens, the authors sought to understand AI-STEM not only as a set of technologies, but as an educational system involving subject, information, medium, environment, and technology elements.

The review screened peer-reviewed empirical studies and identified 63 articles. It categorized AI applications into six groups: learning prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, student behavior detection, automation, educational robots, and other applications (such as AI textbooks and group formation). The review also mapped these AI categories to STEM subjects, educational levels, instructional strategies, mediums, and learning environments.

Across the reviewed studies, the most common context was higher education, especially in technology and science-related courses, though some studies included elementary and secondary learners. The main conclusions were that AI in STEM is most often used to support prediction, personalized tutoring, behavior monitoring, and automated assessment, and that these applications generally show positive effects on learning performance, affective outcomes, higher-order thinking, and efficiency, though a small number of studies found no significant learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: The review includes multiple studies in mathematics and engineering mathematics showing positive effects of AI-supported tools on learning outcomes. For example, an AI-enabled adaptive learning system in Java programming and mathematical problem support were reported to improve performance, and the review notes that AI applications generally had significantly positive effects on learning performance across STEM, including mathematics-focused studies, though the review does not provide a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Learning performance / achievement in mathematics-related STEM courses

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes studies in science and STEM that measured learning achievement, argumentation, and understanding of scientific concepts. Most studies reported positive effects of AI-supported interventions on learning performance, including geoscience and biology learning, with a few null findings; however, no pooled effect size was reported in the review.
finding.measure: Science learning achievement, concept understanding, and scientific argumentation

finding.finding_summary: The review covers technology, engineering, and programming courses, where AI tools were used for prediction, tutoring, automation, and robotics. These applications were generally associated with improved course performance and skills in programming, computer engineering, and engineering-related tasks, although the review does not report a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Programming and engineering course performance, coding-related skills

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that AI applications often improved students' affective perceptions, including attitude, interest, motivation, satisfaction, and engagement. Across 17 studies focused on these outcomes, students generally responded positively to adaptive learning systems, learning analytics, and robots, but the evidence is descriptive and not pooled.
finding.measure: Attitude, interest, motivation, satisfaction, engagement

finding.finding_summary: The review found that AI-supported STEM tools contributed to higher-order thinking outcomes such as problem-solving, computational thinking, self-regulated learning, and argumentation. Several individual studies reported better outcomes for AI-supported groups than comparison conditions, but the review does not provide a meta-analytic effect size.
finding.measure: Problem-solving ability, computational thinking, self-regulated learning, argumentation

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of the reviewed literature examined operational and technological efficiency, including automated assessment accuracy, predictive model performance, and question generation. The review concludes that AI techniques generally performed well in learning prediction and automation, helping reduce instructor workload and improve assessment efficiency, though exact pooled effects were not reported.
finding.measure: Automated assessment accuracy, prediction accuracy, efficiency of AI systems, teacher workload reduction

paper_profiles.title: Evolution and Revolution in Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (review of IJAIED papers across multiple educational levels; no single study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a reflective review of the Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED) field rather than a study of a single intervention. The authors analyze 47 papers published in the International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education from 1994, 2004, and 2014 to identify trends in paper type, domains, interaction styles, collaboration, technology, settings, and learning goals.

The paper’s purpose is to assess what AIED has historically focused on and to argue for future directions. The authors conclude that the field has become more empirical, more focused on STEM, and still heavily centered on step-based tutoring in formal school settings using computers. They argue that while this “evolution” has improved rigor and effectiveness, the field should also pursue a more “revolutionary” agenda: broader technologies, more authentic and collaborative learning, stronger attention to teacher practice and classroom context, and learning beyond the classroom in everyday life.

Because this is a review and conceptual article, it does not evaluate a single AI-personalized feedback system or report original outcome data from a K-12 sample. Instead, it synthesizes patterns across prior AIED studies and uses those trends to make recommendations for the next generation of intelligent learning environments.

finding.finding_summary: Across the 47 IJAIED papers reviewed, the authors find a strong historical shift toward STEM domains, with increasing emphasis on math and science systems and step-based tutoring environments. They do not report a single effect size for learner outcomes; rather, they summarize publication trends and note that the field has increasingly focused on well-defined domain learning problems in formal school settings.
finding.measure: Content analysis of paper domains and interaction styles in IJAIED articles from 1994, 2004, and 2014

finding.finding_summary: The review notes that some AIED papers addressed motivation, satisfaction, and related affective outcomes, especially in 2014, but these were usually measured with surveys and mostly in service of evaluating the systems rather than demonstrating broad transfer. The authors argue that motivation is important, but the reviewed literature still relies heavily on limited self-report measures rather than stronger evidence of lasting impact.
finding.measure: Survey-based measures of satisfaction/motivation in reviewed empirical papers
finding.study_size: varies across reviewed studies; not_reported at paper level

finding.finding_summary: A major theme of the paper is that AIED should move beyond domain knowledge to support durable skills such as metacognition, self-regulated learning, critical thinking, and collaboration. The review finds that a minority of reviewed papers measured these outcomes, often through surveys or limited transfer tasks, and the authors argue that the field needs stronger evaluation of whether such skills improve outside the tutored environment.
finding.measure: Measures of metacognition, self-regulated learning, collaboration, and critical thinking discussed across reviewed studies
finding.study_size: n=47 papers reviewed; subset of empirical studies addressed these skills

finding.finding_summary: The authors characterize much of the AIED literature as having improved learning efficiency, often by producing similar gains in less time through step-based tutoring systems. This is presented as a field-level trend rather than a single estimated effect, with the paper citing prior work on efficiency and reduced practice time.
finding.measure: Learning efficiency and time-on-task trends in reviewed AIED papers

paper_profiles.title: Teacher’s Perceptions of Using an Artificial Intelligence-Based Educational Tool for Scientific Writing
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers (STEM-related disciplines; elementary, middle, and high school teachers)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study examined STEM teachers’ perceptions of an AI-enhanced scaffolding system for scientific writing. The authors were interested in whether hands-on use of an AI-based tool would change teachers’ views of AI in classroom instruction, and what concerns teachers would raise about integrating such technology into schooling.

The intervention was an artificial intelligence-enhanced scaffolding system (AISS) built with GPT-2. Teachers read background literature on AI in education, then used the AISS to complete a short scientific writing task based on an authentic air-quality problem, first drafting independently and then revising with AI-generated expert-modeling support. Afterward, teachers completed brief interviews and their log files were used for triangulation.

Participants were nine STEM teachers from K-12 schools in the southeastern United States, enrolled in a doctoral course at a higher education institution. The sample included elementary, middle, and high school teachers in science, math, physics, and English; all had prior educational technology experience but no prior experience with educational AI. Teachers generally viewed the system positively as superior scaffolding that offered immediate, individualized, and model-based feedback, but they also raised concerns about transparency, reliability, and the possible reduction of the teacher’s role.

Overall, the paper concludes that AI-based scaffolding may be promising for supporting scientific writing and higher-order thinking in STEM classrooms, especially for middle and high school students, but successful adoption will require clearer explanations of AI decisions, professional development, and careful attention to teacher roles in AI-supported instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the AI-based scaffolding supported reasoning, argumentation, and higher-order thinking during scientific writing. Participants described the system as helping them compare claims with evidence, reflect on their thinking, and generate stronger arguments; no quantitative effect size was reported because the study was qualitative (n=9).
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about reasoning, argumentation skills, higher-order thinking, and evidence-based writing during an AI-supported scientific writing task

finding.finding_summary: The AISS was perceived as a helpful tool for scientific writing, particularly for sentence structure, paragraph sequencing, and producing stronger written claims with citations or examples. Teachers said the system provided individualized expert models and immediate feedback that improved their writing process, but the study did not report quantitative literacy outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of scientific writing support; interview themes on writing quality, sentence structure, paragraph organization, and evidence-based writing

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed the AI scaffolded scientific problem solving by helping users connect claims to evidence in an authentic air-quality task. The system was seen as promoting scientific inquiry, deep understanding of scientific content, and application of knowledge in STEM-related contexts; no quantitative test scores or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about scientific writing, scientific problem solving, and understanding of scientific content

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the tool increased interest, engagement, and willingness to interact with the writing task because the AI responses were immediate and surprising. Several comments indicated the experience was motivating and made the writing process more interesting, but the paper did not report quantitative engagement measures.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about interest, motivation, and engagement with the AI-supported writing activity

finding.finding_summary: Participants noted that the AI generated sentences quickly and offered immediate feedback, which they viewed as a potential efficiency benefit compared with human-only support. At the same time, teachers worried they would need time to review AI output for accuracy, so the operational benefit was perceived but not quantified.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about speed of feedback and time needed to review AI-generated text

paper_profiles.title: Integration of AI in STEM Education – Addressing Ethical Challenges in K-12 Settings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how AI is being integrated into K-12 STEM education and what ethical challenges arise from that integration. Rather than reporting new empirical data, it critically reviews recent literature on AI applications such as intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment, predictive analytics, and surveillance tools, with attention to issues of bias, privacy, equity, and pedagogical limits.

The paper’s main contribution is a conceptual framework for responsible AI integration in K-12 STEM. It argues that AI can support personalized learning, real-time feedback, and operational efficiency, but warns that without governance and teacher preparation it may reinforce inequities, narrow pedagogy, and undermine privacy. To address these concerns, the authors propose a three-phased implementation roadmap, a four-phase professional development model grounded in TPACK and critical algorithmic literacy, and equity-centered strategies such as low-resource adaptations, bias audits, and policy alignment.

The paper is situated in K-12 STEM contexts, with examples spanning mathematics, science, and broader STEM classrooms; one implementation scenario focuses on an 8th-grade biology unit. Its conclusions emphasize that AI should be embedded within human-centered, ethically governed STEM instruction, and that future work should examine long-term student outcomes and improve AI literacy assessment tools.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI ethics and algorithmic literacy activities can support critical thinking, ethical reasoning, and critical engagement with AI systems in K-12 STEM. It cites prior work suggesting project-based AI ethics activities show high critical thinking gains, but this paper itself is a conceptual synthesis and does not report new effect sizes.
finding.measure: Critical thinking; ethical reasoning; AI literacy/algorithmic literacy outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper contends that AI tools such as intelligent tutoring systems and automated assessments can improve STEM learning, including science-related reasoning and knowledge integration, by providing personalized feedback and diagnostic support. In its example implementation, 8th-grade biology students use AI to analyze image datasets and detect under-representation bias, but the paper does not report original outcome statistics.
finding.measure: STEM learning, scientific reasoning, knowledge integration, and revision behaviors

finding.finding_summary: The paper consistently states that AI-powered assessment and tutoring tools can reduce teacher workload by automating scoring, providing real-time feedback, and scaling personalized support. These claims are presented as synthesized literature rather than original evaluation results, so no empirical effect size is reported here.
finding.measure: Teacher workload; assessment efficiency; scalability of feedback and scoring

finding.finding_summary: A central focus of the paper is institutional and policy-level governance for AI in K-12 STEM, including bias audits, privacy safeguards, data governance protocols, and alignment with UNESCO/OECD standards. The proposed roadmap and professional development model are intended to drive system-wide adoption while mitigating inequity and surveillance risks, but no original quantitative institutional outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Policy alignment, governance protocols, equity audits, institutional implementation planning

paper_profiles.title: Interactive, Intelligent Tutoring for Auxiliary Constructions in Geometry Proofs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a specific challenge in K-12 geometry learning: helping students discover auxiliary constructions needed to solve proof problems. The authors argue that existing geometry tutors and automated theorem provers either do not teach auxiliary constructions or generate proofs in ways that are opaque to students, limiting their educational value.

To address this, they introduce AGPT (Advanced Geometry Proof Tutor), an interactive geometry tutoring system that combines automated theorem proving with guided student interaction. AGPT uses iGeoTutor as a back-end solver, but instead of simply showing the solution, it pauses the proof search and asks students to match templates and construct auxiliary lines themselves. The system also includes image-based geometry figure recognition, constraint synthesis, interactive feedback, and backtracking so students can work from uploaded problem figures on a mobile-device workflow.

The paper reports a pilot study with 78 ninth-grade students from a local high school, split into three groups: human tutor, iGeoTutor, and AGPT. Students completed pre- and post-tests on geometry proof problems. Results show that all groups improved from pre- to post-test, but when partial credit for correct auxiliary constructions was considered, AGPT produced significantly better gains than iGeoTutor and was not significantly different from the human tutor. The authors conclude that exposing the internal logic of a powerful solver through interactive tutoring can help students learn auxiliary constructions effectively.

finding.finding_summary: AGPT helped students learn geometry proof auxiliary constructions at a level comparable to a human tutor and significantly better than iGeoTutor alone. In the pilot study with 78 ninth-grade students (n=26 per group), the AGPT group showed significant pre- to post-test improvement, and the between-group ANOVA on improvement scores with partial credit indicated a significant difference favoring AGPT over iGeoTutor (F(2,75)=3.23, p=0.045), while AGPT did not differ significantly from the human tutor.
finding.measure: Geometry proof performance on pre-test and post-test; partial-credit score based on correctly identified auxiliary constructions and proof steps

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively targets students' problem-solving and reasoning around auxiliary constructions, which the authors frame as a generalizable skill for geometry proof. Student interaction logs suggest AGPT encouraged exploration and thoughtful problem-solving: 21 students solved at least one problem, 15 used AGPT feedback to obtain solutions, and 8 students found alternative correct solutions distinct from AGPT's reference path.
finding.measure: Student interaction behavior, number of attempts/redirections, and correctness of self-generated constructions/solutions

paper_profiles.title: The cognitive paradox of AI in education: between enhancement and erosion
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an opinion piece that argues AI in education has a dual cognitive effect: it can enhance learning through personalization and efficiency, but it may also erode deeper thinking if students over-rely on AI-generated support. The authors frame the discussion using Cognitive Load Theory, Bloom’s Taxonomy, and Self-Determination Theory to explain how AI can reduce extraneous load, support lower-order skills, and personalize instruction, while also potentially encouraging cognitive offloading, weaker retention, reduced autonomy, and diminished higher-order thinking.

Rather than reporting a new empirical study, the article synthesizes prior research and examples across memory retention, critical thinking/problem-solving, creativity, STEM learning, and language learning. It cites studies on undergraduate and vocational learners as well as secondary students, including findings that pretesting can improve retention before AI use, that AI-assisted practice may improve procedural performance but reduce conceptual understanding, and that AI can support fluency and idea generation while also increasing fixation and lowering creative confidence.

The paper concludes that AI should complement, not replace, human instruction. It recommends structured classroom practices such as reflection prompts, AI-free solving, teacher-guided discussion, source verification, and balanced integration of AI into blended learning so that the technology supports autonomy, engagement, and deep learning rather than dependency.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-based adaptive learning can improve procedural performance and personalization, but may weaken conceptual understanding if students rely on it too heavily. Cited examples include a Stanford report of a 15% score increase on standardized tests for AI tutoring and a University of Pennsylvania finding that Turkish high school students using ChatGPT answered 48% more practice problems correctly but scored 17% lower on a concept understanding test.
finding.measure: standardized test scores; practice problem accuracy; concept understanding test
finding.effect_size: 15% score increase; 48% more problems correct; 17% lower concept understanding

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI can support competence and engagement through personalized learning, but overuse may reduce intrinsic motivation, autonomy, and relatedness. The discussion is theoretical, though it cites prior work suggesting that AI-based technologies can either increase engagement or, when over-relied upon, lead to lower motivation and weaker learner persistence.
finding.measure: motivation; engagement; autonomy; relatedness

finding.finding_summary: This is a central focus of the paper: AI is presented as both an enhancer and an eroder of critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, and creativity. The paper cites evidence that AI may reduce active recall and independent reasoning, and it summarizes studies where AI-supported students showed gains in divergent-thinking fluency, flexibility, and elaboration but also exhibited cognitive fixation and lower creative confidence.
finding.measure: critical thinking; problem-solving; divergent thinking; creativity; retention

finding.finding_summary: The paper briefly notes that AI-based software such as speech recognition, chatbots, and virtual tutors improved English-language communicative competence and fluency in a cited doctoral study. The article also reports that more than 80% of respondents in that cited work believed AI would play a major future role in language teaching.
finding.measure: communicative competence; fluency

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (position paper; discusses K-12 through higher education and professional learning, not a single empirical sample)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT and GPT-3, for education. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, the authors synthesize early examples and likely use cases from the literature and from product capabilities to discuss how LLMs may support learning, teaching, assessment, and educational technology design.

The paper argues that LLMs could be used to personalize feedback, generate practice materials, support writing and problem solving, assist teachers with assessment and lesson planning, and enable more interactive learning experiences. It also highlights substantial risks, including bias, copyright and privacy concerns, overreliance by learners and teachers, difficulty distinguishing human from AI-generated work, and the need for stronger fact-checking and critical-thinking instruction.

The discussion is explicitly broad, spanning elementary, middle, high school, university, and professional settings, with no single population or intervention evaluated experimentally. The main conclusion is that LLMs have strong promise for education, but responsible use requires human oversight, ethical governance, and curricular designs that preserve and strengthen critical thinking rather than replacing it.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models can support critical thinking by generating prompts, explanations, and alternative perspectives, but also warns that effortless answer generation may weaken learners' problem-solving and critical-thinking habits through overreliance. No effect sizes or empirical outcome data are reported because this is a position paper rather than an evaluation study.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, fact-checking, and analytical reasoning (conceptual discussion; no direct measure reported)

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating or semi-automating tasks such as feedback generation, grading support, quiz creation, lesson planning, and content summarization. These are presented as plausible benefits from prior examples rather than quantified empirical results, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, and content-generation efficiency (conceptual discussion; no direct measure reported)

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLMs may improve student engagement, participation, curiosity, and interaction, especially through conversational agents and personalized guidance. However, these claims are framed as opportunities and not backed by a specific empirical evaluation in this paper.
finding.measure: Student engagement, curiosity, and participation (conceptual discussion; no direct measure reported)

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing healthcare: the role of artificial intelligence in clinical practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is being used across clinical practice, with emphasis on diagnosis, treatment selection, population health management, patient support, and implementation challenges. The paper argues that AI can improve accuracy, efficiency, and personalization in healthcare by analyzing large datasets, identifying patterns, and supporting clinician decision-making.

The review synthesizes indexed literature from PubMed/Medline, Scopus, and EMBASE (English-language articles, no date limits). It discusses applications such as medical image diagnosis, clinical laboratory automation, predictive analytics, personalized medicine, dose optimization, virtual health assistants, mental health support, patient education, and guideline development. The authors conclude that AI has strong promise for improving care and reducing workload, but responsible use requires attention to data quality, bias, privacy, transparency, cybersecurity, and the continued involvement of human experts.

This paper is not a K-12 education intervention study and does not directly examine AI-personalized feedback in schools. Its educationally relevant content is limited to broad references to AI in medical education and clinician training, not student learning outcomes or critical thinking measures in K-12 settings.

paper_profiles.title: What if the devil is my guardian angel: ChatGPT as a case study of using chatbots in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the concerns and perceived benefits of using ChatGPT in education, treating ChatGPT as a representative advanced chatbot. The authors ask what concerns arise when chatbots are used in educational settings and explore this through a three-stage qualitative instrumental case study.

The study triangulates three sources of evidence: a social network analysis and sentiment analysis of 2,330 tweets about ChatGPT in education, content analysis of interviews with 19 early adopters who posted public experiences online, and hands-on user experiences conducted by three educators across ten educational scenarios. Across these stages, the paper identifies both enthusiasm and caution: respondents viewed ChatGPT as potentially transformative for teaching and learning, but also raised concerns about accuracy, cheating, privacy, misleading outputs, manipulation, and weakened critical thinking.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT can support education, but it should not be adopted uncritically. The authors argue for safer and more responsible use through updated teaching philosophies, stronger guidance and policy, improved chatbot design, and explicit attention to fairness, privacy, and human-centered educational practices. The paper is exploratory and conceptual rather than efficacy-oriented, and it does not test learning gains in a K-12 intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that ChatGPT may support some aspects of critical thinking by giving users rapid access to information, but it may also weaken critical thinking when learners rely on it for easy answers or unchecked output. This concern appears repeatedly across the tweet analysis, interview themes, and user scenarios; no quantitative learning outcome was measured.
finding.measure: Perceptions and concerns about critical thinking, reasoning, and prompt formulation gathered from tweets, interviews, and scenario-based use
finding.study_size: n=2330 tweets; n=19 interviewees; n=3 educators

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that ChatGPT could reduce teacher workload by helping create quizzes, lesson materials, and outlines, and could provide immediate feedback to students. The paper presents these as perceived efficiency gains rather than measured task-time outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness for instructional design, resource creation, and immediate feedback

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that ChatGPT has the potential to reshape educational practice, but it also raises institutional concerns around cheating, privacy, fairness, misinformation, and policy responses such as school bans. The evidence is qualitative and descriptive, focusing on governance and adoption implications rather than measured institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Policy and governance concerns identified through tweets, interviews, and scenario analyses
finding.study_size: n=2330 tweets; n=19 interviewees; n=3 educators

paper_profiles.title: Examining Science Education in ChatGPT: An Exploratory Study of Generative Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory paper asks how ChatGPT responds to prompts about science education, how educators might use it in science pedagogy, and how it functions as a research tool. The author uses a self-study methodology, entering a set of prompts into ChatGPT and then critically comparing the AI-generated responses with established literature on science teaching. The prompts focus on broad science-pedagogy questions, including effective teaching, teacher-centered versus student-centered approaches, support for struggling students, and the design of a Year 7 unit, rubric, and quiz on renewable and non-renewable energy sources.

The study is not an intervention with students; rather, it is an exploratory analysis of ChatGPT’s output in an educator/researcher context. The paper argues that ChatGPT often produces plausible, pedagogically aligned responses and can be useful for generating drafts of units, rubrics, and quizzes, especially as a starting point for teachers. However, the author emphasizes that the outputs are generic, lack evidence grounding, may reproduce bias, and must be critically reviewed and adapted to context. The paper concludes that generative AI may be a helpful scaffold for educators and researchers, but it does not replace teacher expertise and should be used transparently and responsibly.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT generated science-education responses that often aligned with established research themes, including inquiry-based learning, real-world connections, assessment, and student-centered pedagogy. The paper does not report experimental effect sizes because it is a self-study of AI output rather than a student outcome study.
finding.measure: Alignment of ChatGPT-generated responses with science education literature and pedagogy themes

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly emphasizes critical thinking as a key outcome and teaching goal, arguing that educators should model responsible AI use and critically evaluate AI-generated resources. ChatGPT’s outputs were judged to support critical reflection only indirectly, through prompts that encouraged analysis of pedagogical options and evidence, but no learner data were collected.
finding.measure: Critical thinking reflected in prompts, rubric criteria, and author analysis of AI outputs

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was found to be useful as a drafting and productivity tool for educators and researchers, especially for generating science units, rubrics, quizzes, and for editing/rephrasing text. The paper concludes that the tool can help overcome blank-page problems and improve flow/wording, but outputs still require substantial refinement and contextual adaptation.
finding.measure: Utility for generating teaching resources and editing research text

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.population: Not explicitly studied; broad K-12 and higher education literature overview
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article examines the emerging role of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular emphasis on chatbots and ChatGPT. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the paper synthesizes existing literature to describe how AI tools are being used across teaching, learning, assessment, feedback, and administration, while also highlighting ethical and practical concerns such as bias, privacy, accountability, and academic integrity.

The article discusses AI-supported personalized learning, instant feedback, adaptive tutoring, and automated grading as major educational applications. It also notes that AI may support students’ motivation, engagement, self-regulation, critical thinking, and language learning, and may reduce teachers’ workload through automated scoring and feedback. The paper’s conclusions are conceptual and forward-looking: AI has promise for improving education, but successful use depends on responsible implementation, teacher support, and further research, especially given unresolved ethical and methodological issues. The paper does not report original empirical data from a single K-12 sample.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI tools can reduce teacher and administrator workload by automating grading, scoring, feedback generation, and routine student support. No original data are reported; the claim is supported by cited examples such as automated grading systems and chatbots that collect results and send them to teachers.
finding.measure: Teacher workload; automated grading/scoring and feedback provision

finding.finding_summary: The article synthesizes prior work suggesting that AI-supported learning can increase student motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduce anxiety. It cites studies such as one on an AI math tutor reducing anxiety among middle school students, but this paper itself does not provide a new effect estimate.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, confidence, anxiety

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that AI-based tools can foster critical thinking, creativity, self-reflection, and self-regulated learning, especially through personalized feedback and step-by-step guidance. These are literature-based assertions rather than findings from a new empirical study in this article.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, creativity, self-reflection, self-regulation

finding.finding_summary: The review highlights AI applications for writing support and reading-related outcomes, including personalized feedback on written assignments and improved reading comprehension for students with dyslexia in cited studies. The article does not conduct a literacy experiment itself, so no effect size is reported here.
finding.measure: Writing feedback; reading comprehension

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes that AI chatbots and conversational systems can support language learning and communication skills, including pronunciation correction and speaking performance. These are literature summaries, not original empirical results from the article.
finding.measure: Speaking performance; pronunciation; communication skills

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Peers for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving with Middle School Students: A Participatory Design Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how middle school students perceive AI designed as a peer collaborator, rather than as a tutor, during collaborative mathematical problem solving (CPS). The authors argue that much AI-in-education work has emphasized one-on-one tutoring, leaving open what students actually want from AI when it is embedded in group work and expected to share responsibility for thinking, turn-taking, and problem solving.

To investigate this, the researchers ran a five-day summer camp with 24 rising grades 6–8 students. Students completed human-only CPS tasks and CPS tasks with two AI peers in a technology probe, then took part in participatory design activities, reflections, interviews, poster creation, and preference surveys. The math tasks were aligned to middle-school standards and focused on ratio/proportional reasoning, expressions and equations, and early functions/geometry.

The main findings show that students wanted an AI peer that was scaffold-first, deferential, and clearly under student control. They preferred hints, checks, error detection, and concept refreshers over direct answers; they also wanted explicit control over when the AI spoke and how much help it gave. Quantitatively, AI peers reduced perceived temporal demand, but increased physical demand and lowered social cohesion/coordination. Qualitatively, students criticized overly scripted or teacher-like AI behavior, valued co-agency and emotional support, and rejected peers that felt repetitive, inattentive, or emotionally flat. The paper concludes with design recommendations for youth-centered AI peers in middle school mathematics CPS.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined middle school mathematics collaborative problem solving and students’ experience with AI peers on grade-aligned math tasks. Students preferred math support that offered hints, checks, and concept refreshers rather than direct answers, and the AI condition reduced temporal demand during problem solving (M=5.67, SD=4.38 vs. M=9.62, SD=4.13; p=0.002, d=1.15).
finding.measure: Collaborative mathematical problem-solving tasks; NASA-TLX temporal demand during math CPS
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired quantitative comparisons; n=24 enrolled

finding.finding_summary: Students’ affective experience was worse with AI peers on some dimensions even though the AI reduced time pressure. In GEQ results, Attraction to Group-Social was lower with AI peers (M=5.21, SD=1.81) than in human-only CPS (M=6.50, SD=2.05; p=0.029, d=0.94), and interview data showed students wanted encouragement, empathy, and recognition of frustration.
finding.measure: Group Environment Questionnaire (ATGS) and qualitative accounts of emotional support/frustration
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired quantitative comparisons; interview sample n=18

finding.finding_summary: This paper centrally studied collaboration, co-agency, and negotiation in mathematical groupwork. Students reported lower task coordination with AI peers on GEQ Group Integration-Task (M=4.76, SD=1.58) than in human-only CPS (M=5.54, SD=1.52; p=0.047, d=0.81), and qualitative findings showed students wanted AI that listened, negotiated methods, and supported shared reasoning rather than taking over.
finding.measure: GEQ Group Integration-Task; thematic analysis of reflections/interviews on collaboration and co-agency
finding.study_size: n=22 for paired quantitative comparisons; interview sample n=18

finding.finding_summary: AI peers improved perceived efficiency in one sense but also increased operational burden. Students reported significantly lower temporal demand with AI peers (d=1.15), yet higher physical demand on NASA-TLX (M=8.48, SD=4.65 vs. M=4.90, SD=2.41; p=0.014, d=1.14), reflecting the typing, navigation, and interface management required to work with the text-based probe.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand and physical demand
finding.std_deviation: SD=4.65 (AI condition, physical demand); SD=2.41 (human-only condition, physical demand)

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not report direct achievement or learning-gain outcomes in a non-math academic domain, but it does include brief exposure to AI basics and design activities. These were preparatory activities rather than outcome measures, so there is no substantive academic achievement finding here.
finding.measure: AI basics/card-sort and design activities

paper_profiles.title: Tareas matemáticas abiertas como respuesta didáctica a la inteligencia artificial generativa en contextos post-IA
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a didactic problem arising from the widespread availability of generative AI in school mathematics: many traditional tasks can now be solved automatically, reducing opportunities for students to interpret situations, make decisions, and validate mathematical results. The author argues that in post-AI contexts, simply restricting AI or using it uncritically is insufficient; instead, task design and classroom regulation must be rethought to preserve the formative value of mathematical activity.

The study analyzes one secondary-school classroom experience in which open mathematical tasks were implemented as a response to generative AI. The tasks were mediated by a didactic regulation device called COMPAS, which structures the work into phases such as understanding the situation, organizing assumptions and data, mathematical modeling, producing and exploring results, and validation/socialization. The study uses a qualitative, descriptive-interpretive approach, drawing on student written work, classroom interaction records, and teacher-researcher observations.

The context is secondary education, specifically mathematics lessons where generative AI is available as part of the environment. The analysis focuses on how open tasks, explicit didactic regulation, and human-AI complementarity shape students’ mathematical work. The main conclusion is that when tasks are intentionally designed to require interpretation, assumptions, and validation, students retain epistemic control over the activity, use AI only as a subordinate resource, and engage in meaningful modeling and critical validation rather than passive acceptance of AI-generated answers.

finding.finding_summary: The classroom experience suggests that open mathematical tasks, when regulated through COMPAS, support students' mathematical work in secondary school by requiring interpretation, assumption-building, modeling, and validation rather than direct algorithmic execution. The paper reports that students maintained epistemic control of the mathematical activity even in the presence of generative AI, but it does not provide numerical effect sizes or comparative test outcomes.
finding.measure: Student mathematical task performance and mathematical work observed through written productions, classroom interactions, and modeling/validation processes

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines students' mathematical agency, critical validation, decision-making, and argumentation, all of which align with durable skills such as critical thinking and metacognition. Findings indicate that students compared models, questioned assumptions, and evaluated the plausibility of AI-generated or student-generated solutions, but no quantitative measure or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Students’ agency, critical reasoning, justification of choices, and validation discussions during task resolution

paper_profiles.title: Learning Factors in AI-Augmented Education: A Comparative Study of Middle and High School Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether core learning-perception dimensions remain related in the same way when students learn with AI tools, and whether those relationships differ between middle school and high school students. The authors focus on four dimensions drawn from learning research: experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation.

The study took place in extracurricular computer science/programming courses, where students interacted with AI tools during instructional activities. Middle school students used Teachable Machine in an introductory AI context, while high school students used LLM-based tools such as Gemini and Claude for Python-related activities and vibe coding. The sample included 53 students total (25 middle school, 28 high school), and data came from a 17-item questionnaire with Likert-scale items plus open-ended responses.

Using correlation analysis, Mann-Whitney U tests, and text mining, the authors found that middle school students tended to show tightly connected, holistic perceptions across the four dimensions, whereas high school students showed weaker and more differentiated relationships among dimensions. Ease of use differed significantly by group (U=192.00, p=0.0013), with high school students reporting greater ease. Open-ended responses also suggested that younger students emphasized general learning support, while older students described more analytical and coding-related benefits. The paper concludes that AI-supported learning should be designed with developmental stage in mind, especially in computer science education.

finding.finding_summary: Students generally reported positive experiences with AI tools, but the pattern differed by age group. Middle school students showed stronger interconnections among experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation, while high school students showed more differentiated judgments; the only statistically significant group difference was ease of use (U=192.00, p=0.0013), favoring high school students.
finding.measure: Questionnaire ratings of experience, clarity, comfort, motivation, and ease of use; Mann-Whitney U test and Spearman correlations
finding.study_size: n=53 (middle school n=25; high school n=28)

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines how students perceive AI-supported learning in relation to understanding, explanation, thinking, and code-related reasoning. Text mining of Q7 responses showed that middle school students emphasized learn/understand/helped, while high school students more often linked AI to explanation, think, code, and reasoning tasks, indicating differentiated cognitive support rather than a single uniform effect.
finding.measure: Open-ended questionnaire responses to Q7 ('In what ways do you think the AI tool influenced your learning?') plus co-occurrence network and word frequency analysis
finding.study_size: n=53 (middle school n=25; high school n=28)

paper_profiles.title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teachers should remain “in the loop” when using generative AI to personalize K-12 learning tasks. The authors focus on context personalization in mathematics, asking how middle school teachers prompt ChatGPT to adapt existing curriculum problems to students’ interests, what students think of the resulting problems, and whether the process is efficient for teachers.

Seven middle school math teachers in six U.S. schools worked with GPT-4o/ChatGPT to personalize 143 Illustrative Mathematics problems for 521 seventh-grade students. Teachers first generated personalized versions for Unit 4 (proportional relationships and percentages) and then repeated the process for Unit 6 (expressions, equations, and inequalities), while researchers collected chat logs, video/audio, student ratings, and open-ended feedback. The study used mixed-effects regression models plus inductive coding of prompts and student responses.

The paper finds that teachers mainly used ChatGPT to adjust grain size and realism: they asked for broad or specific popular-culture references, changes to names, locations, age appropriateness, and realistic quantities. Students generally preferred finer-grained personalization tied to specific interests, but they cared less about deeper realism than about whether the topic matched their tastes. On average, personalizing one problem took about 4 minutes and 3.2 prompts, and efficiency did not clearly improve over time; in fact, teachers used more prompts and more time in Unit 6 than Unit 4. Student ratings of interestingness and closeness were modest overall, and were higher when teachers used 3–5 prompts per problem.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and students worked on personalized middle school mathematics problems (n=143 problems assigned to 521 7th-grade students). Student ratings of the problems’ interestingness and closeness to students’ interests were modest overall, but were significantly higher when teachers used 3–5 prompts to create a problem; this optimal prompting range was associated with about a 0.24-point increase on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073).
finding.measure: Student 1–5 ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to interests; teacher-created personalized mathematics problems

finding.finding_summary: The personalized math tasks were intended to increase student interest and engagement, and students’ survey responses showed that some found problems interesting when the context matched their preferences. However, overall ratings were modest (interestingness M=2.46, closeness M=2.53 on 5-point scales), indicating only limited engagement benefits at the group level.
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests; open-ended student feedback
finding.study_size: n=521 students; ratings collected for 53 problems; open-ended feedback for 33 problems

finding.finding_summary: The process of teacher-in-the-loop personalization was not time efficient. Teachers used 558 prompts to create 143 problems, averaging 3.2 prompts per problem (SD=2.6), and each problem took about 246 seconds on average (SD=165.7). Efficiency did not improve over time; in fact, teachers spent more time and used more prompts in Unit 6 than in Unit 4 (time: 204 s vs. 286 s; prompts: 3.2 vs. 4.6).
finding.measure: Prompt counts and time spent creating personalized problems
finding.effect_size: B=1.26 (prompts from Unit 4 to 6); B=70.4 seconds (time from Unit 4 to 6)

finding.finding_summary: The study frames the personalization process as involving design judgment, including how deeply contextualized the tasks were and how much control teachers versus the LLM had over the content. Students and teachers both showed preferences for more fine-grained personalization, but the paper did not directly measure critical thinking or metacognition as student outcomes. The closest evidence is indirect: teachers refined and iterated prompts to improve task quality, and student feedback suggested a preference for specific rather than broad references.
finding.measure: Teacher prompting patterns and qualitative feedback about task depth, grain size, and ownership
finding.study_size: n=7 teachers; n=143 problems; student open-ended feedback on 33 problems

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in K-12 Education: The CyberScholar Initiative
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether CyberScholar, a generative AI writing assistant, can support K-12 students’ writing through formative feedback aligned with teacher rubrics, instructional materials, and classroom expectations. The study is motivated by concerns about declining writing performance and a gap in K-12 research on GenAI tools that provide pedagogically grounded, personalized feedback rather than generic comments.

CyberScholar was piloted in four U.S. public schools across diverse settings, including one middle school and three high schools. The tool was used in English Language Arts, Social Studies, and Modern World History classes with 121 students and 4 teachers, though post-survey and interview participation was smaller. Data came from observations, surveys, and interviews, and were analyzed qualitatively using initial and pattern coding. The paper reports that students generally valued the AI’s detailed feedback, rubric alignment, interactivity, and ability to help them revise writing; some also saw improvements in grammar, transitions, clarity, and rubric scores after revision.

The main conclusion is that CyberScholar shows promise as a formative feedback tool for writing in diverse K-12 subject areas, especially when paired with teacher-defined rubrics and materials. The authors argue that such tools may support writing development, self-regulation, metacognition, and critical thinking, but they also emphasize that AI feedback should complement, not replace, teacher feedback. Because the study is exploratory and qualitative, the findings are suggestive rather than causal, and the authors call for further research with larger and more diverse samples.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers reported that CyberScholar supported writing development through detailed, specific, and rubric-aligned formative feedback. Among 121 participating students, 36 said they would like to use the tool again, and some reported improved rubric scores after revision (for example, one student’s “Compare” and “Contrast” rubric score increased from 0 to 2 after feedback and resubmission).
finding.measure: Writing quality, revision quality, rubric-based writing scores, and student perceptions of writing improvement
finding.study_size: n=121 students; post-survey n=54; interviews n=8 students

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly argues that CyberScholar may deepen students’ critical thinking, self-regulation, and metacognition by prompting revision, reflection, and follow-up questioning. Qualitative evidence from surveys and interviews indicates that students used the AI feedback to rethink structure, clarify arguments, and refine revisions, which the authors interpret as evidence of metacognitive and critical-thinking support.
finding.measure: Student reflections, interview themes, and observed revision processes related to critical thinking, metacognition, and self-regulation
finding.study_size: n=121 students; post-survey n=54; interviews n=8 students

finding.finding_summary: Students described the tool as engaging, interactive, and motivating, with some expressing a desire to use it again. The feedback process was perceived as more dynamic and supportive than static evaluation, and some students said the star ratings motivated them to improve their work in subsequent drafts.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of engagement, motivation, and usefulness of the AI feedback process
finding.study_size: n=121 students; post-survey n=54; interviews n=8 students

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests the tool may save time and reduce workload by quickly identifying areas for improvement and delivering feedback that students described as easier and quicker to use than peer review or self-analysis. Teachers also positioned the system as a way to support feedback processes while managing rather than individually producing all comments.
finding.measure: Perceived time-saving and ease of feedback generation/use

paper_profiles.title: The Path to Conversational AI Tutors: Integrating Tutoring Best Practices and Targeted Technologies to Produce Scalable AI Agents
paper_profiles.population: Not directly studied; discusses K-12 and higher education tutoring systems broadly
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual review and design framework for conversational AI tutors. It asks how generative AI can be combined with lessons from human tutoring and legacy intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) to create scalable tutoring agents that are pedagogically effective, responsive, and aligned with evidence-based practices.

The authors synthesize research on effective human tutoring, older ITS architectures, and emerging generative AI tutoring applications. They propose a keep/change/center/study framework: keep validated ITS components such as knowledge tracing, affect detection, and knowledge graphs; change tutoring delivery by using generative AI for dynamic content generation and dialogic scaffolding; center meaning-making, student agency, and diagnosis of reasoning; and study efficacy, student experience, and human-AI collaboration more deeply.

The paper does not report a new experiment or dataset. Instead, it reviews prior studies and examples such as Khanmigo, Rori, OpenTutor, and human-in-the-loop tutoring systems to argue that conversational AI tutors should be built by integrating structured learner models with generative dialogue. Its main conclusion is that generative AI alone is insufficient; effective conversational tutoring will require hybrid systems grounded in established tutoring science and rigorous future evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is a synthesis rather than a direct empirical study, but it argues that conversational AI tutors can support learning across multiple subjects, including math, science, humanities, and writing, when combined with evidence-based tutoring practices. It cites prior work showing benefits of tutoring and AI tutoring tools, but reports no new effect sizes or primary outcome data of its own.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally argues that tutoring conversations can support motivation, engagement, competence, autonomy, relatedness, and student self-concept, and that conversational AI tutors should center these processes. This claim is based on prior literature reviewed in the paper rather than new empirical data, so no study-specific effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, self-concept, relatedness, autonomy, and affect in tutoring contexts

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is that conversational tutoring can foster metacognition, self-explanation, self-evaluation, and reasoning diagnosis through dialogue. The authors describe these as central opportunities unique to conversational AI tutoring, but they do not present a new intervention or quantitative effect estimate.
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-explanation, reasoning, and diagnosis of misconceptions

paper_profiles.title: Developing and Evaluating a Large Language Model-Based Automated Feedback System Grounded in Evidence-Centered Design for Supporting Physics Problem Solving
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether an LLM-based automated feedback system can provide useful and accurate formative feedback for students solving physics problems. The authors argue that physics problem solving is more complex than conceptual question answering because it requires multiple knowledge types and skills, including conceptual, procedural, factual, mathematical, and metacognitive reasoning.

To support feedback generation, they design a system grounded in Evidence-Centered Design (ECD). The system prompts GPT-4o with the problem statement, the student’s solution, a problem-specific evidentiary scheme, and feedback constraints, aiming to produce short, individualized, analytic feedback rather than full solutions. The study evaluates the system during the first stage of the German Physics Olympiad, where registered secondary school students voluntarily used the online tool while working on olympiad-style physics problems.

Students rated the feedback’s usefulness and factual correctness on 5-point Likert scales, and the generated feedback was also independently checked by human raters. Students generally perceived the feedback as useful (M=3.6, SD=1.7) and highly accurate (M=4.4, SD=1.0). However, human review found that 13 of 64 feedback instances (about 20%) contained errors, ranging from minor calculation mistakes to incorrect concepts or misclassification of valid alternative approaches. Students rarely detected these errors, and perceived accuracy did not significantly differ between correctly and incorrectly generated feedback. The paper concludes that ECD can help ground LLM feedback for complex physics problem solving, but reliability and adaptivity remain major concerns, especially for alternative solution paths.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates LLM-generated feedback for physics problem solving, a scientific reasoning task requiring conceptual, procedural, factual, mathematical, and metacognitive knowledge. Students rated the feedback as useful for problem solving (M=3.6/5, SD=1.7; N=64) and the system’s feedback was judged physically correct in 51/64 cases (about 80%), but 13/64 cases (about 20%) contained 14 errors, including incorrect concepts, assumptions, strategies, and calculations.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness and factual correctness ratings; human-coded correctness of LLM-generated physics feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally targets problem solving and metacognitive aspects of scientific reasoning by providing analytic feedback on students’ solution approaches and evaluating whether the feedback supported students in working through the problem. Students generally viewed the feedback as helpful, but many criticized it as not sufficiently adaptive to their own solution paths, especially when they used valid alternative approaches.
finding.measure: Student ratings of feedback usefulness and written elaborations about adaptivity/solution approach fit

finding.finding_summary: The feedback was intended to support students during a problem-solving task, and students often described it as helpful and motivating for understanding and revising their work. In open-ended responses, 10 students said the feedback was very helpful, and 4 noted its adaptivity; however, some students also found it superficial or not adaptive enough.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness ratings and open-text elaborations

paper_profiles.title: Thinking Twice: Clinical-Inspired Thyroid Ultrasound Lesion Detection Based on Feature Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of accurate thyroid lesion detection in ultrasound images, where noise, blurred boundaries, and low resolution make one-stage detectors vulnerable to missed or incorrect detections. The authors argue that standard feature extraction and fusion pipelines can be improved by mimicking a clinician’s diagnostic workflow: first forming a coarse impression, then revisiting the image with more focused attention.

To implement this idea, they propose a feature feedback mechanism that generates high-semantic prior features from an initial pass and feeds them back into a second feature extraction stage. They combine this with a feature-feedback pyramid, a feedback feature selection module using ASPP plus channel/spatial attention, an improved ConvNeXt backbone, and an adaptive detection head designed to better handle lesions of different sizes and shapes. The method is evaluated on a thyroid ultrasound dataset of 1,023 annotated images from a hospital and additionally on the BUSI breast ultrasound dataset, using AP, AP50, AP75, and related detection metrics.

The main results show improved lesion detection accuracy over FCOS, Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, YOLO variants, DETR, DAB-DETR, and DINO. On the thyroid dataset, the best reported model (ConvNeXt-tiny backbone) reaches AP=70.3, AP50=99.0, and AP75=88.4, with ablation results indicating that ConvNeXt, the adaptive head, and especially the feature-feedback pyramid each contribute to performance gains. The paper concludes that clinically inspired feedback can help detection models suppress noise and focus on lesion regions while meeting real-time requirements, though the work remains limited by small/low-contrast lesions and by sample-imbalance challenges on BUSI.

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on computer vision lesion detection rather than educational outcomes. Its central empirical result is improved thyroid ultrasound lesion detection, with the best model achieving AP=70.3, AP50=99.0, and AP75=88.4 on a dataset of 1,023 annotated images (60/20/20 train/validation/test split). Compared with FCOS, Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, YOLOv3, VarifocalNet, DETR, DAB-DETR, and DINO, the proposed method yields the highest detection accuracy, indicating that the feature-feedback approach improves lesion localization and classification.
finding.measure: Object detection performance on thyroid ultrasound images (AP, AP50, AP75)

paper_profiles.title: A Survey on Feedback Types in Automated Programming Assessment Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how undergraduate students in introductory programming courses perceive and perform under different automated feedback conditions in an automated programming assessment system (APAS). The authors focus on a gap in the literature: although APASs commonly provide compiler output or unit-test feedback, the comparative effects of AI-generated feedback on both student perceptions and task performance had not been directly studied at scale.

The study compares three feedback types within the Artemis APAS: compiler feedback only, traditional unit-test feedback, and AI-generated feedback using OpenAI’s GPT-3.5-Turbo model. Students completed three programming exercises on arrays/matrices in introductory Java courses at two Austrian universities, with each exercise paired with one feedback condition. The researchers collected TAM-based survey responses after each task, system logs, unit-test outcomes, and an open-ended post-study questionnaire, then analyzed the data using nonparametric statistics and thematic analysis.

The sample included 212 university students, mostly first- and second-semester bachelor’s students in computer science and business informatics. Results showed that students rated unit-test feedback as most useful, AI feedback as second, and compiler feedback as least useful. However, AI-generated feedback was associated with significantly better performance than the baseline compiler-only condition, suggesting that AI hints can improve problem solving even when students perceive traditional unit-test feedback as more helpful. The authors conclude that combining unit tests with AI-driven guidance may provide a stronger automated feedback design for programming education.

finding.finding_summary: This study directly examines introductory programming task performance in undergraduate computer science/business informatics courses. Across three exercises, students receiving AI-generated feedback performed significantly better than those receiving compiler-only feedback, while unit-test feedback was rated most useful by students. The paper reports statistically significant differences in performance across feedback conditions (Kruskal-Wallis χ2 = 535.29, p < .001), but does not provide a single effect size for the performance outcome.
finding.measure: Programming task correctness / final solution quality on three introductory Java exercises

finding.finding_summary: The paper also substantively studies students’ problem-solving and debugging behavior while solving programming tasks, which aligns with durable skills such as problem solving and metacognitive regulation. The authors report that AI-generated feedback supported better task performance and that submission logs were used to analyze iteration behavior and problem-solving strategies, but no separate effect size is reported for these process measures.
finding.measure: Submission attempts, time between attempts, and problem-solving behavior during debugging

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses efficiency in completing programming tasks, reporting that students rated the AI and unit-test conditions on perceived usefulness for accomplishing tasks and speed. The post-exercise TAM items included completion speed and ease of accomplishing tasks, and the authors note that AI feedback improved performance, but they do not report a distinct efficiency effect size or a direct time-to-completion comparison as a primary outcome.
finding.measure: Perceived speed / task completion efficiency on TAM survey items and submission logs

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively measures student perceptions of usefulness, ease of use, and feedback quality, which are related to engagement and acceptance of the feedback system. Students preferred unit-test feedback most often (56%), followed by AI feedback (26%), while compiler feedback was least preferred (18%); AI feedback was initially helpful but was sometimes viewed negatively when it produced confusing or hallucinated suggestions. No direct behavioral engagement effect size is reported.
finding.measure: TAM survey ratings and post-study preference questionnaire

paper_profiles.title: Students' Perceived Roles, Opportunities, and Challenges of a Generative AI-powered Teachable Agent: A Case of Middle School Math Class
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how middle school students perceive a generative-AI-powered teachable agent (TA) used in a sixth-grade mathematics classroom. The authors investigate what roles students assign to the TA, what learning opportunities they perceive, and what barriers they experience when interacting with the system.

The intervention was a text-based GenAI-powered TA built with GPT-4-Turbo and a knowledge graph of middle- and high-school math Q&A. The system was used in an authentic 6th-grade rate-and-ratio unit with 108 students across six classes in a public laboratory middle school in the southeastern United States. Students interacted with the TA over two class periods, solving eight math problems through learning-by-teaching conversations; data came from classroom observations, open-ended surveys, and focus-group interviews, and was analyzed thematically.

The main conclusions are that students viewed the TA as a learning companion, facilitator, and collaborative problem-solver, and they reported benefits including a more student-centered learning climate, greater autonomy, stronger cognitive/social/emotional capacities, improved math understanding and application, more enjoyment of math, higher self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, interdisciplinary connections, and more positive attitudes toward AI. Students also identified several barriers, including shallow or poorly sequenced questioning, limited accommodation for different learning styles, weak socio-emotional interaction, technical issues, lack of multimodal input, poor interoperability, and the need for teacher facilitation. Overall, the paper argues that GenAI can extend learning-by-teaching in K-12 math, but design and classroom supports are crucial for effective use.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that interacting with the GenAI-powered teachable agent improved their understanding of the rate-and-ratio math content and helped them apply knowledge in new contexts. In thematic results from 108 sixth-grade students, they described clearer concepts, better recognition of misconceptions, and stronger transfer when explaining math using multiple examples.
finding.measure: Student perceptions from open-ended surveys, focus-group interviews, and classroom observations regarding understanding of rate and ratio and application of mathematical knowledge

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived the TA experience as increasing enjoyment of math, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, and positive attitudes toward learning with AI. The study reports that students were highly engaged during the two-class intervention and described the activity as fun, confidence-building, and energizing, though no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived joy of math, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, engagement, and attitude toward AI from interviews, surveys, and observations

finding.finding_summary: Students reported gains in cognitive, social, and metacognitive capacities, including logical reasoning, reflective analysis, communication, and perspective-taking. The TA’s follow-up prompts such as asking students to elaborate were described as pushing them to explain their thinking, organize ideas, and consider the agent’s perspective; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of reasoning, explanation, perspective-taking, and reflective thinking in qualitative data

paper_profiles.title: Simulations of AGN feedback in galaxy clusters and groups
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is not an education study; it examines how active galactic nuclei (AGN) feedback affects the gas content and X-ray properties of galaxy clusters and groups in cosmological hydrodynamical simulations. The authors ask whether including black hole growth and feedback can resolve long-standing discrepancies between simulated and observed cluster properties, especially excessive gas cooling and overly bright X-ray emission in group-scale halos.

To address this, the study compares high-resolution simulations run with identical initial conditions, once with standard cooling, star formation, and supernova feedback, and once with an additional AGN feedback model. The AGN model includes black hole seeding, accretion, and two feedback modes (quasar and radio) that inject thermal and mechanical energy into the intracluster medium.

The simulations are performed on galaxy clusters and groups, not humans or schools. The main result is that AGN feedback lowers halo gas fractions in poor clusters and groups and suppresses their X-ray luminosities, bringing the simulated gas-fraction and X-ray luminosity–temperature relations into much better agreement with observations. Because the paper is astrophysical rather than educational, it does not address K-12 outcomes such as literacy, critical thinking, or engagement.

paper_profiles.title: Distinguishing Fact from Fiction: Student Traits, Attitudes, and AI Hallucination Detection in Business School Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether undergraduate business school students can detect factual errors in AI-generated text and what student characteristics predict success. The central problem is the risk that generative AI can produce plausible but incorrect answers that students may accept uncritically, which has implications for AI literacy, critical thinking, and assessment design.
