The study uses a summative Year 2 econometrics coursework at a UK business school (n=211) in which students evaluated a ChatGPT 3.5 response to a question about selection bias. Students also completed a related final exam question later in the term, allowing the authors to examine whether detecting hallucinations in the coursework transferred to later performance. Predictors include prior academic performance, interpretive vs. procedural skill, writing/readability, AI sentiment/scepticism, and gender.

The main finding is that only about 20% of students correctly identified the AI hallucination. Better academic performance, stronger interpretive skills, stronger writing skills, and greater scepticism toward AI were associated with higher detection and better articulation of critiques, while procedural knowledge was less helpful. Female students were more likely to detect the error. However, detecting the hallucination did not clearly improve later exam engagement or exam score on the related question, suggesting that the structured feedback given after the coursework may have reduced initial gaps in later performance.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly assesses critical thinking/epistemic vigilance in students’ ability to detect and explain AI hallucinations. Among 211 Year 2 economics and management students, only 20% correctly identified the hallucination, but detection was positively associated with stronger academic performance, interpretive skills, writing quality, and AI scepticism; procedural skills were less useful.
finding.measure: AI hallucination detection (binary Detect) and mark for evaluating the AI response (AI Mark)

finding.finding_summary: The paper uses an econometrics coursework question and finds that statistical proficiency predicts AI hallucination detection. Students with higher marks on statistics-related measures (e.g., Statistics Background and Statistics Year 1 Mark) were more likely to detect and articulate the AI error, indicating that numeracy/domain knowledge supported critical evaluation of the response.
finding.measure: Statistics Background, Statistics Year 1 Mark, and detection of the AI error in an econometrics task

finding.finding_summary: Writing/English proficiency was positively associated with identifying and articulating the AI error. The paper uses readability metrics and a 100-word reflective paragraph to proxy language skill; higher writing-quality scores were linked to better hallucination detection and stronger evaluation marks.
finding.measure: Readability metrics (Flesch-Kincaid, New Dale-Chall) and marker-assigned writing quality for the reflective paragraph

paper_profiles.title: App Planner: Utilizing Generative AI in K-12 Mobile App Development Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents App Planner, a generative-AI-supported conversational tool designed to scaffold K-12 students through the ideation, design, and ethical reflection phases of mobile app development. The authors motivate the tool as a response to a gap in K-12 computing education: students often lack support for brainstorming app ideas, considering user needs, and reflecting on positive and negative societal impacts before implementation.

The tool uses a chat-based interface powered by GPT to provide just-in-time feedback, examples, and suggestions while students fill out structured prompts for defining a problem, designing app features, and evaluating consequences. The authors piloted the tool with five high-school seniors in a university class project, asking them to complete two app-design tasks (day planning and career exploration) with and without App Planner in alternating order.

Findings are based on usability observation and semi-structured interviews rather than quantitative performance measures. Students reported that App Planner made it easier and faster to brainstorm, gave practical design guidance, broadened their ideas, and pushed them to think more about users and the social/ethical consequences of their apps. The study concludes that generative AI can serve as a creative and reflective scaffold for app-development education, especially for supporting ideation and critical thinking in high school contexts.

finding.finding_summary: In a pilot with five high-school students (n=5), App Planner was reported to support critical thinking, metacognitive reflection, and design ideation during mobile app development. Students said the tool helped them think about target users, expand their ideas, and consider both positive and negative impacts of their apps; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Usability observations and semi-structured interview reports about critical thinking, user-centered design, and ethical reflection during app ideation

finding.finding_summary: Participants consistently reported that App Planner made the app-design process easier and faster, helping them brainstorm and proceed when stuck. The study does not report quantitative timing or productivity metrics, but qualitative feedback indicated improved efficiency in moving through app-planning tasks (n=5).
finding.measure: Participant-reported ease, speed, and ability to proceed through app design tasks

paper_profiles.title: Explaining AI Without Code: A User Study on Explainable AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a human-computer interaction problem in explainable AI: no-code machine learning platforms often let users build and deploy models without programming, but they typically do not provide explanations that help users understand, validate, or trust model predictions. The authors argue that this creates an explainability gap, especially for novice users who need accessible explanations and expert users who want deeper diagnostic detail.

To address this, the paper presents DashAI, an open-source no-code ML platform extended with an explainability module that integrates three XAI methods: Partial Dependence Plots (PDP), Permutation Feature Importance (PFI), and KernelSHAP. The module provides both global and local explanations directly within the workflow for tabular classification tasks, so users can inspect models immediately after training without external tools.

The study used a between-subjects user study with 20 participants split evenly between ML novices and ML experts. Participants completed explanation-related tasks and then answered questionnaires measuring explanation satisfaction, usability, and trust. Results showed high task success across all explanation tasks (80% or higher), acceptable reliability for the Explanation Satisfaction Scale (ESS, α = 0.74), and weaker reliability for the Trust in Automation scale (TiA, α = 0.60). Novices generally rated the explanations as more useful, accurate, and trustworthy than experts, while experts wanted more detail and completeness.

Overall, the paper concludes that integrated, human-centered XAI can make no-code ML tools more usable and trustworthy, but that explanation design must balance simplicity for novices with diagnostic depth for experts. The study is about adult ML users in a technical no-code software context rather than K-12 education, and it does not evaluate student learning outcomes or classroom instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The explainability module was usable and supported efficient completion of explanation tasks in the no-code ML workflow. All five explainability tasks achieved at least 80% success (T7=100%, T8=100%, T9=90%, T10=80%, T11=90%) in a study with n=20 participants, indicating that users could complete the explanation-related workflow with relatively little friction.
finding.measure: Task success rate on five explainability tasks in DashAI

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examines users' ability to interpret model explanations, which overlaps with critical-thinking and metacognitive judgment about when to trust AI outputs. Participants reported that explanations improved perceived predictability and confidence in reliance decisions on the Trust in Automation scale (TiA, α = 0.60), and novices in particular rated the explanations more positively than experts.
finding.measure: Explanation Satisfaction Scale (ESS) and Trust in Automation (TiA) questionnaire responses related to comprehension, predictability, and confidence

paper_profiles.title: Evidence-Decision-Feedback: Theory-Driven Adaptive Scaffolding for LLM Agents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a central problem in AI-enabled education: how large language model (LLM) agents can provide adaptive, interpretable scaffolding that supports learning without creating overreliance. The authors argue that many current LLM agents operate as one-size-fits-all systems and therefore struggle to personalize support or make their reasoning understandable to educators and students.

To address this, they propose Evidence-Decision-Feedback (EDF), a theory-driven framework for organizing agent behavior into evidence collection, pedagogical decision-making, and adaptive feedback. They instantiate EDF in Copa, a collaborative peer agent embedded in the C2STEM environment, where students solve open-ended STEM+ problems by building computational models. Copa uses multiple sub-agents and chain-of-thought-style reasoning to infer learner state from log data and dialogue, then adjusts scaffolding based on demonstrated understanding and task mastery.

The study was conducted in an authentic high school science classroom with 33 dyads of sophomore students over six weeks, focused on physics/computing kinematics tasks. The analyses examine whether Copa’s prompts become less probing and more directive as mastery increases, whether students’ verbalized understanding aligns with task mastery, whether reliance on the agent declines over time, and whether the system’s internal reasoning is interpretable. Overall, the paper concludes that the agent’s scaffolding adapted in pedagogically sensible ways, students’ understanding and independence increased with mastery, and Copa’s decisions were traceable to student evidence, though some students still preferred direct answers and were frustrated by the scaffolded interaction style.

finding.finding_summary: Copa’s scaffolding was associated with stronger critical-thinking-aligned support as students’ task mastery increased. The agent significantly reduced PROBE_UNDERSTANDING moves (Spearman’s ρ = -0.34, p = 0.034) and increased SUGGEST_ACTION (ρ = 0.33, p = 0.039) and PUSH_LIMIT (ρ = 0.42, p = 0.007), indicating a shift from eliciting understanding to extending reasoning.
finding.measure: Dialogue policy frequencies across task-mastery quintiles

finding.finding_summary: Students’ demonstrated understanding of kinematics/computational modeling improved as mastery increased. The success rate for correctly explaining code after probing rose significantly with mastery (Spearman’s ρ = 0.40, p = 0.014), and the DEMONSTRATES_UNDERSTANDING state also increased (ρ = 0.34, p = 0.030), suggesting alignment between performance and conceptual reasoning.
finding.measure: Response success rate after probing; dialogue-state occurrence (DEMONSTRATES_UNDERSTANDING)

finding.finding_summary: Student reliance on Copa declined as mastery increased, consistent with growing autonomy and self-regulation. Requests for support dropped significantly across mastery deciles (Spearman’s ρ = -0.26, p < 0.001), with about 59% of support occurring when mastery was low (<40%), indicating decreasing dependence on the agent over time.
finding.measure: Percentage of agent support/interactions across mastery deciles

paper_profiles.title: Rapid Mental Computation System as a Tool for Algorithmic Thinking of Elementary School Students Development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a rapid mental computation system—specifically the Trachtenberg system—can support the development of algorithmic thinking in elementary school students. The authors frame algorithmic thinking as an important early foundation for later informatics/computer science learning and argue that it can be cultivated through mathematics instruction rather than programming alone.

The paper is primarily a conceptual/expository discussion of the Trachtenberg rapid calculation rules, with worked examples for multiplication by 11, 12, 6, 7, 5, 9, 8, 4, and 3. The intervention or approach is not evaluated through a formal classroom study; instead, the authors describe how these step-by-step arithmetic algorithms may help students practice sequencing, rule-following, and problem decomposition in elementary mathematics lessons.

The context is elementary education, with an emphasis on using mathematics lessons to prepare students for secondary-school computer science. The paper concludes that the Trachtenberg system may improve or develop algorithmic thinking and may reduce computation cost in computer algebra implementations, but it does not report direct student outcome data or a controlled empirical evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the Trachtenberg rapid mental computation system can develop or improve elementary students' algorithmic thinking by training them to follow step-by-step rules for arithmetic operations. However, this is a theoretical claim rather than a measured classroom effect; no sample size, effect size, or statistical test is reported.
finding.measure: Algorithmic thinking

finding.finding_summary: The authors present the Trachtenberg system as a way to perform arithmetic computations quickly and accurately, particularly multiplication by several digits. The paper provides worked examples and claims the method can decrease computation cost, but it does not report student test scores or experimental outcome data.
finding.measure: Rapid mental arithmetic / multiplication performance

paper_profiles.title: The cognitive paradox of AI in education: between enhancement and erosion
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an opinion article that examines the tension between the promised benefits of AI in education and the risk that AI can weaken cognition through over-reliance and cognitive offloading. Using Cognitive Load Theory, Bloom’s Taxonomy, and Self-Determination Theory as interpretive lenses, the authors argue that AI can improve personalization, efficiency, and accessibility, but may also reduce active recall, problem-solving, autonomy, and higher-order thinking if students become dependent on machine-generated answers.

The article does not report a new empirical study; instead, it synthesizes prior literature and examples on AI in learning, including adaptive tutoring, conversational AI, language learning, critical thinking, memory retention, and creativity. It recommends implementation practices such as needs analysis, careful tool selection, balanced classroom integration, teacher-led discussion, reflection prompts, AI-free problem-solving, and ongoing monitoring so that AI complements rather than replaces human instruction.

The paper’s main conclusion is that AI in education has a paradoxical character: it can act as both a cognitive enhancer and a cognitive inhibitor. The authors emphasize that responsible AI use should preserve effortful thinking, support metacognition, and avoid dependency, while also promoting fairness, transparency, and human guidance in classroom use.

finding.finding_summary: This is an opinion/synthesis paper, not a primary empirical study. It argues that AI can support higher-order thinking and metacognition when used as a complement to instruction, but that over-reliance may erode critical thinking, independent reasoning, and problem-solving. No original effect size or sample-based estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, higher-order thinking

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can increase competence and personalization, but excessive dependence may reduce autonomy, motivation, and engagement. These claims are presented as conceptual conclusions supported by cited studies rather than results from a new dataset.
finding.measure: Autonomy, motivation, engagement, relatedness

finding.finding_summary: The article claims AI can reduce extraneous cognitive load and improve efficiency by automating redundant work and personalizing learning pathways. However, it does not present original empirical data on productivity or teacher workload, so the evidence is conceptual rather than measured.
finding.measure: Learning efficiency, reduction of redundant work, individualized instruction

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes implementation guidance for educators and policymakers, including fairness, transparency, explainability, and balanced classroom integration. These are normative recommendations rather than measured institutional outcomes, and no empirical policy effect is reported.
finding.measure: Implementation guidance, equity, transparency, explainability

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education learners and teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities, risks, and design requirements of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention experimentally, the authors synthesize early evidence and provide a conceptual framework for how LLMs might support learning, teaching, assessment, and educational innovation while also introducing risks such as bias, plagiarism, overreliance, privacy concerns, and inequitable access.

The paper discusses potential uses across learner and teacher contexts, including personalized feedback, quiz generation, tutoring, language learning support, assessment assistance, and lesson planning. It also highlights K-12-relevant applications such as generating prompts to stimulate children’s curiosity, supporting reading/writing and critical thinking, and helping teachers create differentiated materials. The paper argues that successful integration requires teacher oversight, curricular alignment, fact-checking, age-appropriate interfaces, and strong governance around safety, transparency, and ethics.

Because the article is a position paper and not an empirical study, it does not report original participant-level outcomes or causal effects. Its main contribution is a set of recommendations and risk-mitigation strategies for responsible educational use of LLMs, with particular emphasis on preserving critical thinking, ensuring human oversight, and avoiding misuse or inequitable deployment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can support critical thinking by generating prompts, explanations, hypotheses, and alternative perspectives, but also warns that easy access to generated answers may weaken students’ independent reasoning and problem-solving if used uncritically. The claims are conceptual rather than empirical; no sample, effect size, or outcome measure is reported.
finding.measure: critical thinking, problem-solving, fact-checking, reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating or semi-automating tasks such as personalized feedback, assessment, quiz generation, and lesson planning. These are presented as anticipated benefits rather than measured effects, so no sample size or effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: teacher workload, grading effort, content-generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LLMs may improve student engagement, participation, curiosity, and motivation by providing personalized guidance, interactive dialogue, and curiosity-prompting cues. No original study is reported; the paper summarizes possible benefits and cites prior work, but does not provide quantitative outcome data.
finding.measure: engagement, participation, curiosity, willingness to communicate

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that LLMs can support reading and writing development through grammatical correction, summaries, explanations, style suggestions, and writing feedback. These claims are descriptive and based on cited applications rather than a direct empirical test, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: reading comprehension, writing quality, grammar/style support

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses LLM support for subject-specific learning tasks beyond literacy and math, including science, language, coding, and domain-specific writing. It does not present original empirical evidence; the finding is a conceptual claim that LLMs may help create practice problems, explanations, and summaries across subjects.
finding.measure: subject-specific learning support across disciplines

paper_profiles.title: Shaping integrity: why generative artificial intelligence does not have to undermine education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This opinion paper argues that generative AI (GAI) in education does not have to undermine academic integrity if it is integrated responsibly. The authors frame the issue around two tensions: concerns that AI makes cheating easier and the counterargument that AI tools can support authentic learning, digital literacy, and ethical decision-making when used transparently and with clear boundaries.

Rather than reporting a new empirical study, the paper synthesizes ethical frameworks (deontological ethics, consequentialism, Trustworthy AI, AI4People) and educational theories (constructivism and self-determination theory) to propose how AI can be used to support learning. The discussion highlights potential classroom applications such as AI-generated formative feedback, adaptive learning supports, interactive simulations, collaborative projects, and writing assistance. Across these examples, the paper emphasizes that AI should supplement, not replace, student effort and teacher judgment.

The context is broad K-12 and higher education, but the paper is primarily normative and practice-oriented for educators and administrators. It recommends transparency about AI use, explicit instruction in ethical AI use, professional development for teachers, and iterative monitoring of AI integration. The overall conclusion is that responsible AI implementation can foster autonomy, competence, relatedness, digital literacy, and deeper engagement, thereby supporting rather than eroding academic integrity.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GAI can support writing development through personalized feedback on grammar, tone, and narrative structure. It cites AI-assisted writing examples, but provides no original empirical estimate, sample size, or measured effect; the claims are theoretical and based on prior literature rather than a new study.
finding.measure: Writing quality and academic writing skills

finding.finding_summary: The central claim is that GAI can foster critical thinking, metacognition, and collaborative problem-solving by prompting students to explore, reflect, evaluate outputs, and work together on projects. The paper presents these as expected benefits of constructivist and self-determination-oriented AI use, but does not report original empirical data, sample sizes, or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognition, collaboration, and problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is that GAI can enhance autonomy, competence, relatedness, intrinsic motivation, and academic integrity when used as personalized support. These claims are conceptual and illustrative rather than experimental, so no effect sizes or sample sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Motivation, autonomy, competence, relatedness, and engagement

finding.finding_summary: The article argues for institutional policies on transparent AI use, educator professional development, iterative evaluation, and ethical governance around privacy, bias, fairness, and accountability. These recommendations are presented as best practices, not as outcomes evaluated in an empirical design.
finding.measure: Policy guidance, governance, and institutional implementation practices

paper_profiles.title: Perceptions, strategies, and challenges of teachers in the integration of artificial intelligence in primary education: A systematic review
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Information Technology Education: Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews empirical studies published from 2014 to February 2024 on how artificial intelligence is being integrated into primary education, with a particular focus on teachers’ perceptions, implementation strategies, training, and challenges. Using PRISMA 2020 methods and searches in Web of Science, Scopus, and ERIC, the authors screened a very large initial pool of records and included 28 peer-reviewed studies that addressed AI-supported instruction and teaching in K-12 or primary-school contexts.

The review synthesizes evidence that teachers are generally positive about AI’s potential to personalize learning, support engagement, and strengthen skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, and computational thinking. Across the included studies, common implementation features included AI literacy, teacher digital competence, professional development, and student-AI collaboration; however, adoption was constrained by limited training, inadequate infrastructure, insufficient resources, and weak institutional support, especially in rural or under-resourced settings.

The paper also highlights safety and governance concerns, including privacy, bias, transparency, and the need for policies that support ethical and equitable AI use. Its main conclusion is that effective AI integration in primary education depends less on the tools themselves than on teacher preparation, contextual supports, and coherent policy frameworks that preserve human autonomy and protect students.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, AI was commonly perceived as supportive of durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and computational thinking. The review reports that enhanced AI guidance, student-AI collaboration, and integrating coding/computational thinking into curricula were associated with stronger skill development, but this synthesis does not report a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions and findings from included studies on critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and computational thinking

finding.finding_summary: The review indicates that AI tools were viewed as increasing student engagement, motivation, and confidence in learning, including via humanoid robots, adaptive guidance, and AI translation tools. No pooled effect size is reported, but several included studies described improved engagement and reduced anxiety as benefits of AI integration.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, confidence, and anxiety as reported in included studies and teacher perceptions

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI can improve instructional efficiency by helping with planning, content preparation, activity and assessment design, automated or adaptive feedback, and personalized guidance. The review’s synthesis suggests these efficiency gains are tempered by teacher workload associated with insufficient training and technical support, but no quantitative effect size is provided.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported instructional planning, assessment support, and feedback/automation functions

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that AI integration is shaped by institutional conditions such as infrastructure, funding, training opportunities, policy support, and data-governance safeguards. It emphasizes persistent concerns about privacy, bias, transparency, and equity, and argues that successful adoption requires policies, professional development, and a competency framework for AI literacy rather than tool-level change alone.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, infrastructure, privacy, bias, and institutional support conditions reported across included studies

paper_profiles.title: Transforming K-12 education: A systematic review of AI integration
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology and Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of artificial intelligence (AI) integration in K-12 education, aimed at mapping current AI applications, implementation approaches, and reported impacts on learning outcomes. Using PRISMA procedures and a Scopus search covering 1985 to January 2024, the authors screened 618 records and included 16 studies for final analysis. The review focused on how AI is being used in primary and secondary schooling, what outcomes have been reported, and what barriers and enabling conditions affect successful adoption.

Across the included literature, the paper emphasizes AI-powered chatbots, intelligent tutoring and adaptive systems, AI-enabled mobile apps, and machine-learning-based learning activities as promising tools for supporting personalized learning. The review highlights recurring design features such as goal setting, feedback, personalization, and self-regulated learning support, and it also stresses that successful integration depends on collaboration among teachers, parents, and students. The authors argue that teacher professional development is essential for effective and ethical use of AI, especially given concerns about bias, misinformation, privacy, the digital divide, and cognitive/ethical risks.

The paper's conclusions are synthesized from the included studies rather than from a single primary experiment. It reports that the reviewed AI applications generally improved learning experiences, academic performance, engagement, problem-solving, and critical thinking, but the review does not provide a pooled meta-analytic effect size. It also concludes that future research should address equity, teacher training, ethical implementation, and longitudinal evidence on transfer and sustained impact.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports positive effects for AI-supported literacy-related tasks, especially vocabulary development, writing support, and language learning. Examples include AI-based vocabulary apps, AI feedback for writing, and English-language learning tools, but the paper does not provide a pooled effect size across studies.
finding.measure: Vocabulary learning, English speaking/writing-related outcomes, and formative writing feedback/assessment

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies were described as showing improved English speaking and language-learning outcomes using AI tools such as Google Translate, IMAN Vocab App, and other AI-based language applications. The review’s synthesis is positive overall, but it does not report a combined quantitative effect size or confidence interval.
finding.measure: English speaking skills, language learning, and vocabulary acquisition

finding.finding_summary: The review notes positive learning outcomes from AI-supported STEM and machine-learning activities, including a weather-prediction project-based ML course and robotics/AI learning activities. These studies are presented as improving AI-related learning and subject learning, but the paper does not report a pooled effect size or standardized outcome statistic.
finding.measure: STEM/AI learning outcomes, including project-based machine learning course performance and robotics-related learning

finding.finding_summary: The strongest non-language academic emphasis is on overall academic performance across multiple subjects, including general learning outcomes, subject-specific achievement, and special education assessment. The review states that all four AI application categories in its synthesis showed gains in academic achievement, but it does not provide a pooled numerical estimate.
finding.measure: Academic achievement/performance across subjects; special-needs classroom assessment

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly identifies improved engagement, self-regulated learning, and student participation as major benefits of AI integration. It specifically states that AI chatbots support goal setting, self-assessment, feedback, and personalization for self-regulated learning, and that engagement levels rose over time in the reviewed evidence, though no pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Engagement levels and self-regulated learning indicators

finding.finding_summary: Critical thinking and problem-solving are central outcomes in the review, with the authors explicitly highlighting AI’s potential to improve both. The paper states that reviewed AI interventions were associated with gains in problem-solving ability and that one intervention showed the strongest critical-thinking performance, but it does not give a pooled effect size or confidence interval.
finding.measure: Critical thinking scores and problem-solving ability

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests that AI can support teachers by monitoring student performance, identifying learning gaps, and informing targeted interventions, which may improve instructional efficiency. However, this is synthesized narrative evidence rather than a direct efficiency trial, and no quantitative workload or productivity effect is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher decision-making, monitoring, and targeted intervention support

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that AI adoption in K-12 is shaped by collaboration among teachers, parents, students, and policymakers, but also by barriers such as digital divide, privacy, algorithmic bias, and ethical concerns. It emphasizes teacher professional development and institutional coordination as necessary conditions for successful implementation, while noting unresolved system-level challenges.
finding.measure: Implementation challenges, collaboration, ethics, privacy, digital divide, and teacher professional development

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual discussion of how artificial intelligence, especially large language models such as ChatGPT, can be integrated into education in ways that support learning while reducing misuse. The author argues that AI adoption in classrooms creates both opportunities and risks: personalized support, richer classroom experiences, and help for students with diverse needs on one hand, and hallucinations, overreliance, academic integrity concerns, and teacher uncertainty on the other.

The paper is built around a Swiss University of Applied Sciences case study combined with a narrative literature review. It describes the institution’s internal AI guidelines for student use, including transparency requirements and a rule that AI should be treated as a “sparring partner” rather than a ghostwriter. It also reviews practical classroom uses of AI, such as AI experiments, case-study generation, curriculum design support, gamification, and immersive technologies. The discussion then argues that effective AI integration requires a broader “culture of AI” supported by workshops, budgets, guidelines, and dedicated staff.

A central contribution is the claim that three competencies are essential for AI-era education: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The article lays out subskills and example prompting methods, and it emphasizes that students and teachers should learn to evaluate AI output critically, recognize limitations, and document AI use transparently. The paper’s main conclusion is normative rather than empirical: schools should move beyond bans or unregulated use and instead build structured support for responsible, reflective, and educationally useful AI use.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy and prompt engineering can support critical thinking by requiring students to evaluate AI outputs, recognize hallucinations, and refine prompts. It does not report a controlled effect size; instead, it presents a conceptual and practice-based claim that prompt-based interaction can foster deeper analysis and reflective judgment.
finding.measure: Critical thinking and reflective evaluation of AI output

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes the introduction of institutional AI guidelines at Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences, including documentation requirements for AI use, transparency rules, and permitted/prohibited uses. The main finding is that institutional policy is presented as necessary to manage academic integrity, student fairness, and responsible AI adoption, though no outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Institutional AI policy/guidelines and governance practices

finding.finding_summary: The article suggests AI tools can improve efficiency for educators by helping with curriculum creation, case study development, and classroom planning. These claims are illustrative and based on the author’s discussion and examples rather than empirical measurement, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher curriculum design and lesson-planning efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Learning design to support student-AI collaboration: perspectives of leading teachers for AI in education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers in South Korea (primary and secondary)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines what K-12 learning design should look like when AI is introduced as a collaborative learning agent in classrooms. The authors note that, although AI tools are increasingly used for customized feedback and adaptive support, there is little guidance on how to structure curriculum, interaction, assessment, and school conditions for student-AI collaboration (SAC) in K-12 settings.

The study uses in-depth semi-structured interviews with 10 Korean leading teachers in AI in Education from primary and secondary schools. Using a hybrid deductive-inductive thematic analysis and a distributed cognition framework, the authors identify themes across four areas: curriculum, student-AI interaction, learning environment, and the co-evolution of students and AI over time.

Teachers argued that SAC should aim to build higher-order capacities such as critical thinking, creativity, computational thinking, collaboration, and domain knowledge, while using interdisciplinary, authentic, and creative tasks with process-oriented and collaboration-focused assessment. They also emphasized support for students’ AI literacy, data literacy, debugging, and AI ethics; AI systems with instructional scaffolding, intuitive interfaces, and diverse digital tools; flexible classrooms and digital infrastructure; systemic policy support; teacher capacity building; collaborative school culture; and a safe-to-fail environment. Overall, the paper is a qualitative, design-oriented study that provides teacher perspectives rather than outcome evidence, and it proposes a staged model of SAC development: learn about AI, learn from AI, and learn together.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived SAC as a way to build higher-order and durable skills, especially critical thinking, creativity, analytical thinking, problem-solving, reflection, and collaboration with peers and AI. They argued that students should learn to evaluate AI outputs critically, generate broader solution sets, and work effectively in team-based tasks, but this is a qualitative perception study with no measured effect sizes.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about perceived learning goals and competencies

finding.finding_summary: Teachers also saw SAC as supporting social-emotional development, including motivation, persistence, coping with uncertainty, engagement, and confidence in the face of failure. They highlighted the importance of gamification, AI encouragement, AI ethics education, and a safe-to-fail classroom culture, but the study did not measure student outcomes directly.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about engagement, persistence, motivation, and safe-to-fail learning culture

finding.finding_summary: Teachers viewed SAC as supporting subject-matter knowledge building across disciplines, especially through interdisciplinary learning, authentic problems, and creative tasks. They described students using AI to deepen understanding of content in science, social science, home economics, Korean, and other subjects, but the evidence is perceptual and not an outcome evaluation.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about subject-matter learning and interdisciplinary task design

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper was institutional and policy conditions for SAC, including systematic AIED policy, governance, teacher professional development, flexible school systems, collaborative school culture, and digital infrastructure. Teachers argued these supports are necessary for safe and effective implementation, but again the paper reports stakeholder views rather than measured institutional effects.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about policy, governance, school organization, and implementation conditions

finding.finding_summary: Teachers suggested that AI could reduce repetitive teacher work and improve the efficiency of instruction through personalized learning platforms, automated data processing, and integration with existing school systems. They also stressed that poor interoperability could add workload, so the finding is mixed in implementation terms but generally framed as a potential efficiency gain; no direct workload measures were collected.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about automation, data transfer, and workflow integration

paper_profiles.title: The role of AI in enhancing statistical literacy: A systematic review in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews research on how artificial intelligence (AI) is being used to enhance statistical literacy in statistics education. The review asks which AI tools are used, which statistical literacy competencies they support, what research methods and instruments are used in the underlying studies, who the respondents are, and what overall impact AI has on statistical learning.

Using a systematic literature review protocol, the authors searched Scopus for English-language journal articles published from 2010 to 2024 and screened 173 records down to 11 studies. The reviewed literature includes tools such as ChatGPT, machine learning models, Jupyter Notebook, CODAP, Shiny web applications, eye-tracking, and multimodal learning analytics. Across the 11 studies, AI was associated with three main competency areas: conceptual understanding, data analysis/computational skills, and critical thinking/problem-solving, with additional benefits for engagement and collaborative learning.

The evidence base is mixed in method but generally exploratory: 55% of the included studies were qualitative and 45% quantitative, using instruments such as interviews, observations, surveys, eye-tracking, and learning analytics. The review finds that AI can support statistical literacy, especially through interactive explanation, simulation, visualization, and feedback, but also notes important concerns including algorithmic bias, curriculum integration challenges, transparency, and ethical issues. The authors conclude that more adaptive, ethically responsible, and pedagogically grounded AI implementations are needed, along with more mixed-methods and broader-population research.

finding.finding_summary: Across the 11 studies reviewed, AI tools were reported to improve statistical literacy through better conceptual understanding, data analysis, and computational skills. The review does not report a pooled effect size, but it concludes that tools such as ChatGPT, CODAP, Jupyter Notebook, and machine-learning simulations supported learning of statistical concepts, model evaluation, and data interpretation.
finding.measure: Statistical literacy competencies; conceptual understanding; data analysis and computational skills
finding.study_size: n=11 studies (systematic review); underlying participant totals not reported

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies critical thinking and problem-solving as a central outcome of AI use in statistics education. It reports that ChatGPT and predictive modeling activities helped learners evaluate AI-generated answers, assess statistical assumptions, and interpret data critically, and it also notes decision-tree activities in middle school as supporting heuristic reasoning and problem-solving.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, and evaluative reasoning in statistical tasks
finding.study_size: n=11 studies (systematic review); underlying participant totals not reported

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that AI positively influenced engagement and collaborative learning, particularly through interactive learning analytics-based instruction and multimodal/statistical visualization tools. It also notes that some studies found peer learning engagement was associated with better performance, although the review does not provide pooled effect sizes or a single quantitative estimate.
finding.measure: Student engagement; collaborative learning; motivation/participation indicators

finding.finding_summary: A smaller subset of the reviewed studies focused on learning statistics and data analytics more broadly, including using AI to develop assessment questions, academic writing, instructional materials, and statistical programming skills. These findings suggest AI can support broader academic tasks in statistics education beyond core numeracy outcomes, but the review does not isolate a single effect estimate.
finding.measure: Statistics and data analytics learning tasks; academic writing and instructional-material development in statistics contexts
finding.study_size: n=11 studies (systematic review); underlying participant totals not reported

paper_profiles.title: Can Web-Based AI Be Implemented in the Middle School Science Classroom? A Critical Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a critical literature review of artificial intelligence (AI) in middle school science education, focused on whether web-based AI can be implemented effectively in formal classroom settings. The authors synthesize 17 Scopus-indexed studies published between 2019 and 2023, emphasizing AI-related curricula, web-based learning tools, teacher readiness, practical implementation issues, and potential educational benefits and risks.

The review examines how AI is being used in science learning, including curriculum integration, inquiry-based learning environments, gamified and recommender systems, and tools that support decision-making, ethics, and AI literacy. It also highlights challenges such as limited access to devices, teacher preparedness, language barriers, curriculum alignment, and ethical concerns around bias and overreliance on AI. The paper concludes that AI has meaningful potential to support middle school science learning, especially inquiry, discussion, decision-making, and technological skills, but effective implementation depends on teacher training, infrastructure, and careful curriculum design.

Because this is a review rather than an original empirical study, its conclusions are based on synthesis of prior studies rather than new data collection. The paper is especially relevant to K-12 implementation questions because it discusses teacher integration, readiness, equity concerns, and the need for age-appropriate, practical AI experiences in middle school classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, web-based AI and AI-supported inquiry environments were reported to help middle school students develop science learning, inquiry, and decision-making related to scientific contexts. The review specifically notes that AI can support understanding of complex biological phenomena, question-asking, and discussion-based inquiry, but it does not report a single pooled effect size because it is a critical review of 17 studies.
finding.measure: Science learning outcomes, inquiry/decision-making, and understanding of AI-supported science concepts

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly emphasizes improvements in durable skills such as critical thinking, decision-making, inquiry, and computational empowerment. Examples include students analyzing decision-tree bias, critically examining AI ethics, and using AI-enriched materials to ask questions and reason about technology; no pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, decision-making, inquiry, computational empowerment, and ethical reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The reviewed literature suggests positive effects on motivation, interest, satisfaction, and self-efficacy when AI tools are implemented in engaging, practical ways. For example, the paper reports higher motivation in interactive AI workshops and improved satisfaction/usability in gamified AI applications, but these are narrative summaries across studies rather than a meta-analytic estimate.
finding.measure: Motivation, interest, satisfaction, usability, and self-efficacy

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies substantial institutional barriers and enabling conditions for AI implementation, including teacher training needs, infrastructure and device access, curriculum alignment, policy support, and ethical guidance. It concludes that AI has potential for middle school science education, but successful adoption depends on system-level readiness; the paper does not present a quantified institutional effect.
finding.measure: Teacher readiness, curriculum integration, infrastructure access, and policy/implementation feasibility

paper_profiles.title: Confronting the Challenges of Participatory Culture: Media Education for the 21st Century
paper_profiles.population: Adolescent / K-12 (especially middle school and high school youth)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report argues that youth participation in digital media and online communities is creating new demands for media literacy education. Rather than focusing only on access to technology, the authors frame the central educational problem as helping young people develop the skills, ethical norms, and critical awareness needed to participate fully in contemporary participatory culture.

The report is not an empirical intervention study; it synthesizes prior research, illustrative cases, and policy arguments about learning in informal media environments such as fan communities, games, online publications, and collaborative platforms. It emphasizes three challenges for education: the participation gap (unequal access to meaningful participation), the transparency problem (difficulty recognizing how media shape perceptions), and the ethics challenge (learning norms for responsible participation online).

The paper’s main conclusion is that schools, after-school programs, and parents should take a systemic approach to media education. It argues that participatory culture can support learning, creativity, civic engagement, and workplace-relevant skills, but only if young people are explicitly taught new media literacies such as judgment, networking, collective intelligence, and negotiation. The report also warns that simply providing devices or internet access is insufficient without pedagogical support and critical media literacy instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The report argues that participation in online fan communities, collaborative writing spaces, and other participatory media can support reading and writing development. It cites examples such as beta-reading in fan communities, where peer feedback helps contributors improve sentence construction, narrative structure, and close reading, but it does not present original effect-size evidence.
finding.measure: Reading and writing development in participatory/peer-feedback contexts

finding.finding_summary: The report centrally argues that participatory culture builds durable skills such as critical thinking, judgment, collaboration, networking, multitasking, collective intelligence, and negotiation. These claims are based on synthesis and illustrative examples rather than direct experimental results, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, judgment, collaboration, networking, and related new media literacies

finding.finding_summary: The report suggests that participation in online communities can increase motivation, self-confidence, sense of contribution, and social connection. It describes participatory culture as lowering barriers to expression and fostering feelings that one’s contributions matter, but these are conceptual claims not accompanied by quantitative estimates.
finding.measure: Motivation, self-confidence, sense of belonging, and participation

finding.finding_summary: A major conclusion is that educational systems have not adequately responded to the rise of participatory culture, creating inequities in access and preparation. The report argues that schools, after-school programs, and parents must coordinate a systemic response; it also notes that access initiatives alone are insufficient without educational supports.
finding.measure: Institutional response to participatory culture, access, and media literacy education

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a narrative review and conceptual overview of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular focus on chatbots and ChatGPT. It addresses the promise of AI for improving learning, personalization, feedback, engagement, and teacher productivity, while also foregrounding ethical, practical, and pedagogical concerns such as bias, privacy, academic integrity, and the need for teacher preparation.

The paper does not report an original empirical study or an intervention. Instead, it synthesizes prior literature and examples to argue that AI tools can support individualized instruction, instant feedback, assessment, and administrative efficiency, but only when integrated responsibly and with appropriate pedagogical guidance. The authors emphasize that AI should complement, not replace, teachers, and that successful adoption depends on training, policy, and ongoing oversight.

Because the article is primarily a literature-based discussion, it provides no sample, effect size, or outcome data of its own. Its conclusions are broad and aspirational: AI has substantial potential in education, but ethical safeguards and teacher support are necessary for responsible implementation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools such as chatbots and automated grading systems can reduce teacher workload by evaluating assignments, scoring work, and providing feedback, freeing time for lesson planning, student support, and professional development. This is presented as a conceptual conclusion drawn from prior literature rather than new empirical evidence; no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / grading and feedback efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The article states that AI-supported personalized learning can increase student motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduce anxiety, citing prior studies and examples. These claims are not based on a new empirical dataset in this paper, and no effect sizes or sample sizes are reported here.
finding.measure: Student motivation, engagement, confidence, and anxiety

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-based educational tools can foster critical thinking, creativity, self-reflection, self-directed learning, and self-regulation through personalized feedback and iterative support. The evidence is syntheses of prior literature rather than original results, so no study size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, creativity, self-reflection, self-directed learning, self-regulation

paper_profiles.title: The role of ChatGPT in education: Applications, challenges: insights from a systematic review
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Information Technology Education: Research
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School, High School, Undergraduate, Adult
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic literature review examines empirical research on ChatGPT use in school and higher education, with attention to how the tool is used, what it can and cannot do, and what ethical or practical concerns arise. The authors searched major academic databases for English-language empirical studies published from January 2023 to January 2024 and ultimately synthesized 50 studies across preschool, primary, secondary, and higher education.

The review focuses on use cases such as lesson planning, personalized materials, quizzes, assessment support, language practice, problem-solving, and feedback on writing. Across the included studies, ChatGPT was generally portrayed as useful for supporting learning, especially in language learning, math, physics, and some exploratory tasks, but with important limits in accuracy, depth, creativity, and reliable calculation. The review also identifies recurring risks: hallucinated or outdated answers, fabricated references, academic integrity problems, copyright issues, biased content, privacy concerns, and overreliance that may undermine students’ critical thinking.

For K-12 settings, the review notes relatively fewer studies than in higher education, but reports positive uses in primary and secondary classrooms, including personalized materials, quizzes, feedback, and structured activities such as think-pair-share or prompt engineering. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has promise for education if used with AI literacy, careful teacher guidance, and explicit safeguards, and they call for more empirical K-12 research—especially in primary and secondary education and in underrepresented contexts such as special and non-formal education.

finding.finding_summary: Across the included studies, ChatGPT generally supported literacy-related tasks such as essay writing, reading/writing feedback, and automatic evaluation, especially in language-learning contexts. However, the review also reports limits in response quality and reliability, including superficial or inaccurate feedback and fabricated citations, which constrain literacy benefits.
finding.measure: Writing quality, essay improvement, written feedback, automatic evaluation of assignments

finding.finding_summary: The review reports positive effects on language learning, including language practice, dialogue generation, vocabulary/grammar support, and immediate feedback during writing. These benefits were observed in K-12 and higher education studies, but the review does not provide a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Language practice, dialogue quality, vocabulary/grammar development, writing feedback

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was helpful for explaining mathematical concepts and giving problem-solving steps, particularly in mathematics education. At the same time, the review highlights consistent limitations in numerical computation and inaccurate calculations, especially for more complex STEM problems.
finding.measure: Problem-solving support, conceptual understanding, numerical calculation accuracy

finding.finding_summary: In science-related contexts such as physics, chemistry, and medicine, the review describes generally positive performance for conceptual understanding, question answering, and problem-solving support. It also notes that ChatGPT can outperform students on some tasks, but its limitations are more pronounced in detailed or computational scientific work.
finding.measure: Conceptual understanding, scientific question answering, problem-solving in physics/chemistry/medicine

finding.finding_summary: The review reports positive findings in non-language/non-STEM areas such as history, world religions, journalism, business administration, and teacher education. Examples include improved historical argumentation, knowledge building, task enrichment, and support for lesson planning and assessment design.
finding.measure: Historical thinking, knowledge building, lesson planning, task/assignment quality, domain-specific performance

finding.finding_summary: Several studies in the review found that ChatGPT increased motivation, engagement, persistence, or enjoyment of learning. This pattern appears across history, data science, programming, business administration, and English-related tasks, although one study reported a negative correlation with achievement and motivation.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, persistence, enjoyment of learning

finding.finding_summary: This is one of the central findings of the review: ChatGPT was frequently associated with improvements in critical thinking and higher-order thinking, especially when used for prompt engineering, knowledge construction, problem-solving, and structured classroom activities. The review also cautions that overdependence and low-quality outputs can undermine critical reasoning, so the overall pattern is positive but bounded by important risks.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, higher-order thinking, reasoning, problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: The review shows that educators used ChatGPT to save time and streamline tasks such as lesson planning, quiz creation, assessment design, rubric development, and assignment grading. These uses suggest improved workflow efficiency for teachers and faster task completion for students, though the review does not quantify workload reduction.
finding.measure: Lesson planning, quiz creation, grading, assessment design, task completion speed

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies institution-level concerns and implications around academic integrity, copyright, privacy, bias, and unequal access, all of which affect governance and implementation decisions. It also recommends AI literacy and ethical frameworks for educators and students, but does not present measured policy outcomes.
finding.measure: Academic integrity, privacy, bias, access equity, ethical implementation concerns

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education (HE) published from 2016 to 2022. Its main purpose is to map the state of the field: where studies were conducted, who authored them, what student levels and subject areas were studied, who the intended users were, and how AI was being used in HE.

Using PRISMA methods, the authors screened 371 articles and included 138 peer-reviewed journal articles. They coded studies by geography, first-author affiliation, academic level, subject domain, intended user, and AI use-case. The review found rapid growth in publications in 2021–2022, a geographic shift toward China leading publication counts, a strong concentration in undergraduate populations, and a large share of studies in language learning, computer science, and engineering.

For use-cases, the review identified five major categories: assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. The paper concludes that HE AI research is expanding quickly but remains concentrated in a few countries and disciplines, with relatively limited work on graduate students, managers, and more exploratory or transformative uses of AI. The review is descriptive and does not test intervention effects, but it highlights where the field has evidence and where important gaps remain.

finding.finding_summary: Across the 138-study review, AI was frequently used to reduce instructor workload and automate routine tasks such as assessment, question generation, learning analytics, and instructional design. The paper does not estimate a pooled effect size, but it reports that automatic assessment was the most common assessment use-case (26 studies), and that AI was used to streamline grading, feedback, and student-data management.
finding.measure: Frequency and description of AI use-cases in systematic review coding

finding.finding_summary: The review describes multiple studies where AI supported student persistence, self-regulated learning, emotions, and engagement. For example, AI tools provided immediate personalized feedback, self-testing opportunities, and emotional or motivational support (e.g., volition support and emotion control in an AI change agent), but the review reports these as study-level findings rather than pooled quantitative effects.
finding.measure: Reported study outcomes related to engagement, self-regulation, persistence, and emotion

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly identifies AI use in supporting higher-order and durable skills through personalized tutoring, feedback, and learning analytics. It specifically notes studies involving higher-order thinking, automated personalized feedback, and AI systems that adapt learning paths, with the review emphasizing AI support for student learning strategies and self-regulated learning rather than reporting a pooled effect.
finding.measure: Reported study outcomes related to higher-order thinking, self-regulated learning, and adaptive learning pathways

finding.finding_summary: Literacy-related uses of AI were prominent in language learning, especially writing, reading, and vocabulary acquisition. The review reports that AI tools such as automated feedback systems and intelligent tutoring systems were used to support these literacy outcomes, including a study of Uyghur minority students’ academic writing skills, but it provides no pooled effect estimate.
finding.measure: Writing, reading, vocabulary acquisition, and language-learning outcomes

paper_profiles.title: VLM@school – Evaluation of AI image understanding on German middle school knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VLM@school, a benchmark dataset for evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on German middle school–level tasks that require both image understanding and subject knowledge. The authors argue that many existing multimodal benchmarks are overly English-centric, heavily multiple-choice, and insufficiently reflective of real educational reasoning demands, so they build a dataset of 2,038 open-ended questions paired with 486 images across nine school subjects, including math, biology, history, geography, arts, music, physics, religion, and sports.

The study evaluates thirteen open-weight VLMs on the benchmark using automated LLM-as-a-judge scoring. The models were tested on overall questions and a subset of intentionally adversarial questions designed to be unanswerable from the image alone. Results show that even the strongest models remain below 45% overall accuracy, with especially weak performance on music, math, and adversarial questions. The paper concludes that middle school–level multimodal tasks in German are still highly challenging for current VLMs and that benchmark performance on existing public datasets does not reliably predict performance on this more realistic, open-ended benchmark.

The paper is primarily a benchmark construction and evaluation study rather than an intervention study in classrooms. It does not test teacher use, student learning gains, or implementation of AI feedback in educational practice. Instead, it provides evidence about model capability, domain variation, quantization effects, and failure modes such as hallucination and poor refusal on misleading prompts, with some discussion of implications for future multilingual and more reasoning-oriented VLM evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark includes 308 math questions, and the best-performing model in math reached only 34.09% accuracy (Qwen2.5VL 32B), with several models much lower (e.g., Ovis2 4B at 9.09%). The authors report that models were better at some calculations than at counting or identifying geometric elements, indicating substantial limitations in math-related visual reasoning on middle school content.
finding.measure: Accuracy on open-ended math benchmark questions
finding.study_size: n=308 questions (112 images in the math domain)

finding.finding_summary: Physics questions required interpreting diagrams, reading cues from images, and sometimes explaining causal relationships, but performance remained modest; the best physics score was 47.65% (Qwen2.5VL 32B) and several models were around 32%-46%. The authors note that questions requiring explanations were often answered incorrectly, suggesting weak scientific reasoning beyond surface-level diagram recognition.
finding.measure: Accuracy on physics benchmark questions and explanation-based items

finding.finding_summary: Across non-math, non-science school subjects, models showed uneven performance, with stronger results in history and religion than in music and sports. For example, the best overall domain scores were around 54% in history and religion, but music was much lower (best 31.03%), and the paper reports that these domains revealed major weaknesses in map reading, art-style recognition, musical notation/chord identification, and sports situation interpretation.
finding.measure: Accuracy across arts, geography, history, music, religion, and sports benchmark questions
finding.study_size: n=57-65 images per domain; questions ranged from 154 to 286 per domain

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies models’ ability to handle adversarial questions that require recognizing when an image does not support an answer, which is relevant to critical thinking and epistemic caution. Performance on adversarial items was very low overall, with the best model only reaching 32.83% overall and many models far lower, showing that the models often failed to say 'no' even when the question was misleading or unanswerable from the image.
finding.measure: Accuracy on adversarial/unanswerable questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main institutional contribution is methodological: it argues that benchmark performance on widely used public datasets such as MMMU does not reliably generalize to a German, school-curriculum-aligned benchmark. The authors show that model rankings shift on VLM@school, that quantization can modestly affect results, and that some models with strong public-benchmark performance underperform relative to competitors on this dataset.
finding.measure: Cross-benchmark comparison of model rankings and scores (VLM@school vs MMMU/open VLM leaderboard)

paper_profiles.title: Designing AI Systems that Augment Human Performed vs. Demonstrated Critical Thinking
paper_profiles.venue: AIREASONING-2025-01 (ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning)
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable / no human participants studied
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position paper that examines how generative AI systems should be conceptualized when researchers and designers talk about “critical thinking.” The authors argue that many current studies and AI tools conflate two different constructs: performed critical thinking, meaning independent human cognitive activity without AI assistance, and demonstrated critical thinking, meaning critical thinking that is shown in outputs or processes produced with AI support.

Rather than testing an intervention, the paper synthesizes prior literature from psychology, education, and HCI to propose a conceptual framework for evaluating AI’s effects on critical thinking. It argues that many existing evaluations of GenAI primarily measure improved final outputs rather than improvements in users’ independent reasoning ability. The paper recommends future research designs that separately assess both performed and demonstrated critical thinking, including pre/post or longitudinal designs and learning-science-informed interaction features such as questioning, scaffolding, and guided frameworks.

The paper does not study K-12 learners directly and includes no original empirical sample. Its main contribution is theoretical: clarifying how AI systems might be designed either to improve the quality of AI-assisted outputs or to build users’ independent critical thinking skills over time. The authors specifically suggest that educational design principles could help AI move beyond answer delivery toward scaffolding reasoning processes, but they provide no experimental evidence in this paper.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual paper, not an empirical study. It argues that existing GenAI research often measures demonstrated critical thinking in AI-assisted outputs rather than performed critical thinking, and therefore evidence about whether AI improves independent critical thinking is mixed and potentially overstated. No original sample, effect size, or outcome score is reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of critical thinking definitions and prior studies

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Antitrust and Platform Power in Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: 1st Workshop on Generative AI and Law (co-located with ICML)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how market power is concentrated across the generative AI technology stack and argues that a small number of large technology firms control key inputs needed to build and deploy advanced generative AI systems. The authors frame the issue as an antitrust and competition-law problem, asking how data access, compute, talent, infrastructure, proprietary models, and funding for research contribute to vertical integration and barriers to entry.

The paper does not evaluate an educational intervention or any student-facing AI system. Instead, it synthesizes legal and market observations about generative AI development, including the role of proprietary data, cloud infrastructure, specialized hardware, human feedback labor, and academic influence. It argues that incumbent firms likely have durable advantages that may reinforce concentration, and it suggests that forthcoming regulation such as the EU AI Act could intensify existing inequities if compliance costs favor well-resourced firms.

The context is the broader generative AI ecosystem rather than a specific population or school setting. The main conclusion is normative and policy-oriented: antitrust law and AI governance may need to more carefully address vertical integration and platform power, because current market structures risk limiting competition and entrenching the dominance of large technology companies.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI markets are increasingly concentrated in a few large technology companies and that this concentration may persist or worsen under current and proposed regulation. It does not present empirical estimates of policy impact; rather, it offers a legal-economic analysis of platform power, vertical integration, and likely barriers to entry in generative AI.
finding.measure: Legal-economic analysis of market concentration, vertical integration, and regulatory implications

paper_profiles.title: Natural Language Query Engine for Relational Databases using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of making relational databases accessible to non-technical users who do not know SQL. The author argues that existing natural-language-to-SQL solutions often produce syntactically valid but semantically incorrect queries, fail to incorporate business rules, and do not return user-friendly natural language answers.

To address these issues, the paper proposes a generative-AI-based natural language assistant for relational databases. The system scans database schemas, vectorizes schema and business-rule knowledge in a vector database (Milvus on IBM watsonx.data), uses an LLM (via watsonx.ai) to generate SQL from user questions, and applies a two-step validation process: syntactic execution checks and semantic introspection. It then generates a natural-language response from the retrieved data and supports iterative refinement through user feedback.

The prototype is evaluated on the BIRD-SQL benchmark, a text-to-SQL benchmark for relational databases, rather than an educational setting or K-12 population. Reported results are initial prototype findings: over 50% of benchmark queries were translated correctly on the first attempt, more than 58% for simple queries, and nontechnical users rated natural-language responses as excellent in 90% of test cases. The paper concludes that the approach is promising for enterprise data access, but it also notes limitations around ambiguous queries, execution time, and scalability.

finding.finding_summary: The prototype is designed to improve efficiency by reducing the technical burden of querying relational databases and automating SQL generation, validation, and response drafting. In initial BIRD-SQL evaluation, over 50% of queries were translated correctly on the first attempt (more than 58% for simple queries), suggesting the system can streamline data access for non-expert users; however, the paper does not report a formal efficiency effect size.
finding.measure: SQL translation accuracy / query-response automation on BIRD-SQL benchmark

paper_profiles.title: Provocation: Who benefits from “inclusion” in Generative AI?
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (no K-12 human subjects; speculative case study about marginalized communities and GenAI stakeholders)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a provocation arguing that common participatory AI practices—especially in generative AI development and evaluation—often promise benefits to marginalized communities without adequately accounting for who actually gains access to those benefits, under what conditions, and at what cost. The authors focus on representational harms in text-to-image systems and the ways “inclusion” initiatives can become extractive when community members are asked to provide labor, data, and expertise without meaningful ownership, control, or ongoing compensation.

Rather than reporting a human-subjects experiment, the paper uses a speculative case study centered on a hypothetical Vietnamese community participant invited to label cultural artifacts for a technology company’s T2I model. Through this scenario, the authors trace potential direct and indirect benefits (e.g., improved representation, use by end-users such as educators and artists) and barriers to realizing those benefits, including paywalls, interface accessibility, lack of ownership, weak compensation, and limited ability to translate improved model outputs into social or material gains.

The paper’s main conclusion is that “inclusion” in GenAI is often insufficient unless participation is structured to provide durable agency, control, compensation, and protections against misuse.
