The authors argue for more transparent participatory AI practices and point to alternative models such as community authorship, community-owned models, data licensing, and community-driven refusal or accountability as better ways to align AI development with the interests of marginalized groups.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that current participatory AI structures often benefit technology institutions more than marginalized communities, because institutions can improve and monetize models while community contributors receive only one-time compensation. It is a conceptual/provocation paper, so it does not report empirical effect sizes; instead it identifies governance, ownership, licensing, and policy gaps that shape whether inclusion yields real community benefit.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of participatory AI structures, ownership, compensation, and policy/ governance arrangements

paper_profiles.title: Making AI-Enhanced Videos: Analyzing Generative AI Use Cases in YouTube Content Creation
paper_profiles.venue: CHI EA ’25 (Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how generative AI tools are being used in YouTube video creation and what that suggests about future support for content creators. Rather than evaluating an educational intervention, the authors analyze how-to videos to map the concrete use cases of GenAI across the video production workflow.

The study collected 3,854 YouTube videos via the YouTube Data API, filtered them to 1,046, and then manually reviewed them to produce a final dataset of 274 how-to videos demonstrating generative AI use in video creation. Using thematic analysis of 2,829 segmented clips, the authors developed a conceptual framework spanning four phases: planning, production, editing, and uploading. They identified use cases such as topic ideation, scriptwriting, prompt refinement, AI image/video generation, avatar creation, voiceover generation, lip-syncing, upscaling, subtitle generation, and title suggestion.

The main conclusion is that GenAI is already embedded in creator workflows as a tool for ideation, media generation, editing, and metadata creation. The paper argues that these patterns raise research and design questions about prompt skill development, originality/authenticity, and transparency of AI-generated content, and it suggests future GenAI tools should better support creator workflows while addressing ethical and platform-governance concerns. The paper is exploratory and descriptive, not an effectiveness study.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that creators use GenAI to streamline multiple labor-intensive steps in video production, including scriptwriting, prompt refinement, image/video generation, voiceover creation, lip-syncing, upscaling, subtitle generation, and title suggestion. The evidence is descriptive rather than causal: across 274 how-to videos, GenAI was used in 167 videos for prompting images/videos, 93 for voiceover creation, 28 for subtitles, and 85 for scripting/storytelling, indicating substantial workflow efficiency gains in practice.
finding.measure: Frequency of GenAI use cases in YouTube how-to videos across planning, production, editing, and uploading phases

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses broader platform and governance implications of AI-generated content, including concerns about transparency, disclosure, shadow-banning, demonetization, and algorithmic visibility on YouTube. These are not tested empirically as outcomes, but the study argues that AI content may affect how platforms classify, promote, or demote videos and calls for research on labeling and disclosure practices.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of content-creator practices and discussion of platform governance implications

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally discusses prompting as a skill and ideation as a creative practice, arguing that GenAI may support or hinder originality and creativity. However, it does not directly measure critical thinking or metacognition in learners; instead, it qualitatively infers that creators use GenAI for topic selection, scripting, and prompt crafting, and warns against over-reliance that could reduce originality.
finding.measure: Qualitative thematic analysis of GenAI use cases related to ideation, scripting, and prompt creation

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI Toolkit - A Framework for Increasing the Quality of LLM-Based Applications Over Their Whole Life Cycle
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint addresses the engineering problem of how to develop, test, deploy, and monitor large language model (LLM) applications more reliably across their full life cycle. The authors argue that current LLM application workflows are still too manual, slow, and trial-and-error driven, and they propose the Generative AI Toolkit as an open-source framework to automate key DevOps tasks such as project bootstrapping, user-defined metric creation, repeatable evaluation cases, prompt/model comparison, CI/CD integration, tracing, and production monitoring.

The paper presents the toolkit and walks through several representative use cases, including a text-to-SQL agent, a RAG-based restaurant assistant, and an in-vehicle assistant. These examples are used to illustrate how the toolkit supports automated testing, logging, latency tracking, hallucination detection, and tool-selection checks, with special emphasis on debugging and operational monitoring rather than model training or user studies. The paper also discusses how the toolkit can be used to compare models and prompts under standardized test cases and how it can help reduce manual effort and shorten release cycles.

The context is software development for LLM-based applications, not K-12 education. The main conclusion is that a lifecycle-oriented toolkit can improve quality assurance and operational efficiency for LLM systems by making evaluation and monitoring more systematic and automated. However, the paper does not report controlled empirical evidence from an educational setting; its evidence is primarily illustrative and framework-oriented.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the toolkit reduces manual effort and shortens development and release cycles for LLM applications by automating project setup, evaluation, CI/CD integration, tracing, and monitoring. It does not report a formal controlled experiment; benefits are described qualitatively across representative use cases such as text-to-SQL, RAG, and in-car assistants.
finding.measure: Developer workflow automation, evaluation/monitoring automation, cycle time, manual effort

finding.finding_summary: The toolkit is positioned as supporting better prompt/model iteration, test design, and debugging for LLM-based agents, which are adjacent to analytic and critical-thinking workflows in application development. However, the paper does not study student critical thinking or learning outcomes; the relevance is only indirect through development tooling for evaluation and optimization.
finding.measure: Developer-facing debugging, prompt/model comparison, test case design

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI and Attentive User Interfaces: Five Strategies to Enhance Take-Over Quality in Automated Driving
paper_profiles.venue: MUM’23 Workshop on Interruptions and Attention Management: Exploring the Potential of Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position paper that asks how generative AI could be combined with Attentive User Interfaces (AUIs) to improve takeover quality in Level 3 automated driving. The core problem is that drivers in conditionally automated vehicles may become disengaged from the driving scene and then need to regain situation awareness quickly when a takeover request occurs. The author argues that current explicit alerts can increase workload and stress, whereas subtler, attention-sensitive interventions may better support safe handovers.

Rather than reporting an empirical user study, the paper proposes five design strategies for an intelligent takeover-request assistant: interactive scenario visualizations, conversational primers, context-aware and personalized takeover requests, subtle nudges, and ambient scene generation. The paper also sketches a system architecture that would combine vehicle sensors, cabin sensors, map/V2X data, and personal digital-footprint information to infer driver state and generate tailored interventions. The proposed system is intended to adapt the timing, modality, and content of cues to the driving context and the driver’s attention state.

The paper’s main conclusion is conceptual: generative AI may make takeover support more natural, personalized, and subtle, potentially improving situation awareness and takeover quality. At the same time, the author emphasizes substantial safety, robustness, and regulatory concerns, including hallucinations, bias, lack of explainability, and the challenge of validating nondeterministic systems for safety-critical use. The paper therefore functions as a forward-looking design vision rather than evidence of effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues, at a conceptual level, that generative AI-based attentive user interfaces could improve takeover quality by making driver handovers smoother and more timely. No empirical effect was measured; the claim is based on design reasoning and prior literature rather than a study of outcomes.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Making Physical Objects with Generative AI and Robotic Assembly: Considering Fabrication Constraints, Sustainability, Time, Functionality and Accessibility
paper_profiles.venue: GenAICHI: CHI 2025 Workshop on Generative AI and HCI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This workshop paper asks how 3D generative AI outputs can be translated into physical objects in ways that better account for real-world fabrication constraints. The authors argue that focusing only on improving text-to-3D generation is insufficient; instead, the fabrication method itself should align with the speed, scale, and variability of generative AI.

As a case study, the paper presents a system that combines text-to-3D generation (Meshy.AI) with discrete robotic assembly using a UR10 robotic arm. The system converts AI-generated meshes into component-level representations via voxelization, then applies checks for overhangs, connectivity, and robot reachability to improve assembly feasibility. The paper evaluates the approach along five aspects: fabrication constraints, time, sustainability, functionality, and accessibility.

The context is human-centered digital fabrication research, not a K-12 or education study. The main conclusions are that discrete robotic assembly can better handle variability in generative outputs, can assemble large objects quickly, and can support reuse of modular components for more sustainable fabrication. However, functionality is limited for some objects, and accessibility remains constrained by hardware cost and precision requirements. The paper is primarily a design/technical workshop contribution and does not report educational outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The system substantially improved fabrication throughput relative to the challenge posed by text-to-3D generation: nearly all assembled objects were completed in under five minutes from the user prompt. The paper frames this as a promising prompt-to-physical workflow that could support faster iterative design loops, but it does not report comparative statistics or inferential testing.
finding.measure: Total fabrication/assembly time from user prompt to completed physical object

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that discrete robotic assembly can reduce waste and improve responsible fabrication by enabling disassembly and reuse of the same modular parts across multiple products. Using 40 modular components, the authors assembled seven distinct objects, suggesting a potentially more sustainable fabrication model with broader implications for material use and production practices.
finding.measure: Number of distinct objects assembled from the same set of modular components; reuse/disassembly potential

paper_profiles.title: eRevise+RF: A Writing Evaluation System for Assessing Student Essay Revisions and Providing Formative Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents eRevise+RF, an automated writing evaluation system designed to assess student essay revisions and provide formative feedback on argumentative writing. The core problem is that young writers often receive feedback about evidence use but still struggle to revise effectively; the authors therefore extend prior eRevise work by adding revision-specific feedback that evaluates whether students’ changes actually improve the essay in response to prior feedback.

The system combines NLP-based essay scoring indicators (for number of evidence topics and specificity) with revision classifiers that label sentence-level changes as surface vs. content, evidence vs. reasoning, and successful vs. unsuccessful. It then uses these predictions to generate expert-authored feedback for three evidence-use levels and ten revision-feedback levels. The system was deployed with 6 teachers and 406 students in grades 4-8 across three schools in Pennsylvania and Louisiana, using two response-to-text articles (Millennium Villages Project and Space Exploration) over three sessions.

Results show the NLP components perform reasonably well against human annotations (e.g., QWK=0.67 for number of evidence pieces, 0.82 for specificity, and F1=0.96/0.66/0.70 for revision content, evidence, and success classification). Student essays improved across drafts on word count and evidence-use metrics, and feedback-aligned patterns suggest students responded to both evidence-use feedback and revision feedback. The paper concludes that integrating revision-aware assessment into AWE can support argumentative writing development for younger students, while noting limitations such as small pilot deployment, no control group, and possible classification errors or bias risks.

finding.finding_summary: Across the pilot deployment, student argumentative writing improved from draft 1 to draft 2 and draft 3 on multiple literacy measures. For MVP essays (n=516 essays across 172 students) and SPACE essays (n=450 essays across 150 students), word count, evidence score, number of pieces of evidence (NPE), and specificity (SPC) increased over drafts; for example, predicted NPE rose from 2.56 to 3.34 on MVP and from 3.02 to 4.09 on SPACE, while predicted SPC rose from 8.81 to 13.98 on MVP and from 6.07 to 8.84 on SPACE.
finding.measure: Argumentative writing quality measures: word count, evidence score (ES), number of pieces of evidence (NPE), specificity (SPC), and draft-to-draft revision quality
finding.study_size: n=172 MVP students; n=150 SPACE students (516 MVP essays; 450 SPACE essays)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention targeted students’ revision quality in response to feedback, which is directly tied to metacognitive self-monitoring and evidence-based revision. Feedback-aligned changes were observed: when students received evidence-use feedback, their next drafts generally increased NPE and SPC in the expected direction, and revision feedback also corresponded to improved evidence use in many cases (e.g., annotated NPE increased 128% after EF1 on draft1-draft2; and draft2-draft3 revisions often showed additional evidence and specificity gains).
finding.measure: Feedback-aligned revision behavior; changes in NPE and SPC after evidence-use and revision feedback
finding.study_size: n=172 MVP student essay sequences for feedback analysis; subset counts EF1 N=74, EF2 N=11, EF3 N=87

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating the Design Features of an Intelligent Tutoring System for Advanced Mathematics Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study evaluates two design features of an intelligent tutoring system (ITS) called Xiaomai for advanced mathematics: free-response questions with automatic feedback/self-evaluation, and an error-reflection feature that prompts students to identify why mistakes occurred. The authors ask whether these features improve practice performance and learning outcomes compared with multiple-choice questions and no reflection.

The experiment recruited 120 Chinese college students who had taken advanced mathematics courses. Students were randomly assigned to a 2x2 factorial design: multiple-choice vs. free-response questions, crossed with reflection vs. no reflection. All students completed a pretest, 40 minutes of practice in Xiaomai on three knowledge components, and a posttest. Practice and posttest outcomes were analyzed using ANOVA/ANCOVA, t-tests, and mixed-effects regressions.

The main finding is that the multiple-choice format outperformed the free-response format on practice performance and learning gains, while the reflection feature had no significant positive effect. Students in multiple-choice conditions attempted more questions, answered more correctly, spent less time per question, and showed larger pretest-to-posttest gains than students in free-response conditions. The authors conclude that the current implementation of free-response questions and error reflection in Xiaomai does not improve learning and may need redesign, such as adding better support for free-response evaluation and more informative feedback on incorrect solutions.

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved mathematics learning more in the multiple-choice conditions than in the free-response conditions, but the overall posttest difference was not statistically significant after controlling for pretest scores. The ANCOVA found a marginal main effect of item format on posttest scores (F(1,115)=3.72, p=0.06), with multiple-choice students scoring higher (M=9.21) than free-response students (M=7.94); reflection had no significant effect (F(1,115)=0.07, p=0.79).
finding.measure: Pretest and posttest multiple-choice mathematics scores; pretest-to-posttest learning gain

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly tested an error-reflection feature intended to support metacognition, but it did not improve learning outcomes or practice performance. Reflection showed no significant effect on posttest scores, number of attempts, correctness, or time, and the prior-knowledge moderation test was also nonsignificant.
finding.measure: Reflection on errors / metacognitive error analysis; prior-knowledge moderation of reflection effects

finding.finding_summary: The free-response design reduced practice efficiency relative to multiple-choice items. Students in multiple-choice conditions attempted more questions (M=21.98, SD=8.11) than students in free-response conditions (M=15.41, SD=8.61), and they spent less time per question; item format had a significant effect on time (B=46.26, p<.001) and a marginal effect on correctness (B=0.23, p=0.09).
finding.measure: Practice number of attempts, item correctness, and time per question
finding.std_deviation: SD=8.11; SD=8.61; other SDs reported in paper but effect size not reported

finding.finding_summary: The study’s reflection component was intended to engage self-regulation during learning, but it did not produce measurable gains in learning outcomes or practice behavior. The authors also noted that reflection engagement may have been weak because the system did not verify the quality of students’ reflections.
finding.measure: Self-evaluation and error reflection behavior during ITS practice

paper_profiles.title: V-MATH: An Agentic Approach to the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Mathematics Exams
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of preparing Vietnamese high school students for the National High School Graduation Mathematics Exams (NHSGMEs), which require performance across recognition, comprehension, and application levels and place strong demands on both students and teachers. The authors argue that conventional preparation is constrained by rote learning, static question banks, and limited personalization, while teachers face heavy workload in creating compliant practice materials.

To address this, the paper introduces V-MATH, an agentic AI framework built around a planner-executor architecture with three specialized agents: one for specification-matrix–aligned question generation, one for solving and explaining exam items step by step, and one for personalized learning-path customization based on student performance. The system also incorporates Memento-style memory and a data-extraction pipeline that converts exam PDFs/images into structured LATEX and JSON-like representations, enabling reusable exam banks and adaptive practice.

The study evaluates V-MATH on a newly curated NHSGME dataset (about 500 complete exam sets from 220 official PDFs) and on the VNHSGE benchmark. Results are primarily system-level and benchmark-based rather than student outcome experiments: V-MATH reports very high exact-match accuracy on VNHSGE, strong section-wise performance on held-out NHSGME exams, and improved explanation quality and step completeness with memory augmentation. The paper concludes that the framework is promising for scalable exam preparation and teacher support, while noting future work is needed on latency, robustness, fairness, safety, and teacher-in-the-loop controls.

finding.finding_summary: V-MATH showed strong performance on mathematics exam tasks aligned to the Vietnamese high school graduation exam. On VNHSGE, it achieved 100% exact-match accuracy across 2019–2023 (50 questions per year), and on 50 held-out NHSGME exams it reached 98.1% accuracy in Part I, 93.8% in Part II, and 88.4% in Part III, with 92.1% item accuracy and 64% set-level accuracy on full exams.
finding.measure: Exact-match accuracy, section-wise accuracy, item accuracy, and set-level exam accuracy on Vietnamese high school mathematics exams
finding.study_size: n=250 questions on VNHSGE; n=50 held-out NHSGME exams

finding.finding_summary: The personalized learning agent was associated with improved student engagement and score gains during practice. The paper reports a +11.8 point pre/post score increase, engagement score of 0.76, and reduced repeated skill errors (43% path effectiveness) after students followed recommended learning paths.
finding.measure: Pre/post score gain, engagement score, repeated error reduction, and path effectiveness in personalized practice

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to support step-by-step reasoning, explanation quality, and personalized guidance, and the evaluation suggests these capabilities were improved by the agentic and memory-augmented pipeline. The solver achieved 82.1% step completeness and 4.5/5 explanation quality, while memory increased hard-item accuracy and step completeness, indicating stronger structured problem-solving support.
finding.measure: Step completeness, explanation quality, and hard-item accuracy on math problem solving tasks
finding.study_size: n=250 VNHSGE questions; n=50 held-out NHSGME exams

finding.finding_summary: The framework was explicitly designed to reduce teacher workload by automating compliant question generation and question-bank maintenance. The paper reports high matrix compliance for generated questions (96.7%), low novelty overlap (7.8%), and a teacher rating of 4.6/5, and it argues that automated generation and structured exam extraction reduce manual preparation effort.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings, matrix compliance of generated questions, novelty overlap, and workflow automation for exam/question generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper positions V-MATH as supporting scalable, curriculum-aligned exam preparation for a national high-stakes assessment system and emphasizes alignment with the Vietnamese Ministry of Education and Training specification matrix. It also reports creation of a new dataset of about 500 exam sets from 220 official PDFs, which the authors present as a resource for standardized evaluation and broader educational AI deployment.
finding.measure: Dataset creation, curriculum/specification-matrix alignment, and system-level usability for national exam preparation
finding.study_size: approximately 500 exam sets from 220 official PDFs

paper_profiles.title: Interactive, Intelligent Tutoring for Auxiliary Constructions in Geometry Proofs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a long-standing challenge in K-12 geometry: helping students discover auxiliary constructions needed for proof problems. The authors argue that existing geometry proof tutors either do not teach auxiliary constructions or rely on opaque automated reasoning, making them poor tools for helping students learn a transferable problem-solving strategy.

To address this, they developed AGPT (Advanced Geometry Proof Tutor), an interactive geometry tutoring system that combines image-based geometry figure recognition with an automated theorem prover (iGeoTutor). AGPT does not simply present solutions; instead, it guides students through template matching and construction tasks, using limited hints and backtracking to keep students engaged in the reasoning process. The system was evaluated in a pilot study with 78 ninth-grade students from a local high school, who were assigned to one of three groups: a human tutor, iGeoTutor alone, or AGPT.

The main finding is that AGPT performed about as well as a human tutor and significantly better than iGeoTutor alone on the study’s adjusted improvement measure. On the unadjusted score, all groups improved from pre-test to post-test, but no significant difference was detected; when partial credit for correct auxiliary-construction reasoning was included, AGPT showed a statistically significant advantage over iGeoTutor, with no significant difference between AGPT and the human tutor. The paper concludes that exposing the inner workings of a solver through interactive tutoring can help students learn auxiliary constructions more effectively than viewing a non-interactive proof generator.

finding.finding_summary: AGPT improved students’ performance on geometry proof problems involving auxiliary constructions. In the pilot study with n=78 ninth-grade students, all three groups improved from pre-test to post-test, but when partial credit for correctly identified auxiliary constructions was included, the ANOVA on improvement scores showed a significant difference across conditions (F(2,75)=3.23, p=0.045), and Tukey post hoc tests found AGPT significantly better than iGeoTutor, with no significant difference between AGPT and the human tutor.
finding.measure: Geometry proof problem performance on pre-test/post-test, including partial-credit scoring for correct auxiliary constructions

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was designed to teach and support students’ problem-solving strategy for discovering auxiliary constructions, which the authors frame as a transferable skill in geometry proof solving. The study reports that AGPT’s interactive template-matching and construction process helped students engage in thoughtful problem solving, and that some students found alternative correct solutions, suggesting strategic reasoning beyond rote imitation.
finding.measure: Student success in selecting templates and generating correct auxiliary constructions; interaction logs and post-test performance

finding.finding_summary: AGPT appeared to support persistence and engagement for many students, but some students also became frustrated after repeated failed attempts. The paper reports that 15 students solved at least one problem through AGPT’s feedback mechanism, but also notes that some students displayed noticeable frustration and may have given up after seven attempts.
finding.measure: Interaction logs, number of attempts/redirections, and qualitative observations of student behavior during tutoring
finding.study_size: n=26 per condition in the AGPT group; n=78 total

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in K-12 Education: The CyberScholar Initiative
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether CyberScholar, a generative AI writing assistant, can support K-12 students’ writing development through formative feedback. The central question is how the tool functions in real classroom settings when its feedback is aligned with teachers’ rubrics, instructional materials, and expectations.

The study used an exploratory multiple-case qualitative design across four public schools in the United States, spanning Grades 7, 8, 10, and 11 in English Language Arts, Social Studies, and Modern World History classes. The implementation relied on Retrieval Augmented Generation, prompt engineering, and iterative feedback loops during an agile development process. Data came from classroom observations, surveys, and interviews with 121 students and 4 teachers, though only 54 students and 3 teachers completed the post-survey and 8 students plus 1 teacher were interviewed.

Findings suggest that students perceived CyberScholar as useful for detailed and specific feedback, interactive clarification, improved writing quality, and rubric-aligned ratings. Students reported that the tool helped them revise grammar, transitions, conclusions, and organization, and some saw score improvements after revisions. Teachers’ roles appeared to shift toward guiding AI feedback processes rather than solely evaluating work. The authors conclude that CyberScholar has promise as a formative assessment support tool, but they also note limitations in generalizability, the exploratory nature of the evidence, and the need for further research on ethics, critical thinking, and broader classroom applicability.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers reported that CyberScholar supported writing development through detailed, specific, rubric-aligned formative feedback. Among 121 students, the paper reports that 36 students explicitly said they would like to use the tool again, and some students noted improved rubric scores after revision (e.g., one student’s 'Compare' and 'Contrast' score improved from 0 to 2 after using the feedback).
finding.measure: Student and teacher perceptions of writing support; rubric-based writing revisions and scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that CyberScholar may foster critical thinking, metacognition, and self-regulation by prompting students to reflect on feedback, revise iteratively, and engage in dialogue with the AI. Students described using the feedback to think more carefully about revisions and to ask follow-up questions, but the evidence is qualitative and based on perceptions rather than direct skill measures.
finding.measure: Student perceptions/interviews about revision, reflection, and interactive feedback use

finding.finding_summary: Several students described the tool as engaging, motivating, and helpful, and 36 students said they would use it again while 11 expressed hesitation. The study presents the AI feedback process as potentially supporting student agency and engagement, but it does not report quantitative motivation or self-regulation outcomes.
finding.measure: Student survey responses and interview comments about engagement, motivation, and willingness to reuse the tool
finding.study_size: n=54 post-survey respondents; n=8 interviewed students

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests the tool may save time by quickly identifying areas for improvement and by providing fast, personalized feedback, with one student explicitly noting that it was easier and quicker than peer or self-analysis. These claims come from qualitative feedback rather than a measured analysis of time savings or teacher workload.
finding.measure: Perceptions of speed, convenience, and ease of use

paper_profiles.title: aiPlato: A Novel AI Tutoring and Stepwise Feedback System for Physics Homework
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory study examines whether an AI-enabled homework platform, aiPlato, can support open-ended problem solving in an introductory undergraduate physics course. The paper asks how students use the system’s feedback tools, whether greater engagement is associated with better academic performance, and how students perceive the platform’s usability and learning value.

aiPlato provides stepwise, context-sensitive feedback for free-response physics homework through features such as Evaluate My Work, AI Tutor Chat, Show Next Step, hints, and full-solution access. The platform was deployed in a large-enrollment, calculus-based mechanics course at the University of Texas at Arlington during Spring 2025, where 114 students had access and 87 consented to research use of their data. Students completed four optional extra-credit assignments and the authors analyzed log data, final exam scores, course grades, and end-of-semester surveys.

The study found that higher engagement with aiPlato was associated with higher final exam scores and better overall course grade categories, even after adjusting for prior performance. The high-engagement group scored about 13.86 percentage points higher than the low-engagement group on the final exam, corresponding to an estimated Cohen’s d of approximately 0.81, although the authors emphasize that the design is correlational and self-selection may explain some of the observed differences. Survey and qualitative data suggested that students valued the stepwise feedback and iterative revision workflow, but also reported usability problems such as handwriting recognition issues, lag, and occasional unreliability of AI Tutor Chat.

Overall, the paper presents aiPlato as a feasible model for integrating AI-mediated formative feedback into authentic physics homework. The evidence is promising but preliminary: it supports associations between engagement and performance and provides implementation insights, but it does not establish causal effects or test the system in a K-12 setting.

finding.finding_summary: Students who engaged more frequently with aiPlato tended to achieve higher final exam scores on a cumulative physics assessment. After adjusting for prior academic performance, the high-engagement group scored 13.86 percentage points higher than the low-engagement group, corresponding to an estimated Cohen’s d of approximately 0.81 over four optional assignments (low n=39, medium n=32, high n=16; total consented sample n=87).
finding.measure: Cumulative final exam score in introductory mechanics

finding.finding_summary: Survey and usage data suggest that students were generally engaged and perceived the platform as supporting productive struggle, iterative revision, and motivation to persist on multi-step problems. The most frequently used tool was Evaluate My Work, which students often used multiple times per problem, while qualitative comments indicated that the system helped sustain effort and reduced reliance on instructor email support (survey n=87; usage subset n=87 consented).
finding.measure: Platform engagement patterns; end-of-semester Likert survey and open-ended responses

finding.finding_summary: The platform was designed to support stepwise reasoning, revision, and conceptual explanation during open-ended physics problem solving, and students reported that it helped them understand where their reasoning went wrong. Usage patterns showed repeated use of Evaluate My Work and some use of AI Tutor Chat/Show Next Step, indicating iterative self-correction and feedback-driven problem solving rather than answer seeking (n=87 consented students).
finding.measure: Interaction logs, feedback-tool usage, and student survey feedback about reasoning support

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that built-in feedback tools reduced routine homework-related student emails to the instructor and provided instructor-facing analytics such as proficiency maps and detailed usage logs. This suggests a workflow benefit for teachers, although the paper does not quantify time savings or workload reduction with a formal effect size.
finding.measure: Instructor-reported reduction in homework clarification emails; availability of usage logs and proficiency maps

paper_profiles.title: Towards an intelligent assessment system for evaluating the development of algorithmic thinking skills: An exploratory study in Swiss compulsory schools
paper_profiles.venue: arXiv / Doctoral Dissertation, Università della Svizzera Italiana
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This doctoral dissertation addresses the problem of how to assess algorithmic thinking (AT), a core component of computational thinking, across Switzerland’s compulsory education system. The work is motivated by the lack of scalable, replicable, and context-sensitive assessment tools for CT/AT, especially in a multilingual and decentralized school system with substantial regional variation.

The dissertation develops an age-based competence model for computational thinking, then designs a Cross Array Task (CAT) in two formats: an unplugged paper-based version with manual expert scoring and a virtual digital version with automated logging and scoring. It also proposes an Intelligent Assessment System (IAS) based on Bayesian networks with noisy gates to provide real-time probabilistic assessment of multiple AT-related skills rather than a single holistic score.

The empirical work consists of exploratory classroom studies in Swiss compulsory schools across age groups and educational contexts, including preschool, primary, and lower secondary settings. The findings suggest that the CAT can measure AT competencies across age groups and contexts, that AT develops progressively with age, and that there are no overall gender differences though some school-level variation exists. Performance was influenced by task format and situated context, supporting the need for adaptable assessment instruments and careful contextual interpretation. The dissertation concludes that the proposed instrument and IAS have strong potential for large-scale classroom integration, although broader validation and future tutoring capabilities are still needed.

finding.finding_summary: The dissertation directly studies algorithmic thinking (as a component of computational thinking), which aligns most closely with durable skills/critical thinking. Across exploratory classroom studies, the proposed CAT instrument measured AT competencies across age groups, with evidence of progressive development over time. The work reports no overall gender differences, but variations by school/context, indicating the assessment captures meaningful differences in AT performance.
finding.measure: CAT performance; algorithmic thinking competency levels derived from unplugged and virtual Cross Array Task (CAT) assessments

finding.finding_summary: A central contribution is the development of an intelligent assessment system that automates part of the scoring and provides real-time probabilistic assessment of student skills. The virtual CAT and Bayesian-network-based IAS are intended to reduce reliance on manual expert assessment and support semi-automatic large-scale classroom assessment.
finding.measure: Assessment automation / real-time probabilistic scoring; comparison of manual expert assessment vs digital automated assessment

finding.finding_summary: The dissertation is explicitly framed as a scalable assessment framework for Swiss compulsory schools and discusses integration into real classroom settings across multiple cantons. The work argues that the instrument is adaptable to different educational contexts and highlights its potential for large-scale use in diverse schooling systems.
finding.measure: Applicability across Swiss educational contexts; large-scale classroom integration potential

paper_profiles.title: Socratic Mind: Impact of a Novel GenAI-Powered Assessment Tool on Student Learning and Higher-Order Thinking
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study evaluates Socratic Mind, a generative AI-powered formative assessment tool that uses Socratic questioning to support learning and higher-order thinking in an introductory computing course. The paper asks whether AI-mediated dialogue can improve student engagement, perceived learning, actual academic performance, and self-reported gains in problem-solving, critical thinking, self-reflection, and verbal communication.

The intervention was implemented in a large, fully online asynchronous undergraduate computing course at a U.S. research university. Students completed optional extra-credit AI-based assignments aligned to unit quizzes; the tool used instructor-defined prompts, adaptive follow-up questioning, and immediate personalized feedback. The study used a quasi-experimental mixed-methods design with survey data, system logs, course scores, and thematic analysis of open-ended responses.

Findings suggest that students experienced high behavioral, affective, and cognitive engagement and generally rated the tool as usable and effective. Engagement with the tool was associated with higher perceived learning, and a difference-in-differences analysis indicated that the intervention buffered quiz score declines over time, with stronger gains for lower-performing students. Qualitative responses also indicated perceived improvements in problem-solving, critical thinking, and self-reflection, though evidence for verbal communication gains was weaker. Overall, the paper concludes that Socratic, GenAI-mediated formative assessment can scale personalized feedback and promote deeper learning in higher education.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported high levels of affective, behavioral, and cognitive engagement with the GenAI tool (n=171). Mean engagement scores were high across all three subscales: behavioral engagement M=4.07 (SD=0.61), affective engagement M=3.96 (SD=0.76), and cognitive engagement M=3.96 (SD=0.68) on a 5-point scale. Engagement was positively correlated with perceived learning and UX, indicating the tool was experienced as engaging and motivating.
finding.measure: Affective, behavioral, and cognitive engagement scales; system log behavior measures
finding.std_deviation: Affective SD=0.76; Behavioral SD=0.61; Cognitive SD=0.68

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively examined higher-order thinking outcomes through thematic analysis of open-ended responses (n=141) and found that most students perceived gains in problem-solving (69% positive), critical thinking (62% positive), and self-reflection (60% positive). A smaller share reported change in verbal communication (38% positive), partly because many students typed rather than spoke their responses. These findings suggest the Socratic AI prompts supported reflective and analytical thinking more strongly than communication skill growth.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses on problem-solving, critical thinking, self-reflection, and verbal communication

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved course performance on quizzes, with a difference-in-differences model showing a significant positive treatment-by-post interaction (β=.107, p<.05), indicating the AI assignment buffered the typical decline in quiz scores as the course became harder. The authors report that students in the assignment condition experienced an estimated 3.30-point smaller drop in quiz performance than peers, and lower-performing students appeared to benefit more (pre*treatment B=-0.217, p<.05).
finding.measure: Unit quiz scores and course performance data
finding.study_size: n=171 for final analysis; broader assignment pool n=579

finding.finding_summary: The intervention did not produce a statistically significant improvement in test performance, and subsequent unit assessments/final scores were described as highly similar between groups. In the difference-in-differences test model, the post*treatment interaction was not significant (β=-.053, p>.05), suggesting no detectable effect on higher-stakes test outcomes.
finding.measure: Unit test scores and final course scores

paper_profiles.title: Directive, Metacognitive or a Blend of Both? A Comparison of AI-Generated Feedback Types on Student Engagement, Confidence, and Outcomes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how different types of AI-generated feedback influence student engagement, confidence, and the quality of revised work. The central problem is how to design AI feedback that balances directive, actionable guidance with metacognitive prompts that encourage reflection and self-regulated learning.

The study compares three feedback conditions: directive, metacognitive, and hybrid (a blend of both), implemented in the RiPPLE adaptive learning platform. It uses a semester-long randomized controlled trial with 329 students in an introductory university design and programming course. The feedback was engineered to differ linguistically and functionally, and the authors also analyzed its surface features (word count, imperatives, reflective prompts) to verify the manipulation.

Results showed that the feedback types were clearly distinguishable linguistically: directive feedback contained the most imperatives, metacognitive feedback the most reflective prompts, and hybrid feedback mixed both. Engagement time did not differ significantly across groups, but students receiving metacognitive feedback were less likely to revise than those receiving directive or hybrid feedback, with the hybrid condition showing the highest revision rate. Confidence ratings and resource quality were similar across conditions, suggesting that while feedback type changed revision behavior, it did not produce measurable differences in perceived confidence or final product quality in this context. The authors conclude that hybrid AI feedback may be a promising design for combining immediate actionable guidance with reflective scaffolding, though they note limitations including a single-course setting, high baseline performance, and no evidence of transfer beyond the course.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly compared AI feedback types intended to support metacognition and self-regulated learning. Hybrid feedback produced the most revisions, while metacognitive feedback led to the lowest revision action on feedback (12.1% vs. 21.1% directive and 27.5% hybrid; χ2(2)=8.74, p=.013), but confidence and final resource quality did not differ significantly across conditions.
finding.measure: Revision behavior, action on feedback, confidence ratings on a 1–5 scale, and resource quality scores
finding.effect_size: OR=2.93 for Directive vs. Metacognitive; OR=0.23 for Metacognitive vs. Hybrid; η2 not_reported for behavioral outcome; odds ratios reported from logistic mixed-effects model
finding.confidence_interval: Directive vs. Metacognitive OR 2.93, 95% CI [1.25, 6.88]; Metacognitive vs. Hybrid OR 0.23, 95% CI [0.10, 0.55]; confidence and outcome models non-significant

finding.finding_summary: Feedback type did not significantly affect students' confidence in the quality of their work. Estimated marginal means on the 1–5 scale were similar across Directive (3.63), Metacognitive (3.25), and Hybrid (3.55) conditions, and the omnibus test was non-significant (χ2=0.96, p=.62).
finding.measure: Self-rated confidence in work quality on a 5-point ordinal scale

finding.finding_summary: The study found no statistically significant differences in resource outcome quality across feedback conditions. Estimated marginal means on the rescaled 1–5 quality measure were very close: Directive 3.62, Metacognitive 3.72, and Hybrid 3.75 (χ2=1.40, p=.49).
finding.measure: Resource outcome quality scores based on peer ratings, instructor moderation, and algorithmic adjustments

paper_profiles.title: Metacognitive Training in Professional Development Can Improve and Sustain Student Achievement
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school students; in-service secondary STEM teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a mathematics-and-science professional development system (the MAST System) improved student achievement in secondary schools. The core problem is persistent underperformance in U.S. K-12 mathematics and science, and the paper argues that improving teacher quality through sustained in-service professional development is a promising route to higher student outcomes.

The intervention was a two-year, school-based PD program for secondary STEM teachers in Alliance College-Ready Public Schools in Los Angeles. The program combined workshops, instructional rounds, classroom coaching, debriefing, co-planning, action research, and monthly rubric-based feedback. A central feature was "Defense of Instruction," a metacognitive reflection process in which teachers justified instructional decisions using classroom and student data, with the goal of building adaptive expertise.

The study reports descriptive and comparative evidence from seven schools, 45 teachers, and more than 11,000 students, using California Standards Test mathematics scores as the main outcome and ELA scores as a comparison marker. Schools implementing the MAST System showed larger gains in mathematics than the district and state, while ELA gains were similar across groups, suggesting the effect was specific to mathematics rather than general enrollment change. The authors also report that gains continued for up to two years after the intervention ended, especially in schools where rubric scores indicated stronger implementation of adaptive-expert practices.

Because the paper is not an experimental study and relies on school-level comparison patterns plus rubric correlations, its evidence is best characterized as observational/correlational rather than causal. The main conclusion is that sustained, metacognition-rich professional development may improve secondary mathematics achievement and help institutionalize continuing improvement in schools.

finding.finding_summary: Across seven Alliance secondary schools (45 teachers; over 11,000 students), mathematics performance increased after the two-year MAST intervention. The paper reports a rise in students at or above Proficient from 11% to 29% at the Alliance schools (normalized change <c>=0.20), compared with much smaller changes in the district and state, and one school increased at-or-above-Proficient from 14% to 53% (<c>=0.45) while reducing Below Basic from 58% to 25% (<c>=-0.57).
finding.measure: California Standards Test (CST) mathematics performance categories and normalized change in mathematics scores
finding.effect_size: <c>=0.20 overall at Alliance schools; <c>=0.45 and -0.57 in an example school

finding.finding_summary: The paper also uses English Language Arts CST scores as an internal marker to test whether the mathematics gains reflected broader school change or student composition shifts. ELA improvements at the Alliance schools were similar to the district and state, with normalized changes of <c>=0.08 above Basic and <c>=-0.19 below Basic, suggesting the intervention's strongest effect was specific to mathematics rather than a general testing gain across subjects.
finding.measure: California Standards Test (CST) English Language Arts performance categories and normalized change

finding.finding_summary: A central mechanism of the program was strengthening teachers' metacognition, reflective practice, and adaptive expertise, and the paper reports that schools with higher MAST rubric scores showed larger student gains. Schools in the top quartile of rubric averages had substantially better mathematics normalized changes (e.g., average rubric score 2.3 with +0.18 at/above Proficient and -0.34 below Basic) than schools in the bottom quartile (average rubric score 0.8 with near-zero change), indicating that implementation of reflective, data-driven teaching practices was associated with stronger outcomes.
finding.measure: MAST rubric scores reflecting metacognitive/adaptive-expert teaching practices; association with student mathematics gains
finding.effect_size: Top quartile rubric avg 2.3 vs bottom quartile 0.8; associated normalized changes +0.18 vs near 0 and -0.34 vs near 0

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that achievement gains persisted after the formal two-year PD ended, and four of the five improving schools continued to increase student performance during the two years following the intervention. Across these five schools, average normalized change from the final intervention year to two years later was +0.15 for Advanced/Proficient and -0.33 for Below Basic, which the authors interpret as evidence that the school or teacher culture changed in a sustainable way.
finding.measure: Post-intervention continuation of CST mathematics gains over two years

paper_profiles.title: Developing and Evaluating a Large Language Model-Based Automated Feedback System Grounded in Evidence-Centered Design for Supporting Physics Problem Solving
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether an LLM-based automated feedback system can support students’ physics problem solving when the feedback is grounded in evidence-centered design (ECD). The authors argue that problem solving in physics requires multiple knowledge types and that generic LLM feedback is risky because it can be too holistic, inaccurate, or confabulated. Their design therefore constrains GPT-4o with a problem-specific evidentiary scheme that specifies the conceptual, conditional, procedural, factual, mathematical, and metacognitive evidence expected in student solutions.

The system was implemented as a web-based, two-step feedback tool for students in the German Physics Olympiad. Students submitted written solutions, received short LLM-generated feedback, revised their work, and then received a second round of feedback. The paper evaluates both the design and user perceptions, focusing on perceived usefulness and perceived correctness, and compares those perceptions to expert judgments of actual correctness.

Results from N=64 ratings showed that students generally found the feedback useful (M=3.6/5, SD=1.7) and accurate (M=4.4/5, SD=1.0). However, human raters found that 13 of 64 feedback instances (about 20%) contained errors, ranging from minor calculation mistakes to incorrect concepts, assumptions, or misclassification of valid alternative solutions. Students rarely detected these errors, and perceived accuracy did not differ significantly between correct and incorrect feedback. The authors conclude that ECD-grounded prompting can produce promising feedback, but reliability, handling of alternative solution paths, and explicit safeguards against uncritical acceptance remain major challenges.

finding.finding_summary: The LLM-based system was designed to support physics problem solving, and students generally perceived the feedback as useful for understanding and working on the problem (M=3.6/5, SD=1.7; n=64 ratings). The intervention did not measure learning gains directly, but user ratings suggest the feedback supported scientific problem-solving processes in physics competition tasks.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness of LLM-generated feedback for physics problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies feedback intended to support problem-solving ability and critical reflection on solution approaches, which are durable skills. Students rated the feedback as highly accurate on average (M=4.4/5, SD=1.0; n=64), but expert review found factual/strategy errors in 13 of 64 cases (~20%), and students rarely noticed them, indicating both promise and risk for metacognitive support.
finding.measure: Perceived correctness of feedback; expert-coded correctness of feedback; student recognition of errors

finding.finding_summary: The system was explicitly framed as a scalable, low-cost alternative to human tutoring and automated feedback delivery. The authors estimated the average cost of one response–feedback cycle at approximately USD 0.007, indicating substantial potential efficiency for providing individualized feedback at scale, although no workload study or time-on-task comparison was conducted.
finding.measure: Estimated API cost per feedback cycle

paper_profiles.title: Mentigo: An Intelligent Agent for Mentoring Students in the Creative Problem Solving Process
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of supporting middle school students as they work through creative problem solving (CPS) tasks, especially when teachers have limited time to provide structured, personalized, and emotionally supportive guidance. The authors argue that large language models (LLMs) can be repurposed from task-assistance tools into mentor-like agents that guide students through the full CPS process, from problem discovery to solution implementation.

To do this, the paper presents Mentigo, an LLM-based mentor agent with a controller-mentor architecture. The system was built from authentic classroom data: 80 hours of recorded CPS workshops with 57 middle school students and 12 mentors, yielding 2,362 interaction sequences and coding of 23 student states and 20 mentor strategies. The agent uses stage-based task management, state detection, strategy selection, adaptive feedback, and empathetic prompting to provide personalized guidance across six CPS stages.

The system was evaluated in a within-subject user study with 12 middle school students (ages 12–14) comparing Mentigo to a baseline agent, and also reviewed by five expert teachers. The paper reports that Mentigo improved student engagement and creative outcomes, and helped promote deeper cognitive processes such as analysis and creativity. The authors conclude that structured, adaptive, and empathetic AI mentoring may be a promising way to support middle school CPS, while also reducing the burden on human teachers.

finding.finding_summary: In a within-subject study with 12 middle school students (ages 12–14), Mentigo was reported to improve student engagement relative to a baseline agent. The paper also reports that the system’s adaptive and empathetic interactions supported motivation and emotional comfort during CPS tasks, though exact effect sizes are not reported in the provided text.
finding.measure: Student engagement; perceived usability; cognitive load questionnaires; interview feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies creative problem solving support, including deeper cognitive engagement, analysis, creativity, critical thinking, and reflective reasoning. In the user study with 12 middle school students, Mentigo was described as significantly improving creative outcomes and promoting deeper cognitive processes compared with the baseline system, but the excerpt does not provide numerical effect sizes.
finding.measure: Creative outcomes; depth of reflection; CPS task performance; learning reports; post-test measures

finding.finding_summary: The intervention targets creative problem solving in a school learning context rather than a specific traditional academic subject. The paper reports that Mentigo significantly enhanced creative outcomes in CPS tasks for middle school students, with results based on a controlled within-subject user study and expert teacher review.
finding.measure: Creative problem solving task outcomes; learning reports; expert review

paper_profiles.title: CLASS: A Design Framework for Building Intelligent Tutoring Systems Based on Learning Science Principles
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes CLASS (Conversational Learning with Analytical Step-by-Step Strategies), a design framework for building intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) powered by large language models. The authors argue that effective ITS should do two things well: provide scaffolded, tutor-like step-by-step guidance and support natural conversational interaction. To operationalize this, they create two synthetic GPT-4-generated datasets: a scaffolding dataset containing main problems, subproblems, hints, incorrect responses, and feedback; and a conversational dataset containing simulated student-tutor dialogues with explicit decision logic and response templates.

The proof-of-concept system, SPOCK, is trained on Vicuna-13B and fine-tuned on biology textbooks plus the two CLASS datasets. The domain and evaluation context are introductory college-level biology, not K-12. The paper also introduces subproblem-augmented dual retrieval to fetch relevant educational passages for both the main problem and its subproblems, reporting a 3.5% absolute improvement in LLaMA accuracy on the MMLU College Biology and High School Biology subsets when subproblems are added.

Evaluation is preliminary and largely expert-based. Four biology subject-matter experts reviewed synthetic scaffolding items and interacted with SPOCK through a think-aloud protocol. They rated factual correctness, relevance, completeness, and motivation highly, and the authors conclude that the framework can support explainable, stepwise tutoring with encouraging feedback. However, the study is a proof-of-concept with no student outcome data, and its evidence is centered on college biology content and expert judgments rather than K-12 learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that expert reviewers judged the scaffolding dataset and SPOCK’s biology tutoring behavior to be factually correct, relevant, and useful for breaking questions into subproblems. In a related retrieval experiment, adding subproblems to the main query improved LLaMA accuracy by 3.5% on the MMLU College Biology and High School Biology subsets, suggesting improved question decomposition and reasoning support.
finding.measure: Expert ratings of factual correctness/relevance/completeness; MMLU College Biology and High School Biology accuracy
finding.study_size: n=4 SMEs for human evaluation; benchmark sample size not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Experts reported that SPOCK’s responses were encouraging and motivating, and that its supportive feedback could help students persevere with challenging biology concepts. The evaluation protocol explicitly included a motivation dimension, and the SMEs rated this aspect favorably on a 5-point scale (reported average ratings around 4.0-4.67 across motivation-related items).
finding.measure: Motivation/engagement ratings from SME think-aloud evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The framework aims to reduce manual ITS authoring by using GPT-4 to generate scaffolding items and conversational training data, and by using indexed retrieval to support factual responses. The paper does not measure teacher workload directly, but it presents automation of dataset creation and response generation as a practical efficiency gain for ITS development and maintenance.
finding.measure: Dataset generation and system design features; no direct workload metric reported

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing LLMs for Physics Problem-Solving using Reinforcement Learning with Human-AI Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how to improve large language model performance on high school physics problem solving, with a focus on reasoning quality and answer accuracy. The authors propose Reinforcement Learning with Human and Artificial Intelligence Feedback (RLHAIF), a hybrid feedback pipeline intended to create better preference data than AI-only or human-only approaches.

The study uses the PhyQA dataset, which contains 8,100 high-school physics question-answer pairs scraped from Indian NCERT grades 11–12 textbooks and expanded into preference pairs by generating multiple responses from several models (LLaMA2, WizardMath, Mistral, MAmmoTH, Gemini) and ranking them using GPT-4 with human validation. They then train a reward model and fine-tune LLMs using PPO, DPO, and ReMax. The strongest result is Mistral-PPO, which outperforms the paper’s other settings and the cited SciPhy-RAG benchmark on text-generation metrics, reaching 58.67 METEOR and 87.49 BERTScore.

The paper also includes a small manual evaluation on 100 randomly sampled problems, reporting 38/100 correct for Mistral-PPO and an error analysis showing that computation errors are the most common failure mode. Overall, the paper concludes that combining human and AI feedback can improve physics reasoning in LLMs, but the approach is computationally expensive and still struggles with multi-step arithmetic and deduction.

finding.finding_summary: The RLHAIF pipeline improved high school physics problem-solving performance, especially for Mistral-PPO. On the paper’s main evaluation table, Mistral-PPO achieved 58.67 METEOR and 87.49 BERTScore, outperforming the cited SciPhy-RAG benchmark on text-generation metrics and exceeding other model/settings in the study.
finding.measure: Physics question-answering performance on the PhyQA benchmark; automatic text-generation metrics (METEOR, BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore) and a 100-item human correctness check
finding.study_size: n=8100 for training/evaluation dataset; n=100 for manual accuracy/error analysis

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates reasoning-related skills such as critical assumption, problem deduction, arithmetic calculation, logical reasoning, conceptual understanding, and error detection. In a 100-response manual reasoning assessment of Mistral-PPO, the model showed strengths in some reasoning dimensions but still had substantial weaknesses, especially in arithmetic calculation (reported as a major challenge in about 91% of cases).
finding.measure: Human-rated reasoning score distribution across six skills: critical assumption, problem deduction, arithmetic calculation, logical reasoning, conceptual understanding, and error detection

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved performance on high-school physics textbook problems drawn from NCERT grades 11–12. In the 100-example accuracy check, Mistral-PPO achieved 38/100 correct responses, compared with 21/100 for Mistral SFT and 18/100 for LLaMA2-7B PPO, indicating better performance on this specific academic task.
finding.measure: Correct/incorrect accuracy on sampled high-school physics questions from PhyQA

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education from 2007 to 2018. The authors ask how the literature has developed over time, how AI in education is conceptualized, what ethical issues are discussed, and what kinds of AI applications have been studied in higher education.

Using an explicit search strategy across EBSCO Education Source, Web of Science, and Scopus, the review identified 2,656 records, screened 1,549 titles/abstracts, retrieved 291 full texts, and ultimately included 146 articles. The reviewed studies mostly came from Computer Science and STEM fields, used quantitative methods, and focused on four application areas: profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalisation, and intelligent tutoring systems.

The review concludes that the field is dominated by technical and predictive work, with relatively little educational or pedagogical grounding and very limited critical reflection on ethical risks such as privacy. Most studies addressed undergraduate contexts and academic support or institutional services, and many reported promising prototype or pilot results, but longitudinal evidence and educator-centered perspectives were scarce. The paper argues that AI in higher education needs stronger connections to educational theory, ethics, and the practical concerns of educators.

finding.finding_summary: Across 146 reviewed studies, AI applications were frequently framed as tools to reduce workload and improve efficiency in higher education. Examples included automated grading, feedback generation, admissions prediction, student-risk detection, and administrative decision support; many studies reported high classification or agreement accuracy (e.g. 81.19% dropout prediction accuracy with ANN in one study, and 94.6%–98.2% agreement for automated essay scoring).
finding.measure: Accuracy, agreement with human raters, and administrative/teacher workload reduction described across reviewed studies
finding.study_size: n=146 articles reviewed; individual primary-study samples varied

finding.finding_summary: A substantial share of the reviewed literature examined institutional and administrative uses of AI, including admissions decisions, course scheduling, drop-out prediction, student profiling, and support for policy or management decisions. The review reports that 48 studies (32.8%) focused on institutional/administrative services, and the remaining results suggest these systems can support timely intervention and decision-making at scale.
finding.measure: Institutional and administrative decision-support applications coded across studies

finding.finding_summary: Some reviewed AI systems targeted student engagement, motivation, self-regulation, and persistence, especially through early-warning systems and intelligent tutoring environments. The review notes that several studies used behavioral data to identify low-engagement students or predict motivation, but most were short-term pilot studies and the overall evidence was described as preliminary rather than definitive.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, and related behavioral indicators
finding.study_size: n=146 articles reviewed; individual study samples varied

finding.finding_summary: The review includes a smaller set of studies on durable skills, especially collaboration and metacognitive/self-regulatory support through intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive systems. Some applications provided collaborative problem solving, automated feedback, or support for learning strategies, but the review emphasizes that evidence was limited, often short-term, and frequently based on prototype implementations rather than rigorous long-term tests.
finding.measure: Collaboration, self-regulation, learning strategies, and related learner-process outcomes
finding.study_size: n=146 articles reviewed; individual study samples varied

finding.finding_summary: The review covers automated essay scoring, writing feedback, and reading/writing tutoring systems, which generally reported encouraging results such as high computer-human agreement and improved revision or feedback processes. However, the authors also note ongoing concerns about feedback quality and genre suitability, so the overall picture is positive but qualified.
finding.measure: Writing quality, automated essay scoring agreement, and feedback outcomes
finding.study_size: n=146 articles reviewed; individual study samples varied

finding.finding_summary: A subset of the reviewed intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning studies targeted mathematics or quantitatively oriented coursework, including mathematics, statistics, and related STEM subjects. The review reports generally positive preliminary results for these systems, but the evidence base is small and mainly short-term pilot work.
finding.measure: Performance in mathematics/statistics-related tutoring and learning environments
finding.study_size: n=146 articles reviewed; individual study samples varied

finding.finding_summary: Several AI applications were used in STEM and science-oriented contexts, including virtual laboratories, engineering courses, medicine, and computer science. These studies often reported positive preliminary results for tutoring, feedback, and adaptive support, but the review does not identify robust causal evidence or long-term validation.
finding.measure: Performance in STEM/science learning tasks, virtual labs, and content mastery
finding.study_size: n=146 articles reviewed; individual study samples varied

finding.finding_summary: The review includes AI applications across other academic subjects such as business, languages, psychology, and engineering. These studies generally reported promising performance for tutoring, personalization, and assessment tools, but the evidence is fragmented across domains and mostly descriptive or pilot in nature.
finding.measure: Course and subject-specific academic performance across non-literacy, non-numeracy domains
finding.study_size: n=146 articles reviewed; individual study samples varied

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings / position paper (venue not reported in provided text)
paper_profiles.population: All educational levels (primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional development); not a K-12 empirical sample
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the potential opportunities and challenges of large language models—especially ChatGPT—for education. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it surveys emerging uses of LLMs for students and teachers, including content generation, personalized learning support, feedback, assessment, tutoring, and educational dialogue. It also discusses risks such as bias, privacy, copyright, overreliance, academic integrity, and the difficulty of distinguishing AI-generated from human-generated text.

The paper is framed as a conceptual and normative analysis grounded in examples from recent early studies and use cases across education settings. It argues that LLMs could support learning by providing personalized explanations, prompts, practice tasks, and feedback, and could help teachers with lesson planning, assessment, and feedback generation. However, the authors emphasize that these benefits depend on careful implementation, human oversight, ethical governance, and curricular supports that foster critical thinking and fact-checking.

The target context spans elementary through higher education and professional training, with examples drawn mostly from research literature rather than a single study sample. The paper concludes that LLMs are promising but require responsible integration, clear institutional policies, and further empirical research on best practices and educational outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can support durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, and question-asking when they are used to generate prompts, alternative perspectives, explanations, and scaffolds. At the same time, it warns that overreliance on model-generated answers may weaken students’ critical thinking and independent inquiry; these claims are conceptual rather than based on a direct empirical effect estimate.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of critical thinking, problem-solving, and question-asking support/risk

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly claims that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by assisting with lesson planning, feedback generation, assessment, quiz creation, and summarization. It cites prior examples such as semi-automated grading and feedback generation, but the paper itself does not present original empirical data; therefore no effect size can be extracted.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, assessment efficiency, and content generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is the institutional implications of adopting LLMs in education, including governance, privacy, copyright, fairness, sustainability, and academic integrity. The authors argue that responsible adoption requires policy frameworks, human oversight, training, and access strategies; these are conceptual recommendations rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: Policy/governance implications, privacy, fairness, integrity, and sustainability considerations

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education published from 2016 to 2022. The authors use PRISMA-guided searching, screening, and coding to map where the research was conducted, who conducted it, what student levels and subject domains were studied, who the AI was intended to support, and the main functions AI served in higher education.

The review identified 371 records through electronic and hand searching, screened 138 full-text articles, and excluded 237 studies, leaving 138 peer-reviewed journal articles for analysis. The paper does not evaluate a single intervention; instead, it synthesizes the field and finds growth in publications in 2021–2022, a shift in publication leadership from the US to China, and a strong concentration on undergraduate students and language learning. The most common AI uses were assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning, with students the primary intended users. The authors conclude that AI in higher education is expanding quickly but remains concentrated in a few countries and disciplines, with gaps in graduate-level research, managerial uses, and more innovative applications.

finding.finding_summary: The review found that language learning was the most common subject domain (17%), including writing, reading, and vocabulary acquisition. AI was frequently used for automated feedback on writing and text-based support, suggesting that AI applications were often aimed at improving literacy-related outcomes in higher education, though the paper does not report pooled effect sizes.
finding.measure: Language learning activities and literacy-related AI uses (writing, reading, vocabulary; automated feedback systems)

finding.finding_summary: Durable-skill outcomes were a recurring focus, especially critical thinking, higher-order thinking, and metacognitive/self-regulated learning processes. The review notes studies that evaluated reflections, achievement goals, community identity, and higher-order thinking, and reports that AI was used to support self-regulated learning and student decision-making, but it does not aggregate effect sizes.
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking, reflections, achievement goals, self-regulated learning, and related cognitive processes

finding.finding_summary: The paper documents AI uses aimed at motivation, persistence, and emotion-related support, including a virtual change agent that supported goal initiation, planning, action control, and emotion control. It also notes studies using AI to determine student emotions while learning, but no quantitative synthesis is reported.
finding.measure: Student emotions, persistence/volition, and engagement-related supports

finding.finding_summary: Operational efficiency was a major theme, with AI used for automatic assessment, generating questions, learning analytics, curriculum sequencing, instructional design, and administrative data analysis. The review states that automatic assessment was the most common specific use within assessment/evaluation (26 studies) and that AI reduced instructor grading time and supported organizational tasks, but it does not report pooled effect sizes.
finding.measure: Assessment automation, question generation, learning analytics, instructional design, and student-data management
