Across 45 student Python solutions, the models achieved 84.44%–88.89% accuracy in judging correctness, but feedback quality was uneven: 63% of hints were accurate and complete while 37% contained errors such as wrong line identification, incorrect explanations, or hallucinated issues.
finding.measure: Accuracy of correctness classification and categorized quality of generated programming feedback hints
finding.study_size: n=45 student solutions; 190 feedback hints across four LLMs

finding.finding_summary: The study substantively examines whether LLMs can support reasoning and problem-solving by identifying student logic mistakes in code. The authors report that while the models often detected surface-level issues, they frequently struggled to pinpoint deeper reasoning errors, and 37% of hints were flawed in some way.
finding.measure: Quality of model-generated hints for reasoning mistakes in student code

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames LLM feedback generation as a way to automate and scale instructional feedback in programming courses, reducing the burden of providing timely individualized comments. While it does not measure teacher workload directly, the results suggest the approach could improve feedback production efficiency, though reliability limitations remain significant.
finding.measure: Automated generation of feedback for programming assignments

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI as a Tool for Enhancing Reflective Learning in Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI, specifically large language models (LLMs), can support reflective learning by scaffolding student self-assessment, deeper analysis of experiences, and critical thinking. The authors frame the problem as a scalability challenge in traditional reflective pedagogy: teachers may not have the time or expertise to provide individualized, timely feedback that sustains meaningful reflection.

The study uses a simulated project-based learning scenario in which GPT-4o acts as a reflective tutor and a simulated student engages in multi-turn dialogue about a completed group project on designing smart devices for campus environmental protection. The paper focuses on prompt engineering for reflective dialogue, comparing richer prompt guidance with a truncated prompt, and then evaluates the resulting sessions with GPT-4o as an automatic judge using reflection rubrics and Bloom’s taxonomy. Five dialogue sessions were generated, and the authors also analyze tutor prompts and student responses qualitatively.

The paper concludes that pedagogically aligned prompts can make LLMs useful for scalable reflective guidance, producing dialogues that elicit balanced reflection, insights about collaboration and project-based learning, and forward-looking action plans. However, the evidence is based on simulated interactions rather than authentic students, so the authors explicitly caution that future work should test these approaches in real educational contexts and consider risks such as over-reliance, bias, and hallucinations.

finding.finding_summary: In a simulated project-based learning reflection task, GPT-4o-guided dialogue supported deeper reflective thinking, including analysis of teamwork, disagreement, shared vision, and future planning. The paper reports five dialogue sessions averaging about 5 turns and over 130 words per turn, and the selected session was rated 8/10 for depth of reflection and 9/10 for insights and learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Reflective dialogue quality; reflection rubric scores; Bloom’s taxonomy classification of student responses

paper_profiles.title: Developing and Evaluating a Large Language Model-Based Automated Feedback System Grounded in Evidence-Centered Design for Supporting Physics Problem Solving
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether a large language model (LLM)-based automated feedback system can support students’ physics problem solving, and whether students can judge the quality of that feedback accurately. The authors argue that problem solving is more complex than conceptual recall and therefore requires feedback grounded in evidence about multiple knowledge types and skills, including conceptual, conditional, procedural, factual, mathematical, and metacognitive components.

To address this, they developed a web-based feedback system for physics problems using Evidence-Centered Design (ECD) to constrain GPT-4o-generated feedback. The system presents a problem, a student solution, and a problem-specific evidentiary scheme, then returns short, targeted feedback intended to be analytical rather than a full solution. The system was evaluated during the first stage of the German Physics Olympiad, where participating secondary school students voluntarily used it as an online problem-solving training tool.

The evaluation focused on perceived usefulness and perceived correctness, plus an expert check of actual correctness. Students generally rated the feedback as useful (M=3.6/5, SD=1.7, n=64) and highly accurate (M=4.4/5, SD=1.0, n=64). However, human raters found that 13 of 64 feedback instances (about 20%) contained errors, including calculation mistakes, wrong concepts, and misclassification of valid alternative approaches. Students rarely noticed these errors, and perceived accuracy did not differ significantly between correct and incorrect feedback (Mann–Whitney U=363, p=0.543). The paper concludes that ECD-grounded LLM feedback shows promise but still requires stronger safeguards, better handling of alternative solution paths, and improved student awareness of possible AI errors.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that an ECD-grounded GPT-4o feedback system can provide scientifically appropriate feedback for physics problem solving, and students generally rated it as useful and accurate. In the main evaluation, 64 student ratings showed perceived usefulness of M=3.6/5 (SD=1.7) and perceived accuracy of M=4.4/5 (SD=1.0), while human raters judged 51 of 64 feedback instances correct (about 80%) and found 13/64 (about 20%) contained errors.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness/accuracy ratings for physics problem-solving feedback; expert review of feedback correctness

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was designed to support physics problem-solving processes, including analytical reasoning and metacognitive aspects such as identifying relevant evidence and next steps. Students generally found the feedback helpful for working on the problem, but a substantial minority criticized it as insufficiently adaptive to their own solution paths, and the paper notes that correct alternative approaches were sometimes misclassified as incorrect.
finding.measure: Student ratings/comments on usefulness and adaptivity of feedback for problem solving; expert review of feedback alignment with student solutions

finding.finding_summary: Students’ subjective evaluations suggest the system was generally engaging/helpful enough to be perceived as supportive during problem solving, but the paper does not directly measure motivation, persistence, or self-regulation. The closest reported evidence is that several students explicitly described the feedback as helpful or adaptive in open-text responses, while others noted frustration with non-adaptive feedback.
finding.measure: Open-text elaborations and Likert ratings of perceived usefulness

paper_profiles.title: Where’s the Line? A Classroom Activity on Ethical and Constructive Use of Generative AI in Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical instructional problem: how to help students think critically about the ethical and educational implications of generative AI use in coursework. Rather than proposing a technical AI tutor or an automated feedback system, it describes a classroom activity intended to help students reason about where AI use supports learning, where it undermines learning, and where it crosses into academic dishonesty.

The activity is designed for physics courses and is built around 10–12 short scenarios involving generative AI, small-group ranking and boundary-setting, class discussion, and optional reflective writing or AI use policy drafting. The paper situates the activity in social constructivist learning theory, metacognition, and ethics education, emphasizing student dialogue, shared norm-setting, and reflective judgment.

The paper is largely descriptive and pedagogical rather than evaluative. It reports that, across implementations, students’ reflections suggested greater clarity about appropriate AI use, more awareness of prompt design and metacognitive learning, and more nuanced ethical reasoning about when AI supports or bypasses understanding. However, these claims are based on informal student reflections and discussion rather than formal outcome measures, so the paper does not provide causal evidence of effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: The activity is intended to strengthen metacognition, ethical reasoning, and collaborative judgment through scenario ranking, boundary-setting, and class discussion. The paper reports that students’ reflective writing and discussion suggested increased clarity about appropriate AI use, greater awareness of how prompt design affects learning, and more nuanced reasoning about when AI supports versus bypasses understanding, but these observations are not based on formal assessment measures.
finding.measure: Student reflective writing and class discussion

finding.finding_summary: The activity aims to shape classroom norms and student understanding of academic integrity by engaging learners in participatory policy and boundary-setting. The paper argues that this approach can help cultivate a dynamic, shared culture of integrity around generative AI use, but it does not report formal institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Student discussion of institutional academic integrity frameworks and optional AI use policy drafting

paper_profiles.title: Learning Analytics from Spoken Discussion Dialogs in Flipped Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether features extracted from students’ in-class spoken discussion dialogs in a flipped classroom can predict group learning outcomes. The central question is whether conversational properties such as topic relevance, sentiment, cognitive processing, information exchange, and context cohesion are associated with exam performance on the week’s course topic.

The study was conducted in a freshman engineering mathematics course at a university, where students watched lecture videos before class and then solved problems in small groups during class. The authors recorded and manually transcribed 9 weeks of discussion for 10 groups (90 group-discussion samples total), then computed speech, semantic, LIWC, and acoustic features at the segment and group levels. Statistical analyses showed that higher learning outcomes were associated with more topic-relevant, more positive, more logically structured, and more cohesive discussions, as well as greater information exchange. A support vector machine trained on statistically significant features achieved 78.9% accuracy in predicting high/mid/low group learning outcome, suggesting that spoken discussion analytics can be used to characterize and predict collaborative learning performance in a flipped classroom.

finding.finding_summary: The study focused on a freshman engineering mathematics flipped classroom and used exam performance on topic-specific midterm and final questions as the learning outcome. Topic-relevant discussion features were positively associated with better math learning outcomes, and an SVM using selected discussion features predicted high/mid/low group outcome with 78.9% accuracy (90 group-discussion samples).
finding.measure: Topic-specific midterm and final examination scores mapped to weekly mathematics topics; group learning outcome ranking
finding.study_size: n=90 group discussions (10 groups across 9 weeks)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly analyzes discussion indicators related to collaboration, logical thinking, and conversational quality, all framed as indicators of durable skills in group problem solving. Higher learning outcomes were associated with more turns, more logical language (e.g., causation, conjunction, comparison), higher topic relevance, and greater cohesion in discussion dialogs.
finding.measure: Discussion dialogue features: number of turns, LIWC cognitive-processing categories, topic relevance score, cohesion score

finding.finding_summary: The study found that sentiment-related features in group discussions were associated with learning outcome. High-performing groups showed more positive sentiment (e.g., assent) and lower negative sentiment (e.g., negative emotion, anger, anxiety, risk, negation) than low-performing groups; no standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: LIWC sentiment categories; acoustic proxy for emotion (Min H1-H2)

paper_profiles.title: Human-Generative AI Collaborative Problem Solving Who Leads and How Students Perceive the Interactions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how undergraduate students collaborate with ChatGPT during a maze design and problem-solving activity, focusing on who leads the interaction, how students perceive the interaction experience, and how those perceptions relate to agency and collaborative problem-solving. The authors frame the work as an exploratory study of human-generative AI collaboration in an educational setting, motivated by concerns that students may over-rely on AI and lose agency while solving complex tasks.

The study involved 79 undergraduate students in Singapore enrolled in an interdisciplinary digital literacy course. Students worked in small groups on a 3D Maze task with ChatGPT available as a flexible support tool; they were not given rigid instructions on how to use the AI. After the activity, students completed surveys on collaborative problem-solving and sense of agency, and wrote reflections about their and ChatGPT’s contributions and their interaction experiences.

Content analysis of reflections identified three collaboration patterns: human leads, even contribution, and AI leads, with human leads and even contribution comprising 77.21% of cases. Students also reported mostly positive or mixed interaction experiences (67.09%). In correlational and regression analyses, the only significant predictor of collaborative problem-solving was sense of negative agency, which negatively predicted students’ self-reported collaborative problem-solving (b = -0.34, p = .006, adjusted R2 = .108). The authors conclude that while many students use ChatGPT as a supportive tool, a meaningful minority appear to let AI lead, and feelings of lost control may undermine collaborative problem-solving.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies collaborative problem-solving as a durable skill in the context of human-ChatGPT collaboration. In the sample of 79 undergraduates, 77.21% reported human-led or even-contribution collaboration, while 15.19% reported AI-led collaboration. In regression, sense of negative agency significantly and negatively predicted collaborative problem-solving (b = -0.34, p = .006), with the model explaining 10.8% of the variance (adjusted R2 = .108; n = 72).
finding.measure: Self-reported collaborative problem-solving survey; reflection-coded collaboration type; multiple linear regression predicting collaborative problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: The study substantively examines students’ sense of agency and interaction experience with ChatGPT, both of which are social-emotional constructs. More positive interaction experiences were positively correlated with sense of positive agency (r = 0.26*), while sense of negative agency was negatively correlated with collaborative problem-solving (r = -0.35**) and negatively correlated with positive agency (r = -0.41***).
finding.measure: Sense of Positive Agency scale; Sense of Negative Agency scale; self-reported interaction experience with ChatGPT
finding.std_deviation: SoPA SD=0.71; SoNA SD=0.75; InterExp SD=0.76

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes student reflections on whether ChatGPT supported the maze-design task efficiently, and reports that many students perceived the interaction as positive or mixed. However, the paper does not directly measure time saved or productivity gains, so evidence for operational efficiency is indirect and based on perceived ease, speed, and support from the tool.
finding.measure: Students’ written reflections on interaction experience, including ease of use and response speed

paper_profiles.title: Using Think-Aloud Data to Understand Relations between Self-Regulation Cycle Characteristics and Student Performance in Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.venue: The 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how self-regulated learning (SRL) processes relate to moment-by-moment problem-solving performance in intelligent tutoring systems (ITS). Prior work had largely examined SRL in relation to overall learning gains; the authors instead focus on whether the timing and sequence of SRL behaviors predict correctness on the very next tutoring step.

The study uses think-aloud data from 10 undergraduate and graduate students working on stoichiometry chemistry problems in two ITSs: Stoichiometry Tutor and ORCCA Tutor. Students’ verbalizations were transcribed with Whisper, then human-coded for four SRL categories grounded in the Winne and Hadwin cyclical model: processing information, planning, enacting, and realizing errors. The authors then linked coded utterances to subsequent step correctness using mixed-effects logistic regression, comparing models that used only the immediately preceding SRL code versus models that also captured SRL cycle characteristics such as whether a student was inside or outside an SRL loop, how many attempts had elapsed since the last loop, and average attempts per cycle.

The main finding is that SRL timing mattered: correctness was lower after utterances coded as processing information or realizing errors, and higher after enacting utterances. The model including SRL cycle characteristics fit the data better than the model with only in-the-moment SRL codes, and longer cycles / more attempts since the last loop were associated with higher correctness. The authors conclude that live SRL support in tutoring systems should consider not only whether a student is processing or planning, but also where they are in their SRL cycle; they also suggest that automated think-aloud transcription can be used to support scalable SRL research and future adaptive scaffolding.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies self-regulated learning behavior during problem-solving in an ITS. In a mixed-effects logistic regression with 630 attempts, attempts immediately preceded by processing information were less likely to be correct (OR=0.53, 95% CI [0.31, 0.91], p=.014), enacting was more likely to be correct (OR=1.55, 95% CI [1.01, 2.37], p=.046), and realizing errors was less likely to be correct (OR=0.34, 95% CI [0.14, 0.84], p=.015); planning was not significant (OR=1.05, p=.869).
finding.measure: Next-attempt correctness in the tutoring system predicted from coded think-aloud SRL utterances

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally examines SRL cycle characteristics as a form of metacognitive regulation and process-oriented thinking. A model including cycle features fit the data significantly better than a model using only the immediately preceding SRL code (likelihood-ratio test χ2(3)=14.08, p=.003). In that model, more attempts per cycle (OR=1.48, 95% CI [1.15, 1.89], p=.002) and more attempts since the last closed loop (OR=1.33, 95% CI [1.01, 1.73], p=.039) were associated with higher correctness.
finding.measure: Mixed-effects logistic regression of step correctness on SRL cycle characteristics derived from think-aloud coding

paper_profiles.title: Safe Generative Chats in a WhatsApp Intelligent Tutoring System
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This workshop paper examines how to make LLM-backed chat interactions safer inside an existing intelligent tutoring system (ITS). The authors focus on a WhatsApp-based math tutor, Rori, used by low-income middle-school students in Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ghana, and Rwanda, and ask how to prevent harmful, inappropriate, or off-topic conversational behavior while preserving a structured, personalized tutoring experience.

The intervention is a semi-structured generative chat designed to teach growth mindset before math practice begins. The system combines prompt engineering, a simple word-list filter, and OpenAI’s moderation API to classify student and system messages as low risk or high risk, then either redirects the student or ends the conversation for human review. The design was evaluated through educator red-teaming, an in-classroom usability test (109 students, 252 conversations), and a field deployment (8,168 students, 8,755 conversations; 126,278 messages analyzed). The authors report that GPT-3.5 rarely produced objectionable content, while problematic student messages were more common; the main remaining issue was subtle yea-saying or insufficiently corrective responses to objectionable student inputs. Overall, the paper concludes that this moderation-and-management approach was effective for basic safety, but that future work should better handle nuanced student misconduct and sensitive disclosures.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that a lightweight moderation-and-redirection system can be operationalized at scale inside an ITS with ongoing monitoring. Across 8,755 field-deployment conversations (126,278 messages), GPT-3.5 generated almost no objectionable content and the moderation setup required only limited intervention, suggesting the design is feasible for routine deployment and safety oversight.
finding.measure: Safety moderation performance and deployment feasibility in student conversations

finding.finding_summary: The generative chat was intentionally designed to promote growth mindset before math practice, and the authors argue the conversation was acceptable and mostly effective in sustaining student engagement through the structured sequence. In the usability test (n=252 conversations), 60% were completed and only 6.3% of rated conversations were below five stars, with no clear qualitative evidence of major student dissatisfaction.
finding.measure: Conversation completion and student satisfaction ratings

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper is about a growth-mindset chat, it does not directly measure critical thinking or metacognitive gains. The only evidence is that the conversation scaffold attempted to elicit reflection on practice and learning, but no outcome data on durable skills were reported, so no substantive effect can be established.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Math learning is the broader tutoring context, but this paper does not evaluate math achievement or numeracy outcomes. It describes a pre-practice growth-mindset conversation embedded in a math tutor, yet provides no test scores, learning gains, or numeracy measures attributable to the intervention.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: MindScratch: A Visual Programming Support Tool for Classroom Learning Based on Multimodal Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: ACM conference paper (conference name not specified in provided text)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a common challenge in K-12 programming education: how to support young learners’ creative Scratch-based projects while keeping them aligned with teacher-set learning objectives, classroom pacing, and required content. The authors argue that existing programming support tools either give too much freedom, provide insufficient scaffolding, or do not fit structured classroom workflows.

To address this, they developed MindScratch, a visual programming support tool powered by multimodal generative AI. The system combines a mind map interface, a dialogic question-answering agent, AI-assisted drawing and audio generation, and scaffolded logic/code suggestions. Teachers can set learning objectives and themes, and the system uses those objectives to guide student work, highlight relevant nodes, and support step-by-step project development without generating complete solutions directly.

The evaluation included a formative study with six programming educators, a within-subject classroom study with 24 fifth-grade students comparing MindScratch to Scratch, long-term follow-up with three students over four weeks, and interviews with educators. The study reports that MindScratch helped students better achieve learning objectives, improved computational thinking and creativity, and supported richer project development. Educators also saw potential for reducing routine support demands and enabling more timely feedback, though the paper remains primarily a prototype-and-user-study contribution rather than a large-scale efficacy trial.

finding.finding_summary: In a within-subject study with 24 fifth-grade students, MindScratch improved students’ computational thinking performance relative to Scratch. The paper reports significant gains on CT-related outcomes, including higher code quality as measured by the Dr.Scratch rubric and better pre/post CT survey results in a 4-week follow-up with 3 students, indicating stronger critical-thinking-like programming skills.
finding.measure: Dr.Scratch rubric; CT Skills Survey pre/post tests

finding.finding_summary: The tool was designed to increase student engagement and creativity during classroom programming, and the authors report that students showed deeper engagement and more extensive mind map expansion when using MindScratch. Questionnaire and interview data indicate that the system provided effective creative support and helped sustain participation in project work.
finding.measure: Creativity Support Index questionnaire; interview feedback; mind map node expansion

finding.finding_summary: Educator interviews suggested that MindScratch could reduce teacher workload by helping students progress more independently through scaffolded guidance, thereby freeing teachers to provide more timely and constructive feedback. This finding is based on teacher perceptions from six programming educators rather than a direct workload time study.
finding.measure: Semi-structured educator interviews
